title: Test-Input Generation for Tensor Programs: What Actually Finds Kernel Bugs
comment: 8 pages, 1 figure, LNCS format. Companion paper: arXiv:2606.20128 (P1). Additional companions (P2, P4) to follow on arXiv this week; IDs will be added in a v2 replace
summary: Test-input generation for tensor kernels is folkloric. Most projects pick a representative shape and dtype, run a fixed-shape allclose-style check, and ship. We make the choices explicit and measure them. Using the gpuemu op-schema-aware seeded fuzzer (arXiv:2606.20128), we evaluate seven test-generation strategies across a 26-op corpus (16 correct controls and 10 LLM-style buggy variants seeded with documented transcription patterns) on an RTX 3060 GPU instance. Strategies vary the shape candidate set, the dtype mix, and the input value distribution. We report each strategy on two axes: bug recall and control false-positive (FP) rate. Boundary-only shape sampling is the operationally safe winner: 78% recall on the 10 buggy kernels with 0% FP on the 16 controls. Adversarial value sampling reaches higher recall (99%) but inflates control FP to 94% because the strategy injects NaN and Inf inputs and the validator's NaN check fires on every kernel that propagates them, not only on buggy kernels. On the two softmax tail-mask bugs the "regular" strategy (no boundary shapes) catches 0%, while boundary raises recall to 100% and 62% respectively. That gap is the clearest single signal in the data. The corpus result is about which seeded bug patterns each strategy catches, not about the bug rate of any specific deployed LLM.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates seven test-input generation strategies for tensor kernels across 26 kernels (16 correct, 10 buggy), measuring bug recall and false-positive rates. Boundary-only shape sampling emerges as the safest strategy with 78% recall and 0% false positives, while adversarial value sampling achieves 99% recall but 94% false-positive rate due to NaN/Inf propagation issues.
AI.motivation: Tensor kernel testing currently relies on ad-hoc, folkloric practices—picking representative shapes and dtypes without systematic justification. The authors aim to make these choices explicit, measurable, and evidence-based by rigorously evaluating how different test-generation strategies affect bug detection and false-positive rates.
AI.method: Using the gpuemu op-schema-aware seeded fuzzer, the authors evaluate seven test-generation strategies varying in shape candidate sets, dtype mixes, and input value distributions. The evaluation corpus comprises 16 correct control kernels and 10 buggy variants seeded with documented LLM-style transcription errors, tested on an RTX 3060 GPU. Each strategy is assessed on two metrics: bug recall and control false-positive rate.
AI.result: Boundary-only shape sampling achieved 78% recall on buggy kernels with 0% false positives on controls, making it the operationally safest strategy. Adversarial value sampling reached 99% recall but caused 94% FP due to NaN/Inf injection triggering validators indiscriminately. For softmax tail-mask bugs, "regular" strategy caught 0% while boundary sampling raised recall to 100% and 62% respectively—the clearest signal in the data.
AI.conclusion: Boundary-only shape sampling is the recommended default strategy for tensor kernel testing, offering strong bug detection with zero false positives. The work emphasizes that strategy choice matters significantly—naive strategies can miss entire bug classes—and that the findings pertain to which seeded bug patterns each strategy catches rather than any specific LLM's bug rate.

title: Implementing GenAI-Supported Learning in Software Engineering and Computer Science Education using Bloom's Taxonomy
summary:
Context: Generative AI adoption in software engineering education raises opportunities for learning support alongside concerns about superficial learning and academic integrity.
  Objective: This study investigates how explicit instructional guidance aligned with Bloom's taxonomy supports responsible GenAI use in SE/CS education, exploring student and instructor perceptions of GenAI-supported learning.
  Method: We designed a Bloom-aligned GenAI framework that articulated appropriate GenAI roles at different cognitive levels. The framework was embedded in course instructions, labs, and assessment across multiple SE/CS courses at Queen's University Belfast and Azerbaijan Technical University. Data were collected via anonymous questionnaires and learning artifacts, analyzed using thematic analysis with Bloom's taxonomy as an analytic lens.
  Results: Students perceived GenAI as most valuable for higher-order cognitive activities (analysis, evaluation, reflection) and less suitable for foundational learning. Explicit Bloom-level guidance influenced students to use GenAI reflectively, with delayed or intentional non-use when independent thinking was prioritized. Both students and instructors reported pedagogical benefits alongside challenges in cognitive effort and instructional design workload.
  Conclusion: GenAI's educational value lies in intentional alignment between cognitive learning goals, instructional guidance, and learner self-regulation. Bloom's taxonomy provides a scalable, pedagogy-driven framework for responsible GenAI use in SE/CS education, offering a practical alternative to enforcement-focused responses.

AI.tldr: A study across two universities found that aligning GenAI use guidelines with Bloom's taxonomy encourages reflective, pedagogically sound adoption in software engineering education — students benefit most at higher-order cognitive levels while requiring structured guidance at foundational levels.
AI.motivation: Generative AI is increasingly adopted in software engineering and computer science education, creating tension between its potential as a learning aid and concerns about superficial learning and academic dishonesty. The authors seek to move beyond enforcement-focused responses toward a pedagogy-driven framework for responsible GenAI integration.
AI.method: The authors designed a Bloom-aligned GenAI framework specifying appropriate GenAI roles at each cognitive level (Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyze, Evaluate, Create) and embedded it into course instructions, labs, and assessments across multiple SE/CS courses at Queen's University Belfast and Azerbaijan Technical University. Anonymous questionnaires and learning artifacts were collected and analyzed using thematic analysis with Bloom's taxonomy as the analytic lens.
AI.result: Students perceived GenAI as most valuable for higher-order activities (analysis, evaluation, reflection) and less suitable for foundational learning. Explicit Bloom-level guidance promoted reflective GenAI use, including delayed or intentional non-use when independent thinking was prioritized. Both students and instructors reported pedagogical benefits but also challenges related to cognitive effort and increased instructional design workload.
AI.conclusion: Responsible GenAI integration hinges on intentional alignment among cognitive learning goals, instructional guidance, and learner self-regulation. Bloom's taxonomy offers a scalable, pedagogy-driven framework for guiding GenAI use in SE/CS education, providing a practical alternative to purely enforcement-based academic integrity responses.

title: Formal Grammars in Business Process Management: A Systematic Literature Review
summary: Business Process Management (BPM) is concerned with the systematic design, execution, monitoring, and improvement of business processes. Formal grammars have emerged as a particularly fruitful formalism for BPM, offering generative, declarative, and analytical capabilities that are uniquely well-suited to process-oriented concerns. This paper presents a systematic literature review of 34 primary studies at the intersection of formal grammars and BPM. We identify seven research streams: (i) process grammars for organizational process design; (ii) process modeling languages evaluated as grammars under the Bunge-Wand-Weber ontological framework; (iii) production-rule grammars for process structural specification and variant management; (iv) attribute grammars for the declarative specification and distributed execution of workflows; (v) graph grammars for the transformation, generation, and semantic analysis of process models; (vi) grammatical inference for process mining and discovery; and (vii) process algebras as grammar-like compositional frameworks for behavioral specification and verification. For each stream, we synthesize contributions, formalisms employed, and limitations. The review reveals that formal grammars have influenced BPM across every lifecycle phase (from organizational design to formal verification and data-driven discovery) yet the seven streams have developed largely in parallel, without cross-stream synthesis. We identify five corpus-grounded open challenges and argue that a deeper, unified exploitation of grammatical theory holds significant promise for advancing the state of the art in BPM.

AI.tldr: A systematic literature review of 34 studies examining how formal grammars have been applied across BPM, identifying seven distinct research streams that have developed in parallel without cross-stream synthesis, and proposing five open challenges for unified grammatical approaches to BPM.
AI.motivation: Despite formal grammars offering generative, declarative, and analytical capabilities well-suited to BPM, no prior review has systematically mapped how grammatical formalisms have been applied across the full BPM lifecycle. The authors aim to consolidate fragmented research and identify opportunities for deeper, unified exploitation of grammatical theory.
AI.method: The authors conducted a systematic literature review (SLR) following established guidelines, yielding 34 primary studies. They categorized these into seven distinct research streams based on the type of grammatical formalism and BPM application, then synthesized contributions, formalisms, and limitations for each stream.
AI.result: Seven research streams were identified: (1) process grammars for organizational design, (2) Bunge-Wand-Weber ontological evaluation of modeling languages, (3) production-rule grammars for process structure and variants, (4) attribute grammars for declarative workflow specification and execution, (5) graph grammars for model transformation and semantic analysis, (6) grammatical inference for process mining, and (7) process algebras as grammar-like frameworks for behavioral verification. These streams cover all BPM lifecycle phases but have evolved in isolation.
AI.conclusion: Formal grammars have permeated every phase of the BPM lifecycle, yet the seven streams remain disconnected. The authors identify five open challenges — including cross-stream synthesis, tooling integration, and scalability — arguing that a unified grammatical approach holds significant promise for advancing BPM.

title: Recall Before Rerank: Benchmarking Deep Learning Models for Large-Scale Code-to-Code Retrieval
summary: Semantic code search and clone detection are essential for software development, maintenance, and reuse. This paper evaluates the effectiveness, efficiency, and scalability of contemporary deep learning models for first-stage recall in large-scale code-to-code search engines. Benchmarking across multiple programming languages and datasets reveals critical limits in the precision and scalability of these models on Terabyte-scale source-code collections. We present LLM-based code normalisation and query-rewriting schemes that yield significant gains in precision for lower-performing models. Our results question the sustainability of resource-constrained deployment and the assumed robustness of current code-specialised LLMs across datasets. We conclude with actionable insights for building scalable, efficient code-retrieval systems.

AI.tldr: Evaluates deep learning models for code-to-code search at terabyte scale, finds critical precision/scalability limits, and proposes LLM-based code normalization and query rewriting to improve low-performing models.
AI.motivation: Current deep learning models for semantic code search and clone detection lack rigorous benchmarking at realistic terabyte-scale corpora. Their effectiveness, efficiency, and sustainability under resource-constrained deployment remain unverified across diverse languages and datasets.
AI.method: Benchmarks contemporary deep learning code-retrieval models across multiple programming languages and datasets for first-stage recall. Introduces LLM-based code normalisation and query-rewriting schemes to boost precision. Evaluates scalability, precision, and robustness under terabyte-scale conditions.
AI.result: Reveals critical precision and scalability limits of current models on terabyte-scale source-code collections. LLM-based normalisation and query rewriting yield significant precision gains, particularly for lower-performing models. Questions the assumed cross-dataset robustness of code-specialised LLMs and the sustainability of resource-constrained deployments.
AI.conclusion: Current code-specialised LLMs are not robust or scalable enough for terabyte-scale code retrieval. LLM-based normalisation and query rewriting offer practical mitigation. Actionable insights are provided for building scalable, efficient code-retrieval systems.

title: HandMade: Spatial Prompting for Generative 3D Creation with Part-Labeled VR Sketches
summary: Text-to-3D generation lowers the barrier to 3D content creation, but text alone is a weak interface for specifying spatial intent: where parts should be placed, how they relate, and how an object should be organized in 3D. We present HandMade, a workflow that combines VR 3D sketching and language for open-domain 3D asset generation. HandMade treats coarse, part-labeled 3D sketches not as incomplete geometry to reconstruct directly, but as spatial prompts for existing generative models. It converts segmented VR strokes into multi-view part guidance and structured prompts, allowing users to specify object layout and part relationships through 3D sketching while using language for identity, material, style, and local details. A technical evaluation shows that HandMade better preserves user-authored spatial scaffolds than text-only and sketch-based baselines on 20 varied examples. A user study with eight participants characterizes how users make use of 3D sketching for spatial layout and language for identity, materials, and details across initial authoring and subsequent revision. HandMade contributes an interaction paradigm and interface-to-generation pipeline for spatially guided 3D creation.

AI.tldr: HandMade combines VR 3D sketching with language prompts for open-domain 3D asset generation, treating part-labeled sketches as spatial prompts rather than incomplete geometry. A pipeline converts segmented VR strokes into multi-view part guidance, enabling users to specify layout via sketching and identity/style/details via text. Evaluation on 20 examples and a user study (n=8) demonstrate superior preservation of spatial scaffolds over text-only and sketch-based baselines.
AI.motivation: Text alone is a weak interface for specifying 3D spatial intent — part placement, relationships, and object organization. Existing text-to-3D methods lack precise spatial control, while direct 3D reconstruction from sketches fails to leverage the generative power of pretrained models. The gap motivates a hybrid interface that uses sketching for spatial layout and language for appearance/identity.
AI.method: HandMade is an interaction paradigm and generation pipeline: (1) users create coarse, part-labeled 3D sketches in VR; (2) segmented strokes are converted into multi-view part guidance (e.g., depth, segmentation masks from virtual camera views); (3) structured prompts combining sketch-derived spatial constraints and user-provided language (identity, material, style, details) are fed into existing generative models. The sketch serves as a spatial scaffold, not geometry to be reconstructed.
AI.result: A technical evaluation on 20 diverse examples shows HandMade preserves user-authored spatial scaffolds significantly better than text-only and sketch-based baselines. A user study with eight participants characterizes how users leverage 3D sketching for spatial layout and language for identity, materials, and details across both initial authoring and iterative revision.
AI.conclusion: HandMade contributes a novel interaction paradigm and interface-to-generation pipeline that effectively combines VR 3D sketching with language for spatially guided 3D asset creation, demonstrating both quantitative and qualitative advantages over existing approaches.

title: SidConArena: An Environment Evaluating Agents in Open-Ended,Positive-Sum Bargaining Game
summary: Evaluating LLM agents requires dynamic environments that go beyond static reasoning and zero-sum games. Real-world economic interaction is often open-ended and mixed-motive: agents must negotiate, create positive-sum surplus, compete for scarce assets, and plan under delayed returns. We introduce SidConArena, a new benchmark framework for evaluating LLM agents in open-ended, positive-sum bargaining. SidConArena formalizes a multi-player economy as a finite-horizon partially observable stochastic game with three coupled phases: natural-language negotiation with binding trades, deterministic converter-based production, and sealed-bid auctions for long-term assets. The framework combines structured observations, phase-aware agent dispatching, a neural-symbolic action interface, and asynchronous execution, enabling free-form interaction while preserving rule-grounded evaluation. Across homogeneous and heterogeneous tournaments, stronger frontier models achieve higher economic outcomes, yet agents still misvalue resources, bargain passively, and remain limited in long-horizon investment planning.

AI.tldr: SidConArena introduces a multi-phase economic benchmark for evaluating LLM agents in open-ended, positive-sum bargaining scenarios. Frontier models perform better in tournaments but still exhibit significant strategic limitations in resource valuation, negotiation assertiveness, and long-horizon planning.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM agent benchmarks focus on static reasoning or zero-sum games, failing to capture the open-ended, mixed-motive nature of real-world economic interactions where agents must negotiate, create value, compete for resources, and plan under delayed returns.
AI.method: SidConArena formalizes a multi-player economy as a finite-horizon partially observable stochastic game with three coupled phases: (1) natural-language negotiation with binding trades, (2) deterministic converter-based production, and (3) sealed-bid auctions for long-term assets. It integrates structured observations, phase-aware agent dispatching, a neural-symbolic action interface, and asynchronous execution to enable free-form interaction while maintaining rule-grounded evaluation.
AI.result: In both homogeneous and heterogeneous tournaments, stronger frontier models achieved higher economic outcomes. However, all agents demonstrated notable weaknesses: misvaluing resources, engaging in passive bargaining, and showing limited capacity for long-horizon investment planning.
AI.conclusion: SidConArena provides a robust framework for assessing LLM agents in complex economic settings. While frontier models show promising economic reasoning capabilities, persistent strategic deficiencies in valuation, negotiation, and long-term planning highlight important directions for future agent development.

title: Formalizing Latent Thoughts: Four Axioms of Thought Representation in LLMs
summary: We introduce an axiomatic evaluation framework for latent thought representations in LLMs, comprising metrics that are independent of downstream benchmark scores and reveal representational failures that benchmark accuracy masks. Existing evaluations conflate representation quality with model capacity. Therefore, failures cannot be attributed to the representation rather than to the model that processes it. We formalize four functional axioms (Causality, Minimality, Separability, and Stability) and define a quantitative measure for each, computed directly on the representation independently of downstream accuracy. We audit open-weight LLMs across 23 reasoning tasks (e.g., Spatial Reasoning, Factual QA). We find that no candidate satisfies all four axioms simultaneously, that the representations distinguish task type reliably but cannot distinguish between two questions within the same task, and that the representations encode little information beyond what is already present in the input embedding. The failure is consistent across dense, reasoning-distilled, and RL-trained model families, indicating that the gap is structural rather than a property of model size or training procedure.

AI.tldr: Proposes an axiomatic framework with four metrics (Causality, Minimality, Separability, Stability) to evaluate LLM latent thought representations independently of downstream benchmarks. Auditing 23 reasoning tasks across multiple model families reveals that no representation satisfies all axioms, representations encode little beyond input embeddings, and this failure is structural rather than tied to model size or training.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluation methods conflate representation quality with the model capacity that processes those representations, making it impossible to isolate whether failures stem from the representation itself or from downstream processing. A representation-centric evaluation framework is needed.
AI.method: Four functional axioms are formalized: (1) Causality — the representation should causally influence correct outputs; (2) Minimality — it should contain only necessary information; (3) Separability — it should distinguish different tasks/questions; (4) Stability — it should be robust to irrelevant perturbations. Quantitative measures are defined for each axiom and computed directly on latent representations from open-weight LLMs across 23 reasoning tasks (Spatial Reasoning, Factual QA, etc.), spanning dense, reasoning-distilled, and RL-trained model families.
AI.result: No candidate representation satisfies all four axioms simultaneously. Representations reliably distinguish task types but fail to discriminate between questions within the same task. They encode minimal information beyond what is already present in the input embedding. The failure pattern is consistent across dense, reasoning-distilled, and RL-trained architectures, indicating a structural gap.
AI.conclusion: The gap in latent thought representations is structural rather than a consequence of model scale or training procedure. Current LLM representations serve primarily as task-type discriminators and add little beyond input-level information, highlighting a fundamental limitation in how LLMs internally represent reasoning.

title: A Sensitivity-Aware Test Collection for Search Among Personal Information
summary: Traditional search tasks aim to satisfy user information needs by returning a subset of a collection of documents, ranked by the documents' relevance to a user query. However, some collections that contain useful information also contain sensitive personal information. Recently, there has been increasing interest in the development of Sensitivity-Aware Search (SAS) retrieval models to provide users with effective retrieval results without revealing such sensitive information. To develop such systems, test collections containing both sensitive and non-sensitive information, a set of queries, and query-document relevance assessments are required. The Enron email corpus contains real business-related emails, where some emails also contain sensitive personal information. However, the original Enron collection does not contain queries or query-relevance assessments. To this end, we crowdsource 150 query formulations for 50 different topics and 11,471 query-relevance assessments for a subset of the Enron documents that have been manually labelled for sensitivity. We follow best practices for using large language models (LLMs) in Information Retrieval evaluation to extend the collection further with additional LLM judged query-relevance assessments and sensitivity labels. We present baseline performances for relevance, sensitivity classification, and sensitivity-aware search on the collection. We make the collection available, including through the popular ir_datasets package, and provide pre-built sparse and dense indices on Huggingface to facilitate easy experimentation.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a new test collection built from the Enron email corpus, augmented with 150 queries, 11,471 crowdsourced relevance assessments, and LLM-extended sensitivity labels, to support research in Sensitivity-Aware Search (SAS)—retrieving relevant documents while protecting sensitive personal information.
AI.motivation: Traditional search systems rank documents solely by relevance, ignoring the risk of exposing sensitive personal information. There is growing interest in SAS, but no suitable benchmark exists. The Enron corpus contains both business and sensitive personal content but lacks queries and relevance judgments, motivating the authors to construct the first publicly available SAS test collection.
AI.method: The authors crowdsource 150 query formulations across 50 topics and collect 11,471 query-document relevance judgments on a sensitivity-labeled subset of Enron. They then apply best practices for LLM-based IR evaluation to extend the collection with additional LLM-judged relevance assessments and sensitivity labels. The collection is released via ir_datasets with pre-built sparse and dense indices on HuggingFace.
AI.result: The paper reports baseline performances for three tasks on the new collection: standard relevance ranking, sensitivity classification, and sensitivity-aware search. The collection comprises 11,471 human-assessed query-document pairs plus LLM-extended judgments, with pre-computed indices provided for reproducibility and ease of experimentation.
AI.conclusion: The constructed test collection fills a critical gap in SAS research by providing a standardized benchmark with queries, relevance assessments, and sensitivity labels. The open release through ir_datasets and Huggingface, along with baseline results, enables the community to develop and fairly compare sensitivity-aware retrieval models.

title: When the Aggregator Cheats: Data-Free Backdoors in Federated LLM-based QA Systems
comment: Accepted at the 35th USENIX Security Symposium (USENIX Security 2026)
summary: Large Language Model (LLM)-based question-answering (QA) systems are increasingly deployed in sensitive domains such as healthcare, mental health counseling, and legal consultation. Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative training without sharing raw client data, for which locally trained models are aggregated at a central server (i.e., a cloud service provider) to obtain a global model. In this paper, we explore the potential vulnerability where a malicious aggregator, who may collude with a third-party vendor, stealthily implants advertisement-type backdoors into federated QA models, without ever accessing client data. The attacker's goals are twofold: (1) preserve clean QA fidelity (i.e., the poisoned model behaves like a clean model on non-triggered queries); and (2) generate highly natural, contextually relevant responses with target advertisements when a trigger appears. Achieving these two goals simultaneously is highly challenging, as naive backdoor injection without knowledge about private data may degrade model's clean performance or fail to inject the target. Motivated by this, we propose to leverage clients' uploaded gradients during training, and develop a two-stage framework for data-free and stealthy poisoning: (1) recover representative training samples from client gradients, and (2) construct poisoning datasets utilizing recovered samples and trigger phrases to inject backdoors into the global model. Experiments across representative QA datasets and LLM families under full fine-tuning and LoRA settings demonstrate that, our method achieves nearly 100% Attack Success Rate (ASR) while incurring negligible degradation on clean tasks. Crucially, reconstructing only 5-20% of gradients suffices to mount a reliable attack, exposing a practical blind spot in the pipeline of federated training of QA LLMs.

AI.tldr: This paper reveals a vulnerability in federated learning for LLM-based QA systems where a malicious aggregator can implant advertisement backdoors without accessing client data, by reconstructing training samples from client gradients and using them to craft poisoned data, achieving ~100% attack success with minimal clean performance degradation.
AI.motivation: Federated QA systems in sensitive domains (healthcare, legal, mental health) rely on a central aggregator that could be malicious or collude with third parties. Existing backdoor attacks assume access to private data, which is unrealistic in FL. The challenge is injecting ads while preserving clean QA performance without any client data access — naive approaches fail at both goals simultaneously.
AI.method: A two-stage data-free poisoning framework: (1) Gradient-based data reconstruction — recover representative training samples from uploaded client gradients using gradient inversion techniques; (2) Poisoning dataset construction — pair recovered samples with adversarial trigger phrases and target advertisement responses, then inject these into the global model via malicious aggregation. Tested under full fine-tuning and LoRA settings.
AI.result: The attack achieves nearly 100% Attack Success Rate (ASR) across representative QA datasets and LLM families, with negligible degradation on clean tasks. Remarkably, reconstructing only 5-20% of gradients is sufficient to mount a reliable attack, exposing a critical blind spot in federated QA LLM training pipelines.
AI.conclusion: Federated training of QA LLMs harbors a practical and stealthy vulnerability: a malicious aggregator can implant effective advertisement backdoors without any client data access, using only partial gradient information. This exposes a significant security blind spot requiring urgent attention from the FL community.

title: OverFlowLight: Real-Time Gridlock Prevention and Traffic Signal Optimization for Urban Intersections
summary: Queue overflow, a severe consequence of urban traffic congestion, occurs when vehicle queues exceed intersection capacity, obstructing upstream traffic and triggering cascading gridlocks. Prevailing traffic signal control (TSC) algorithms, primarily optimized for throughput, often fail to address overflow during peak hours, exacerbating congestion and creating safety hazards. We propose OverFlowLight, a real-time framework designed to preemptively resolve overflow and enhance overall TSC performance. It first introduces a mechanism to accurately detect overflow in real-time by leveraging multi-modal sensing from cameras and radars. Upon detection, it dynamically generates and inserts dedicated overflow phases into the signal cycle to clear the blocking queues. This is orchestrated by a hybrid control design that combines rapid rule-based overflow intervention with controller back ends such as reinforcement learning (RL) for longer-horizon efficiency. We conducted extensive real-world deployments of OverFlowLight across 43 intersections in three major cities. The framework demonstrates seamless integration with existing RL-based TSC agents, highlighting its modularity and practical applicability. Empirical results show that OverFlowLight reduces overflow incidents by 60.4% and increases network throughput by 18.2% compared to deployed baselines. Furthermore, it substantially diminishes the need for manual intervention common with expert-tuned signal plans. This work presents the first practical, scalable, and data-driven framework for actively preventing traffic gridlock, offering a crucial component for building resilient and efficient urban transportation systems. Our demonstration videos, codes and datasets are available at the anonymous URL, https://anonymous.4open.science/r/OverFlowLight-FBF9.

AI.tldr: OverFlowLight is a real-time traffic signal control framework that detects and preemptively resolves queue overflow at intersections using multi-modal sensing (cameras + radars) and a hybrid control design (rule-based overflow intervention + RL backend), achieving 60.4% fewer overflow incidents and 18.2% higher throughput across 43 real-world deployments in three cities.
AI.motivation: Existing traffic signal control algorithms prioritize throughput optimization and fail to address queue overflow during peak hours, where vehicle queues exceed intersection capacity, block upstream traffic, and trigger cascading gridlocks. This creates both congestion and safety hazards that require costly manual intervention.
AI.method: OverFlowLight employs: (1) multi-modal sensing (cameras and radars) for real-time overflow detection; (2) dynamic generation and insertion of dedicated overflow phases into the signal cycle upon detection; and (3) a hybrid control architecture combining rapid rule-based overflow intervention with reinforcement learning-based controller backends for long-horizon efficiency. The framework is designed to be modular and integrate seamlessly with existing RL-based TSC agents.
AI.result: Deployed across 43 intersections in three major cities, OverFlowLight reduced overflow incidents by 60.4%, increased network throughput by 18.2% compared to deployed baselines, and substantially reduced the need for manual intervention by traffic engineers.
AI.conclusion: OverFlowLight represents the first practical, scalable, data-driven framework for actively preventing traffic gridlock, serving as a critical component for resilient and efficient urban transportation systems. Its modular integration with existing RL-based TSC agents demonstrates real-world applicability.

title: AI-Model Network: Concept, Current State and Future
summary: While the primary function of computers lies in computation and processing, the core value of the Internet is rooted in sharing and collaboration. Computers create the Internet, and the Internet empowers the value of computers. The rapid development of the Internet, cloud computing, and big data is pushing artificial intelligence into the era of large models (LMs). However, the practical application of LMs is currently hindered by high training costs and deployment complexities, driving a shift toward lightweight, private, and domain-specific models. With the rapid proliferation and wide distribution of heterogeneous models, enabling effective interaction and collaboration among them has emerged as a critical bottleneck that urgently needs to be addressed in LM development. Drawing inspiration from the development of the Internet, this paper proposes the concept, vision, and system architecture of world wide AI-model network (AI-ModelNet). It is a novel paradigm that achieves interconnection, capability sharing, and collaborative reasoning by establishing pathways between models. We first briefly review the current state of single-model and multi-model research. Subsequently, the systemic vision and hierarchical architecture of AI-ModelNet are articulated, followed by validation of the framework's feasibility through a prototype system and diverse application cases. Finally, key directions for future research are discussed preliminarily.

AI.tldr: Proposes the "world wide AI-model network" (AI-ModelNet) — a paradigm inspired by the Internet that interconnects heterogeneous models for capability sharing and collaborative reasoning, addressing the bottleneck of isolated domain-specific models via a layered architecture validated through a prototype system.
AI.motivation: Large models face high training costs and deployment complexities, driving adoption of lightweight, private, domain-specific models. As these heterogeneous models proliferate, enabling effective interaction and collaboration among them becomes an urgent bottleneck — analogous to how the Internet unlocked the value of individual computers through interconnection.
AI.method: The paper draws an analogy between the Internet's evolution and the current state of AI models. It proposes a hierarchical system architecture for AI-ModelNet that establishes pathways between models for interconnection, capability sharing, and collaborative reasoning. Feasibility is validated through a prototype system and diverse application cases.
AI.result: A prototype system and multiple application cases demonstrate the feasibility of the AI-ModelNet framework, showing that interconnecting heterogeneous models through structured pathways can enable effective collaboration and capability sharing.
AI.conclusion: AI-ModelNet represents a novel paradigm shift toward networked AI, where models — like computers on the Internet — gain amplified value through interconnection. Key future research directions are identified, though discussed only preliminarily.

title: Towards Evaluation of Implicit Software World Models in Coding LLMs
comment: Accepted to DL4Code workshop at ICML 2026
summary: Software engineering, whether performed by humans or by AI agents, requires reasoning about how software behaves. We call the internal model that supports such reasoning the software world model, and view current code-execution benchmarks as covering one well-studied slice of it -- control flow. In this paper, we take a step toward a broader evaluation by shifting the observable axis to execution resources: alongside test outcome and exception class, we predict peak memory, wall-clock time, and ranked profiler outputs at method and line granularity. We use SWE-bench Verified as the source of data to hold the test close to real-world software engineering tasks. All tested models, frontier ones included, show modest performance and brittle behaviour, suggesting a notable lack of understanding of how software is executed, as opposed to how its source code is written.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the concept of a "software world model" and expands code-execution benchmarks beyond control flow to include execution resource prediction (peak memory, wall-clock time, profiler outputs). Using SWE-bench Verified, the authors find that even frontier models perform modestly and exhibit brittle behavior, indicating poor understanding of software execution.
AI.motivation: Current code-execution benchmarks focus narrowly on control flow (test outcomes, exceptions), neglecting other critical dimensions of software behavior such as resource usage. The authors argue that a true "software world model" — the internal representation enabling reasoning about software behavior — must encompass execution resources as well, motivating a broader evaluation paradigm.
AI.method: The authors shift the evaluation axis from control flow to execution resources. Using SWE-bench Verified as the data source to maintain real-world relevance, they task models with predicting: (1) peak memory usage, (2) wall-clock execution time, and (3) ranked profiler outputs at both method and line granularity — alongside traditional test outcomes and exception classes.
AI.result: All tested models, including frontier models, demonstrated only modest performance and exhibited brittle behavior across the resource-prediction tasks. This reveals a significant gap between models' ability to reason about source code syntax/structure and their understanding of how software actually executes at runtime.
AI.conclusion: There is a notable lack of understanding among current models regarding how software is executed, as opposed to how source code is written. Broadening evaluation to include execution-resource prediction exposes this weakness and points toward the need for richer software world models in AI-based software engineering.

title: Context-Aware Explanations for Spatialized Document Layouts
comment: 10 pages, 4 figures, accepted to Graphics Interface 2026 (GI 2026)
summary: Spatialized document layouts are widely used for exploratory analysis of text corpora, but interpreting the spatial organization of documents and the relationships between regions remains challenging. Existing approaches primarily summarize document content or explain how layouts are generated, providing limited support for understanding spatial relationships within the layout itself. We present CAPE, a context-aware explanation framework that generates natural-language explanations grounded in both document semantics and layout-derived spatial context. CAPE identifies salient spatial patterns (e.g., clusters, subgroups, outliers, and bridging documents) and constructs multi-level contextual representations to guide LLM-based explanation generation. It supports both AI-guided overview and user-driven exploration, with explanations available at multiple levels of detail. We demonstrate CAPE on news and scholarly document layouts and evaluate it in a controlled user study against keyword-based and content-only LLM baselines. Our results suggest that spatially grounded explanations are perceived as more helpful than content-only baselines for interpreting the spatial organization of document layouts.

AI.tldr: CAPE generates spatially grounded, natural-language explanations for document layouts by combining semantic content with layout-derived spatial context, helping users interpret clusters, outliers, and bridging documents more effectively than keyword-based or content-only baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing document layout exploration tools either summarize content or explain layout generation, but fail to help users interpret the spatial relationships among documents within the layout itself—such as why certain documents cluster together or what connects disparate regions.
AI.method: CAPE identifies salient spatial patterns (clusters, subgroups, outliers, bridging documents) and builds multi-level contextual representations that encode both document semantics and spatial layout information. These representations guide an LLM to generate explanations at varying levels of detail, supporting both AI-driven overview and user-driven interactive exploration.
AI.result: A controlled user study comparing CAPE against keyword-based and content-only LLM baselines on news and scholarly document layouts showed that spatially grounded explanations were perceived as significantly more helpful for interpreting spatial organization.
AI.conclusion: Integrating spatial context into natural-language explanations substantially improves users' ability to interpret and make sense of spatialized document layouts, suggesting a promising direction for future visual text analysis systems.

title: Delayed Verification Destabilizes Multi-Agent LLM Belief: Instability Thresholds and Optimal Corrector Placement
comment: 20 pages, 5 figures, 1 table. Code and data: https://github.com/YehudaItkin/delayed-verification-llm
summary: Multi-agent large language model (LLM) systems often rely on verifier and critic agents to suppress hallucinations, but verification is delayed. During this delay, false claims can propagate through the agent network. We model this process as delayed consensus on a graph with grounded corrector nodes. Spectral decomposition by the grounded Laplacian yields a closed-form stability threshold for the verification dose: correction that is too strong or too delayed can turn consensus into oscillation. The most unstable regime occurs when the communication and verification delays coincide; for delay two, the threshold is the inverse golden ratio. The same framework gives a supermodular placement objective and a greedy (1-1/e)-approximation rule for assigning a limited corrector budget to influential nodes. Experiments across five open models confirm the predicted dose-delay oscillations. By contrast, grounded factual answering makes truth an absorbing boundary and eliminates the effect, suggesting that the instability is specific to signed-belief tasks while grounded verification remains stabilizing

AI.tldr: This paper models hallucination propagation in multi-agent LLM systems as delayed consensus on a graph with grounded corrector nodes. Using spectral decomposition of the grounded Laplacian, it derives a closed-form stability threshold showing that verification dose and delay interact nonlinearly — overly strong or delayed correction induces oscillation rather than consensus. The worst-case instability occurs when communication and verification delays coincide. The framework also yields a supermodular placement objective with a greedy (1-1/e)-approximation for optimal corrector assignment. Experiments confirm predicted dose-delay oscillations, while grounded factual answering eliminates the effect, indicating the instability is specific to signed-belief tasks.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent LLM systems use verifier/critic agents to combat hallucinations, but verification is inherently delayed. During this latency, false claims can propagate and compound through the agent network. Existing approaches lack a formal understanding of how verification delay and intensity interact to affect system stability — specifically, when correction transitions from stabilizing to destabilizing.
AI.method: The paper models the multi-agent system as delayed consensus dynamics on a graph, where some nodes are "grounded correctors" (agents with access to ground truth). It applies spectral decomposition via the grounded Laplacian matrix to derive a closed-form stability threshold. The analysis reveals the threshold as a function of correction strength and delay, with the most unstable regime at coincident communication and verification delays. For delay-2 systems, the threshold equals the inverse golden ratio. The framework also formulates corrector placement as a supermodular optimization problem, yielding a greedy algorithm with (1-1/e) approximation guarantee.
AI.result: Experiments across five open-source LLMs confirm the predicted dose-delay oscillations: correction that is too strong or too delayed causes belief oscillations rather than convergence. Grounded factual answering — where truth serves as an absorbing boundary — eliminates these oscillations, suggesting the instability phenomenon is specific to signed-belief (subjective/opinion-based) tasks rather than grounded verification tasks.
AI.conclusion: Verification in multi-agent LLM systems exhibits a fundamental stability threshold governed by the interplay of correction strength and delay. The derived spectral criteria provide principled guidance for designing stable verification protocols. Optimal corrector placement is a supermodular problem admitting efficient approximation. The instability is restricted to signed-belief tasks; grounded factual verification remains inherently stabilizing.

title: Position: The Term "Machine Unlearning" Is Overused in LLMs
comment: 13 pages; ICML 2026 Position Paper Track. Sangyeon Yoon and Yeachan Jun contributed equally
summary: Large language models increasingly face demands to "forget" training data, knowledge, or behaviors due to regulatory deletion obligations, copyright/licensing disputes, and safety or product-policy requirements. This position paper argues that machine unlearning is overused as a term in LLM research and should be reserved for dataset-defined deletion: removing the training influence of a precisely specified forget set such that the resulting model is approximately indistinguishable from retraining without that data. We contend that many tasks currently labeled "unlearning" (e.g., refusal for harmful requests, entity/knowledge removal, or targeted suppression) pursue different, often policy-dependent objectives and therefore require different terminology and baselines (e.g., alignment, suppression, editing, obfuscation). We further argue that this confusion is not cosmetic: because papers make different implicit guarantees under the same label, metrics and benchmarks are frequently reused outside their intended scope, rewarding surface-level non-disclosure (e.g., low ROUGE/forget accuracy) even when retraining-equivalence is not tested and derived capabilities remain. We conclude by calling for stricter terminology tied to explicit guarantees and reference models, and for evaluations that match the claimed objective.

AI.tldr: This position paper argues that "machine unlearning" is overused and misapplied in LLM research. It contends the term should be strictly reserved for dataset-defined deletion where the model becomes indistinguishable from retraining without the forget set. Many tasks labeled as "unlearning" actually pursue different objectives (alignment, suppression, editing) and require distinct terminology, baselines, and evaluation metrics.
AI.motivation: The proliferation of papers claiming "unlearning" under different implicit guarantees has led to conceptual confusion, metric misuse (e.g., low ROUGE scores misinterpreted as successful unlearning), and a failure to test for retraining-equivalence. This undermines both scientific rigor and practical compliance with regulatory, copyright, and safety requirements.
AI.method: This is a position paper, so it employs conceptual analysis and argumentation rather than experiments. The authors taxonomize LLM deletion-related tasks, distinguish dataset-defined unlearning from policy-defined objectives (alignment, suppression, editing, obfuscation), and critique how mismatched terminology enables inappropriate reuse of benchmarks and metrics across fundamentally different task types.
AI.result: The paper identifies that many "unlearning" methods only achieve surface-level non-disclosure (e.g., refusing to output memorized text) without demonstrating retraining-equivalence. It highlights that derived capabilities often persist despite apparent success on narrow metrics, revealing a gap between claimed and actual guarantees.
AI.conclusion: The authors call for stricter, guarantee-tied terminology in LLM deletion research: "unlearning" should be reserved for retraining-equivalent dataset removal, while other objectives should adopt terms like alignment, suppression, editing, or obfuscation. Evaluations must be matched to each task's explicit claims.

title: Intuition-Guided Latent Reasoning for LLM-Based Recommendation
summary:
Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive reasoning capabilities in complex problem-solving tasks, motivating their use for preference reasoning in recommender systems. Latent reasoning, which operates in continuous hidden spaces rather than discrete tokens, has recently emerged as a promising paradigm for LLM-based recommendation. However, existing methods often start from unconstrained reasoning points, where hidden representations are misaligned with target item embeddings, leading to suboptimal reasoning trajectories.
  Inspired by cognitive neuroscience, which suggests that human multi-step reasoning is guided by intuition as a latent prior, we propose \emph{IntuRec}, a two-stage framework that anchors latent reasoning with \emph{recommendation intuition}. In the extraction stage, the LLM-based recommender generates a top-$K$ candidate set based on users' histories as the source of intuition. In the injection stage, the candidate set is transformed into a preference-aligned intuition embedding using self- and cross-attention mechanisms, which initializes the reasoning start point and guides subsequent latent reasoning. By providing a semantically grounded starting point, IntuRec efficiently explores the preference space along more accurate reasoning trajectories. Extensive experiments on multiple real-world datasets demonstrate that IntuRec consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. We release our code at https://github.com/Ten-Mao/IntuRec.

AI.tldr: IntuRec introduces a two-stage framework that anchors latent LLM reasoning with a preference-aligned "intuition" embedding derived from a top-K candidate set, improving recommendation accuracy by starting reasoning from semantically grounded points.
AI.motivation: Existing latent reasoning methods for LLM-based recommendation start from unconstrained, misaligned hidden representations, producing suboptimal reasoning trajectories. The authors draw inspiration from cognitive neuroscience, where human multi-step reasoning is guided by intuition as a latent prior.
AI.method: IntuRec is a two-stage framework: (1) Extraction stage — the LLM recommender generates a top-K candidate set from user history as a source of intuition; (2) Injection stage — the candidate set is transformed into a preference-aligned intuition embedding via self- and cross-attention mechanisms, which initializes the reasoning start point and guides subsequent latent reasoning in continuous hidden space.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on multiple real-world datasets show IntuRec consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines.
AI.conclusion: Anchoring latent reasoning with recommendation intuition provides a semantically grounded starting point, enabling more efficient exploration of the preference space and more accurate reasoning trajectories for LLM-based recommendation.

title: On the Inseparability of Instructions and Data in Shared-Embedding Sequence Models
summary:
Prompt injection is the top security risk for LLM-integrated applications, yet every defense proposed so far has been broken. We prove this is not a coincidence: in shared-embedding architectures that lack enforced control-data separation, perfect prompt-injection prevention is mathematically impossible. We formalize prompted systems as Prompted Action Models whose outputs include control-authoritative actions: refusal decisions, tool authorization, policy routing, and memory writes. We define Semantic-Faithful Control (SFC), the property that such behavior depends only on the meaning of untrusted input, not on how it is encoded. We then prove SFC is unachievable within the shared pipeline, via three results: a provenance-recovery impossibility (shared representations make trusted and untrusted content statistically inseparable, bounded by total variation distance); control-path exposure (untrusted tokens enter control-relevant computation through the same attention value-aggregation that determines outputs); and a finite-coverage invariance gap (finite training cannot certify invariance over infinite semantic-equivalence classes). We ground each quantity in measurements on production tokenizers and models.
  The result is structural, not a gap in current defenses. It mirrors the code-data confusion in Von Neumann machines that gives rise to buffer overflows, a vulnerability class that took decades of layered defenses (DEP, Write-XOR-Execute, ASLR, stack canaries, and ultimately memory-safe languages) to contain, because no single mechanism sufficed. The implication is the same: prompt injection cannot be eliminated by better in-pipeline classification or alignment alone. It requires architectural separation of instruction and data channels. We identify the root cause and the class of solution it demands.

AI.tldr: Prompt injection is proven mathematically impossible to prevent in shared-embedding LLM architectures lacking control-data separation. The paper formalizes this via three theorems—provenance-recovery impossibility, control-path exposure, and finite-coverage invariance gap—and argues the only solution is architectural separation of instruction and data channels, analogous to how buffer overflows required decades of layered defenses in Von Neumann machines.
AI.motivation: Every proposed defense against prompt injection in LLM-integrated applications has been broken. The authors aim to demonstrate this is not coincidental but structural—a fundamental architectural limitation rather than a gap in current defense mechanisms. They seek to formally characterize why prompt injection persists and identify the class of solution actually required.
AI.method: The authors formalize prompted LLM systems as Prompted Action Models (PAMs), where outputs include control-authoritative actions (refusal, tool authorization, policy routing, memory writes). They define Semantic-Faithful Control (SFC) as the property that control behavior depends only on the semantic meaning of untrusted input, not its encoding. Three impossibility proofs are then developed: (1) provenance-recovery impossibility—trusted and untrusted representations are statistically inseparable under shared embeddings, bounded by total variation distance; (2) control-path exposure—untrusted tokens influence control-relevant computation through the same attention value-aggregation mechanism that determines outputs; (3) finite-coverage invariance gap—finite training cannot certify invariance over infinite semantic-equivalence classes. Each result is grounded with empirical measurements on production tokenizers and models.
AI.result: All three theorems hold: shared embeddings make trusted/untrusted content statistically inseparable; attention mechanisms expose control paths to untrusted tokens; and finite training cannot cover infinite semantic-equivalence classes. The structural impossibility is grounded in measurements on production systems. The authors draw a direct analogy to buffer overflows in Von Neumann architectures, where code-data confusion enabled exploits that required decades of layered mitigations (DEP, W^X, ASLR, stack canaries, memory-safe languages) to contain.
AI.conclusion: Prompt injection cannot be eliminated through better in-pipeline classification or alignment alone. The root cause is architectural: shared embedding spaces conflate instruction and data, creating an irreducible vulnerability. The required solution class is architectural separation of instruction and data channels—akin to the memory-safety evolution in systems security. No single defense mechanism suffices; layered architectural changes are necessary.

title: RANSAC Scoring Done Right
summary: The most widely used RANSAC variants score candidate models by counting inliers or summing per-point scores that saturate beyond a residual threshold. Every such score requires a user-supplied parameter that is a function of the inlier scale, which must itself be estimated from contaminated data. We remove this dependence by reversing the usual order of inference: rather than estimating the scale and then scoring against it, we marginalize the inlier scale analytically in closed form under a conjugate Inverse-Gamma prior for a fixed inlier partition, then optimize over partitions. A single closed-form expression spans the non-informative Jeffreys limit and informative empirical-Bayes priors, so the same score adapts across data-rich and data-scarce regimes without any change to the algorithm. The proposed RANSAC score is the first in which the inlier scale is genuinely absent from the formula. The score admits O(N log N ) computation via sort-and-sweep. On a benchmark of nearly 70 000 image pairs spanning different two-view estimation problems and both engineered and learned feature pipelines, the proposed score exceeds the state of the art (RANSAC, MSAC, GaU, MAGSAC): it stays nearly flat under threshold miscalibration where baselines degrade, reaches near-optimal accuracy from as few as two validation pairs where baselines need ont he order of 100 times more,. and tightens its prior regularization as validation data grows scarce.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a novel RANSAC scoring function that analytically marginalizes out the inlier scale parameter under an Inverse-Gamma prior, removing the need to manually set an inlier threshold. The method adapts automatically across data-rich and data-scarce regimes and achieves state-of-the-art performance on a large-scale two-view geometry benchmark.
AI.motivation: All existing RANSAC variants require a user-specified inlier threshold that depends on the unknown inlier scale, creating a chicken-and-egg problem: accurate scale estimation requires a good model, but model scoring requires a threshold derived from the scale. This parameter is notoriously difficult to tune and miscalibration severely degrades performance. The authors aim to eliminate this dependency entirely.
AI.method: The authors reverse the conventional inference order: instead of estimating the inlier scale and scoring models against it, they marginalize the inlier scale analytically in closed form using a conjugate Inverse-Gamma prior, conditioned on a fixed inlier/outlier partition. The resulting score spans from the non-informative Jeffreys prior to informative empirical-Bayes priors within a single expression. Optimization then proceeds over partitions. The score is computed efficiently via O(N log N) sort-and-sweep.
AI.result: On a benchmark of ~70,000 image pairs covering different two-view estimation problems with both handcrafted and learned features, the proposed score outperforms RANSAC, MSAC, GaU, and MAGSAC. It remains nearly flat under threshold miscalibration (where baselines degrade), achieves near-optimal accuracy from as few as two validation pairs (vs. ~100x more needed by baselines), and tightens prior regularization as validation data becomes scarce.
AI.conclusion: The proposed marginalization-based RANSAC score is the first to genuinely eliminate the inlier scale from the scoring formula, enabling fully automatic robust estimation that adapts to varying amounts of prior information without algorithmic changes, while achieving state-of-the-art accuracy and robustness to miscalibration.

title: When Does Personality Composition Matter for Multi-Agent LLM Teams?
summary: Personality prompting shapes how large language models communicate, yet whether these behavioral shifts affect objective task outcomes remains under-explored. Prior work shows that agents prompted with low agreeableness produce adversarial language, while those prompted with high agreeableness become cooperative, but the relationship between communication style and task performance has not been systematically examined across multiple domains. In this work, we investigate whether personality composition matters for multi-agent team performance by manipulating personality traits across frontier LLMs on three task domains: structured coding, open-ended research collaboration, and competitive bargaining. We find that personality effects depend critically on task structure. In coding tasks, low agreeableness leads to large communication shifts that have little effect on milestone completion. In open-ended collaboration and bargaining, the same manipulation substantially degrades performance. We discuss implications for multi-agent system design and the limits of personality manipulation.

AI.tldr: This study examines whether manipulating personality traits (specifically agreeableness) in LLM-based agents affects multi-agent team performance across coding, open-ended research collaboration, and bargaining tasks. Low agreeableness shifts communication style significantly but only degrades performance in open-ended and competitive tasks, not in structured coding tasks.
AI.motivation: Prior work has shown personality prompting changes LLM communication behavior (e.g., low agreeableness → adversarial language, high agreeableness → cooperative language), but the downstream impact on objective task outcomes in multi-agent settings remains unexplored. The authors seek to close this gap by systematically testing personality effects across diverse task structures.
AI.method: The authors manipulate personality traits (focusing on agreeableness) across frontier LLMs and deploy them as multi-agent teams in three distinct task domains: (1) structured coding with clear milestones, (2) open-ended research collaboration, and (3) competitive bargaining. They compare both communication shifts and task performance metrics under different personality compositions.
AI.result: Personality effects are task-dependent. In structured coding, low agreeableness produces large communication shifts but negligible impact on milestone completion. In open-ended collaboration and bargaining, the same manipulation substantially degrades performance.
AI.conclusion: Personality composition matters for multi-agent system design, but only for certain task types. The findings caution against unqualified personality engineering in LLM agents and highlight the need to match agent personality configurations to task structure.

title: Speculative Refinement: A Hybrid Autoregressive Diffusion Decoding Strategy and Its Behavior Across Benchmarks
summary: How should we evaluate generation systems that combine autoregressive (AR) and diffusion decoding? We study this question through Speculative Refinement (SpecRef), a training-free hybrid method that warm-starts a masked diffusion language model from an AR draft using entropy-guided selective masking. Evaluating SpecRef across six benchmarks (HumanEval, MBPP, GSM8K, BBH, ARC-Challenge, HellaSwag) with three distinct evaluation protocols (execution-based pass@1, exact-match, log-likelihood scoring), we surface several findings relevant beyond our specific system: (1) code benchmarks conflate structural discovery with logical correctness: providing a syntactic scaffold lifts accuracy from near zero to over 20% without changing the model, indicating that much of the baseline failure is structural; (2) a refinement tension phenomenon where multi-stage correction degrades already-correct tokens, exposing benchmark saturation ceilings invisible to single-model evaluation; (3) log-likelihood and generative evaluation produce different model rankings for the same model pair, suggesting they measure different capabilities; (4) standard Python post-processing silently breaks code evaluation for non-AR generators. These observations apply to any multi-stage or non-autoregressive generation pipeline and point toward more diagnostic evaluation practices.

AI.tldr: The paper examines how to evaluate hybrid generation systems combining autoregressive and diffusion decoding, using Speculative Refinement (SpecRef) as a testbed. Through systematic evaluation across six benchmarks and three protocols, it uncovers four key findings: code benchmarks confound structure with logic, a refinement tension phenomenon saturates benchmarks, log-likelihood and generative evaluations produce different model rankings, and standard Python post-processing breaks non-AR evaluation. These findings inform better evaluation practices for multi-stage generation pipelines.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluation protocols are designed for single-stage autoregressive models and may be inadequate or misleading when applied to hybrid AR-diffusion generation systems. The authors aim to systematically surface evaluation pitfalls that generalize beyond any specific system.
AI.method: The authors introduce SpecRef, a training-free hybrid decoding method that uses an AR model to generate a draft, then selectively masks tokens based on entropy for a masked diffusion LM to refine. They evaluate SpecRef across six benchmarks (HumanEval, MBPP, GSM8K, BBH, ARC-Challenge, HellaSwag) using three protocols: execution-based pass@1, exact-match, and log-likelihood scoring, systematically probing each protocol's failure modes.
AI.result: Four key findings: (1) Providing a syntactic scaffold via AR draft lifts code benchmark accuracy from near zero to >20%, showing structural confounds; (2) Refinement tension causes multi-stage correction to degrade already-correct tokens, exposing saturation ceilings; (3) Log-likelihood and generative evaluation rank the same model pairs differently; (4) Standard Python post-processing (e.g., stopping at newlines) silently breaks non-AR generator evaluation.
AI.conclusion: The findings diagnose systematic issues in how multi-stage and non-autoregressive generation systems are evaluated, and the authors call for more diagnostic, multi-protocol evaluation practices that are sensitive to structural, refinement, and post-processing confounds.

title: Typing Behavior in Human-LLM Interaction: Keystroke Dynamics Reveal Cognitive Effort During Prompting
summary: As Large Language Models (LLMs) become increasingly integrated into daily routines, understanding how users interact with these systems is crucial for effective human-AI collaboration. This work investigates keystroke dynamics as a behavioral measure of user mental effort and perceived output usefulness in human-LLM interaction. We conducted a user study (N = 36) to examine how task difficulty (easy vs. hard) and device type (desktop vs. mobile) influence typing behavior and workload (NASA-TLX) during interactions. Our results indicate that hard tasks led to significantly more keystrokes, slower typing, increased pauses, and higher self-reported workload. Device type had weaker effects, with mobile use slightly reducing input length and typing speed. While keystrokes captured differences in cognitive effort, they did not predict perceived LLM output usefulness. These findings highlight the potential of keystroke dynamics as real-time indicators of cognitive effort during LLM prompting, while also showing their limitations in capturing perceived collaboration success.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates keystroke dynamics as a behavioral proxy for cognitive effort during human-LLM interactions. A user study (N=36) manipulating task difficulty and device type found that harder tasks significantly increased keystrokes, pauses, and typing latency, but keystroke patterns did not predict perceived LLM output usefulness.
AI.motivation: As LLMs become embedded in daily workflows, there is a need for real-time, unobtrusive measures of user cognitive effort to improve human-AI collaboration. Keystroke dynamics offer a passive, fine-grained behavioral signal that could complement traditional self-report measures like NASA-TLX.
AI.method: A controlled user study (N=36) with a 2×2 within-subjects design crossing task difficulty (easy vs. hard) and device type (desktop vs. mobile). Participants engaged in LLM prompting tasks while keystroke dynamics (total keystrokes, inter-key intervals, pause frequency) were logged. Subjective workload was measured via NASA-TLX, and perceived output usefulness was collected post-task.
AI.result: Hard tasks significantly increased keystroke count, slowed typing speed, raised pause frequency, and elevated NASA-TLX scores. Device type showed weaker effects — mobile use slightly reduced input length and speed. Critically, keystroke dynamics captured cognitive effort variations but failed to predict perceived LLM output usefulness.
AI.conclusion: Keystroke dynamics show promise as real-time, implicit indicators of cognitive load during LLM prompting, but they are insufficient for capturing the perceived quality or usefulness of AI-generated responses. This suggests a dissociation between behavioral effort markers and subjective collaboration success, pointing to the need for multi-modal sensing approaches.

title: Glite ARF: Verifier-Driven Research with Parallel LLM Coding Agents
comment: 13 pages, 6 figures, 7 tables. Open-source framework (Apache-2.0) and a public demo project at https://github.com/GliteTech/glite-arf and https://github.com/GliteTech/research-ace-cefr
summary: LLM coding agents make it tempting to automate empirical research by delegating experiments to them directly, but naive delegation does not scale to large projects: low-rate instruction lapses compound into broken, irreproducible artefacts. To address this problem, we present Glite ARF, an open-source Python framework for running many LLM coding agents in parallel on a research repository without sacrificing reproducibility or auditability. The framework defines a three-role stack: a human researcher chooses which hypotheses to test, coding agents (Claude Code, Codex CLI) implement individual tasks under a fixed structure, and deterministic Python verifier scripts enforce task isolation, immutability of completed work, a corrections overlay, and a materialised project overview. We call this verifier-driven research: the rules of the research process live in code that fails loudly when violated, not in prose that agents are merely asked to follow. Using Glite ARF, we developed our submission to the BEA 2026 vocabulary-difficulty shared task, placing first in the closed track and second in the open track on all three target languages (Spanish, German, Mandarin) and reducing the official baseline RMSE by 29.9% (closed) and 35.9% (open). The campaign comprised 273 tracked tasks (146 experiment runs) across 129 feature sets, run by up to twelve parallel agents orchestrated from a single laptop - with some model training on rented A100s - at approximately \$450 in LLM API spend (\$498 total third-party cost), and structured per-fold provenance let us catch and strip four target-leaking feature sets, correcting an implausible 0.609 RMSE to 0.802. Across three campaigns in three domains, the framework's structural machinery adds only about 1% of wall-clock time. Framework and a public demo project accompany this paper.

AI.tldr: Gilte ARF is an open-source framework that enables parallel LLM coding agents to conduct empirical research at scale while maintaining reproducibility through verifier-driven rules enforced by deterministic Python scripts, demonstrated by winning first place in the BEA 2026 shared task.
AI.motivation: Naive delegation of empirical research to LLM coding agents fails at scale because low-rate instruction lapses compound, producing broken and irreproducible results. A systematic framework is needed to harness LLM agents' capabilities while enforcing reproducibility and auditability.
AI.method: A three-role stack: (1) human researchers select hypotheses, (2) coding agents (Claude Code, Codex CLI) execute tasks under a fixed structure, and (3) deterministic Python verifier scripts enforce task isolation, work immutability, a corrections overlay, and a materialized project overview. This "verifier-driven research" encodes rules in code that fails loudly on violation rather than in prose instructions.
AI.result: The framework was used to develop the winning submission to the BEA 2026 vocabulary-difficulty shared task, placing 1st (closed track) and 2nd (open track) across Spanish, German, and Mandarin, reducing baseline RMSE by 29.9% and 35.9% respectively. The campaign included 273 tracked tasks, 146 experiment runs, 129 feature sets, 12 parallel agents, at ~$450 API cost. It also caught and corrected four target-leaking feature sets. The framework's overhead is ~1% of wall-clock time across three campaigns.
AI.conclusion: Verifier-driven research, where process rules are enforced by code rather than prose prompts, enables scalable, reproducible, and auditable LLM-driven empirical research with minimal overhead.

title: A Survey of Automated Presentation Coaching: Systems, Methods, and Open Challenges
comment: accepted into the BEA 2026 workshop at ACL
summary: Automated coaching for oral presentations sits at the intersection of computer-assisted pronunciation training (CAPT), prosody modeling, and speech synthesis, yet no prior work has systematically surveyed and compared existing systems along these dimensions. This survey reviews and categorizes automated presentation coaching systems, spanning pronunciation tutors, fluency and prosody coaches, multimodal trainers, and conference Q&A practice tools. We introduce a five-dimensional task taxonomy - covering segmental pronunciation, lexical stress, suprasegmental prosody, pacing, and content faithfulness - and explicitly map surveyed systems onto it to reveal coverage gaps. We further review the core technical methods these systems employ: TTS-based exemplar generation and diagnostic methods for pronunciation, prosody, and fluency assessment. Key open challenges include the scarcity of annotated presentation corpora, achieving accent-fair feedback across diverse L1 backgrounds, and delivering low-latency diagnostics for real-time rehearsal.

AI.tldr: A systematic survey of automated oral presentation coaching systems, proposing a five-dimensional task taxonomy (segmental pronunciation, lexical stress, suprasegmental prosody, pacing, content faithfulness) and reviewing underlying TTS-based and diagnostic methods, while identifying key open challenges including data scarcity, accent fairness, and low-latency feedback.
AI.motivation: No prior work has systematically surveyed and compared automated presentation coaching systems across the intersecting dimensions of CAPT, prosody modeling, and speech synthesis, leaving a gap in understanding system capabilities, coverage, and limitations.
AI.method: The authors conduct a comprehensive literature review and categorization of existing systems (pronunciation tutors, fluency/prosody coaches, multimodal trainers, Q&A practice tools), introduce a novel five-dimensional task taxonomy, map surveyed systems onto this taxonomy to identify coverage gaps, and review core technical approaches including TTS-based exemplar generation and pronunciation/prosody/fluency diagnostic methods.
AI.result: The mapping reveals coverage gaps across the five dimensions; key open challenges identified include scarcity of annotated presentation corpora, difficulty in achieving accent-fair feedback for diverse L1 backgrounds, and the need for low-latency diagnostics to enable real-time rehearsal.
AI.conclusion: Automated presentation coaching remains an underexplored, interdisciplinary field with significant technical and resource gaps. Future progress hinges on building richly annotated corpora, developing accent-inclusive assessment models, and engineering real-time capable diagnostic pipelines.

title: Bifocal Diffusion Language Models: Asymmetric Bidirectional Context for Parallel Generation
summary: Discrete diffusion language models (dLLMs) recover masked tokens in parallel, offering significant speedups over autoregressive (AR) generation. However, such promising frameworks face a fundamental architectural design dilemma: \ding{182} Adopting bidirectional attention achieves strong generation quality by allowing each position to access the full context, but is inherently incompatible with KV caching, limiting inference throughput in batch-serving scenarios; \ding{183} Conversely, causal attention enables efficient cached inference but loses all right-side context, substantially degrading generation quality. This paper introduces Bifocal dLLMs, a new paradigm that resolves this dilemma through \emph{asymmetric bidirectional context}. Analogous to bifocal lenses, we instantiate the paradigm as \textbf{R2LM} (Right-to-Left Mamba), which combines two complementary mechanisms: $a$) standard causal attention providing precise left-context with full KV cache compatibility, while $b$) a lightweight reverse Mamba SSM sidecar supplying compressed right-side context without breaking cacheability.
