Comprehensive experiments on continued pretraining of Qwen3-1.7B with 60B tokens demonstrate that R2LM achieves $2.4\times$ to $12.9\times$ higher throughput than bidirectional dLLMs and $1.9\times$ to $2.9\times$ speedup over AR baselines in batch serving through parallel decoding with KV caching, while exceeding the causal baseline on most benchmarks and surpassing the bidirectional dLLM on average.

AI.tldr: Bifocal dLLMs (R2LM) resolve the dilemma between generation quality and inference throughput in discrete diffusion language models by pairing causal attention (left context, KV-cacheable) with a lightweight reverse Mamba SSM (compressed right context), achieving significant speedups over both bidirectional dLLMs and AR models while maintaining strong generation quality.
AI.motivation: Discrete diffusion language models face a fundamental architectural trade-off: bidirectional attention yields high generation quality but is incompatible with KV caching (hurting throughput), while causal attention enables fast cached inference but loses right-side context (degrading quality). The authors aim to break this dilemma by enabling access to both left and right context without sacrificing KV-cache compatibility.
AI.method: The authors propose Bifocal dLLMs, instantiated as R2LM (Right-to-Left Mamba). The architecture combines two asymmetric components: (a) standard causal attention for precise left-context modeling with full KV cache compatibility, and (b) a lightweight reverse Mamba SSM sidecar that supplies compressed right-side context without breaking cacheability. This asymmetric bidirectional context design is validated through continued pretraining of Qwen3-1.7B on 60B tokens.
AI.result: R2LM achieves 2.4× to 12.9× higher throughput than bidirectional dLLMs and 1.9× to 2.9× speedup over AR baselines in batch-serving scenarios via parallel decoding with KV caching. In terms of generation quality, R2LM exceeds the causal baseline on most benchmarks and surpasses the bidirectional dLLM on average.
AI.conclusion: The Bifocal dLLM paradigm, specifically R2LM, successfully reconciles generation quality with inference efficiency for discrete diffusion language models, making them practical for real-world batch-serving deployment by achieving both strong benchmark performance and substantial throughput gains.

title: AdvScan: Black-Box Adversarial Example Detection at Runtime through Power Analysis
comment: 15 pages, 10 figures. Published in IEEE Transactions on Information Forensics and Security
summary: TinyML models deployed on edge devices are increasingly adopted in safety/security-critical applications, making them a prime target for adversarial example (AE) attacks where inputs are modified to cause misclassifications. However, existing AE detection methods either require white-box model access, which is often unavailable in licensed black-box deployments, or rely on input pre-processing stages that add non-trivial latency and resource overhead, often exceeding what mission-critical applications can afford on their inference path. To address these challenges, we propose AdvScan, a runtime power analysis-based methodology for AE detection that operates in a black-box scenario while inducing minimal latency. AdvScan is based on the observation that AEs produce anomalous neuron activations, which in turn generate distinctive power-consumption signatures. The algorithm initially constructs a baseline distribution of power signatures from known benign inputs; then, at runtime, it applies a one-sample t-test to determine whether a test input's power signature significantly deviates from this baseline, thereby detecting AEs. We evaluated AdvScan using three adversarial example generation algorithms: Fast Gradient Sign Method (FGSM), Projected Gradient Descent (PGD), and Carlini-Wagner (C&W), on three MLPerf Tiny benchmark models implemented on two target devices: the STM32F303RC (ARM Cortex-M4) and STM32L562RE (ARM Cortex-M33) microcontrollers. Across 318,400 total test inputs, AdvScan detects 99.984% of AEs with only 40 false negatives and zero false positives. These results demonstrate the viability of power-based AE detection for secure, accuracy-critical TinyML deployments in black-box environments.

AI.tldr: AdvScan proposes a black-box adversarial example detection method for TinyML edge devices using runtime power analysis, achieving 99.984% detection rate with zero false positives by identifying anomalous power signatures from perturbed neuron activations.
AI.motivation: TinyML models in safety/security-critical edge applications are vulnerable to adversarial example (AE) attacks, but existing AE detection methods either require white-box model access (unavailable in black-box commercial deployments) or impose prohibitive latency and resource overhead on the inference path. A lightweight, black-box, minimal-latency detection approach is needed.
AI.method: AdvScan leverages the observation that AEs induce anomalous neuron activations producing distinctive power-consumption signatures. It constructs a baseline power signature distribution from benign inputs during an offline phase. At runtime, it applies a one-sample t-test to determine whether a test input's power signature statistically deviates from the baseline, flagging deviations as AEs. The approach operates fully black-box with no input preprocessing on the inference path.
AI.result: Evaluated across three AE generation algorithms (FGSM, PGD, C&W), three MLPerf Tiny benchmark models, and two ARM Cortex-M microcontrollers (STM32F303RC/M4 and STM32L562RE/M33). Out of 318,400 total test inputs, AdvScan detected 99.984% of AEs with only 40 false negatives and zero false positives.
AI.conclusion: Power analysis-based AE detection is a viable and effective approach for securing accuracy-critical TinyML deployments in black-box environments, offering high detection rates with minimal runtime overhead.

title: Unified Zero-Shot Time Series Forecasting: A Darts Foundation
summary: Since its initial release in 2020, Darts has become a widely used open-source Python library for time series analysis. A series of foundation models have recently claimed accuracy improvements in zero-shot forecasting, promising a paradigm shift from training custom models to harnessing pre-trained general-purpose forecasters. Foundation models, however, are often released as isolated packages with fragmented interfaces and limited interoperability with common tooling, making joint evaluation and integration within complete pipelines difficult. In Darts, we developed a unified $\texttt{FoundationModel}$ class collection (Chronos-2, TimesFM 2.5, TiRex, PatchTST-FM) that provides standardized, full-cycle forecasting interfaces with minimal external dependencies for integrating foundation models into the ecosystem. Existing Darts pipelines can now use foundation models with only a name change; new pipelines can use them for zero-shot or fine-tuned forecasting, uncertainty estimation, and backtesting, combined with data processing and evaluation tooling, all within a unified framework.

AI.tldr: Darts has integrated multiple foundation models (Chronos-2, TimesFM 2.5, TiRex, PatchTST-FM) into its time series library via a unified FoundationModel class, enabling zero-shot forecasting, fine-tuning, uncertainty estimation, and backtesting within existing pipelines with minimal code changes.
AI.motivation: Foundation models for time series forecasting promise a paradigm shift from custom model training to general-purpose zero-shot forecasting, but they are released as isolated packages with incompatible interfaces and poor interoperability with standard tooling, hindering joint evaluation and integration into complete workflows.
AI.method: The authors developed a unified FoundationModel abstract class within the Darts library that wraps four foundation models (Chronos-2, TimesFM 2.5, TiRex, PatchTST-FM) behind standardized, full-cycle forecasting interfaces. The class provides consistent APIs for zero-shot forecasting, optional fine-tuning, uncertainty estimation, and backtesting, with minimal external dependencies.
AI.result: Existing Darts pipelines can now swap in foundation models by changing only the model name. New pipelines can leverage these pre-trained forecasters alongside Darts' existing data processing, evaluation, and backtesting tooling within a single unified framework.
AI.conclusion: By providing a standardized interface for foundation models, Darts lowers the barrier to adopting and fairly comparing general-purpose forecasters, enabling practitioners to integrate state-of-the-art zero-shot forecasting into production workflows without sacrificing the benefits of a cohesive ecosystem.

title: Internalizing the Future: A Unified Agentic Training Paradigm for World Model Planning
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents have demonstrated strong capability in sequential decision-making, yet they remains fundamentally reactive in long-horizon tasks. Unlike humans who employ "what-if" reasoning to evaluate potential plans before commitment, standard agents lack an internal world model to simulate future outcomes. Therefore, we propose to internalize future-aware planning by training a single autoregressive model to verbalize both a prospective state rollout and a plan-conditioned success estimate-a textual analogue of the Q-value. Crucially, we identify a format-capability gap: simply fine-tuning agents on look-ahead traces during post-training leads to superficial mimicry of foresight without genuine predictive grounding. To bridge this gap, we introduce a three-stage training paradigm: (i) World Model Agentic Mid-Training (WM-AMT) to inject latent predictive capabilities into the policy; (ii) Format-Eliciting SFT (FE-SFT) to structure this injected capability; and (iii) Foresight-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning (FC-RL) to refine the calibration and utility of the generated simulations. Evaluated on search and mathematical reasoning tasks, our approach consistently outperforms other training baselines. Our results demonstrate that effective internal world modeling in LLM agents requires a capability-first training pipeline to achieve grounded and calibrated foresight.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses LLM agents' lack of internal world models for future-aware planning. It proposes training a single autoregressive model to verbalize prospective state rollouts and plan-conditioned success estimates (textual Q-values). A three-stage training paradigm—WM-AMT, FE-SFT, and FC-RL—bridges the "format-capability gap" to achieve grounded, calibrated foresight, outperforming baselines on search and math reasoning tasks.
AI.motivation: LLM agents excel at sequential decision-making but remain fundamentally reactive in long-horizon tasks. They lack the human-like "what-if" reasoning capability—an internal world model to simulate and evaluate future outcomes before committing to actions. Existing post-training approaches that fine-tune on look-ahead traces result only in superficial mimicry of foresight without genuine predictive grounding, revealing a "format-capability gap."
AI.method: The authors propose internalizing future-aware planning by training an autoregressive model to verbalize both a prospective state rollout and a plan-conditioned success estimate (a textual analogue of Q-values). Their three-stage training paradigm consists of: (i) World Model Agentic Mid-Training (WM-AMT) to inject latent predictive capabilities; (ii) Format-Eliciting Supervised Fine-Tuning (FE-SFT) to structure this injected capability into the desired verbalized format; and (iii) Foresight-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning (FC-RL) to refine the calibration and decision utility of the generated simulations.
AI.result: Evaluated on search and mathematical reasoning tasks, the proposed three-stage approach consistently outperforms other training baselines. The results validate that effective internal world modeling requires a capability-first training pipeline to achieve grounded and calibrated foresight, rather than superficial mimicry through direct fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: Effective internal world modeling in LLM agents necessitates a capability-first training pipeline—first injecting latent predictive capabilities, then eliciting them into structured formats, and finally refining them via RL. This yields grounded, calibrated foresight that meaningfully improves long-horizon sequential decision-making over reactive baselines.

title: Contextual Associations Between Webpage Elements for Web Accessibility: An Empirical Study
comment: 11 pages, 2 Figures, 1 Table, submitted to ESEIW 2026 ESEM - Registered Reports Track
summary: [Context] Screen reader users navigating webpages by element list often encounter accessible names such as "Read more" that are valid under the W3C Accessible Name and Description Computation specification but uninterpretable in isolation. The surrounding elements that would make these names meaningful exist in the page but are not linked to the target by any mechanism. No prior work has empirically studied how to select which surrounding elements are contextually relevant to a given target. [Objective] This registered report investigates whether human-perceived contextual associations between webpage elements can be recovered from the accessibility tree using link prediction, and whether the learned associations generalize across websites. [Method] We will construct a dataset of human-annotated contextual associations on 35 websites, stratified across the Tranco top-million list, with three independent annotators per page. Each page is represented as a graph derived from its accessibility tree, augmented with spatial and semantic features from the DOM and CSS. We compare four machine learning models (MLP, GCN, GAT, and SEAL) against two heuristic baselines under leave-one-site-out cross-validation with a pre-registered statistical framework, using Hit@K and MRR. [Results] We have conducted a five-site author-annotated pilot study to establish the pipelines and parameterize the power simulation, with pilot Hit@10 ranging from 0.16 to 0.85 across four learned models and 0.08 to 0.30 across two heuristic baselines. The final results will be reported after the planned experiments and analyses are completed. [Conclusion] The study contributes a human-annotated dataset of contextual associations on webpages, an empirical evaluation of link prediction for context selection on accessibility-tree graphs, and a cross-site generalization analysis.

AI.tldr: This registered report proposes using link prediction on accessibility-tree graphs to recover human-perceived contextual associations between webpage elements, aiming to help screen reader users interpret otherwise ambiguous accessible names like "Read more" by identifying contextually relevant surrounding elements.
AI.motivation: Screen reader users navigating by element list encounter accessible names (e.g., "Read more") that are technically valid per W3C specifications but semantically uninterpretable in isolation. While surrounding contextual elements exist in the page, no mechanism links them to the target element, and no prior work has empirically studied how to select contextually relevant surrounding elements.
AI.method: A dataset of human-annotated contextual associations will be constructed across 35 websites stratified from the Tranco top-million list, with three annotators per page. Pages are modeled as graphs derived from accessibility trees augmented with spatial and semantic features from DOM/CSS. Four ML models (MLP, GCN, GAT, SEAL) are compared against two heuristic baselines under leave-one-site-out cross-validation with pre-registered statistical tests using Hit@K and MRR. A five-site pilot study parameterized the power simulation.
AI.result: Pilot study results (5 sites, author-annotated) show Hit@10 ranging from 0.16–0.85 for the four learned models and 0.08–0.30 for the two heuristic baselines, indicating learned approaches significantly outperform heuristics. Final results are pending completion of the planned experiments.
AI.conclusion: The study will contribute (1) a human-annotated dataset of contextual associations on webpages, (2) an empirical evaluation of link prediction for context selection on accessibility-tree graphs, and (3) a cross-site generalization analysis.

title: Functional outcomes and naturalistic engagement with a purpose-built conversational AI for mental health (Ash)
summary:
Background: Conversational AI chatbots designed for mental health may offer an accessible, scalable avenue for supporting psychological well-being, yet prior evaluations have largely focused on clinical symptom reduction rather than broader indicators of day-to-day functioning, and have rarely monitored for potential harms such as inflated self-perception.
  Objective: We examined within-person change in psychological functioning indicators among real-world users of Ash, a purpose-built conversational AI for mental health support, over the first four weeks of use, and whether these changes were associated with engagement metrics.
  Methods: In this single-arm observational cohort study, new users (n = 1,284) completed in-app single-item measures of psychological functioning (life satisfaction, relationship satisfaction, sleep quality, behavioral activation), working alliance, and grandiosity (inflated self-perception), at baseline and Week 4. Paired-sample t-tests examined within-person change; ANCOVAs tested engagement-outcome associations at Week 4, controlling for baseline.
  Results: At baseline, participants reported below-average life satisfaction and fair sleep quality. Significant within-person improvements emerged across all functioning indicators and working alliance (ps < .001; d = 0.14-0.26), with no change in grandiosity. Active days, total sessions, and total minutes consistently predicted Week 4 psychological functioning and working alliance (ps <= .006; partial R^2 range: 0.58-2.15%; controlling for baseline), whereas user message volume did not.
  Conclusion: Findings provide preliminary data for the potential of evidence-based conversational AI to extend mental health support for broad psychological functioning, extending the existing literature beyond symptom-based outcomes.

AI.tldr: A 4-week observational study of 1,284 users of the mental health chatbot "Ash" found significant within-person improvements in life satisfaction, relationship satisfaction, sleep quality, behavioral activation, and working alliance, with no increase in grandiosity. Engagement metrics (active days, sessions, minutes) predicted outcomes, while message volume did not.
AI.motivation: Prior evaluations of mental health chatbots have focused narrowly on clinical symptom reduction rather than broader psychological functioning, and have rarely monitored for potential iatrogenic effects such as inflated self-perception (grandiosity). This study aimed to fill that gap.
AI.method: Single-arm observational cohort study. New users (n=1,284) of the Ash chatbot completed in-app single-item measures at baseline and Week 4 assessing life satisfaction, relationship satisfaction, sleep quality, behavioral activation, working alliance, and grandiosity. Paired-sample t-tests examined within-person change; ANCOVAs tested associations between engagement metrics and Week 4 outcomes, controlling for baseline.
AI.result: Significant within-person improvements were found across all functioning indicators and working alliance (all ps < .001; Cohen's d = 0.14–0.26), with no significant change in grandiosity. Active days, total sessions, and total minutes each significantly predicted Week 4 outcomes (ps ≤ .006; partial R² range: 0.58–2.15%), while user message volume did not.
AI.conclusion: The findings offer preliminary evidence that evidence-based conversational AI can support broader psychological functioning beyond symptom reduction, and suggest that engagement dose (frequency/duration) rather than verbosity drives benefit, all without inflating grandiosity.

title: QueenBee Planner: Skill-Evolving Communication Topologies for Token-Efficient LLM Multi-Agent Systems
summary: Large language model (LLM) multi-agent systems increasingly depend not only on how individual agents reason, but also on how agents are connected. This paper introduces QueenBee Planner, a framework that treats inter-agent communication topology as a retrievable and self-improving design skill. A pool of worker agents, the task adapter, and the scoring function are frozen; only an outer LLM planner learns to generate temporal communication DAGs specifying who sends information to whom, in which round, who merges messages, and who emits the final answer. Execution traces are distilled into evidence-backed design rules with three actions: \emph{Preserve}, \emph{Modify}, and \emph{Avoid}. To prevent self-evolution from turning lucky runs or plausible but false explanations into policy, QueenBee uses held-out acceptance gates, variance-aware credit, motif-level attribution, transfer trust, insight falsification, and structural deduplication. We evaluate the method on Count-Frequency aggregation and Silo-Bench-style distributed coordination tasks. With fixed workers, self-evolved graph generation produces communication structures that improve over fixed topologies and cold generation. In the CF fulltest setting, the best generated graph reduces RMSE from 12.53 for the strongest fixed topology to 7.87 while also reducing messages, model calls, and token cost; Silo-style results show the same direction of improvement over cold and fixed-topology baselines. These results suggest that multi-agent systems can learn reusable architectural design knowledge rather than merely memorizing task answers.

AI.tldr: QueenBee Planner treats inter-agent communication topology as a self-improving design skill. An outer LLM generates temporal DAGs specifying communication patterns, with execution traces distilled into evidence-backed rules (Preserve, Modify, Avoid). Self-evolution is safeguarded by multiple verification gates. On aggregation and coordination tasks, self-evolved graphs outperform fixed topologies and cold generation, reducing RMSE from 12.53 to 7.87 while lowering costs.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent LLM systems' performance depends on both individual agent reasoning and inter-agent communication topology. Fixed topologies are suboptimal across diverse tasks, and existing approaches lack mechanisms to treat topology design as a retrievable, reusable, and self-improving skill grounded in evidence rather than memorized answers.
AI.method: QueenBee Planner freezes worker agents, task adapter, and scoring function. An outer LLM planner generates temporal communication DAGs (who sends to whom, in which round, who merges, who emits final answer). Execution traces are distilled into design rules using three actions: Preserve, Modify, Avoid. Six safeguards prevent spurious self-evolution: held-out acceptance gates, variance-aware credit, motif-level attribution, transfer trust, insight falsification, and structural deduplication.
AI.result: On Count-Frequency aggregation, the best self-evolved graph reduces RMSE from 12.53 (strongest fixed topology) to 7.87, while also reducing messages, model calls, and token cost. Silo-Bench-style distributed coordination tasks show consistent improvement over both cold generation and fixed-topology baselines.
AI.conclusion: Multi-agent systems can learn reusable architectural design knowledge — specifically communication topology — rather than merely memorizing task answers. Self-evolving topology generation with evidence-backed rule distillation and rigorous safeguards yields both better performance and lower resource costs.

title: Causal Connections: Leveraging Multilingual Fine-Tuning for Financial QA@FinCausal 2026
summary: This paper describes team HSA_CORAL's submission to the FinCausal 2026 shared task on extracting cause-effect relations from financial narratives via extractive question answering in English and Spanish. We compare three modeling families: (i) encoder-only token tagging with multilingual BERT, (ii) encoder-decoder generation with multilingual BART, and (iii) decoder-only LLMs (Llama 3.1 and GPT variants) using prompt refinement, few-shot demonstrations, and supervised fine-tuning. Across settings, prompting and few-shot examples yield competitive performance, while supervised fine-tuning provides the largest gains. Our best system, GPT-4.1 Mini fine-tuned on combined English and Spanish training data, achieves a tied highest score on the English subtask (score 4.8140) and ranks third on Spanish (score 4.7753) under the shared task's LLM-as-a-judge metric. Overall, the results highlight the value of task-specific adaptation and multilingual fine-tuning for cross-lingual transfer in financial causality QA.

AI.tldr: Team HSA_CORAL's submission to FinCausal 2026 explores extractive QA for financial causality, comparing encoder-only (mBERT), encoder-decoder (mBART), and decoder-only LLMs (Llama 3.1, GPT variants). Supervised fine-tuning of GPT-4.1 Mini on combined English-Spanish data yields the best results, tying for first on English (4.8140) and ranking third on Spanish (4.7753) under an LLM-as-judge metric.
AI.motivation: Extracting cause-effect relations from financial narratives is challenging, particularly across languages. The shared task provides a structured benchmark (FinCausal 2026) for evaluating how well different modeling paradigms — and specifically LLMs — can perform this task in English and Spanish, with an emphasis on cross-lingual transfer.
AI.method: The authors compare three modeling families: (1) encoder-only token tagging using multilingual BERT, (2) encoder-decoder generation using multilingual BART, and (3) decoder-only LLMs (Llama 3.1 and GPT variants) under three strategies: prompt refinement, few-shot demonstrations, and supervised fine-tuning (SFT). The best system fine-tunes GPT-4.1 Mini on combined English and Spanish training data. Evaluation uses the shared task's LLM-as-a-judge metric.
AI.result: Prompting and few-shot methods yield competitive baselines, but supervised fine-tuning provides the largest performance gains. GPT-4.1 Mini fine-tuned on bilingual data achieves a tied best score of 4.8140 on the English subtask and third place (4.7753) on Spanish.
AI.conclusion: Task-specific adaptation via supervised fine-tuning, combined with multilingual training data, substantially benefits financial causality extraction. Decoder-only LLMs, when fine-tuned, outperform encoder-only and encoder-decoder approaches, and multilingual fine-tuning supports effective cross-lingual transfer.

title: End-to-End Dynamic Sparsity for Resource-Adaptive LLM Inference
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) inference is typically deployed under a static resource assumption, where models execute a fixed computational graph regardless of the runtime environment. However, real-world cloud infrastructure is inherently dynamic, characterized by fluctuating availability (e.g., spot instance preemption) and tiered Quality-of-Service requirements. In such volatile settings, static models are inflexible: they either crash under resource constraints or waste compute on redundant operations. To bridge this gap, we propose Learning to Allocate (L2A), an end-to-end framework for resource-adaptive inference. Unlike prior methods that condition only on input difficulty, we formulate inference as a constrained allocation problem conditioned on both the input and the runtime resource budget itself. We introduce lightweight, budget-conditioned and input-aware gating networks integrated into the LLM. These gates are trained via a unified objective that jointly optimizes task performance, logical consistency, and resource costs along three axes matching how real-world dynamics manifest: layer skipping for memory and depth pressure, head pruning for throughput contention, and reasoning-token reduction for latency tightening. This lets the model learn a budget-aware policy beyond input difficulty alone: it adaptively configures its computational footprint with respect to real-time resource dynamics, maximizing reasoning depth when resources permit while enforcing strict frugality when budgets tighten. A single L2A model traces the entire compute-accuracy Pareto frontier on Llama-3-8B and Qwen-3-4B: at up to 34% realized layer sparsity, it stays within 0.6% of the dense baseline on GSM8K, with the same gap holding zero-shot on out-of-distribution tasks, while every static or heuristic baseline requires a separately tuned model and still drops by 5-10% at comparable inference time.

AI.tldr: L2A proposes resource-adaptive LLM inference via lightweight, budget-conditioned gating networks that jointly optimize layer skipping, head pruning, and reasoning-token reduction, enabling a single model to trace the entire compute-accuracy Pareto frontier across dynamic cloud environments.
AI.motivation: Static LLM inference fails under dynamic cloud conditions (e.g., spot instance preemption, fluctuating resource availability, tiered QoS). Existing adaptive methods condition only on input difficulty and cannot respond to runtime resource constraints, leading to either crashes or wasted computation.
AI.method: L2A formulates inference as a constrained allocation problem conditioned on both input and runtime resource budget. It integrates lightweight, budget-conditioned, input-aware gating networks into the LLM, trained with a unified objective optimizing task performance, logical consistency, and resource costs across three axes: (1) layer skipping for memory/depth pressure, (2) head pruning for throughput contention, and (3) reasoning-token reduction for latency constraints.
AI.result: On Llama-3-8B and Qwen-3-4B, a single L2A model traces the full compute-accuracy Pareto frontier. At up to 34% layer sparsity, it stays within 0.6% of the dense baseline on GSM8K, with the same margin holding zero-shot on out-of-distribution tasks. In contrast, static/heuristic baselines require separately tuned models and drop 5-10% at comparable inference time.
AI.conclusion: L2A enables a single LLM to adapt its computational footprint in real time to dynamic resource conditions, achieving near-dense accuracy under severe sparsity constraints while eliminating the need for per-budget model tuning.

title: Reliable Homomorphic Matching for Fuzzy Labeled PSI at Scale
summary: Fuzzy Labeled Private Set Intersection (FLPSI) lets a receiver learn the labels of enrolled records similar to its query, and nothing else. Constructions based on a set-threshold reduction reach practical performance: a query matches a record when the two agree on a threshold number of components, and the private matching is delegated to an inner set-threshold kernel. We study its homomorphic form, which combines leveled-BFV homomorphic encryption (HE), a garbled circuit, and secret sharing to decide the match under encryption and release the record's label. We identify a composition gap in this kernel: efficiency is bought with a per-trial false-accept probability, but one query runs a trial for every record, so the error compounds with the database size into the kernel's realization soundness error (RSE), the rate at which it accepts a query the plaintext matcher would reject. The RSE is a reliability property of the cryptographic matching layer, not the matcher's accuracy, and a sound kernel must contribute zero or negligible RSE of its own. We formalize this as a composable security property, give a closed-form bound on the receiver's advantage, and close the gap with CSTPSI, a kernel that runs independent token rounds and raises the per-trial bound to a matching power. We prove CSTPSI secure in the semi-honest model. The bound sets the round count: two token rounds suffice for million-scale databases and three for billion-scale at the $10^{-6}$ engineering threshold. Our evaluation confirms this: at a million records the baseline kernel's RSE reaches 100% while CSTPSI holds it at 0 in every measured configuration. For large labels at small to moderate scale CSTPSI is more than 20x faster than the baseline, with up to 93% less communication, converging to the baseline only at million-scale. Our implementation, with a one-command reproducibility harness, is publicly available.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies a composition flaw in Fuzzy Labeled Private Set Intersection (FLPSI) where per-trial false-accept probabilities compound with database size into a non-negligible Realization Soundness Error (RSE). It proposes CSTPSI, a kernel using independent token rounds with a matching-power bound, eliminating the RSE with only 2–3 rounds needed for million-to-billion-scale databases, and demonstrates significant performance improvements over the baseline.
AI.motivation: Existing FLPSI constructions based on set-threshold reduction suffer from a composition gap: the per-trial false-accept probability of the inner matching kernel compounds across all database records, yielding a Realization Soundness Error (RSE) that can reach 100% at scale. The cryptographic matching layer must contribute zero or negligible RSE independently of the matcher's accuracy, but prior work fails this requirement.
AI.method: The authors formalize RSE as a composable security property and derive a closed-form bound on the receiver's advantage. They propose CSTPSI, a kernel that runs independent token rounds and raises the per-trial bound to a matching power, thereby neutralizing the composition effect. The construction combines leveled-BFV homomorphic encryption, garbled circuits, and secret sharing. Security is proven in the semi-honest model, and the round count is analytically determined (2 rounds for million-scale, 3 for billion-scale at $10^{-6}$ threshold).
AI.result: At one million records, the baseline kernel's RSE reaches 100% while CSTPSI holds it at 0 in all measured configurations. For large labels at small-to-moderate scale, CSTPSI is over 20x faster than the baseline with up to 93% less communication, converging to the baseline only at million-scale. The implementation with reproducibility harness is publicly available.
AI.conclusion: CSTPSI successfully closes the composition gap in FLPSI by eliminating the compounding RSE through independent token rounds. The approach is practical, requiring only 2–3 rounds for real-world database scales, and offers substantial efficiency gains, making it a sound and performant replacement for prior set-threshold kernels.

title: PairSAE: Mechanistic Interpretability from Pair Representations in Protein Co-Folding
comment: Accepted at the Machine Learning in Structural Biology (MLSB) 2025 workshop
summary:
Foundation models for structural biology have achieved remarkable performance in predicting biomolecular structure and show promise for the design of proteins and small molecules. Yet understanding which internal features drive their outputs remains challenging. Standard sparse autoencoders (SAEs), effective on transformer-style sequence embeddings, do not transfer cleanly to pairformer-like architectures: naively operating on pairwise representations yields a quadratic blow-up of features and obscures concepts distributed jointly across sequence and pair representations.
  We introduce PairSAE, which summarizes pairwise tensors via an N-mode SVD into token-wise interaction roles, then uses a sparse autoencoder to learn a shared set of token-level features that decode into both sequence and pair representations. Evaluated on Boltz-2 activations for PLINDER protein-ligand complexes, PairSAE yields interpretable features that align with UniProt annotations and predict Boltz-2 affinity values. These results indicate that PairSAE links the latent space of foundation models for structural biology to interpretable structural concepts, clarifying what the model "knows" while avoiding pairformer-induced pitfalls that limit conventional SAEs.

AI.tldr: PairSAE introduces a sparse autoencoder method for pairformer-like architectures that uses N-mode SVD to decompose pairwise tensors into token-wise interaction roles, enabling interpretable feature extraction from structural biology foundation models without quadratic feature blow-up.
AI.motivation: Standard sparse autoencoders (SAEs) work well on transformer sequence embeddings but fail on pairformer architectures because operating directly on pairwise representations causes a quadratic explosion of features and obscures concepts distributed jointly across sequence and pair representations.
AI.method: PairSAE first summarizes pairwise tensors via N-mode SVD into token-wise interaction roles, then trains a sparse autoencoder to learn a shared set of token-level features that decode into both sequence and pair representations.
AI.result: Evaluated on Boltz-2 activations for PLINDER protein-ligand complexes, PairSAE yields interpretable features that align with UniProt annotations and predict Boltz-2 affinity values.
AI.conclusion: PairSAE successfully links the latent space of structural biology foundation models to interpretable structural concepts, clarifying model knowledge while avoiding the pairformer-induced pitfalls that limit conventional SAEs.

title: Odyssey: Constructing Verifiable Local Truth-Preserving Foundation Models
summary: We introduce a categorical framework called ODYSSEY for constructing verifiable, local truth-preserving foundation models as compositions of foundries: building-block architectural components that specify a cover of local contexts, local representation families, restriction maps, gluing rules, obstruction policies, update obligations, and human-facing views. A foundry is an organized sheaf of knowledge that carries within it an argumentation component. Concrete foundries are built from generic foundries such as evidence/argument, operational decision, institutional/financial, market meaning, scientific challenge, research-program, assistant-build, and evaluation-harness foundries. Universal Foundry Learning (UFL) formalizes foundry construction as a composition of left and right Kan extensions, with left Kan extension rolling local artifacts into candidate foundries and right Kan extension enforcing the restriction, gluing, obstruction, and argumentation conditions required for promotion. Foundry SQL (FSQL) is a small typed query surface for slicing maintained foundry artifacts that uses TICKET (Topos Integration using Causal Kan Extension Transformers) certification for admitting external or pre-built models into durable ODYSSEY state. ODYSSEY is fully implemented and tested across a wide spectrum of concrete foundries, showing that the same categorical machinery supports domain construction, artifact replay, sheaf diagnostics, grounded Toulmin/local-LLM scrutiny, residual-obstruction ledgers, and optimized TICKET-compatible causal-claim extraction across heterogeneous sources. This paper is to be presented as a 2.5 hour tutorial at ICML 2026. The tutorial home page is at https://bit.ly/4ajS0nA.

AI.tldr: ODYSSEY is a categorical framework for building verifiable, truth-preserving AI foundation models by composing modular "foundries"—sheaf-like architectural units with built-in argumentation. It uses Kan extensions (UFL) for construction, a typed query language (FSQL) for slicing artifacts, and TICKET certification for integrating external models, all implemented and tested across diverse domains.
AI.motivation: Current foundation models lack verifiable, local truth-preservation guarantees and structured composability. There is a need for a principled categorical framework that can construct models from modular components while enforcing consistency, gluing conditions, and argumentation, enabling scrutiny and durable integration of heterogeneous knowledge sources.
AI.method: The framework organizes knowledge as foundries—sheaf-like structures specifying local contexts, representation families, restriction maps, gluing rules, obstruction policies, update obligations, and human-facing views. Universal Foundry Learning (UFL) formalizes construction via left Kan extensions (rolling up local artifacts into candidates) and right Kan extensions (enforcing restriction, gluing, obstruction, and argumentation conditions). Foundry SQL (FSQL) provides a typed query surface, and TICKET (Topos Integration using Causal Kan Extension Transformers) certifies external models for admission into ODYSSEY state.
AI.result: ODYSSEY is fully implemented and tested across a wide spectrum of concrete foundries (evidence/argument, operational decision, institutional/financial, market meaning, scientific challenge, research-program, assistant-build, evaluation-harness). The same categorical machinery supports domain construction, artifact replay, sheaf diagnostics, grounded Toulmin/local-LLM scrutiny, residual-obstruction ledgers, and optimized TICKET-compatible causal-claim extraction across heterogeneous sources.
AI.conclusion: The categorical sheaf-theoretic approach embodied in ODYSSEY provides a unified, implementable framework for constructing verifiable, truth-preserving foundation models. It demonstrates that the same formal machinery generalizes across diverse domains and supports rigorous auditing, integration, and querying of knowledge artifacts.

title: Test Case Selection for Deep Neural Networks: A Replication Study on LLMs for Code
comment: Accepted at ISSTA 2026, the 35th ACM SIGSOFT International Symposium on Software Testing and Analysis
summary: Recently, test case selection (TCS) techniques have been explored to support the operational evaluation of deep neural networks (DNNs) under limited testing budgets, where labeling cost is a primary concern and uncovering model failures early is a key objective. Although prior studies report promising results, existing empirical evaluations focus almost exclusively on vision-based DNNs and datasets, leaving it unclear whether prior findings generalize to LLM code models. This paper presents a large-scale replication study of TCS techniques in the context of LLM code models. We re-examine established TCS strategies originally proposed for DNNs and complement them with statistical sampling strategies not previously evaluated for TCS. We assess their effectiveness on three code-related classification tasks: clone detection, vulnerability detection, and technical debt prediction. The study spans 17 task-specific fine-tuned model instances, 7 predictive features, and 13 selection strategies, including 12 feature-aware strategies and simple random sampling (SRS) as a feature-agnostic baseline. We evaluate performance along two dimensions: accuracy estimation and early failure discovery. The results indicate that only a subset of findings reported for vision-based DNNs generalize when TCS is applied to LLMs for code. In particular, uncertainty-based features are effective for early failure discovery, while representation-based features are more robust for accuracy estimation. At the same time, performance varies substantially across tasks and models, indicating that TCS effectiveness is context-dependent. Overall, this study provides empirical evidence on the replicability of TCS techniques beyond vision-based deep learning and offers insights into their use for the operational evaluation of LLMs for code.

AI.tldr: A large-scale replication study examining whether test case selection (TCS) techniques developed for vision-based DNNs generalize to LLM code models across three code classification tasks, finding that generalizability is partial and context-dependent: uncertainty-based features aid early failure discovery, while representation-based features excel at accuracy estimation.
AI.motivation: Existing TCS techniques have been evaluated almost exclusively on vision-based DNNs and datasets. It is unclear whether prior findings — particularly regarding which features and strategies are effective — generalize to LLMs for code-related tasks, where labeling costs are high and early failure discovery is critical for operational evaluation.
AI.method: The authors conduct a replication study across three code classification tasks (clone detection, vulnerability detection, technical debt prediction) using 17 fine-tuned model instances. They evaluate 13 selection strategies (12 feature-aware + random sampling baseline) spanning 7 predictive features. Performance is assessed along two dimensions: accuracy estimation (how well selected subsets estimate full-test-set accuracy) and early failure discovery (how effectively failures are surfaced under budget constraints).
AI.result: Only a subset of findings from vision-based DNNs generalize: uncertainty-based features are effective for early failure discovery, while representation-based features are more robust for accuracy estimation. Substantial performance variation exists across tasks and models, indicating that TCS effectiveness is context-dependent rather than universally transferable.
AI.conclusion: TCS technique replicability beyond vision-based deep learning is limited and task/model-dependent. Practitioners should consider uncertainty-based features when prioritizing failure discovery and representation-based features when estimating accuracy. The study provides empirical evidence to guide TCS adoption for operational evaluation of LLMs for code.

title: DysLexLens: A Low-Resource LLM Framework for Analysing Dyslexic Learners Insights from Online Forums
summary: Dyslexic learners increasingly use artificial intelligence (AI) tools to support reading, writing, organisation, and study-related tasks. However, their lived experiences with these tools remain largely underexamined. This paper proposes DysLexLens, a low-resource LLM framework, designed to analyse dyslexic learners experience with AI through online forum discussions. DysLexLens is designed as an end-to-end, evidence-traceable architecture which transforms noisy social media posts into a dictionary-driven corpora, provides knowledge-graph (KG)-based question reasoning, generates verifiable query responses, and enables response evaluation through quantitative and human-grounded assessment. DysLexLens has four key features. First, it employs a dictionary-driven filtering method to construct a more focused Reddit corpus on dyslexia and AI, filtering out noisy and weakly related posts to improve the relevance of data collected from low-resource forum contexts. Second, it integrates LLM-assisted semantic analysis with KG-based query reasoning to uncover meaningful patterns. Third, it has quantitative evaluation metrics (RAGAS and Query Robustness) to measure LLM-generated response performance. Fourth, it provides structured qualitative validation guidelines for assessing response quality, with a specific focus on hallucination and evidence alignment. We demonstrate the effectiveness of DysLexLens using dyslexia-related Reddit forum data and 30 questions. The results show its potential generalisability to other low-resource forum data contexts. DysLexLens, sample data, questions and evaluation results are available at Github to support reproducibility.

AI.tldr: DysLexLens is a low-resource LLM framework that extracts and analyzes dyslexic learners' experiences with AI tools from noisy Reddit forum posts using dictionary-driven filtering, KG-based reasoning, and structured evaluation, demonstrating effectiveness on 30 questions with reproducible artifacts.
AI.motivation: Dyslexic learners increasingly use AI tools, yet their lived experiences remain underexamined. Existing approaches lack systematic, evidence-traceable methods for analyzing user experiences from low-resource, noisy social media contexts.
AI.method: The DysLexLens framework comprises four components: (1) dictionary-driven filtering to construct a focused Reddit corpus on dyslexia and AI; (2) LLM-assisted semantic analysis integrated with knowledge-graph-based query reasoning; (3) quantitative evaluation via RAGAS and Query Robustness metrics; and (4) structured qualitative validation guidelines targeting hallucination and evidence alignment.
AI.result: The framework was validated using dyslexia-related Reddit data and 30 questions, demonstrating effectiveness in generating verifiable, evidence-aligned responses from low-resource forum contexts, with potential generalizability to other domains.
AI.conclusion: DysLexLens provides a reproducible, end-to-end architecture for analyzing user experiences in low-resource social media settings, with all artifacts (framework, sample data, questions, and evaluation results) publicly available on GitHub.

title: GenWorld: Empirically Grounded Urban Simulation Infrastructure for Scalable LLM-Agent Studies
comment: 27 pages, 24 figures. Code: https://github.com/Perseus1993/genworld. Project page: https://genworld1993.netlify.app/
summary: LLM-agent simulation faces a joint grounding and scaling problem: agents should act in environments that reflect real urban constraints, yet direct online LLM calls for city-scale populations are computationally prohibitive. We present GenWorld, an empirically grounded urban simulation infrastructure that combines a building-level synthetic city, a structured agent-environment interface, and offline compilation of LLM-derived decision signals into lookup policies for scalable rollout. In a reference instantiation for Higashihiroshima, Japan, GenWorld grounds 196,608 synthetic residents in census and geospatial data, validates demographic consistency against census tabulations, and uses YJMob100K mobile-phone data as a commuting-distance diagnostic. We demonstrate the infrastructure through three reproducible cases: a full-city weekday rollout, a weekday-weekend behavioral contrast, and a warning-response perturbation with auditable replanning traces. These cases support GenWorld as a reproducible platform for grounded and scalable LLM-agent studies, while calibrated forecasting for traffic, evacuation, or policy outcomes remains future work.

AI.tldr: GenWorld is an urban simulation platform that grounds LLM agents in real geospatial/census data and compiles LLM decision signals into offline lookup policies, enabling scalable, city-scale agent simulations without costly online LLM calls.
AI.motivation: LLM-agent simulations face a dual challenge: they must be grounded in realistic urban constraints (e.g., demographics, geography), but running LLMs online for every agent at city scale is computationally infeasible. Existing approaches fail to jointly address grounding and scalability.
AI.method: GenWorld combines (1) a building-level synthetic city grounded in census and geospatial data, (2) a structured agent-environment interface, and (3) offline compilation of LLM-derived decision signals into lookup policies. This decouples LLM reasoning (done once offline) from rollout execution, enabling massive-scale simulation. The reference instantiation models 196,608 synthetic residents in Higashihiroshima, Japan, validated against census tabulations and YJMob100K mobile-phone commuting data.
AI.result: GenWorld produces demographically consistent agent populations validated against census data. Three case studies are demonstrated: a full-city weekday rollout, a weekday-weekend behavioral contrast, and a warning-response perturbation with auditable replanning traces, all run reproducibly at city scale.
AI.conclusion: GenWorld establishes a reproducible, grounded, and scalable platform for LLM-agent urban simulation. Calibrated forecasting for traffic, evacuation, and policy outcomes is deferred to future work.

title: Developmental approach reveals the statistical learning of Neural Language Models: Transformers generalize from the most abstract statistical patterns
comment: 10 pages, 7 figures, oral presentation at Interdisciplinary Advances in Statistical Learning
summary: In this study, we use a developmental approach to investigate the statistical learning and mental representation of neural language models (NLM). A series of Generative Transformer models are trained on a synthetic grammar. The model states are saved at multiple stages in the course of training. Through analyzing how the internal representations of these models change in the developmental path, we found that NLMs acquire the most abstract global statistical knowledge at the beginning of learning and later acquire the relatively local statistical dependencies. This learning path contains many over-generalizations from the very beginning and these over-generalizations are gradually constrained in the later stage of learning. Based on this observation, we propose a new framework to explain the statistical learning and language cognition of NLMs.

AI.tldr: Neural language models learn abstract global statistics first, then local dependencies, with early overgeneralizations gradually constrained — revealing a developmental trajectory that informs a new framework for statistical learning in NLMs.
AI.motivation: To understand how statistical knowledge is acquired and mentally represented in neural language models (NLMs) by examining their internal representational changes over the course of training, analogous to a developmental approach in cognitive science.
AI.method: A series of Generative Transformer models were trained on a synthetic grammar, with model states saved at multiple stages during training. The internal representations were analyzed across these developmental checkpoints to trace how statistical knowledge emerges and evolves.
AI.result: NLMs first acquire the most abstract, global statistical knowledge at the beginning of learning, and only later acquire relatively local statistical dependencies. The learning trajectory exhibits substantial overgeneralizations early on, which are progressively constrained in later stages.
AI.conclusion: The observed developmental learning path — global-to-local with initial overgeneralization followed by constraint — motivates a new explanatory framework for statistical learning and language cognition in neural language models.

title: From Bootstrapping to Sequence Modeling: A Unified Generative Framework for Personalized Landing-Page Modeling
comment: arXiv admin note: text overlap with arXiv:2507.23459
summary: Modern online platforms increasingly adopt multi-page architectures to accommodate diverse user needs. On these platforms, page navigation (the process of directing users to specific functional pages upon app entry) serves as a critical gateway that shapes user's first impression and significantly influences subsequent engagement. To optimize this process, Kuaishou formulated the task of Personalized Landing Page Modeling (PLPM) and proposed KLAN, a reinforcement learning framework built upon Conservative Q-Learning (CQL). However, CQL-based approaches suffer from two fundamental limitations: (1) the Markov assumption fails to capture the strong non-Markovian temporal dependencies inherent in real-world user behaviors, and (2) TD learning with bootstrapping incurs severe cumulative errors and credit assignment difficulties under delayed rewards, particularly in long-horizon settings where users enter the app multiple times daily. To address these limitations, we propose GLAN (Generative Landing-page Adaptive Navigator), a sequence modeling framework built on Decision Transformer to tackle PLPM from a unified global-local perspective. Specifically, GLAN incorporates two key modules. First, we design the L-RTG module that captures users' inter-day consumption dynamics to provide accurate global guidance for all page assignments within a day. Furthermore, we propose the HRM module that decomposes session-level feedback into fine-grained signals, enabling precise local supervision for each page assignment. Extensive online experiments conducted on the Kuaishou platform demonstrate the effectiveness of GLAN, achieving +0.158\% and +0.108\% improvements on Daily Active Users (DAU) and user Lifetime (LT) respectively.

AI.tldr: Kuaishou proposes GLAN, a Decision Transformer-based framework for personalized landing page assignment that replaces CQL-based RL methods. It uses an L-RTG module for inter-day global guidance and an HRM module for session-level local supervision, achieving +0.158% DAU and +0.108% user lifetime improvements in online experiments.
AI.motivation: Existing CQL-based approaches (KLAN) for Personalized Landing Page Modeling suffer from two key issues: (1) the Markov assumption fails to model non-Markovian temporal dependencies in real user behavior, and (2) TD learning with bootstrapping causes cumulative errors and credit assignment difficulties under delayed, sparse rewards in long-horizon settings where users open the app multiple times daily.
AI.method: GLAN is a sequence modeling framework using Decision Transformer that addresses PLPM from a global-local perspective. It has two modules: (1) L-RTG (Local Return-To-Go) captures inter-day consumption dynamics to provide global guidance for daily page assignments, and (2) HRM (Hierarchical Reward Modeling) decomposes session-level feedback into fine-grained signals for precise local supervision per page assignment.
AI.result: Online A/B testing on Kuaishou showed GLAN achieved +0.158% improvement on Daily Active Users (DAU) and +0.108% improvement on user Lifetime (LT) compared to prior methods.
AI.conclusion: GLAN effectively addresses the limitations of CQL-based methods by leveraging sequence modeling (Decision Transformer) with hierarchical reward decomposition. The global-local design enables better handling of non-Markovian dependencies and long-horizon credit assignment, leading to measurable business metric gains on a large-scale industrial platform.

title: Exploring and Exploiting Synchrony Limitations of Time-Triggered Network-Agnostic Guardians
comment: Presented at the "29th International Symposium on Real-Time Distributed Computing" ISORC 2026
summary: Time-triggered communication protocols rely on trusted components known as guardians to enforce adherence to predetermined network schedules. Network-agnostic guardians offer an efficient and scalable distributed solution with reduced implementation cost and complexity compared to network-aware alternatives. However, this efficiency is based on the guardian's dependence on the controlled node for clock synchronization, which introduces a vulnerability: a malicious node can exploit this dependency to launch timing attacks against its guardian and eventually interfere with messages from other nodes on the network. In this paper, we establish a theoretical lower bound on the attainable clock synchronization precision between a node and its network-agnostic guardian. Building on this result, we introduce a timing attack that leverages the unavoidably imperfect clock synchrony to cause controlled and undetected de-synchronization of the guardian. The attack enables a malicious node to cause collisions with targeted critical network messages. We evaluate the effectiveness of the attack using a FlexRay field bus network model implemented in the OMNeT++ simulation framework. Our results show that the attack is able to remain undetected with 100% success and disrupts the transmission of the critical messages of the target node by causing collisions with them with 100% success.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies a vulnerability in network-agnostic guardians used in time-triggered protocols: a malicious node can exploit imperfect clock synchronization to stealthily de-synchronize its guardian and cause collisions with critical messages from other nodes, achieving 100% success in both evasion and disruption in FlexRay simulations.
AI.motivation: Network-agnostic guardians are preferred for their efficiency and scalability over network-aware guardians, but they depend on the controlled node for clock synchronization. This dependency creates a security vulnerability that has not been formally characterized, motivating the authors to investigate whether a malicious node can exploit imperfect synchrony to launch timing attacks.
AI.method: The authors first derive a theoretical lower bound on clock synchronization precision between a node and its network-agnostic guardian. They then design a timing attack that exploits this imperfect synchrony to cause controlled, undetected de-synchronization of the guardian. The attack is evaluated using a FlexRay field bus network model implemented in the OMNeT++ simulation framework.
AI.result: The proposed timing attack achieves 100% success in remaining undetected and 100% success in disrupting critical message transmissions of the target node by causing collisions.
AI.conclusion: Network-agnostic guardians, despite their practical advantages, are fundamentally vulnerable to timing attacks due to the unavoidable imprecision in clock synchronization. This challenges the security assumptions underlying their design and highlights the need for more robust guardian architectures in time-triggered communication systems.

title: Learning in Markovian bandits with non-observable states and constrained decision epochs
summary: This paper studies the problem of regret minimization in Markovian bandits with \emph{non-observable states} and possibly \emph{constrained} decision epochs. The focus is restricted to a ``pure'' regret benchmark, that compares the performance of the learning algorithm to the best \emph{pure policy} which -- akin to optimal policies of stochastic bandits -- picks the optimal arm from start to finish without ever switching. We introduce a generalization of rested Markovian bandits, \emph{self-degrading Markovian bandits}, for which pure policies are always asymptotically optimal.We show that without prior knowledge on the underlying bandit, the regret of algorithms that switch arms rarely necessarily scales super-logarithmically for every bandit, i.e., as $ω(\log(T))$, where $T$ is the learning horizon. Despite the unreachability of the logarithmic regime, we design UCB-NOM, an optimistic algorithm inspired by UCB, of which the regret is nearly logarithmic. Lastly, we show that given prior knowledge on the Markovian bandit in the form of a bound on the bias functions of its arm, a proper instantiation of UCB-NOM achieves $O(\log(T))$ regret. We further show that this prior knowledge allows for a $O(\sqrt{T \log(T)})$ worst-case regret bound for UCB-NOM. Notably, our regret bounds do not depend on the number of states of the underlying Markov chains. Our findings suggest that the non-observability of states is a mild inconvenience in self-degrading Markovian bandits.

AI.tldr: This paper studies regret minimization in Markovian bandits with hidden states and constrained decision epochs, introducing "self-degrading Markovian bandits" where pure (switch-free) policies are asymptotically optimal. Without prior knowledge, regret must be ω(log T); with a bound on arm bias functions, UCB-NOM achieves O(log T) regret and O(√(T log T)) worst-case regret, with bounds independent of the number of states.
AI.motivation: The paper is motivated by bandit problems where the underlying system has non-observable Markovian states that evolve over time, and where decision-making is constrained (e.g., limited opportunities to switch arms). In such settings, the authors aim to understand whether low-regret learning is possible relative to the best "pure policy" that never switches arms — a natural benchmark when switching is costly or infeasible.
AI.method: The authors first define self-degrading Markovian bandits, a subclass of rested Markovian bandits where each arm's state evolves only when pulled and degrades (or improves) monotonically in a way that makes pure policies asymptotically optimal. They prove a lower bound showing that without prior knowledge, any algorithm that rarely switches arms incurs ω(log T) regret. They then propose UCB-NOM (UCB for Non-Observable Markovian bandits), an optimistic algorithm that estimates arm performance without observing the latent state. When given prior knowledge in the form of a bound on the bias functions of each arm, UCB-NOM is instantiated to achieve near-logarithmic regret.
AI.result: Key results include: (1) a super-logarithmic lower bound (ω(log T)) on regret for any algorithm without prior knowledge; (2) UCB-NOM achieves nearly logarithmic regret in the agnostic case; (3) with a known bound on bias functions, UCB-NOM attains O(log T) regret; (4) a O(√(T log T)) worst-case regret bound also holds with this prior knowledge. Notably, all bounds are independent of the number of underlying Markov states.
AI.conclusion: The non-observability of states in self-degrading Markovian bandits is only a "mild inconvenience": while the logarithmic regret regime is unreachable without prior knowledge, providing a bound on arm bias functions suffices to recover O(log T) regret via UCB-NOM. This suggests that state observability is not critical for efficient learning in this bandit subclass.

title: LLM-Assisted Model-Based GUI Testing for Vue.js Web Applications
summary: Vue.js is a popular framework for building modern web applications. As Vue.js functionality and tooling support grow, ensuring its reliability (through automated testing) is becoming increasingly important. Although model-based testing has been successfully used to automate graphical user interface (GUI) testing on other platforms, its application to Vue.js remains challenging: Transition candidates, which are spread across router configurations and single-file components (SFCs), must be concretized and normalized into an executable page transition graph (PTG) for testing. To address this, we propose the LLMVue framework, which uses a large language model (LLM) to generate a PTG from Vue.js source code. LLMVue infers component hierarchies and route transitions, merging them into a unified PTG across multiple SFCs. We evaluated LLMVue on a collection of ten open-source Vue.js projects from GitHub, using GPT-4o as the LLM backbone. The constructed graphs demonstrate high precision and recall, with low graph edit distance. LLMVue -guided testing also significantly improves the coverage and exploration efficiency, compared to a random exploration baseline (with the same time constraints). To the best of our knowledge, this is the first use of LLMs for model-based GUI testing of Vue.js applications using source-level PTG extraction.

AI.tldr: LLMVue leverages GPT-4o to automatically extract page transition graphs (PTGs) from Vue.js source code, unifying router configurations and single-file components for model-based GUI testing. Evaluated on ten open-source projects, it achieves high precision/recall and significantly outperforms random exploration in coverage and efficiency.
AI.motivation: Vue.js lacks robust model-based GUI testing approaches because transition candidates are scattered across router configurations and single-file components (SFCs), making it difficult to concretize and normalize them into an executable page transition graph. Existing model-based testing techniques from other GUI platforms do not directly address this fragmentation.
AI.method: LLMVue uses GPT-4o to infer component hierarchies and route transitions from Vue.js source code, merging them into a unified page transition graph (PTG) spanning multiple SFCs. This PTG then guides model-based automated testing of the application.
AI.result: On ten open-source Vue.js GitHub projects, LLMVue-constructed PTGs showed high precision and recall with low graph edit distance. LLMVue-guided testing significantly improved coverage and exploration efficiency over random exploration under identical time constraints.
AI.conclusion: This work represents the first application of LLMs for model-based GUI testing of Vue.js via source-level PTG extraction, demonstrating that LLMs can effectively bridge the gap between scattered transition information and executable test models.

title: GBC: Gradient-Based Connections for Optimizing Multi-Agent Systems
comment: 15 pages, 8 figures, accepted by SIGDIAL 2026 Long Papers
summary: Multi-agent systems (MAS) built on large language models (LLMs) provide a promising framework for solving complex tasks through role specialization and structured interaction. However, their performance is often limited by miscoordination and, more fundamentally, the lack of fine-grained credit assignment across agents. Existing approaches typically rely on coarse-grained feedback, making it difficult to identify which agents or interaction steps are responsible for errors. We propose Gradient-Based Connections (GBC), an approach for fine-grained attribution and optimization of multi-agent systems. GBC models a MAS as a computational graph and introduces gradient-based connection weights to quantify the influence of each agent's output on downstream agents at the token level. By constructing an attribution graph and propagating task-specific loss signals backward, our method enables precise identification of error sources and targeted prompt optimization. We further develop AgentChord, an efficient implementation that leverages prefix-based gradient computation. Experiments on MultiWOZ and τ-bench show that GBC improves multi-agent performance and outperforms strong single-agent and multi-agent baselines, and higher attribution quality is associated with greater optimization effectiveness. Code is available at: https://github.com/yxc-cyber/AgentChord.

AI.tldr: GBC introduces token-level gradient-based attribution for multi-agent LLM systems, modeling them as computational graphs to pinpoint error sources and enable targeted prompt optimization, outperforming baselines on MultiWOZ and τ-bench.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent LLM systems suffer from miscoordination and lack fine-grained credit assignment; coarse feedback cannot identify which agents or interaction steps cause errors, limiting optimization.
AI.method: GBC models the MAS as a computational graph with gradient-based connection weights quantifying token-level influence between agents. It constructs an attribution graph, backpropagates task-specific loss signals, and identifies error sources for targeted prompt optimization. AgentChord implements this efficiently via prefix-based gradient computation.
AI.result: GBC improves multi-agent performance on MultiWOZ and τ-bench, outperforming both single-agent and multi-agent baselines. Higher attribution quality correlates with greater optimization effectiveness.
AI.conclusion: Fine-grained gradient-based attribution enables precise error identification and targeted optimization in MAS, significantly improving task performance over existing coarse-grained feedback methods.

title: Supersede: Diagnosing and Training the Memory-Update Gap in LLM Agents
comment: 11 pages, 4 figures, 3 tables. Code, environment, model, and dataset: https://github.com/Vrin-cloud/supersede
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents operate over long, multi-session interactions in which facts change: a user moves, a price updates, a plan is revised. Acting correctly requires using the current value of a fact and discarding values that have been superseded. We isolate this ability on real conversational data and show that it is a distinct, unsolved failure. On the knowledge-update subset of LongMemEval, replacing an agent's full context with a bounded, self-maintained memory drops accuracy from 92% to 77% even on a frontier model (gpt-5.4), a gap that is statistically significant (paired McNemar p<0.005) and persists across model scale while full-context accuracy saturates near 92%. The bottleneck is therefore memory maintenance, not comprehension, and is not closed by a stronger model. We then ask whether this is merely an undersized memory, and find it is not: as the conversation grows 24x, accuracy falls further (from 68% to 28%), and granting the agent proportionally more memory yields no detectable recovery (28% to 28%, n=25). The failure scales with the length of the conversation, not the compression ratio. We release Supersede, an open reinforcement-learning environment (on the verifiers / prime-rl stack) that turns this measurement into a training signal: agents are rewarded for answering from the current value and penalized for stale ones. Finally, we close the loop and show the gap is trainable: GRPO fine-tuning a small open model (Qwen2.5-3B) on this environment nearly doubles its held-out supersession accuracy on real, unseen conversations (9.0% to 16.7%, a single run), along a monotonic checkpoint curve indicating the learned policy, not the harness, carries the gain. To our knowledge this is the first trainable environment whose reward targets temporal fact-currency, and the first evidence the supersession gap can be trained down, not only measured.

AI.tldr: LLM agents fail at maintaining fact-currency over long conversations where facts change; this "supersession" gap stems from memory maintenance, not comprehension, cannot be fixed by scaling models or memory, but is trainable via a new RL environment (Supersede).
AI.motivation: LLM agents in long, multi-session interactions must track changing facts (e.g., updated prices, revised plans) and use only current values, discarding stale ones. Prior work has not isolated this failure mode on real conversational data nor shown it to be trainable.
AI.method: Authors isolate the "supersession" ability using the knowledge-update subset of LongMemEval. They test frontier models (GPT-5.4) comparing full-context vs. bounded self-maintained memory, vary conversation length 24x, and vary memory size proportionally. They release Supersede, an open RL environment (verifiers/prime-rl stack) rewarding current-value answers and penalizing stale ones, then fine-tune Qwen2.5-3B with GRPO and evaluate on held-out real conversations.
AI.result: Replacing full context with bounded memory drops accuracy from 92% to 77% (p<0.005), persistent across model scales. Scaling conversation 24x drops accuracy from 68% to 28%; proportional memory increase yields no recovery (28%→28%). GRPO fine-tuning on Supersede nearly doubles held-out supersession accuracy (9.0%→16.7%) with a monotonic checkpoint curve.
AI.conclusion: The supersession gap is a memory-maintenance bottleneck — not a comprehension problem solvable by stronger models or larger memory — but it is trainable. Supersede is the first RL environment targeting temporal fact-currency, providing the first evidence that the gap can be reduced via training.

title: An LLM-Powered Semantic Alignment Framework for Journal Recommendation
summary: Journal recommendation is an important task in scholarly information systems. Existing approaches typically rely on supervised learning models, manually engineered features, or historical interaction data, which may limit their generalizability and interpretability. We propose an LLM-powered semantic alignment framework that formulates journal recommendation as a semantic matching problem between manuscript content and journal scope descriptions. The framework enables large language models (LLMs) to infer journal suitability directly from article titles, abstracts, keywords, and candidate journal information without task-specific training. Experiments are conducted using DeepSeek-V3 on a dataset of 23,609 articles from 49 journals in statistics and related fields. The proposed framework achieves Top-3, Top-5, and Top-10 accuracies of 40.23\%, 53.67\%, and 70.05\%, respectively. Additional analyses show that incorporating reference information generally improves recommendation performance and that recommendations remain highly stable across repeated runs, with an average Top-5 Jaccard similarity of 84\%. The framework also generates interpretable reasoning outputs that provide insights into the recommendation process. These findings demonstrate the potential of LLMs as a training-free and scalable paradigm for journal recommendation and scholarly decision support.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a training-free, LLM-powered framework for journal recommendation that matches manuscript content (title, abstract, keywords) to journal scope descriptions using semantic alignment. Tested with DeepSeek-V3 on 23,609 articles across 49 statistics journals, it achieves Top-3/5/10 accuracies of 40.23%, 53.67%, and 70.05%, with high stability (84% Jaccard similarity) and interpretable reasoning outputs.
AI.motivation: Existing journal recommendation methods depend on supervised learning, handcrafted features, or historical interaction data, which suffer from limited generalizability across domains and poor interpretability. The authors aim to leverage the semantic understanding capabilities of LLMs to bypass these limitations with a zero-shot, training-free paradigm.
AI.method: A semantic alignment framework where LLMs (specifically DeepSeek-V3) are prompted with a manuscript's title, abstract, and keywords alongside candidate journal scope descriptions. The model infers suitability rankings without any task-specific fine-tuning. Experiments also incorporate reference information as an auxiliary signal and evaluate output stability via repeated-run Jaccard similarity.
AI.result: The framework achieves Top-3 accuracy of 40.23%, Top-5 of 53.67%, and Top-10 of 70.05% on 23,609 articles from 49 statistics journals. Incorporating references improves performance. Repeated runs yield an average Top-5 Jaccard similarity of 84%, indicating high stability. The LLM also produces interpretable natural-language rationales for each recommendation.
AI.conclusion: LLMs offer a viable, scalable, and interpretable alternative to traditional journal recommendation systems, requiring no task-specific training. The semantic alignment approach generalizes across journals and provides transparent decision support for authors.

title: Self-Verifying Measurement Records: Hash-Linked Evidence Graphs for Hardware Benchmarking
comment: 17 pages, 3 figures, 7 tables. Ancillary files (anc/) contain the full source code, the raw observations, the hash-linked evidence graph, and a SHA-256 manifest; the record audits offline with a standard-library script
summary: Performance numbers reported for hardware are accepted on trust: the reader cannot recompute them, the apparatus is gone, and the silicon itself can be silently wrong, with fleet studies reporting on the order of one core in a thousand returning incorrect arithmetic with no error raised. We make a reported hardware measurement a tamper-evident, independently checkable record. Every quantity in the text, a table, or a figure is bound, by its content hash, to the observation and the verification behind it; the whole is a hash-linked, append-only structure (a transparency log for measurement) that a verifier audits offline without trusting its producer. Matrix products are verified by a probabilistic identity (Freivalds) at O(k n^2) cost under a tolerance we derive from floating-point error analysis and calibrate to the device's own measured residual floor, so a wrong product is rejected with probability 1 - 2^(-k); quantities with no such identity carry an algebraic checksum and a measured reproducibility class.
