We then treat the check itself as a security object: a probe seed committed for offline reproducibility is an attack surface, and a probe-aware adversary can hide a corruption in the probe's null space, fooling even a quorum of bit-identical witnesses, while a Fiat-Shamir challenge derived from the claimed output closes this. Driving the device from an unprivileged tenant's reach, with a di/dt power virus and a thermal soak, neither moves the calibrated tolerance nor produces a silent error, placing the physical-fault threat at the rare defective part or the privileged attacker and marking the boundary at which the record must compose with a hardware root of trust. We demonstrate the construction across Blackwell and Hopper GPUs and report a residual-floor and reproducibility map by precision, size, and device.

AI.tldr: A system for making reported hardware benchmark results tamper-evident and independently verifiable by binding every quantity to a hash-linked transparency log, using probabilistic verification (Freivalds) for matrix products and Fiat-Shamir challenges to defeat probe-aware adversaries, demonstrated on Blackwell and Hopper GPUs.
AI.motivation: Hardware performance results are trusted on faith — readers cannot recompute them, the hardware is inaccessible, and silicon can silently produce incorrect arithmetic (~1 in 1000 cores) without raising errors. This creates a trust crisis where reported measurements are unverifiable and potentially fraudulent or corrupted.
AI.method: The paper constructs a tamper-evident measurement record where (1) every quantity is content-hash-bound to its observation and verification, (2) the whole forms a hash-linked append-only transparency log auditable offline without trusting the producer, (3) matrix products use Freivalds probabilistic verification at O(k n²) cost with a tolerance derived from floating-point error analysis, calibrated to the device's measured residual floor, achieving rejection probability 1-2^(-k), (4) non-matrix quantities carry algebraic checksums and reproducibility classes, and (5) Fiat-Shamir challenges derived from claimed outputs replace committed probe seeds to close the null-space attack surface where a probe-aware adversary could hide corruption. Stress testing via di/dt power viruses and thermal soaking is used to characterize the fault boundary.
AI.result: The construction was demonstrated on Blackwell and Hopper GPUs. Results include a residual-floor and reproducibility map across precision, matrix size, and device. Di/dt power viruses and thermal soaking did not shift the calibrated tolerance nor produce silent errors, indicating the physical-fault threat is limited to rare defective parts or privileged attackers.
AI.conclusion: Hardware measurement integrity can be achieved through a transparency log architecture with probabilistic verification, turning reported results into independently checkable records. The system bounds the silent-error threat to defective hardware or privileged attackers, at which point composition with a hardware root of trust becomes necessary.

title: Prism Transformer: Progressive Head Schedules for Hierarchical Attention Processing
summary: Multi-head attention conventionally partitions the hidden dimension equally across all heads at every layer, enforcing an identical representational subspace dimension (dh = dmodel/h) throughout the models depth. In this work, we identify this uniform allocation as a fundamental structural bottleneck: due to their restricted dimensional space, early-layer heads are unable to faithfully capture complex, high-dimensional contextual patterns. To resolve this, we introduce the Prism Transformer, a novel architectural paradigm that replaces the static, uniform head configuration with a progressive head schedule. By monotonically increasing the head count across layers, the Prism Transformer naturally establishes a local-to-global representational hierarchy: early layers leverage fewer, exceptionally wide heads to capture complex, local compositional patterns, while deep layers deploy many, narrow heads to decompose these patterns into specialized linguistic features. Crucially, this structural shift is parameter-neutral, compute-neutral, and introduces zero training or inference overhead, preserving identical weight matrices and FLOP budgets as the standard Transformer. Across three model scales (124M, 354M, and 757M), the Prism Transformer consistently outperforms uniform baselines, achieving consistent reductions in validation loss alongside consistent gains on downstream zero-shot benchmarks (including PIQA, HellaSwag, ARC-Easy, and WinoGrande). Our findings demonstrate that non-uniform subspace allocation unlocks latent capacity within the standard Transformer budget, enabling more effective use of model capacity.

AI.tldr: The Prism Transformer replaces the standard uniform multi-head attention subspace allocation with a progressive schedule — fewer wide heads in early layers, many narrow heads in deep layers — achieving consistent gains over uniform baselines at zero parameter/compute overhead.
AI.motivation: Standard Transformers allocate equal hidden dimension per head (d_h = d_model/h) across all layers. The authors identify this as a bottleneck: early-layer heads, restricted to narrow subspaces, cannot adequately capture complex high-dimensional contextual patterns. A non-uniform allocation is hypothesized to better match the representational demands at different depths.
AI.method: The Prism Transformer monotonically increases head count across layers, creating a local-to-global hierarchy: early layers use few wide heads (large d_h) to capture complex local compositions; deep layers use many narrow heads (small d_h) to decompose these into specialized linguistic features. This is achieved via a progressive head schedule that is parameter-neutral, compute-neutral, and requires no additional training or inference overhead — weight matrices and FLOPs remain identical to the standard Transformer.
AI.result: Across three model scales (124M, 354M, 757M), the Prism Transformer consistently outperforms uniform baselines on validation loss and downstream zero-shot benchmarks including PIQA, HellaSwag, ARC-Easy, and WinoGrande.
AI.conclusion: Non-uniform subspace allocation unlocks latent capacity within the standard Transformer budget, enabling more effective use of model capacity without increasing parameters or compute.

title: MER-R1: Multimodal Emotion Reasoning via Slow-Fast Thinking Synergy
summary: We find that explicit reasoning does not necessarily translate into better multimodal emotion recognition (MER) accuracy, even though it makes predictions more interpretable. Specifically, for reasoning-based MLLMs, fast thinking by triggering direct answers often outperforms slow thinking after deliberative reasoning. Our empirical analyses show that fast thinking improves recall with broader and more confident predictions, whereas slow thinking favors precision through conservative filtering of incorrect categories. Building on these insights, we propose MER-R1, a reinforcement learning framework that turns slow-fast complementarity into explicit optimization. Dual-objective disentanglement separates recall and precision into two optimization signals, allowing them to be jointly optimized rather than traded off against each other. Slow-fast confidence calibration further aligns the final slow-thinking answer with fast-thinking intuition, strengthening correct emotions while suppressing incorrect ones. In this way, MER-R1 unifies the recall-oriented intuition of fast thinking with the precision-oriented selectivity of slow thinking. We further provide theoretical justification for this synergy, showing that it mitigates variance-induced interference during optimization. Extensive experiments on MER-UniBench and MME-Emotion show that MER-R1 achieves state-of-the-art performance and makes reasoning genuinely benefit emotion recognition.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates the disconnect between explicit reasoning and multimodal emotion recognition (MER) accuracy, finding that "fast thinking" (direct answers) often outperforms "slow thinking" (deliberative reasoning) despite the latter being more interpretable. The authors propose MER-R1, a reinforcement learning framework that jointly optimizes recall and precision via dual-objective disentanglement and slow-fast confidence calibration, achieving state-of-the-art results on MER-UniBench and MME-Emotion.
AI.motivation: Explicit reasoning in MLLMs improves interpretability for MER but does not reliably improve accuracy — fast thinking (direct answering) often beats slow thinking (reasoning-based). The authors aim to understand this phenomenon and leverage the complementarity between fast (recall-oriented, broad/confident) and slow (precision-oriented, conservative) thinking to make reasoning genuinely beneficial.
AI.method: MER-R1, a reinforcement learning framework with two key components: (1) **Dual-objective disentanglement** — separates recall and precision into distinct optimization signals for joint optimization rather than trade-off; (2) **Slow-fast confidence calibration** — aligns slow-thinking outputs with fast-thinking intuition to reinforce correct emotions and suppress incorrect ones. Theoretical justification shows this synergy mitigates variance-induced interference during optimization.
AI.result: MER-R1 achieves state-of-the-art performance on two benchmarks: MER-UniBench and MME-Emotion, demonstrating that reasoning can be made to genuinely benefit emotion recognition.
AI.conclusion: Fast and slow thinking exhibit complementary strengths (recall vs. precision) that can be unified through explicit optimization. By disentangling objectives and calibrating confidence across thinking modes, MER-R1 enables reasoning-based MLLMs to achieve superior MER performance, reconciling the accuracy-interpretability tension.

title: BashCoder-R1: Towards Robust and Explainable Bash Code Generation with Robustness-Aware Group Relative Policy Optimization
summary: Bash scripts are the cornerstone of system administration and DevOps automation, where code quality directly impacts system stability and security. In automated Bash script generation using Large Language Models (LLMs), two interconnected failures emerge: unauditable "black box" reasoning and critical robustness vulnerabilities in generated code. To address both, we propose BashCoder-R1, a novel framework for robust and explainable Bash script generation. Our pipeline combines: (1) Continual Pre-training (CPT) to specialize the model on Bash paradigms; (2) Long Chain-of-Thought Supervised Fine-Tuning (L-CoT SFT) on expert-validated reasoning-and-code samples to emulate proactive risk-aware thinking; and (3) Robustness-Aware Group Relative Policy Optimization (R-GRPO), a reinforcement learning phase optimizing a weighted reward for syntax correctness, robustness (via shellcheck), and format correctness. We evaluate on BashBench, a new benchmark of 952 real-world tasks (773 single-line, 179 multi-line). BashCoder-R1 achieves SyntaxPass (100.00%/94.97%), RobustWarnRate (4.01%/16.47%), RobustPass (95.99%/79.33%), FuncRate (93.01%/93.85%), and FullRate (90.04%/73.18%) for single-line/multi-line tasks, outperforming the strongest baseline DeepSeek-V3.2 (Reasoning) by 37.82% and 20.18% in FullRate. Human evaluation on Functionality, Robustness, and Clarity further confirms BashCoder-R1 achieves the highest quality ratings.

AI.tldr: BashCoder-R1 introduces a three-stage training pipeline (CPT, L-CoT SFT, R-GRPO) that produces robust, explainable Bash scripts from LLMs, achieving state-of-the-art results on the new BashBench benchmark and significantly outperforming DeepSeek-V3.2.
AI.motivation: Automated Bash script generation via LLMs suffers from two critical issues: (1) "black box" reasoning that is unauditable, and (2) robustness vulnerabilities in the generated code that threaten system stability and security. Existing approaches fail to address both simultaneously.
AI.method: A three-phase framework: (1) Continual Pre-training (CPT) to specialize the model on Bash paradigms; (2) Long Chain-of-Thought Supervised Fine-Tuning (L-CoT SFT) on expert-validated reasoning-and-code samples to instill proactive risk-aware thinking; (3) Robustness-Aware Group Relative Policy Optimization (R-GRPO), an RL phase using a weighted reward combining syntax correctness, robustness (via shellcheck), and format correctness. Evaluation uses BashBench, a new benchmark of 952 real-world tasks.
AI.result: BashCoder-R1 achieves single-line/multi-line scores of: SyntaxPass (100.00%/94.97%), RobustWarnRate (4.01%/16.47%), RobustPass (95.99%/79.33%), FuncRate (93.01%/93.85%), and FullRate (90.04%/73.18%). It outperforms DeepSeek-V3.2 (Reasoning) by 37.82% (single-line) and 20.18% (multi-line) in FullRate. Human evaluation confirms superior Functionality, Robustness, and Clarity.
AI.conclusion: BashCoder-R1 effectively addresses both the explainability and robustness gaps in LLM-based Bash generation through its specialized three-stage pipeline, demonstrating that explicit reasoning combined with robustness-aware RL training yields substantial improvements over general-purpose reasoning models.

title: Triadic Werewolf: A Jester Role for Multi-Hop Theory of Mind in LLMs
summary: Theory-of-mind evaluations of large language models typically use dyadic social-deduction games, where every observable cue points to a single hidden side, so a model with strong language priors can score well without ever simulating opponents' incentives. We extend the Werewolf game with a Jester, a third faction whose utility on peer suspicion is inverted because it wins by being voted out, so optimal play requires reasoning across three opposing utility functions. Across 60 games on GPT-4.1, DeepSeek-V3.1, and Llama-3.3-70B with Jester self-learning on and off, the Jester wins 60-70% of games while Werewolves never exceed 20%, and GPT-4.1 wolves vote the Jester out on day 1 in 60-70% of games, a strictly self-defeating action. Self-learning helps DeepSeek and Llama but hurts GPT-4.1, with the cost landing on Villagers rather than Werewolves. Only DeepSeek learns the subtle strategy of looking suspicious without looking intentionally suspicious, and it gains the most from the loop. Triadic incentive structure exposes a layer of multi-agent reasoning that dyadic deduction games leave invisible.

AI.tldr: Introducing a third faction (Jester) with inverted win conditions into the Werewolf game exposes fundamental failures in LLMs' multi-agent reasoning. While dyadic social-deduction games allow models to succeed via language priors alone, the triadic incentive structure reveals that LLMs struggle to simulate opponents' utility functions, with GPT-4.1 exhibiting strictly self-defeating behavior and only DeepSeek learning genuinely subtle deceptive strategies through self-play.
AI.motivation: Existing theory-of-mind benchmarks for LLMs rely on dyadic social-deduction games where all observable evidence points to a single hidden state, enabling models to exploit surface-level language correlations rather than genuinely modeling opponents' beliefs and incentives. The authors aim to demonstrate this limitation and propose a triadic game structure that forces models to reason across multiple, opposing utility functions simultaneously.
AI.method: The authors modify the Werewolf game by adding a Jester role whose utility is inverted: the Jester wins by being voted out rather than surviving. This creates a triadic incentive structure (Villagers, Werewolves, Jester) where each faction has a distinct, opposing utility function. Three LLMs — GPT-4.1, DeepSeek-V3.1, and Llama-3.3-70B — play 60 games under two conditions: with and without Jester self-learning (agents retain memory across games). Performance is measured by win rates and strategic behavior analysis.
AI.result: The Jester dominates across all models, achieving 60–70% win rates, while Werewolves never exceed 20%. GPT-4.1 Werewolves exhibit a catastrophic failure: they vote out the Jester on day 1 in 60–70% of games — an action that directly benefits the Jester's win condition and harms the Werewolves' own objectives. Self-learning improves DeepSeek and Llama performance but degrades GPT-4.1's, with the cost borne by Villagers rather than Werewolves. Only DeepSeek successfully learns the nuanced strategy of appearing suspicious without appearing intentionally suspicious, and it derives the greatest benefit from the self-learning loop.
AI.conclusion: Triadic incentive structures reveal a critical layer of multi-agent reasoning that dyadic deduction games fail to test. Current LLMs, particularly GPT-4.1, show severe deficits in simultaneously modeling multiple opposing utility functions, leading to self-defeating strategic choices. Self-learning helps some models but can also amplify failures, suggesting that genuine multi-agent theory-of-mind remains an open challenge for language models.

title: The Context-Ready Transformer
summary: We introduce the context-ready transformer, a new recurrent neural network architecture built from a D-layer transformer block that pre-contextualizes each token before it enters the block. During left-to-right generation, a correction network combines the previous position's block output -- a cached summary of past context -- with the current token embedding, so the tokenenters the block already contextualized rather than as a raw embedding. At sequential inference, the correction chain makes the architecture a recurrent neural network. For training, we unroll the correction process K times over the full sequence, processing all positions in parallel at each step. A pretrained transformer can also be converted to a context-ready model by adding a zero-initialized correction FFN and fine-tuning. We evaluate across widths, depths, block sizes, and two datasets, with all comparisons against standard transformers, variants, and ablations. A D=5 model beats a 12-layer transformer while generating 1.7x faster on an A100. With K=10, a single-layermodel (D=1) beats a 6-layer transformer with a 2.6x inference speedup, and sequential inference matches parallel K=10 to within 0.01 PPL. The architecture benefits most from wide representations and long contexts. On a pointer-chasing task, D=1 trained with BPTT solves all 10 composition levels, while standard transformers exhibit staircase-like depth dependence.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the context-ready transformer, a recurrent architecture where each token is pre-contextualized via a correction network before entering a D-layer transformer block. During inference, it operates as an RNN with cached context; during training, the correction process is unrolled K times over the sequence. A D=5 model outperforms a 12-layer transformer with 1.7x faster generation; a D=1 model with K=10 beats a 6-layer transformer with 2.6x speedup. The approach excels with wide representations and long contexts, and solves all 10 levels of a pointer-chasing task where standard transformers show staircase depth dependence.
AI.motivation: Standard transformers suffer from a compute-quality tradeoff: deeper models achieve better perplexity but are slower at sequential inference. The authors aim to decouple representational capacity from inference cost by enabling a shallow (or single-layer) transformer block to match or exceed the performance of much deeper standard transformers via recurrent pre-contextualization, yielding faster generation without sacrificing quality.
AI.method: The context-ready transformer consists of a D-layer transformer block preceded by a correction network. At each generation step, the correction network fuses the previous position's block output (a cached summary of past context) with the current token embedding, so the token enters the block already contextualized. This creates a recurrent computational chain (correction → block → correction → ...). During training, the correction process is unrolled K times across the full sequence, processing all positions in parallel at each unroll step. A pretrained standard transformer can be converted by adding a zero-initialized correction FFN and fine-tuning. The architecture is evaluated across varying widths, depths, block sizes D, and unroll steps K, with ablations against standard transformers and variants.
AI.result: A D=5 context-ready model surpasses a 12-layer standard transformer while generating 1.7× faster on an A100 GPU. With K=10 unroll steps, a single-layer (D=1) model outperforms a 6-layer transformer with 2.6× inference speedup. Sequential (autoregressive) inference matches parallel K=10 training to within 0.01 perplexity, validating the recurrent formulation. Wider representations and longer contexts yield the largest gains. On a pointer-chasing benchmark, a D=1 model trained with BPTT solves all 10 composition levels, whereas standard transformers exhibit staircase-like depth dependence (requiring deeper models to handle more composition levels).
AI.conclusion: The context-ready transformer successfully decouples representation quality from inference cost by shifting contextualization into a recurrent correction mechanism. This allows shallow blocks to match or exceed deep standard transformers while being significantly faster at sequential generation. The architecture is particularly effective for wide models, long-range dependencies, and compositional reasoning tasks, suggesting a promising direction for efficient and powerful sequence modeling.

title: Listwise Explanation of Embedding-Based Rankings via Semantic Chunk Grouping
summary: Dense embedding rankers score documents through contextual sentence- and passage-level representations. Yet many listwise explanation methods still attribute rankings to isolated words. This feature-unit mismatch leaves word-level features too fragmented for dense semantic ranking. We introduce ChunkGroupSHAP, a listwise Shapley method that clusters semantically related chunks into shared cross-document features. Masking a group perturbs all documents with related evidence, attributing rankings at a granularity closer to dense representations while preserving the listwise setup. Our findings across MS MARCO, FinanceBench, AILACaseDocs, and FinQA with E5 rankers and BM25 show that the best explanation unit is setting-dependent: word features for lexical BM25, corpus-level groups for dense rankers, and query-local grouping for heterogeneous web retrieval. Feature units should thus follow both the ranker's representational granularity and the structure of the retrieved corpus.

AI.tldr: ChunkGroupSHAP introduces a listwise explanation method that clusters semantically related text chunks into shared cross-document features, aligning explanation granularity with dense ranker representations. The optimal feature unit depends on both the ranker type and corpus structure.
AI.motivation: Existing listwise explanation methods attribute rankings to isolated words, creating a feature-unit mismatch with dense embedding rankers that operate on contextual sentence- and passage-level representations. This fragmentation obscures how dense rankers actually make decisions.
AI.method: ChunkGroupSHAP extends Shapley-based listwise explanation by clustering semantically related chunks into shared cross-document feature groups. Masking a group perturbs all documents containing related evidence, enabling attribution at a granularity matching dense representations while maintaining the listwise ranking setup.
AI.result: Experiments across MS MARCO, FinanceBench, AILACaseDocs, and FinQA using E5 dense rankers and BM25 reveal that the optimal explanation unit is setting-dependent: word-level features suit lexical BM25, corpus-level groups suit dense rankers, and query-local grouping works best for heterogeneous web retrieval.
AI.conclusion: Feature units for ranking explanations should align with both the ranker's representational granularity and the structure of the retrieved corpus. There is no universally optimal explanation unit; the choice must be conditioned on the ranker architecture and retrieval context.

title: Agentic AI-Powered Re-Identification: An Emerging, Scalable Threat to Mobility Microdata Privacy
summary:
The widespread collection of fine-grained location data by commercial data brokers creates a re-identification risk that is not widely recognised by the public. While prior research has established that mobility traces are highly unique and that individuals can, in principle, be identified from a handful of spatio-temporal points, such attacks have historically required significant manual effort from skilled analysts, limiting their practical scale.
  In this feasibility study, we demonstrate in a real world setting that agentic AI fundamentally changes this threat model. We present an end-to-end pipeline in which large language model agents autonomously search the open web, cross-reference public records and social media, and resolve raw coordinate sequences to candidate identities - without human intervention. We evaluate the pipeline on a spatio-temporal dataset containing simulated location points anchored at and around true home and work addresses, focusing on a high-risk disclosure scenario. Our results demonstrate that, from spatio-temporal data and public sources alone, our agentic AI successfully re-identified 18 of the 25 re-identifiable individuals (72%) and 18 of 43 cases overall (41.9%).
  We discuss implications for Statistical Disclosure Control (SDC) practice and outline the near-future escalation that data custodians and regulators must anticipate. De facto anonymity - an implicit foundation of SDC practice - is shifting. Agentic AI strengthens the case that re-identification is reasonably likely by any means under the GDPR Recital-26 standard, at costs of minutes-and-dollars per target.

AI.tldr: Agentic AI (LLM agents) can autonomously re-identify individuals from raw location data by cross-referencing public web sources, achieving 72% success on re-identifiable targets, fundamentally altering the threat model for statistical disclosure control.
AI.motivation: Commercial data brokers collect fine-grained location data at scale, creating a re-identification risk the public underestimates. Prior attacks required skilled manual effort, limiting practical scale. The authors investigate whether agentic AI fundamentally changes this threat model by enabling fully automated, low-cost re-identification.
AI.method: An end-to-end pipeline where LLM agents autonomously: (1) search the open web, (2) cross-reference public records and social media, and (3) resolve raw GPS coordinate sequences to candidate identities — all without human intervention. Evaluated on a spatio-temporal dataset with simulated location points anchored at true home/work addresses, focusing on a high-risk disclosure scenario (25 re-identifiable individuals among 43 total cases).
AI.result: The agentic AI successfully re-identified 18 of 25 re-identifiable individuals (72%) and 18 of 43 cases overall (41.9%), using only spatio-temporal data and public sources, at a cost of minutes and dollars per target.
AI.conclusion: De facto anonymity — the implicit foundation of Statistical Disclosure Control — is shifting. Agentic AI strengthens the case that re-identification is "reasonably likely by any means" under GDPR Recital 26, and data custodians/regulators must anticipate near-future escalation of this threat.

title: Operator Learning for Cubic Nonlinear Schrödinger Equation on Periodic Domains
summary: We consider the cubic nonlinear Schrödinger (NLS) equation on two-dimensional flat tori with varying aspect ratios. In this formulation, the choice of aspect ratio governs the Fourier resonance structure, so rational and irrational geometries can exhibit different high-frequency cascade behaviors. We present a geometry-conditioned Fourier neural operator (FNO) for the cubic defocusing NLS equation, where the input consists of the real and imaginary parts of the solution together with the aspect-ratio parameter \(ω^2\). The model is trained to approximate the one-step solution operator and is evaluated on unseen trajectories generated from random-phase initial data using Fourier pseudospectral method. Our numerical experiments show that the learned operator captures the main solution dynamics on both tori and reproduces the distinct Sobolev norm behavior of the two geometries, with stronger \(H^2\)-growth on the rational torus and more constrained behavior on the irrational torus, consistent with the findings of \cite{hrabski2021energy}. We perform ablation studies to examine the roles of retained Fourier modes, activation functions, Fourier-layer depth, and explicit geometry conditioning. The results indicate that including $ω^2$ improves long-time predictive accuracy, especially for the rational geometry, and supports the use of geometry-aware neural operators for learning spectral-transfer phenomena in nonlinear dispersive partial differential equations.

AI.tldr: A geometry-conditioned Fourier neural operator (FNO) is proposed for the cubic defocusing NLS equation on 2D flat tori, where the aspect ratio ω² governs Fourier resonances. The model takes real/imaginary solution components and ω² as input, learns the one-step solution operator, and successfully captures distinct Sobolev norm growth behaviors on rational vs. irrational tori, consistent with prior analytical results.
AI.motivation: The cubic NLS equation on 2D tori exhibits qualitatively different high-frequency cascade behaviors depending on whether the aspect ratio is rational or irrational, due to differences in Fourier resonance structure. Traditional numerical methods require separate simulations per geometry, motivating a geometry-aware learned operator that can generalize across aspect ratios and capture these distinct spectral-transfer phenomena.
AI.method: A Fourier neural operator (FNO) is conditioned on the aspect-ratio parameter ω², taking as input the real and imaginary parts of the complex wavefunction alongside ω². The model approximates the one-step time-evolution operator. Training data is generated via Fourier pseudospectral method from random-phase initial conditions. Ablation studies examine the effects of retained Fourier modes, activation functions, Fourier-layer depth, and explicit geometry conditioning.
AI.result: The geometry-conditioned FNO captures the main solution dynamics on both rational and irrational tori. It reproduces the distinct Sobolev norm behavior: stronger H²-growth on the rational torus and more constrained growth on the irrational torus, matching Hrabski et al. (2021). Including ω² improves long-time predictive accuracy, especially for the rational geometry. Ablation studies support the importance of explicit geometry conditioning.
AI.conclusion: Geometry-aware neural operators, specifically FNOs conditioned on the aspect ratio, are effective for learning spectral-transfer phenomena in nonlinear dispersive PDEs. Explicit geometry conditioning significantly improves long-time prediction accuracy, particularly for rational tori where resonant interactions are richer.

title: ToE: A Hierarchical and Explainable Claim Verification Framework with Dynamic Multi-source Evidence Retrieval and Aggregation
summary: The rapid spread of fake news poses increasing threats to information ecosystems, especially as AI-generated misinformation under Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) poisoning allows adversarially crafted content to be systematically surfaced by retrieval systems, contaminating LLM reasoning. In this paper, we propose Tree of Evidence (ToE), a hierarchical evidence reasoning framework for automated fact-checking that models each claim as a dynamically expanding argument tree. ToE integrates a reinforcement learning-driven multi-source retrieval agent, an evidence evaluation agent, and an argument tree aggregation algorithm to iteratively decompose, retrieve, and verify claims through an explainable evidence chain. We further provide a theoretical analysis of the retrieval process, deriving a formal error bound that guarantees the learned policy converges to a neighborhood of the information-theoretically optimal policy. Experiments across multiple datasets and backbone LLMs demonstrate that ToE achieves improvements ranging from 4 to 24 percentage points over competitive baselines, with particularly pronounced gains on adversarially poisoned inputs.

AI.tldr: Tree of Evidence (ToE) is a hierarchical evidence reasoning framework for automated fact-checking that uses a reinforcement learning-driven retrieval agent to build argument trees, achieving 4–24 pp improvements over baselines, especially on adversarially poisoned inputs.
AI.motivation: Fake news and AI-generated misinformation under Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) poisoning can systematically contaminate retrieval systems and LLM reasoning. Existing fact-checking methods lack structured, explainable, and robust evidence reasoning capable of handling adversarial content.
AI.method: ToE models each claim as a dynamically expanding argument tree, integrating three components: (1) a reinforcement learning-driven multi-source retrieval agent, (2) an evidence evaluation agent, and (3) an argument tree aggregation algorithm. These work together to iteratively decompose, retrieve, and verify claims via explainable evidence chains. A theoretical analysis derives a formal error bound showing the learned policy converges near the information-theoretically optimal policy.
AI.result: Experiments across multiple datasets and backbone LLMs show ToE achieves improvements of 4 to 24 percentage points over competitive baselines, with especially pronounced gains on adversarially poisoned inputs.
AI.conclusion: ToE provides a robust, explainable, and theoretically grounded approach to automated fact-checking that effectively counters GEO-style adversarial poisoning of retrieval systems.

title: UNICS: Multilingual Code Search via Unified Pseudocode and Contrastive Transfer Learning
comment: Accepted to the ACM International Conference on the Foundations of Software Engineering (FSE 2026). 24.pages
summary: While pre-trained models have achieved remarkable success in code search, their multilingual capabilities remain a major hurdle, plagued by data imbalance, cross-lingual semantic interference, and the loss of critical information from existing unified representations like Abstract Syntax Trees (ASTs) or Intermediate Representations (IRs). Furthermore, conventional contrastive learning strategies often rely on simplistic hard negative sampling while overlooking the potential of mining hard positives to learn code's intrinsic semantic invariance. To address these challenges, we introduce UNICS, a framework for multilingual code search built on a two-stage training strategy. In the first stage, UNICS is pre-trained on a novel dataset we constructed, which uses pseudo-code as a unified representation to learn a cross-lingual, algorithm-level logic that preserves full semantic fidelity. The second stage employs a multi-task transfer learning strategy that adapts this general knowledge to specific languages by decomposing code into semantic slices (e.g., API calls, function bodies) and incorporating tasks for hard positive mining and cross-lingual dynamic hard negative sampling. Experimental results demonstrate that UNICS achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple multilingual and cross-lingual benchmarks, showcasing superior generalization and performance balance, especially in zero-shot transfer tasks to low-resource languages.

AI.tldr: UNICS introduces a two-stage framework for multilingual code search that uses pseudo-code as a unified representation for pre-training, followed by multi-task transfer learning with hard positive mining and dynamic hard negative sampling, achieving SOTA results especially in low-resource zero-shot transfer.
AI.motivation: Existing pre-trained models for code search suffer from three key problems: (1) data imbalance across languages, (2) cross-lingual semantic interference, and (3) information loss from existing unified representations like ASTs or IRs. Additionally, conventional contrastive learning relies heavily on hard negative sampling while neglecting hard positive mining to capture intrinsic semantic invariance.
AI.method: UNICS employs a two-stage training strategy. Stage 1: Pre-training on a newly constructed dataset using pseudo-code as a unified, language-agnostic representation to learn algorithm-level logic with full semantic fidelity. Stage 2: Multi-task transfer learning that adapts general knowledge to specific languages by decomposing code into semantic slices (API calls, function bodies, etc.), incorporating hard positive mining tasks and cross-lingual dynamic hard negative sampling.
AI.result: UNICS achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple multilingual and cross-lingual benchmarks, demonstrating superior generalization and balanced performance, with particularly strong gains in zero-shot transfer to low-resource languages.
AI.conclusion: The two-stage approach combining pseudo-code unified pre-training with decomposition-based multi-task transfer learning effectively addresses multilingual code search challenges. Hard positive mining and dynamic hard negative sampling complement each other to better capture semantic invariance, enabling robust cross-lingual generalization even for underrepresented languages.

title: Towards Value-Constrained Credit Assignment in Fully Delegated AI Cooperatives
summary: We propose a framework for reward allocation in fully delegated AI cooperatives where humans are represented by agents that contribute data and participate in model updates under heterogeneous value constraints. The key idea is to credit only those updates that remain admissible after screening them against each principal's value profile. We formulate value-conditioned gradient filtering, online marginal contribution signals, and cumulative revenue settlement within a traversal learning (TL) substrate. TL is especially attractive here because it performs decentralized backpropagation without the quality loss associated with aggregation-centric distributed learning and, we argue, offers a finer attribution substrate than FedAvg-style federated learning by preserving explicit traversal and gradient paths. The framework is positioned against data valuation, federated contribution estimation, personalized federated learning, and pluralistic alignment.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a reward allocation framework for AI cooperatives where human-representing agents contribute data and model updates, using value-conditioned gradient filtering to credit only admissible updates. It leverages Traversal Learning (TL) as a decentralized backpropagation substrate that preserves explicit gradient paths, offering finer attribution than FedAvg-style federated learning.
AI.motivation: Existing federated learning and data valuation methods lack fine-grained, value-aligned attribution mechanisms for rewarding contributors in decentralized AI cooperatives. There is a need for a system that screens contributions against individual principals' heterogeneous value constraints before crediting them, ensuring fairness and alignment.
AI.method: The framework employs value-conditioned gradient filtering to screen updates against each principal's value profile, online marginal contribution signals for real-time attribution, and cumulative revenue settlement for reward distribution. These components operate on a Traversal Learning (TL) substrate — a decentralized backpropagation approach that preserves explicit traversal and gradient paths, avoiding the quality loss of aggregation-centric distributed learning.
AI.result: The framework is positioned analytically against four related paradigms: data valuation, federated contribution estimation, personalized federated learning, and pluralistic alignment. TL is argued to provide a finer attribution substrate than FedAvg-style federated learning by maintaining explicit gradient paths.
AI.conclusion: Traversal Learning offers a principled substrate for value-conditioned reward allocation in fully delegated AI cooperatives, enabling decentralized, attributable, and value-aligned contribution crediting that surpasses aggregation-based federated approaches in attribution granularity.

title: EntMTP: Accelerating LLM Inference with Entropy Guided Multi Token Prediction
summary: Multi-token prediction has been shown to increase data density during training, improve downstream text-generation quality, and serves as the defacto approach for self-speculative decoding. Existing foundation and open source models that use MTP heads commit to a static tree-based attention topology throughout the entire generation sequence, meaning the speculation depth, and thus the compute required during verification, stays constant regardless of the context. This is fundamentally misaligned with the entropy patterns of natural language where low-entropy regions often support reliable multi-step drafting, while high-entropy regions require more conservative speculation. To address this, we propose Entropy-guided Multi-Token Prediction (EntMTP), a training-free scheduler that toggles between tree-based attention topologies from a set of task-specific pareto-optimal trees conditioned on a running estimate of local generation entropy. By matching speculation depth to context predictability, EntMTP maximizes expected accepted-token throughput across the full distribution of generated text without sacrificing generation quality. When evaluated across Humaneval, ShareGPT, GSM8k, and Litbench benchmarks, EntMTP consistently achieves a 1.15x speedup against Hydra and peak speedup of 1.36x against Medusa baselines respectively.

AI.tldr: EntMTP is a training-free scheduling method that dynamically adjusts multi-token prediction tree depth based on local generation entropy, achieving up to 1.36x speedup over Medusa while maintaining generation quality.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-token prediction (MTP) models use a static tree-based attention topology with constant speculation depth regardless of context. This is misaligned with natural language entropy patterns: low-entropy regions can support aggressive multi-step drafting, while high-entropy regions require conservative speculation. Static topologies therefore waste compute or miss opportunities.
AI.method: EntMTP is a training-free scheduler that dynamically selects from a set of task-specific Pareto-optimal tree-based attention topologies based on a running estimate of local generation entropy. It toggles between these topologies to match speculation depth with context predictability, maximizing expected accepted-token throughput without retraining the underlying MTP model.
AI.result: Evaluated across Humaneval, ShareGPT, GSM8k, and Litbench benchmarks, EntMTP consistently achieves a 1.15x speedup against Hydra and a peak speedup of 1.36x against Medusa baselines, without sacrificing generation quality.
AI.conclusion: Entropy-guided dynamic topology scheduling effectively aligns MTP speculation depth with local text predictability, yielding significant inference speedups over static baselines in a training-free manner.

title: Fast and Feasible: Permutation-based Constrained Reranking for Revenue Maximization
summary: Search and recommender systems have produced highly relevant search results. A natural next step in the development of such systems in e-commerce is to rerank these results to increase the platform's revenue from paid promotion products. However, maximizing revenue alone may degrade the user experience by reducing relevance or increasing fraud risk. To avoid this, we state the reranking problem as an integer linear program ($ILP$) that maximizes revenue subject to per-query constraints on other metrics, e.g., relevance. Since solving $ILP$ exactly for every query is slow for deployment to the online service, we propose a lightweight permutation-based reranking approximation algorithm PermR. At each step, the algorithm selects a pair of neighboring items and swaps them to either improve the objective or repair a violated constraint. We evaluate PermR across multiple categories of a large classified platform in offline and online settings. PermR achieves about 63\% of the ILP revenue improvement, within production latency limits, preserving all constraints. In a 14-day online A/B test over 56 million search queries, PermR increased revenue by $2$\%.

AI.tldr: Proposes PermR, a lightweight permutation-based reranking algorithm for e-commerce search that approximates an integer linear program (ILP) to maximize revenue from paid promotions while preserving constraints on relevance and fraud risk. Achieves 63% of optimal ILP revenue gain with low latency, and a 2% revenue increase in a large-scale online A/B test.
AI.motivation: Search systems need to incorporate paid promotion reranking to boost platform revenue, but naive revenue maximization can degrade user experience (relevance) or increase fraud risk. Exact ILP solutions are too slow for online deployment, creating a need for a fast, constraint-preserving approximation.
AI.method: Formulates the reranking problem as an integer linear program (ILP) maximizing revenue subject to per-query constraints (e.g., relevance, fraud risk). Proposes PermR, a greedy approximation algorithm that iteratively selects and swaps neighboring item pairs to improve the objective or repair constraint violations. Evaluated via offline experiments and a 14-day online A/B test across 56M queries on a large classified ads platform.
AI.result: PermR achieves approximately 63% of the ILP's revenue improvement, satisfies all constraints, and operates within production latency limits. In the online A/B test over 56 million search queries, PermR increased revenue by 2%.
AI.conclusion: PermR provides a practical, deployable solution for revenue-aware reranking in e-commerce search, balancing revenue gains with user experience constraints and meeting stringent latency requirements.

title: Decoys Cannot Go Everywhere: Mapping the Deception Surface in MITRE ATT&CK
summary: Cyber deception research often assumes that a decoy can be placed wherever there is attacker behavior. This work tests that assumption across MITRE ATT&CK v18.1. We introduce a four-criterion rubric for infrastructure deception and apply it to all 250 ATT&CK techniques. The rubric evaluates whether a defender-controlled decoy can be placed, whether an attacker is likely to interact with it, what intelligence that interaction can yield, and whether the interaction reliably indicates malice. The resulting deception surface is sparse: only 80 techniques (32%) admit a decoy the attacker could plausibly reach. For the remaining 170 techniques, there is no defender-controlled asset in the attacker's path that can be fabricated as a decoy. Decoy placement across those 80 techniques falls into two patterns we call Sweep and Seek. In Sweep, the attacker moves broadly through assets in range and encounters the decoy as part of that activity. In Seek, the attacker looks for a specific kind of asset and interacts with a fabricated version of it. These patterns give a simple placement rule: a decoy must either sit on a sweep path or imitate a sought asset. We also show that decoys usually have useful intelligence potential, but whether an attacker interacts with them at all, and whether that interaction reliably indicates malice, both vary. We release the rubric, decision rules, and per-technique assessment as an auditable baseline for future deception research and deployment planning, and show that infrastructure decoys cannot be assumed to apply to all attacker behavior.

AI.tldr: The paper challenges the assumption that decoys can be placed anywhere in attacker workflows. Using MITRE ATT&CK v18.1, the authors apply a four-criterion rubric to all 250 techniques and find only 32% admit plausible decoy placement. Two placement patterns—Sweep and Seek—emerge, and the work provides an auditable baseline for deception deployment.
AI.motivation: Cyber deception research and practice often operate under the unexamined assumption that a decoy can be positioned at any point where attacker behavior occurs. The authors seek to empirically test this assumption, revealing the actual "deception surface" and providing defenders with a rigorous, technique-level framework for determining where infrastructure decoys are genuinely feasible.
AI.method: The authors introduce a four-criterion rubric for infrastructure deception: (1) whether a defender-controlled decoy can be placed, (2) whether an attacker is likely to interact with it, (3) what intelligence the interaction yields, and (4) whether the interaction reliably indicates malice. They apply this rubric to all 250 ATT&CK v18.1 techniques, producing a per-technique assessment. From the results, they derive two archetypal placement patterns and release the rubric, decision rules, and full assessment as a reproducible baseline.
AI.result: Only 80 of 250 techniques (32%) support plausible decoy placement. The remaining 170 techniques lack a defender-controlled asset in the attacker's path. Two placement patterns emerge: Sweep (attacker encounters the decoy while moving broadly through assets) and Seek (attacker searches for a specific asset and interacts with a fabricated version). Decoys generally offer useful intelligence, but the likelihood of attacker interaction and the reliability of malice indicators both vary across techniques.
AI.conclusion: Infrastructure decoys cannot be assumed to apply universally to all attacker behaviors. The deception surface is sparse, and effective placement follows a simple rule: a decoy must either sit on a sweep path or imitate a sought asset. The released rubric and per-technique assessment serve as an auditable baseline for future deception research and operational deployment planning.

title: The Curse of Multiple Mediators: Hidden Interaction Effects in Activation Patching
summary: Activation patching is the primary tool in mechanistic interpretability. It attributes causal responsibility for a model behavior to each of its individual components by estimating its natural indirect effect (NIE). Re-deriving the activation patching estimand from causal mediation analysis, we find that the NIE does not solely capture the causal effect through the specific component. It also contains interaction effects (INT) that measure how much the component's causal effect itself depends on the state of other components in the model. A natural response may be to try to eliminate INT by adjusting the estimator or unit of analysis, but each of these potential remedies has predictable failure modes. We demonstrate these failure modes in the GPT-2 IOI circuit; components whose causal importance is conditional on the state of other components are either invisible or artificially inflated, and INT variance explains the previously documented instability of faithfulness scores. We prove that INT scales with the distance between clean and patched component activations, is negligible when the model is locally affine, and decomposes combinatorially into pairwise and higher-order group interactions. Despite its inevitability, INT is not a nuisance to be eliminated, but rather a diagnostic for interpretability studies. Its individual and group-level magnitude and sign signal when causal conclusions are prompt-dependent, and when greedy NIE-based component ranking will miss mechanisms only discoverable through combinatorial search.

AI.tldr: Activation patching, widely used in mechanistic interpretability, estimates the natural indirect effect (NIE) but inadvertently captures interaction effects (INT) that depend on other components' states. The authors demonstrate that INT is irreducible through estimator or unit-of-analysis adjustments, show its empirical consequences in GPT-2 IOI circuits, prove its theoretical properties, and argue that INT should be treated as a diagnostic signal rather than a nuisance.
AI.motivation: Activation patching is the dominant method for attributing causal responsibility in mechanistic interpretability, yet its estimand (the NIE) has been uncritically adopted from causal mediation analysis without examining whether it actually isolates the targeted component's effect. The authors aim to rigorously re-derive what activation patching estimates, expose the presence of interaction effects, and address the resulting implications for interpretability research.
AI.method: The authors re-derive the activation patching estimand from the perspective of causal mediation analysis. They decompose the NIE into a direct component-specific effect plus interaction effects (INT). They test potential remedies (adjusting the estimator or unit of analysis) and document their failure modes. Empirically, they apply their analysis to the GPT-2 IOI (Indirect Object Identification) circuit. Theoretically, they prove that INT scales with activation distance, is negligible under local affinity, and admits a combinatorial decomposition into pairwise and higher-order group interactions.
AI.result: Interaction effects are inevitable in activation patching. Attempted remedies (estimator or unit-of-analysis adjustments) have predictable failure modes: components with conditional causal importance become invisible or artificially inflated. INT variance explains previously documented instability in faithfulness scores. Theoretically, INT is small when the model behaves locally affinely and grows with the distance between clean and patched activations. INT decomposes combinatorially into pairwise and higher-order interactions. Its magnitude and sign serve as diagnostics: they signal when causal conclusions are prompt-dependent and when greedy NIE-based ranking will miss mechanisms requiring combinatorial search.
AI.conclusion: INT is not a nuisance to eliminate but a valuable diagnostic for interpretability studies. Researchers should examine INT magnitude and sign to assess prompt-dependence of their causal conclusions and to detect when NIE-based component ranking overlooks mechanisms discoverable only through combinatorial search.

title: Towards Reliable and Robust LLM Planning: Symbolic Feedback-Driven Iterative Self-Refinement Framework
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have attracted widespread attention from academia and industry, yet their deployment raises critical security concerns regarding robustness and reliability. Planning, a core component of intelligent behavior, remains challenging for LLMs, which often produce infeasible or incorrect solutions in long-horizon decision-making tasks due to inherent complexity. In this paper, we propose a symbolic feedback-driven iterative self-refinement framework to enhance the robustness and reliability of LLMs in long-horizon planning. Specifically, a natural language prompting mechanism is introduced to map logical symbols into natural language descriptions, enabling LLMs to better capture task constraints and semantics. We further design a symbolic verifier that identifies errors and converts them into corrective instructions interpretable by the LLM, thereby guiding self-refinement. In addition, we leverage a plan recognizer to infer goal reachability, facilitating more effective guidance toward desired goals. Empirical results demonstrate that the proposed framework consistently improves both feasibility and correctness in long-horizon planning tasks. This highlights its effectiveness in enhancing the reliability of LLM-based planning and potential to enable more trustworthy AI systems.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a symbolic feedback-driven iterative self-refinement framework that combines natural language prompting, symbolic verification, and plan recognition to improve the feasibility and correctness of LLM-based long-horizon planning.
AI.motivation: LLMs struggle with long-horizon decision-making tasks, frequently producing infeasible or incorrect solutions. Existing approaches lack robust mechanisms to verify constraint satisfaction and guide iterative correction, motivating the need for a framework that enhances planning reliability and trustworthiness.
AI.method: The framework consists of three components: (1) a natural language prompting mechanism that maps logical symbols into natural language to help LLMs capture task constraints and semantics; (2) a symbolic verifier that detects planning errors and generates corrective instructions interpretable by the LLM; (3) a plan recognizer that infers goal reachability to provide effective goal-directed guidance. These components operate in an iterative self-refinement loop.
AI.result: Empirical results show that the proposed framework consistently improves both feasibility and correctness on long-horizon planning tasks, demonstrating its effectiveness over baseline LLM planning approaches.
AI.conclusion: The symbolic feedback-driven iterative self-refinement framework effectively enhances LLM planning robustness and reliability, offering a promising direction for building more trustworthy AI systems capable of complex, long-horizon decision-making.

title: Reasoning Beyond Prediction: From Data-Driven to Causal Software Engineering
comment: Accepted for publication in Communications of the ACM
summary: Software engineering is an intellectually demanding, creative discipline that juggles a web of interdependent tasks to design, build, and assure the quality of increasingly complex systems. As our expectations from software soar - with demands spanning AI-driven products, pervasively distributed and cloud-native architectures, and deeply embedded cyber-physical environments - its complexity steadily increases. In response, a new wave of co-engineering methods and tools, fueled by deep learning, has emerged to augment the process, enhancing automation and decision support. Yet, these advances remain far from delivering the kind of intelligent support that modern software development demands. We call for a new paradigm of human-machine cooperation: one where machines don't just automate routine tasks or predict from learned patterns, but actively amplify engineers' reasoning through the lens of causation. As software becomes smarter, a smarter support is needed.

AI.tldr: This paper advocates for a paradigm shift in software engineering tooling: moving from deep learning-based automation and prediction toward human-machine cooperation grounded in causal reasoning, where machines actively amplify engineers' reasoning rather than merely automating routine tasks.
AI.motivation: Software systems are growing increasingly complex due to AI-driven products, cloud-native architectures, and cyber-physical environments. Current deep learning-based co-engineering tools provide automation and decision support but fall short of delivering the truly intelligent assistance that modern software development requires.
AI.method: The authors propose a new paradigm of human-machine cooperation centered on causal reasoning — machines would actively amplify engineers' reasoning through the lens of causation, rather than merely automating routine tasks or predicting from learned patterns.
AI.result: The paper is a vision/position statement rather than an empirical study, so it does not report experimental results. It identifies a gap between current DL-based tooling capabilities and the intelligent support needed for modern software engineering.
AI.conclusion: As software becomes smarter, smarter support is needed. The field must pivot toward causation-driven human-machine cooperation to meet the demands of increasingly complex software systems.

title: Estimation--Prediction Tradeoff in Causal Probabilistic Temporal Graphs
summary: Temporal link prediction is usually evaluated by predictive performance on unseen edges, but in probabilistic temporal graphs this criterion can conflate model error with irreducible uncertainty. We study this issue by characterising an inherent estimation--prediction tradeoff in binary logistic models where regimes that maximise Fisher information and improve parameter recoverability are also those with the highest entropy, making individual predictions intrinsically harder even under perfect parameter recovery. We propose a probabilistic causal framework for generating temporal graphs with transient edges and known ground-truth causal structure, allowing temporal link prediction to be evaluated jointly with causal parameter recovery. For the proposed binary logistic parametrisation, we derive the Cramér--Rao bound and validate the tradeoff between parameter estimation error and irreducible predictive loss. Our results show that predictive accuracy alone may not reflect whether a model has learned the underlying causal mechanism, motivating benchmarks that distinguish reducible model error from intrinsic process uncertainty.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies an estimation–prediction tradeoff in temporal link prediction: regimes optimal for parameter recovery (maximizing Fisher information) also exhibit high entropy, making individual predictions inherently uncertain. The authors propose a probabilistic causal framework with known ground truth, derive Cramér–Rao bounds for a binary logistic model, and demonstrate that predictive accuracy alone fails to distinguish model error from irreducible process uncertainty.
AI.motivation: In probabilistic temporal graphs, standard evaluation of temporal link prediction using predictive accuracy on unseen edges conflates model error with irreducible uncertainty inherent to the stochastic process. There is a need to distinguish whether poor predictions stem from a misspecified model or from fundamental unpredictability in the data-generating mechanism.
AI.method: The authors construct a probabilistic causal framework that generates temporal graphs with transient edges and known ground-truth causal structure. They adopt a binary logistic parametrisation, derive the Cramér–Rao bound to establish the theoretical limit on parameter estimation error, and jointly evaluate temporal link prediction accuracy alongside causal parameter recovery to reveal the estimation–prediction tradeoff.
AI.result: Regimes that maximise Fisher information (yielding better parameter recoverability) coincide with those of highest entropy, making individual link predictions intrinsically harder even when parameters are perfectly recovered. The Cramér–Rao bound formally validates an inverse relationship between parameter estimation error and irreducible predictive loss.
AI.conclusion: Predictive accuracy alone is an insufficient metric for assessing whether a model has captured the underlying causal mechanism. Benchmarks should explicitly separate reducible model error from intrinsic process uncertainty to provide a more faithful evaluation of temporal link prediction models.

title: Ko-WideSearch: A Korean Breadth-Search Benchmark for Exhaustive Set Enumeration by Web Agents
summary: Web-agent benchmarks overwhelmingly measure depth -- pinning one obscure answer behind a chain of constraints -- while breadth, exhaustively enumerating a closed set and filling each item's attributes, is barely evaluated, especially outside English. Breadth is also hard to build: certifying that a gold set is complete and every cell correct is far costlier than checking a single answer. I introduce \textsc{Ko-WideSearch}, a Korean breadth-search benchmark built by an automated synthesize-and-verify pipeline. Each task names a set-parent entity -- a TV season, a dynasty, a league, an administrative region, an election -- and asks for its full membership plus a per-item attribute table, graded by Item-, Column-, and Row-F1. It spans 228 tables over 190 entities and sixteen categories across three difficulty tiers, set by two structural knobs I dial independently -- table width and a 2-D composite key -- so cross-product membership climbs from 0\% to 100\% across the tiers. A single normalization-aware comparator is shared between gold construction and grading, so stable date and count columns are not over-dropped on formatting alone. Across twenty web agents, the failure is consistent: agents recover the set but not the rows (e.g.\ Item-F1 92.8 against Row-F1 53.7), accuracy falls steadily as the knobs harden, and neither more search nor more spend closes the gap. Broken down by cell, the hard part is finding the right value, not formatting it: open-ended free-text cells fail most, while cells with a standard answer such as a date or a name usually come out right.

AI.tldr: Ko-WideSearch is a Korean breadth-search benchmark with 228 tables across 190 entities and 16 categories at three difficulty tiers. It evaluates web agents on exhaustive set enumeration and attribute filling using Item-, Column-, and Row-F1 metrics. Across 20 agents, a consistent failure pattern emerges: agents recover sets well (Item-F1 92.8) but struggle with complete rows (Row-F1 53.7), and difficulty knobs (table width, composite keys) systematically degrade performance.
AI.motivation: Existing web-agent benchmarks overwhelmingly measure depth (finding one obscure answer behind a constraint chain) while breadth — exhaustively enumerating a closed set and filling each item's attributes — is barely evaluated, especially outside English. Moreover, constructing breadth benchmarks is costly because certifying a complete gold set with correct cells is far harder than checking a single answer.
AI.method: The author built Ko-WideSearch using an automated synthesize-and-verify pipeline. Each task names a set-parent entity (e.g., TV season, dynasty, league) and asks for full membership plus a per-item attribute table. Difficulty is controlled via two independent structural knobs: table width and a 2-D composite key, making cross-product membership vary from 0% to 100% across three tiers. A single normalization-aware comparator is shared between gold construction and grading to avoid over-dropping stable date/count columns on formatting differences. Evaluation uses Item-F1, Column-F1, and Row-F1 metrics.
AI.result: Across 20 web agents, results show a consistent failure pattern: agents recover the set (Item-F1 92.8) but fail on complete rows (Row-F1 53.7). Accuracy falls steadily as difficulty knobs harden, and neither more search steps nor higher computational spend closes the gap. Cell-level breakdown reveals that finding the right value (not formatting it) is the bottleneck: open-ended free-text cells fail most, while cells with standard answers like dates or names typically succeed.
AI.conclusion: Breadth search is a distinct and under-evaluated capability for web agents, where the primary failure mode is locating correct values for open-ended cells rather than formatting them. Ko-WideSearch provides a structured, multi-tier, non-English benchmark to systematically measure this capability.

title: SHARD: cell-keyed residual splitting for alignment-resistant private dense retrieval
comment: arXiv admin note: text overlap with arXiv:2606.26373
summary:
Dense embeddings underpin semantic search and RAG, yet a leaked vector store hands much of the underlying text back to whoever holds it. The attacks that make this possible (few-shot alignment, zero-shot inversion, unsupervised cross-space translation) share one weakness: the protected store is a single global geometry that can be aligned to a known one. A secret global rotation, the usual lightweight defence, is no exception: orthogonal Procrustes recovers it once the attacker has about the subspace dimension in known pairs.
  We introduce Shard, a retrieval-preserving embedding transform that removes this weak axis. The centred embedding is split into a short public prefix (for stage-1 retrieval) and a private residual sharded into C cells under separate secret keys; the residual is reranked under CKKS, where the keys cancel and leave the inner product exact. A single parameter C runs the design from the global-linear baseline it replaces (C=1) to per-document micro-keys (C=N). Because the rerank is full-dimensional, Shard returns the raw-space nDCG@10 that half-SVD truncation gives up; and because the residual is keyed cell-locally, mapping it back to a common frame under a diffuse known-plaintext leak costs roughly C times more anchors (median 200 to 102,400 at C=256), for a few encrypted queries. The short public prefix leaks far less neighbour structure, and a micro-key limit drives the residual graph to zero with an unlinkable, renewable template. The barrier holds against learned, non-linear and unsupervised aligners, and where a matched-utility noise defence de-anonymises almost every probe, Shard de-anonymises none. We are plain about the limits: within a cell the keys cancel, a targeted attacker needs only about d_priv anchors, and an overlapping reference corpus still leaks through the prefix. Shard is an attack-aware geometric defence, not a cryptographic guarantee.

AI.tldr: Shard splits embeddings into a public prefix for fast retrieval and a private residual sharded across cells under separate keys, using CKKS homomorphic encryption for exact inner-product reranking. This forces attackers to gather C× more anchor pairs to align the private geometry, while preserving full-dimensional retrieval quality.
AI.motivation: Existing embedding inversion and alignment attacks exploit a single global geometry. Defenses like secret global rotation are brittle — orthogonal Procrustes recovers the rotation with ~d known pairs. A defense is needed that eliminates this global geometric weak axis without sacrificing retrieval utility.
AI.method: Shard decomposes each centred embedding into: (1) a short public prefix for approximate stage-1 retrieval, and (2) a private residual partitioned into C cells, each randomized by a distinct secret key. Stage-2 reranking uses CKKS fully homomorphic encryption: keys cancel within each cell, yielding exact inner products. The parameter C spans from C=1 (global baseline) to C=N (per-document micro-keys). The residual is full-dimensional, avoiding the nDCG loss of half-SVD truncation.
AI.result: At C=256, anchor requirements for alignment rise from ~200 to ~102,400 (median). The public prefix leaks substantially less neighbour structure; at the micro-key limit, the residual graph becomes zero (unlinkable, renewable template). Shard withstands learned, non-linear, and unsupervised alignment attacks. Under a matched-utility noise defense, nearly all probes are de-anonymized, whereas Shard de-anonymizes none. Within-cell key cancellation, ~d_priv anchors needed by a targeted attacker, and prefix leakage from overlapping reference corpora are acknowledged limits.
AI.conclusion: Shard is a practical, attack-aware geometric defense that raises the cost of embedding inversion by removing the global alignment axis, while preserving exact retrieval quality via CKKS-based reranking. It is not a cryptographic guarantee but substantially hardens vector stores against realistic leakage scenarios.

title: Boundary condition fidelity for bottom-hole pressure and CO2 plume prediction in geological carbon storage
summary: Accurate prediction of bottom-hole pressure (BHP) and CO2 plume migration is essential for safe geological carbon storage, yet practical simulations often rely on truncated domains where artificial boundaries distort pressure diffusion and CO2 saturation footprints. In this study, we evaluate how boundary-condition fidelity affects BHP and CO2 plume prediction by comparing ten reduced-domain boundary treatments against full-domain reference simulations in homogeneous and heterogeneous reservoirs. We test uniform pore-volume multipliers, transmissibility modifiers, corner-adjusted pore-volume corrections, layered corrections, and gradual modifiers using BHP RMSE, NRMSE, peak pressure deviation, and plume Intersection over Union (IoU) as performance metrics. Our results show that conserving corner pore volume is the most important requirement for truncated-domain modeling. We find that uniform treatments which neglect corner storage generate large pressure errors, with BHP RMSE of 362 to 382 psi in the homogeneous model and 250 to 304 psi in the heterogeneous model, and yield plume IoU values near 0.80 to 0.84, indicating roughly 16 to 20% of the combined plume area is misrepresented. Corner-adjusted scenarios substantially reduce pressure errors and raise plume IoU above 0.94, but we observe that transmissibility correction is not universally beneficial. In homogeneous reservoirs, uniform transmissibility adjustment improves pressure fidelity; in heterogeneous reservoirs, it can over-restrict flow across variable-permeability boundary faces, increasing BHP error and contracting the predicted plume. We find the gradual modifier with transmissibility correction provides the most consistent performance, achieving BHP NRMSE below 3.7% and plume IoU above 0.97 in both reservoir types.

AI.tldr: Evaluated ten reduced-domain boundary treatments for CO2 storage simulation; corner-adjusted methods substantially outperform uniform methods, with gradual modifier plus transmissibility correction achieving BHP NRMSE <3.7% and plume IoU >0.97 across reservoir types.
AI.motivation: Truncated-domain reservoir simulations introduce artificial boundary effects that distort bottom-hole pressure (BHP) prediction and CO2 plume migration estimates, compromising the reliability of geological carbon storage models. There is a need to systematically evaluate which boundary-condition treatments best preserve simulation fidelity.
AI.method: Compared ten reduced-domain boundary treatments (uniform pore-volume multipliers, transmissibility modifiers, corner-adjusted pore-volume corrections, layered corrections, and gradual modifiers) against full-domain reference simulations in both homogeneous and heterogeneous reservoirs. Performance evaluated using BHP RMSE, NRMSE, peak pressure deviation, and plume Intersection over Union (IoU).
AI.result: Uniform treatments neglecting corner storage produced large BHP errors (RMSE 362–382 psi homogeneous, 250–304 psi heterogeneous) and plume IoU ≈0.80–0.84 (~16–20% misrepresentation). Corner-adjusted scenarios reduced pressure errors substantially and raised plume IoU above 0.94. Transmissibility correction was beneficial in homogeneous reservoirs but over-restricted flow in heterogeneous cases, contracting the predicted plume. The gradual modifier with transmissibility correction performed most consistently (BHP NRMSE <3.7%, plume IoU >0.97) in both reservoir types.
AI.conclusion: Conserving corner pore volume is the single most critical requirement for truncated-domain CO2 storage modeling. Transmissibility correction is not universally beneficial and can degrade predictions in heterogeneous reservoirs. The gradual modifier with transmissibility correction offers the most robust, reservoir-type-agnostic performance.

title: Understanding Rollout Error in Graph World Models
summary: World models are often used for planning by rolling learned dynamics forward. Many planning environments, however, are not vectors or images; they are graphs of agents, tools, skills, routes, and dependencies. In these settings, a local prediction error may stay local or spread through the graph, and the failure mode changes again when edges are predicted rather than fixed. This paper studies long-horizon rollout error in Graph World Models (GWMs). We formulate a unified fixed-edge and dynamic-edge GWM framework with action nodes for node-, edge-, and graph-level decisions. We develop graph-valued rollout bounds that separate topology-induced amplification from model-induced amplification, and we introduce a joint node-edge operator for dynamic-edge rollouts. Guided by the analysis, we propose Error-Aware GWM, which combines spectral regularization, rollout consistency, and critical-node weighting. Across synthetic topologies and heterogeneous agent-graph testbeds, rollout error and planning regret grow with horizon, dynamic-edge training is needed when structure evolves, and Error-Aware GWM prevents long-horizon divergence while preserving prediction accuracy. Real-world graph benchmarks clarify the scope of GWMs: they are most useful for dynamic graph rollout and agent planning, while specialized graph models remain strong on static or sparse prediction tasks.

AI.tldr: The paper formalizes Graph World Models (GWMs) with both fixed and dynamic edges, derives rollout error bounds that separate topology-driven and model-driven amplification, and proposes Error-Aware GWM — combining spectral regularization, rollout consistency, and critical-node weighting — to mitigate long-horizon divergence in graph-structured planning.
AI.motivation: Standard world models assume vector or image state spaces, but many real-world planning domains (multi-agent systems, skill/tool graphs, logistics networks) are inherently graph-structured. In these settings, local prediction errors can propagate non-locally through the graph topology, and the failure mode shifts when edges themselves must be predicted rather than being fixed. No prior work has formally analyzed long-horizon rollout error accumulation in graph world models.
AI.method: The authors (1) define a unified GWM framework with action nodes supporting node-, edge-, and graph-level decisions; (2) derive graph-valued rollout error bounds that isolate topology-induced amplification (via spectral properties of the graph operator) from model-induced amplification; (3) introduce a joint node-edge operator for dynamic-edge rollouts; and (4) propose Error-Aware GWM with three components: spectral regularization to control the Lipschitz constant, rollout consistency training to align single-step and multi-step predictions, and critical-node weighting to focus learning on high-impact nodes.
AI.result: On synthetic topologies and heterogeneous agent-graph testbeds, rollout error and planning regret grow with horizon; dynamic-edge training proves essential when graph structure evolves during rollouts. Error-Aware GWM prevents long-horizon divergence without sacrificing single-step prediction accuracy. On real-world benchmarks, GWMs excel at dynamic graph rollout and agent planning but are outperformed by specialized static graph models on stationary or sparse prediction tasks.
AI.conclusion: GWMs offer a principled approach to model-based planning on graphs, with the proposed error-aware techniques effectively controlling compounding errors. Their practical utility is greatest for dynamic, agent-driven graph environments; static graph tasks are better served by dedicated graph learning models.

title: Evolution-Aware Regression Test Prioritization of ML-Enabled Systems Using Gradient-Based Behavior Vectors
comment: Accepted to the 41st IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering (ASE 2026)
summary: The machine learning(ML) component of an ML-enabled system evolves through retraining, fine-tuning, and optimization, so previously valid test results may no longer hold. A single evolution step can worsen performance on some test cases while improving others, making regression test prioritization inherently directional.
