We present Gradient-based Behavior Vector-Parameter Delta(GBV-PD), the first approach to operationalize the behavior vector space for evolution-aware regression test prioritization. GBV-PD represents each test case as a gradient-based vector(GBV), a low-dimensional projection of its loss gradient under the original model. It then projects the observed parameter update of the evolved model onto the same PCA basis and uses the resulting alignment to estimate whether each test case's loss is likely to increase or decrease, without running the evolved model on test cases during prioritization. In an empirical study across classification and regression tasks, GBV-PD consistently outperformed non-directional baselines and remained competitive with a full-gradient reference, while offering better time and storage profiles for repeated updates via reusable GBV caching. These results show that behavior-space ideas can be operationalized into a practical and efficient mechanism for repeated-update regression testing of evolving ML-enabled systems.

AI.tldr: GBV-PD introduces a gradient-based behavior vector approach for evolution-aware regression test prioritization in ML systems. By projecting test case loss gradients and model parameter updates onto a shared PCA basis, it predicts per-test loss directionality (increase/decrease) without executing the evolved model, outperforming non-directional baselines while enabling efficient reusable caching.
AI.motivation: ML-enabled systems undergo frequent evolution (retraining, fine-tuning, optimization), invalidating prior test results. A single evolution step can simultaneously improve some test cases while degrading others, making regression test prioritization inherently directional. Existing approaches lack a practical mechanism that accounts for this directionality without requiring expensive re-execution of the evolved model on all test cases.
AI.method: GBV-PD represents each test case as a Gradient-based Behavior Vector (GBV) — a low-dimensional PCA projection of the loss gradient computed under the original model. When the model evolves, the observed parameter delta is projected onto the same PCA basis. The alignment (inner product) between the test case's GBV and the projected parameter delta estimates whether that test case's loss is likely to increase or decrease, enabling directional prioritization without executing the evolved model. GBVs are cached for reuse across repeated updates.
AI.result: In an empirical study spanning classification and regression tasks, GBV-PD consistently outperformed non-directional baselines and remained competitive with a full-gradient reference method, while offering superior time and storage profiles due to reusable GBV caching.
AI.conclusion: Behavior-vector-space concepts can be operationalized into a practical, efficient mechanism for repeated-update regression testing of evolving ML-enabled systems, providing both directional awareness and computational efficiency.

title: Agent-Native Immune System: Architecture, Taxonomy, and Engineering
summary: The transition from static chat bots to autonomous agents--equipped with persistent memory, tool-use protocols, and multi-agent collaboration--has fundamentally expanded the AI threat landscape. Current defense mechanisms, such as perimeter security and training-time alignment, remain external to the agent's active reasoning loop. Consequently, they fall short: a fully aligned agent remains highly vulnerable to runtime hijacking via memory poisoning, tool-chain manipulation, or multi-agent protocol attacks. To address this critical gap, we introduce the Agent-Native Immune System (ANIS), the first biologically inspired, endogenous defense architecture embedded directly within the agent's cognitive loop. Our framework presents four primary contributions. First, we design a six-layer Immune Tower (L0-L5), distinctly incorporating Barrier Immunity (L1) as a non-cognitive, physical-and-logical isolation layer. Second, we establish a unified taxonomy of Agent Viruses and Agent Vaccines, formalizing the critical distinction between superficial non-parametric defenses and robust parametric vaccines. Third, we conceptualize the Harness Triad--Meta, Self, and Auto--a self-monitoring, meta-cognitive automation backbone that drives Continual Immune Learning (CIL), enabling vaccines to dynamically adapt to novel threats. Finally, we establish a rigorous theoretical demarcation between model alignment and agent immunity: while alignment provides a static "constitutional" value foundation during training, ANIS serves as the dynamic "law enforcement" mechanism during runtime. We conclude by framing open challenges for the field, including immune protocol standardization, novel evaluation metrics such as the Autoimmunity Rate (false-positive intervention rate), and the co-evolutionary dynamics between pathogens and vaccines within collective intelligence ecosystems.

AI.tldr: ANIS is a biologically inspired, endogenous defense architecture embedded within an agent's cognitive loop, featuring a six-layer Immune Tower, a formal taxonomy of Agent Viruses/Vaccines, and a Harness Triad for Continual Immune Learning, positioning agent immunity as runtime "law enforcement" distinct from static training-time alignment.
AI.motivation: Current AI defense mechanisms (perimeter security, training-time alignment) operate outside the agent's active reasoning loop, leaving aligned agents vulnerable to runtime attacks such as memory poisoning, tool-chain manipulation, and multi-agent protocol exploits. No existing framework provides endogenous, in-loop immunity.
AI.method: The authors propose ANIS with four components: (1) a six-layer Immune Tower (L0-L5) with Barrier Immunity (L1) as a non-cognitive isolation layer; (2) a unified taxonomy distinguishing Agent Viruses from parametric/non-parametric Agent Vaccines; (3) the Harness Triad (Meta, Self, Auto) driving Continual Immune Learning (CIL) for dynamic adaptation; and (4) a theoretical demarcation between static alignment (constitutional foundation) and dynamic immunity (runtime enforcement).
AI.result: The paper delivers a conceptual architecture and theoretical framework rather than empirical results. Key constructs include the Immune Tower taxonomy, the virus/vaccine formalism, the CIL mechanism, and the alignment-vs-immunity distinction. It also identifies open challenges: immune protocol standardization, Autoimmunity Rate metrics, and pathogen-vaccine co-evolutionary dynamics.
AI.conclusion: ANIS redefines AI safety by shifting defense from external, static mechanisms to an internal, adaptive immune system operating within the agent's cognitive loop, and calls for standardization, novel evaluation metrics, and study of co-evolutionary dynamics in multi-agent ecosystems.

title: Narrative-UFET: Narrative Generation for Ultra-Fine Entity Typing
summary: Ultra-fine entity typing (UFET) assigns highly specific types to entity mentions, but current approaches struggle with types in the long tail. We hypothesize that a key limitation is the reliance on sentence-level context, since disambiguating evidence is often spread across multiple sentences. Testing this has been difficult because all existing UFET resources are sentence-level. We present Narrative-UFET, a controlled extension of UFET in which each entity mention is paired with an automatically generated short, coherent narrative. Synthesizing narratives lets us isolate the effect of specific discourse properties. We experiment with two paired variants: one in which the entity's type is held constant across the narrative (Maintain) and one in which it shifts (Change). We show that narrative context yields consistent improvements on long-tail types over sentence-level baselines, with the Change variant providing the stronger signal. A comparison against naturally occurring contexts shows that synthetic narratives yield stronger gains, indicating that controlled discourse construction can surface signals that real text leaves implicit. Substantial room for improvement remains, suggesting open directions in both discourse modeling and narrative construction.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Narrative-UFET, a benchmark that pairs entity mentions with synthetic narratives to study how discourse-level context improves ultra-fine entity typing, especially for long-tail types. It finds that multi-sentence narratives consistently outperform sentence-level baselines, with type-shifting narratives providing the strongest signal, and that synthetic narratives can surface signals that naturally occurring text leaves implicit.
AI.motivation: Current UFET approaches rely on sentence-level context and struggle with long-tail types. The authors hypothesize that disambiguating evidence is often spread across multiple sentences, but testing this has been impossible because all existing UFET resources are sentence-level. They aim to isolate the effect of discourse-level properties on entity typing.
AI.method: The authors construct Narrative-UFET by automatically generating short, coherent narratives for each entity mention. They create two controlled variants: Maintain (entity type held constant across the narrative) and Change (entity type shifts). These synthetic narratives allow controlled manipulation of discourse properties, enabling comparison against sentence-level baselines and naturally occurring contexts.
AI.result: Narrative context yields consistent improvements on long-tail types over sentence-level baselines. The Change variant provides a stronger typing signal than Maintain. Synthetic narratives produce stronger gains than naturally occurring contexts, indicating controlled discourse construction surfaces signals implicit in real text. Substantial room for improvement remains.
AI.conclusion: Discourse-level context significantly benefits UFET for long-tail types. Controlled narrative synthesis is an effective method for isolating discourse effects, and the Change condition (type shift) is particularly informative. The work opens directions in both discourse modeling and narrative construction for entity typing.

title: AdvancedShelLM: A Stateful Multi-Agent LLM Honeypot for SSH Deception
summary: LLM-based SSH honeypots can generate believable interactions, but evaluations indicate they remain somewhat identifiable to determined attackers, indicating the need for a better scaffolding. We present a new LLM-based honeypot design that uses a multi-agent, multi-LLM architecture to address the limitations of the previous shelLM LLM honeypot. Our honeypot, called AdvancedShelLM, uses two LLM agents, a Manager and a Worker, that better understand the commands while reducing incorrect responses and increasing deception. It implements an advanced permanent filesystem, allowing many simultaneous attackers to see the same changing files for the first time. It was evaluated with: (i) unit tests for generative capabilities, (ii) an AI attacker (ARACNE) to assess realism and deception, (iii) human attackers to assess its deceptive capability, and (iv) an Internet deployment to evaluate deception in real-world attacks. In unit test results, AdvancedShelLM achieved a pass rate of up to 99.02%. The AI attacker ARACNE had issues making a decision if the system is honeypot or not, but showed slight bias towards saying honeypot, even for a real Ubuntu shell. With human attackers, AdvancedShelLM deceived more humans than Cowrie, but had similar results as shelLM. The Internet deployment showed concrete evidence that the output of AdvancedShelLM can influence the behaviour of real-life attackers.

AI.tldr: AdvancedShelLM is a multi-agent, multi-LLM SSH honeypot that improves upon shelLM by using Manager-Worker agents and a shared persistent filesystem, achieving 99.02% unit test pass rate and demonstrating effective deception against both AI and human attackers in lab and real-world deployments.
AI.motivation: Previous LLM-based SSH honeypots like shelLM produce believable interactions but remain identifiable to determined attackers. A better scaffolding is needed to reduce incorrect responses, improve command understanding, and enhance deception, particularly by supporting multi-attacker scenarios with consistent state.
AI.method: AdvancedShelLM employs a dual-agent architecture (Manager and Worker LLMs) to parse commands and generate responses more accurately. It introduces an advanced permanent filesystem enabling multiple simultaneous attackers to observe consistent, changing file state. Evaluation used four approaches: (i) unit tests for generative quality, (ii) the ARACNE AI attacker for realism assessment, (iii) human attacker studies comparing against Cowrie and shelLM, and (iv) live Internet deployment to observe real attacker behavior.
AI.result: Unit tests yielded up to 99.02% pass rate. ARACNE struggled to definitively classify the system, showing slight honeypot bias even against real Ubuntu shells. Human studies showed AdvancedShelLM deceived more attackers than Cowrie, with deception rates comparable to shelLM. Internet deployment confirmed the honeypot's output tangibly influenced real attacker behavior.
AI.conclusion: The multi-agent, multi-LLM design with a shared persistent filesystem improves command interpretation and reduces errors, though deception rates remain similar to shelLM against humans. The architecture represents a meaningful step toward more resilient, scalable LLM-based honeypots but still exhibits identifiable characteristics that warrant further refinement.

title: Productionized Fairness Measurement Under Privacy Constraints
summary: Fairness measurements in the form of disaggregated evaluations often rely on demographic signals that are legally constrained or culturally sensitive. Race and ethnicity signals are among the more difficult signals to curate and use for this task. This paper presents Privacy-Preserving Probabilistic Race/Ethnicity Estimation (PPRE) as a method for enabling fairness measurements with respect to race/ethnicity for U.S.\ LinkedIn members in a privacy-preserving manner. PPRE applies privacy technologies (specifically: secure two-party computation, differential privacy, and additive homomorphic encryption) on top of two race/ethnicity demographic signal sources (the Bayesian Improved Surname Geocoding estimator and a sparse golden survey set of self-reported demographics) to power a fairness measurement solution with respect to US-based race/ethnicity demographics. We detail its privacy guarantees and demonstrate its application on candidate- and viewer-side fairness measurements. We close with a transferable framework for institutions seeking to implement similar privacy-preserving measurement infrastructure.

AI.tldr: LinkedIn introduces PPRE, a privacy-preserving method that combines Bayesian Improved Surname Geocoding with self-reported survey data, secured by differential privacy, secure two-party computation, and additive homomorphic encryption, enabling race/ethnicity-based fairness measurements on their platform without exposing individual demographic signals.
AI.motivation: Fairness evaluations in algorithmic systems require disaggregated demographic data, but race and ethnicity signals are legally constrained, culturally sensitive, and difficult to curate. Organizations need a method to perform fairness measurements without directly collecting or exposing protected demographic attributes.
AI.method: PPRE integrates two demographic signal sources: the Bayesian Improved Surname Geocoding (BISG) estimator (probabilistic race/ethnicity inference from surname and geography) and a sparse golden survey set of self-reported race/ethnicity. Three privacy technologies are layered on top: (1) secure two-party computation to keep signals split across parties, (2) differential privacy to bound information leakage from outputs, and (3) additive homomorphic encryption to enable computation over encrypted data. The system is applied to U.S. LinkedIn members for candidate-side and viewer-side fairness measurements.
AI.result: The paper demonstrates successful implementation of PPRE for fairness measurements on LinkedIn's platform, providing formal privacy guarantees while enabling both candidate-side (e.g., job applicants) and viewer-side (e.g., content consumers) disaggregated fairness evaluations with respect to U.S. race/ethnicity demographics.
AI.conclusion: PPRE offers a transferable framework for institutions that need to conduct fairness measurements with respect to sensitive demographic signals like race/ethnicity while complying with privacy constraints and regulations. The approach balances measurement utility with rigorous privacy protections.

title: Grounded Iterative Language Planning: How Parameterized World Models Reduce Hallucination Propagation in LLM Agents
summary: World models for language agents come in two useful forms. An agent-based world model calls an LLM API and reasons flexibly in language, but its errors appear as hallucinated state changes that are hard to score with ordinary regression losses. A parameterized world model is a trained transition predictor; its errors are easier to measure with quantities such as NodeMSE, delta accuracy, and validity accuracy, but it is usually weaker as a standalone planner. We compare these two families on four graph-structured planning benchmarks and introduce operational hallucination metrics for the agent-based case. The comparison motivates \textbf{Grounded Iterative Language Planning} (GILP), which trains only a small parameterized backbone and combines it with API-based agent reasoning. The backbone supplies valid actions, predicted state deltas, risk, and value; the LLM drafts an action and imagined delta; and a consistency gate asks for revision when the two disagree. On real GPT-4o-mini calls, GILP reduces hallucinated-state rate from 0.176 to 0.035. In calibrated simulator ablations, it raises success from 0.668 to 0.838 while adding only ~22% extra LLM calls.

AI.tldr: This paper compares agent-based and parameterized world models for language agents, introduces hallucination metrics for agent-based models, and proposes Grounded Iterative Language Planning (GILP), which combines a small trained backbone with LLM reasoning to reduce hallucination rates and improve planning success.
AI.motivation: Agent-based world models (LLM-driven) offer flexible reasoning but suffer from hallucinated state changes that are difficult to quantify. Parameterized world models provide measurable errors but are weaker planners. The paper seeks to understand this trade-off and develop a hybrid approach that captures the strengths of both families while mitigating their weaknesses.
AI.method: The authors compare both world model families on four graph-structured planning benchmarks, introducing operational hallucination metrics for the agent-based case. They then propose GILP: a small parameterized backbone is trained to supply valid actions, predicted state deltas, risk, and value estimates. An LLM drafts actions and imagined deltas, and a consistency gate triggers revision when the backbone and LLM disagree. The approach is evaluated on real GPT-4o-mini API calls and in calibrated simulator ablations.
AI.result: GILP reduces the hallucinated-state rate from 0.176 to 0.035 on real GPT-4o-mini calls. In calibrated simulator experiments, success rate improves from 0.668 to 0.838 with only ~22% additional LLM calls.
AI.conclusion: Combining a lightweight parameterized world model backbone with LLM-based reasoning via a consistency gate effectively reduces hallucinations and boosts planning performance, offering a practical and efficient hybrid approach for grounded language planning.

title: SBridge: Identifying Source-to-Binary Function Similarity via Cross-Domain Control Block Matching
summary: We present SBridge, a precise approach for identifying functions in binaries that are similar to the given source code functions. Identifying reused code in binaries is critical for security, particularly for detecting propagated vulnerabilities. Although binary-to-binary comparison is feasible, leveraging source code as the reference is more practical because source code is easier to collect and analyze directly without compilation. However, significant gaps between source and binary representations, including function inlining, create challenges in cross-domain function detection. Existing approaches primarily rely on string literals or structural similarities between entire functions, failing to capture detailed code behavior and generating many false alarms. SBridge addresses these limitations through a key innovation: control block-based function matching, which encapsulates essential functional features by segmenting functions into meaningful units such as conditionals and loops. Leveraging control blocks as a cross-domain representation, SBridge enables precise measurement of function similarity between source and binary code, effectively overcoming challenges posed by function inlining and stripped binaries. For evaluation, we collected 3,904 real-world C/C++ binaries from BinKit. In experiments identifying binary functions identical to input source functions, despite approximately 40% of binary functions being inlined, SBridge achieved 75.13% recall@1 and 80.98% recall@5, outperforming existing approaches, which achieved up to 43.31% recall@1 and 50.2% recall@

AI.tldr: SBridge is a cross-domain (source-to-binary) function matching approach that uses control blocks (conditionals, loops) as an intermediate representation to precisely identify reused functions, achieving 75.13% recall@1 and 80.98% recall@5 despite ~40% inlining rates.
AI.motivation: Detecting propagated vulnerabilities requires identifying reused code in binaries. Source code is easier to collect and analyze than binary-to-binary comparison, but cross-domain matching is hard due to gaps like function inlining and stripped binaries. Existing methods relying on string literals or whole-function structural similarity produce many false alarms and miss inlined functions.
AI.method: SBridge introduces control block-based function matching: both source and binary functions are segmented into meaningful control blocks (conditionals, loops, etc.) that encapsulate essential functional features. These control blocks serve as a cross-domain intermediate representation, enabling precise similarity measurement that is robust to function inlining and symbol stripping.
AI.result: Evaluated on 3,904 real-world C/C++ binaries from BinKit, with ~40% of binary functions inlined, SBridge achieved 75.13% recall@1 and 80.98% recall@5, significantly outperforming prior approaches (43.31% recall@1 and 50.2% recall@5).
AI.conclusion: Control block-based matching effectively bridges the semantic gap between source and binary code, overcoming inlining and stripping challenges. SBridge sets a new state-of-the-art for cross-domain function identification, enabling more accurate detection of propagated vulnerabilities in real-world binaries.

title: Democratic ICAI: Debating Our Way to Steering Principles from Preferences
comment: Accepeted to the ICLR 2026 HCAIR Workshop, 40 pages
summary: Preference-based alignment often struggles to capture the reasoning that underlies human judgments. Many evaluations rely on multiple interacting criteria, yet pairwise labels reveal only the final choice rather than the considerations that shape preferences. Inverse Constitutional AI (ICAI) improves interpretability in decision making by summarizing preferences into natural-language principles, but its single-pass explanations miss much of the nuance involved in complex decisions. We introduce Democratic ICAI, a novel approach that gathers multiple competing rationales through structured persona debate, offering a broader and more expressive account of the factors influencing each comparison. From these richer signals, we derive clearer and more comprehensive steering principles and use them to guide decision modeling through both LLM-based and decision-tree judges. Experiments on creative preference benchmarks, MuCE-Pref and LiTBench, across multiple creative task categories show that Democratic ICAI yields a more faithful preference structure. It improves average preference prediction across tasks relative to deliberative prompting and principle-based baselines, while producing constitutions that LLM annotators prefer.

AI.tldr: Democratic ICAI enhances interpretability in preference alignment by using structured persona debates to gather multiple competing rationales for human judgments, then distills these into clearer steering principles. It outperforms deliberative prompting and principle-based baselines on creative preference benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Preference-based alignment methods typically capture only binary choices without the underlying reasoning. Inverse Constitutional AI (ICAI) attempts to extract natural-language principles, but its single-pass explanations lack the nuance required for complex, multi-criteria decisions. There is a need for richer, more expressive accounts of the factors driving human preferences.
AI.method: Democratic ICAI introduces structured persona debates where multiple competing rationales are gathered for each pairwise comparison. From these richer signals, clearer and more comprehensive steering principles are derived. These principles guide decision modeling through both LLM-based and decision-tree judges.
AI.result: On creative preference benchmarks (MuCE-Pref and LiTBench) across multiple creative task categories, Democratic ICAI yields more faithful preference structures. It improves average preference prediction relative to deliberative prompting and principle-based baselines, while also producing constitutions that LLM annotators prefer.
AI.conclusion: Democratic ICAI provides a more faithful and interpretable preference alignment framework by capturing diverse rationales through debate, leading to better preference predictions and more human-preferred constitutions than prior single-pass approaches.

title: Masked Language Flow Models
summary: Masked Diffusion Models (MDMs) promise fast, parallel language generation, but their reverse transition factorises across token positions -- an approximation that breaks down in the few-step sampling regime where parallel generation ought to provide the greatest efficiency gains. Flow Language Models (FLMs) sidestep this limitation by learning a continuous flow that transports noise toward clean sequences represented in Euclidean space, inducing a flow map that can be distilled for single-step generation. However, this makes complex tasks requiring multi-step reasoning problematic for FLMs, as FLMs are forced to decode every token during generation. To address this, we introduce Masked Language Flow Models (MLFMs), which incorporate masking into FLMs using a continuous stochastic interpolant to bridge partially masked and clean sequences. This design enables conditional generation via continuous flows and allows pretrained MDMs to be converted into MLFMs through a simple, lightweight adaptation. Leveraging this flexibility, we propose a novel sampler that alternates continuous denoising with the discrete unmasking of confident tokens to better support multi-step reasoning. We evaluate our approach on GSM8K and MT-Bench and find, for the first time, that flow-based language models can be scaled to solve downstream reasoning and instruction-following tasks.

AI.tldr: Masked Language Flow Models (MLFMs) integrate masking into continuous flow language models via a stochastic interpolant bridging masked and clean sequences. This enables conditional generation, allows lightweight conversion of pretrained MDMs, and supports a hybrid sampler alternating continuous denoising with discrete unmasking for multi-step reasoning, achieving state-of-the-art results on reasoning benchmarks.
AI.motivation: MDMs are fast but their token-wise independent reverse transition factorisation fails in few-step regimes. FLMs enable single-step distillation via continuous flows but struggle with multi-step reasoning since they must decode all tokens simultaneously. The goal is to unify the strengths of both paradigms — continuous flows with iterative unmasking — for efficient, reasoning-capable language generation.
AI.method: The authors propose MLFMs, which define a continuous stochastic interpolant between partially masked sequences and clean sequences in Euclidean embedding space. This formulation supports conditional generation via continuous flows. A lightweight adaptation procedure converts pretrained MDMs into MLFMs. A novel hybrid sampler alternates between continuous flow-based denoising steps and discrete unmasking of high-confidence tokens, enabling iterative refinement suited to multi-step reasoning.
AI.result: MLFMs are evaluated on GSM8K (math reasoning) and MT-Bench (instruction following), demonstrating for the first time that flow-based language models can scale to solve downstream reasoning and instruction-following tasks.
AI.conclusion: MLFMs successfully bridge masked and flow-based language modeling paradigms, combining the efficiency of continuous flows with the iterative refinement capability of masking. This enables flow-based models to tackle complex reasoning tasks and opens the door to converting existing MDMs into more capable flow-based architectures.

title: Ghost Without Shell: Measuring Non-Interactive SSH Attacks on Honeypots
summary: Cyber deception research has focused on improving honeypot deception capabilities to increase attacker engagement and extend their interactions to collect more and better intelligence. For SSH honeypots, this relies on the assumption that attackers log in, open a shell, and type. We tested whether this still held by deploying eleven SSH honeypots that served both interactive and non-interactive session requests for fifteen days. We collected 177,622 authenticated sessions and validated our results against an independent Cowrie dataset over the same time window. We found that 99.23% of sessions were non-interactive. Interactive sessions account for only 0.10%. The same pattern held in the comparative third-party dataset used for evaluation. This finding is important because a honeypot that focuses on interactive shells or evaluates success based on session length and the number of commands can miss most authenticated attacks and draw the wrong conclusions about what attackers do after login.

AI.tldr: This paper challenges a foundational assumption in SSH honeypot design — that attackers log in and interactively type commands. Through a large-scale deployment of eleven honeypots, the authors found that 99.23% of authenticated sessions are non-interactive, with interactive shells comprising only 0.10%, suggesting current honeypot metrics may misrepresent attacker behavior.
AI.motivation: Cyber deception research has heavily invested in improving the interactive deception capabilities of SSH honeypots, operating under the assumption that attackers establish shells and type commands. The authors questioned whether this assumption still holds empirically and aimed to test it through real-world deployment.
AI.method: The authors deployed eleven SSH honeypots over a 15-day period, configured to serve both interactive shell sessions and non-interactive session requests (e.g., SCP, SFTP, port forwarding, command execution without a full shell). They collected 177,622 authenticated sessions and categorized them as interactive or non-interactive. Results were validated against an independent, contemporaneous Cowrie dataset as a comparative benchmark.
AI.result: 99.23% of all authenticated sessions were non-interactive. Interactive shell sessions constituted only 0.10% of the total. This distribution was corroborated by the independent Cowrie dataset, confirming the pattern is not an artifact of the authors' honeypot configuration.
AI.conclusion: Honeypots that exclusively focus on interactive shells — or evaluate effectiveness using session length and command counts — risk missing the vast majority of authenticated attacks and may draw erroneous conclusions about post-login attacker behavior. The community should reconsider how SSH honeypot success is measured and what attacker activity is prioritized for observation.

title: Quantum Generative Diffusion Model for Real-World Time Series
summary: Generative models have achieved remarkable success in data synthesis, though recent advances driven by increasing model scale have introduced challenges in computational cost and efficiency. Quantum machine learning offers a promising alternative, representing complex data distributions using compact, highly expressive models. Here, we propose QDiffusion-TS, the first quantum generative diffusion model for time series synthesis, and validate it on the IQM quantum processor. The framework extends a classical diffusion architecture by replacing feed-forward components within the denoising transformer with quantum neural networks, yielding a hybrid quantum transformer that reduces the number of trainable parameters in each replaced component by nearly three orders of magnitude. Evaluated on financial time series from Apple and Amazon, the model generates synthetic data that more accurately reproduces the real distributions, reducing Wasserstein distance by approximately 44% relative to its classical counterpart across both datasets. In a downstream forecasting task, augmentation with the generated data improves predictive performance by up to 71% in RMSE over a baseline trained solely on real data. These results show that quantum enhanced architectures can consistently match and frequently surpass classical performance with substantially fewer parameters, establishing a practical framework towards more efficient and scalable data-driven generative modelling.

AI.tldr: QDiffusion-TS introduces a hybrid quantum-classical diffusion model for time series synthesis, replacing feed-forward layers in a denoising transformer with quantum neural networks. This reduces trainable parameters by ~1000× while improving distribution fidelity (44% lower Wasserstein distance) and downstream forecasting performance (up to 71% RMSE improvement).
AI.motivation: Generative models are scaling up rapidly, incurring prohibitive computational costs. Quantum machine learning offers compact, highly expressive parameterizations that could mitigate this efficiency bottleneck while maintaining or improving generative quality.
AI.method: The authors propose QDiffusion-TS, a hybrid quantum diffusion model for time series. It extends a classical denoising diffusion transformer by substituting feed-forward components with quantum neural networks (variational quantum circuits), resulting in a hybrid quantum transformer. The model is validated on the IQM quantum processor using financial time series data (Apple, Amazon).
AI.result: The quantum-enhanced model reduces trainable parameters in each replaced component by nearly three orders of magnitude. It lowers Wasserstein distance by ~44% compared to its classical counterpart across both datasets. In a downstream forecasting task, synthetic data augmentation improves RMSE by up to 71% over a baseline trained only on real data.
AI.conclusion: Quantum-enhanced architectures can match or surpass classical performance with substantially fewer parameters, establishing a practical and scalable framework for efficient data-driven generative modelling.

title: ATOD: Annealed Turn-aware On-policy Distillation for Multi-turn Autonomous Agents
summary: Training small language-model agents for long-horizon interactive tasks requires both fast imitation and reward-driven improvement. On-policy distillation (OPD) provides dense teacher guidance and typically improves rapidly in the early stage, but its gains saturate once the student approaches the teacher, limiting the final performance ceiling. Reinforcement learning (RL) directly optimizes environment rewards and encourages exploratory improvement toward a higher reward-defined ceiling, but sparse and delayed feedback makes early-stage learning much less efficient than OPD. In this paper, we propose ATOD (Annealed Turn-aware On-policy Distillation), a hybrid online distillation algorithm that explicitly exploits this complementarity. (1) ATOD uses an annealed OPD-RL schedule: OPD dominates early training to approach teacher-level behavior, while RL is gradually strengthened to drive reward-based exploration. (2) ATOD introduces Turn-level Disagreement-Uncertainty Reweighting (T-DUR), which softly amplifies high-utility turns and improves dense supervision in long trajectories. Experiments on ALFWorld, WebShop, and Search-QA show that ATOD consistently outperforms competing post-training baselines: across the three student sizes, ATOD improves average success rate by 3.03 points over OPD and 23.62 points over GRPO, while surpassing the corresponding teacher models by 2.16 points.

AI.tldr: ATOD is a hybrid online distillation algorithm that combines annealed on-policy distillation (OPD) with reinforcement learning (RL), using a turn-level disagreement-uncertainty reweighting mechanism. It outperforms both pure OPD and RL baselines, surpassing teacher models on ALFWorld, WebShop, and Search-QA.
AI.motivation: On-policy distillation provides fast early improvement but saturates near teacher performance; RL enables higher reward ceilings but suffers from sparse/delayed feedback early on. Existing approaches fail to exploit the complementary strengths of these two training paradigms for small language-model agents on long-horizon interactive tasks.
AI.method: ATOD combines two innovations: (1) an annealed OPD-RL schedule where OPD dominates early training and RL is gradually strengthened; (2) Turn-level Disagreement-Uncertainty Reweighting (T-DUR), which softly amplifies high-utility turns to improve dense supervision in long trajectories.
AI.result: Across three student sizes on ALFWorld, WebShop, and Search-QA, ATOD improves average success rate by 3.03 points over OPD, 23.62 points over GRPO, and surpasses teacher models by 2.16 points.
AI.conclusion: ATOD effectively bridges the gap between imitation-based distillation and reward-driven RL, achieving both rapid early improvement and a high final performance ceiling that exceeds the teacher models.

title: The ARDoCo Tool Landscape: REST API, TraceView, and TraceViz for Architecture Traceability
comment: Accepted at ASE'26 Tools and Datasets
summary: Context and Problem. Software development produces interrelated artifacts like software architecture documentation (SAD), software architecture models (SAMs), and source code, whose relationships are essential for maintenance and consistency checking. However, automatically recovering links between these artifacts (traceability link recovery (TLR)) remains difficult to deploy in practice. Method and Aim. We present an accessible tool landscape for ARDoCo's TLR approaches: the ARDoCo REST API exposes four TLR pipelines (SAD-SAM, SAM-Code, SAD-Code, and SAD-SAM-Code) via HTTP endpoints with asynchronous execution and caching; TraceView is a browser-based frontend with a guided wizard and interactive multi-panel exploration of recovered links and inconsistencies; and TraceViz, which is a VS Code extension that overlays trace links directly onto documentation in the IDE. Results and Conclusion. All three components are publicly deployed and usable. A preliminary study for TraceViz's in-IDE visualization confirmed that it improves developer comprehension during software understanding tasks. The tool landscape makes state-of-the-art TLR accessible to architects, developers, and tool integrators. Video. We provide a screencast of our ARDoCo Tool Landscape and how it is used here: https://youtu.be/IOTEPZQ3tVs

AI.tldr: ARDoCo provides a tool landscape (REST API, browser frontend TraceView, and VS Code extension TraceViz) that makes traceability link recovery between software architecture documentation, models, and source code accessible and deployable, with preliminary evidence that in-IDE visualization improves developer comprehension.
AI.motivation: Automatically recovering traceability links between software artifacts (SAD, SAM, source code) is essential for maintenance and consistency checking, yet existing TLR approaches remain difficult to deploy in practice. The work aims to bridge this gap by making state-of-the-art TLR accessible.
AI.method: The authors present three integrated components: (1) ARDoCo REST API exposing four TLR pipelines (SAD-SAM, SAM-Code, SAD-Code, SAD-SAM-Code) via HTTP with asynchronous execution and caching; (2) TraceView, a browser-based frontend with a guided wizard and interactive multi-panel exploration of recovered links and inconsistencies; and (3) TraceViz, a VS Code extension that overlays trace links directly onto documentation in the IDE. A preliminary user study evaluated TraceViz's impact on developer comprehension.
AI.result: All three components are publicly deployed and usable. The preliminary study confirmed that TraceViz's in-IDE visualization improves developer comprehension during software understanding tasks.
AI.conclusion: The ARDoCo tool landscape successfully makes state-of-the-art traceability link recovery accessible to architects, developers, and tool integrators, lowering the barrier to practical TLR deployment.

title: Cross-Platform Chinese Offensive Comment Detection via Dual-Threshold Hard Example Mining
summary: Cross-platform deployment of offensive comment detection for Chinese social media suffers performance degradation. The paper proposes a dual-threshold hard mining method to address this. First, the clean-Chinese-base RoBERTa is finetuned on COLD to establish a binary baseline for fair comparison. Second, a three-class fine-labeled test set covering Weibo, Xiaohongshu, Tieba, and Zhihu is constructed, domain distances from the source are quantified using Jaccard and Proxy-A Distance, as well as the degradation bottleneck of the baseline under domain shift is systematically revealed. Herein, a dual threshold hard example mining strategy is proposed. High- and low-confidence error-prone samples are filtered from unlabeled corpora by prediction confidence. The model is secondarily finetuned under implicit contexts with merely a small set of manually labeled hard examples, realizing low-cost cross-platform domain adaptation. Experiments reveal significant performance gains of the optimized model across four platforms.

AI.tldr: A dual-threshold hard example mining method is proposed for low-cost cross-platform domain adaptation of Chinese offensive comment detection, using secondary fine-tuning on error-prone samples to mitigate performance degradation across social media platforms.
AI.motivation: Cross-platform deployment of Chinese offensive comment detection models suffers significant performance degradation due to domain shift. Existing approaches lack a systematic understanding of this degradation bottleneck, and low-cost adaptation methods are needed to avoid expensive full re-labeling for each target platform.
AI.method: Clean-Chinese-base RoBERTa is fine-tuned on the COLD dataset as a binary classification baseline. A three-class fine-labeled test set is constructed spanning Weibo, Xiaohongshu, Tieba, and Zhihu. Domain distances from the source are quantified using Jaccard distance and Proxy-A Distance to systematically reveal degradation under domain shift. The core contribution is a dual-threshold hard example mining strategy: high-confidence and low-confidence error-prone samples are filtered from unlabeled target corpora based on prediction confidence, then the model undergoes secondary fine-tuning using only a small set of manually labeled hard examples under implicit contexts, achieving low-cost domain adaptation.
AI.result: Experiments demonstrate significant performance gains of the optimized model across all four platforms (Weibo, Xiaohongshu, Tieba, Zhihu), validating the effectiveness of the dual-threshold hard mining strategy for cross-platform adaptation.
AI.conclusion: The dual-threshold hard example mining method effectively addresses cross-platform domain shift in Chinese offensive comment detection at low labeling cost, offering a practical solution for real-world multi-platform deployment.

title: ToolPrivacyBench: Benchmarking Purpose-Bound Privacy in Tool-Using LLM Agents
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have increasingly moved from standalone text generation systems to agents that invoke external tools, access environments, and execute multi-step tasks. However, conventional function-calling benchmarks mainly evaluate task completion and API correctness, while privacy evaluation benchmarks typically focus on final responses or privacy judgments. Neither perspective captures purpose-bound information flow across an executed multi-tool trajectory. Motivated by this limitation in current agent evaluation, ToolPrivacyBench audits whether task-private atoms are routed only to authorized tools and downstream sinks, thereby evaluating both task completion and privacy over-disclosure during tool use. The benchmark contains 2,150 cases, including 1,150 fully synthetic privacy-sensitive business workflows and 1,000 cases adapted from existing multi-tool and function-calling benchmarks. Each case is represented by a policy knowledge base. After an agent executes against mock business backends, the evaluator compares recorded tool arguments and backend audit logs with this policy knowledge base. The evaluation covers nine widely used agents to characterize purpose-bound privacy over-disclosure. The results show that successful tool execution does not imply appropriate privacy disclosure: an agent may complete a task while transmitting unnecessary private information through intermediate tool calls. ToolPrivacyBench therefore formalizes a need-to-know disclosure boundary, under which each tool should receive only the information necessary for its stated purpose, and uses trajectory-level auditing to identify privacy over-disclosure in multi-tool workflows.

AI.tldr: ToolPrivacyBench is a benchmark auditing whether LLM agents disclose task-private information only to authorized tools during multi-step workflows, using 2,150 cases and trajectory-level policy enforcement to reveal that task completion does not guarantee appropriate privacy disclosure.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks evaluate either task completion/API correctness (function-calling benchmarks) or final-response privacy (privacy benchmarks), but neither captures purpose-bound information flow across an entire multi-tool trajectory. This gap motivates auditing whether private atoms are routed only to authorized tools and sinks during execution.
AI.method: ToolPrivacyBench contains 2,150 cases: 1,150 synthetic privacy-sensitive business workflows and 1,000 adapted from existing benchmarks. Each case has a policy knowledge base specifying which tools are authorized to receive which private information. Agents execute against mock business backends; tool arguments and backend audit logs are compared against the policy knowledge base to detect privacy over-disclosure at the trajectory level.
AI.result: Evaluation across nine widely used agents shows that successful tool execution does not imply appropriate privacy disclosure — agents frequently complete tasks while transmitting unnecessary private information through intermediate tool calls.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark formalizes a need-to-know disclosure boundary where each tool should receive only information necessary for its stated purpose. Trajectory-level auditing effectively identifies privacy over-disclosure in multi-tool workflows, highlighting a critical gap in current agent evaluation.

title: hia-gat: A Heterogeneous Interaction-Aware Graph Attention Network For Frame-Level Traffic Conflict Risk Prediction On Freeways
summary: This paper formulates frame-level freeway risk assessment as a multi-agent scene graph-level binary classification problem, where each video or trajectory frame is labeled risky if any TTC- or PET-based conflict violates a specified severity threshold. We construct a relation-aware graph per frame with vehicles as nodes and two interaction types as edges: same-lane (longitudinal) and adjacent-lane (lateral), augmented with physics-informed edge features aligned to rear-end and lane-change conflict mechanisms. Building on a structured benchmarking suite of non-graph models and graph baselines, we propose HIA-GAT, a dual-stream heterogeneous graph attention network that processes longitudinal and lateral interactions through dedicated attention pathways and fuses them via a conflict-type-aware gating mechanism with event-level gate supervision derived from SSM conflict attribution. Experiments on the NGSIM I-80 and US-101 freeway datasets across nine TTC and PET threshold configurations show that HIA-GAT achieves the best average risk-ranking performance (AUC 0.835 on I-80 and 0.867 on US-101), with the largest gains on PET-only (lane-change) settings where relational structure is essential. Beyond accuracy, the learned gate provides interpretable per-vehicle attribution of dominant conflict type, supporting actionable, real-time freeway safety monitoring. We show that graph structure is critical for modeling lateral conflict risk, while longitudinal risk can often be captured by non-relational aggregation.

AI.tldr: Proposes HIA-GAT, a dual-stream heterogeneous graph attention network for frame-level freeway risk assessment that processes longitudinal and lateral vehicle interactions through dedicated attention pathways with a gating mechanism, achieving top AUC on NGSIM datasets and providing interpretable conflict-type attribution.
AI.motivation: Existing methods struggle to model both longitudinal (rear-end) and lateral (lane-change) conflict types jointly in freeway risk assessment. Graph-based approaches are underutilized, and the relative importance of relational structure for different conflict types is unclear.
AI.method: Formulates risk assessment as multi-agent scene graph binary classification. Constructs relation-aware graphs with vehicles as nodes and two edge types (same-lane longitudinal, adjacent-lane lateral) with physics-informed edge features. Proposes HIA-GAT: a dual-stream heterogeneous graph attention network with dedicated attention pathways per interaction type and a conflict-type-aware gating mechanism supervised by SSM-based conflict attribution. Benchmarked against non-graph and graph baselines on NGSIM I-80 and US-101 across nine TTC/PET threshold configurations.
AI.result: HIA-GAT achieves best average AUC of 0.835 on I-80 and 0.867 on US-101. Largest gains occur in PET-only (lane-change) settings where relational structure is essential. Longitudinal risk can often be captured without graph structure, while lateral conflict modeling critically depends on it. The learned gate provides interpretable per-vehicle conflict-type attribution.
AI.conclusion: Graph structure is critical for modeling lateral conflict risk but less necessary for longitudinal risk. HIA-GAT's dual-stream heterogeneous design with gated fusion effectively captures both conflict types and offers interpretable, actionable outputs for real-time freeway safety monitoring.

title: NormAct: A Benchmark for Hidden Social Norm Compliance in Embodied Planning
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are increasingly deployed as embodied planners in egocentric environments, where task success requires not only achieving instructed goals but also acting in socially appropriate ways. While explicit goals may render certain actions optimal, implicit social norms often impose hidden constraints. Existing evaluations typically focus on explicit goal achievement or direct norm knowledge, seldom assessing whether planners can infer and apply these hidden constraints within action sequences. We introduce NormAct, a benchmark for embodied social-norm interactions that evaluates plans on Goal Achievement, Norm Compliance, and overall Task Success. NormAct uniquely embeds hidden norms within ordinary tasks, testing whether models can realize them without explicit instruction. Experiments with state-of-the-art MLLMs (GPT-5.4, Claude Opus 4.7, Gemini 3 Pro) reveal a significant gap: models achieve explicit goals in 67.3\% of cases, but comply with hidden norms in only 26.4\%. Cue-condition experiments indicate that this gap stems not from a lack of general social knowledge, but from challenges in activating and grounding relevant norms in context. To address this, we propose NormPerceptor, a context-conditioned cue generator that infers scene-relevant norms prior to planning, increasing Task Success from 24.2\% to 46.7\%. Our results underscore the importance of enabling embodied agents to proactively detect hidden norms, ground them in visual evidence, and integrate them as action-planning constraints. Our benchmark is publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/Caleb196x/NormAct.

AI.tldr: NormAct is a benchmark evaluating whether multimodal LLMs can infer and comply with unspoken social norms during embodied planning. State-of-the-art models achieve explicit goals well (67.3%) but rarely comply with hidden norms (26.4%). The proposed NormPerceptor, a context-conditioned cue generator, boosts task success from 24.2% to 46.7% by inferring scene-relevant norms before planning.
AI.motivation: Embodied MLLM planners are evaluated on explicit goal achievement, but real-world tasks also demand compliance with implicit social norms — unstated constraints that render certain actions socially inappropriate even if goal-optimal. No existing benchmark assesses whether planners can infer and apply these hidden constraints within action sequences.
AI.method: The authors introduce NormAct, a benchmark embedding hidden social norms within ordinary egocentric planning tasks. Tasks are evaluated on three axes: Goal Achievement, Norm Compliance, and overall Task Success (requiring both). Cue-condition experiments test whether failures stem from missing social knowledge versus failure to activate it in context. NormPerceptor is proposed as a pre-planning module that generates context-conditioned norm cues from visual scene evidence.
AI.result: GPT-5.4, Claude Opus 4.7, and Gemini 3 Pro achieve 67.3% explicit goal achievement but only 26.4% norm compliance. Overall Task Success is just 24.2%. Cue-condition experiments show models possess relevant social knowledge but fail to ground it contextually. NormPerceptor raises Task Success to 46.7%.
AI.conclusion: The gap between goal achievement and norm compliance reveals a critical weakness in current MLLMs for embodied planning: not a lack of social knowledge, but an inability to proactively detect, ground, and integrate implicit norms. The NormPerceptor approach demonstrates that context-conditioned norm inference significantly mitigates this, underscoring the need for proactive norm-awareness in embodied agents.

title: How Humans, Bots, and Agents Communicate About Vulnerabilities in Pull Requests
summary: Developers may reference vulnerabilities in pull request discussions through both explicit identifiers, such as CVEs or GHSAs, and implicit security-related language (e.g., "unauthorized access" or "SQL injection"). Prior work has primarily focused on explicit identifiers, potentially overlooking vulnerability discussions that lack formal references. Bots and coding agents are becoming more common in pull requests, raising new questions about how different accounts communicate about vulnerabilities. In this registered report, we describe our planned study of vulnerability communication in pull requests by humans, bots, and coding agents. Building on the AIDev-pop dataset, we analyze explicit vulnerability references and implicit security-related signals across pull request titles, descriptions, review comments, commit messages, and timeline discussions. We further investigate whether these references are associated with vulnerabilities introduced or fixed in the modified code and how they relate to pull request review activity and outcomes. This study contributes a large-scale empirical investigation of vulnerability communication practices in modern software development.

AI.tldr: This registered report outlines a planned large-scale empirical study investigating how humans, bots, and coding agents communicate about vulnerabilities in pull requests, examining both explicit identifiers (CVEs, GHSAs) and implicit security-related language across multiple PR text fields, and analyzing their relationship to code-level vulnerabilities and review outcomes.
AI.motivation: Prior research has narrowly focused on explicit vulnerability identifiers (e.g., CVEs), potentially missing substantial vulnerability discussions conveyed through implicit security-related language. Additionally, the growing presence of bots and coding agents in pull requests raises unexplored questions about how different account types participate in vulnerability communication.
AI.method: The study builds on the AIDev-pop dataset and analyzes explicit vulnerability references (CVEs, GHSAs) and implicit security signals (e.g., "unauthorized access," "SQL injection") across PR titles, descriptions, review comments, commit messages, and timeline discussions. It further investigates associations between these references and vulnerabilities introduced or fixed in the modified code, as well as correlations with PR review activity and outcomes.
AI.result: As a registered report, results are not yet reported; the paper presents the study design, research questions, and methodology for the planned investigation.
AI.conclusion: This work will provide the first large-scale empirical characterization of vulnerability communication practices spanning humans, bots, and coding agents, informing tooling and best practices for security-related collaboration in modern software development.

title: Yuvion LLM: An Adversarially-Aware Large Language Model for Content And AI Safety
summary: As large language models are increasingly deployed in real-world systems, safety failures can still lead to harmful outputs and dangerous misuse. We argue that the essence of safety is adversarial: many failures arise not from natural inputs alone, but from strategic attempts to evade model policies and safeguards. However, existing general-purpose model development largely overlook this adversarial nature, and often remain insufficient for realistic safety scenarios involving planning, tool use, and multi-step reasoning, causing measured safety performance to overestimate real deployment robustness. To address this gap, we present Yuvion LLM, a large language model built for adversarially robust content safety and broader AI safety. Yuvion LLM treats adversarial robustness and agentic capability as first-class objectives. Its pipeline combines adversarially aware data construction, knowledge-enhanced continued pretraining, and policy-grounded multi-task safety post-training, including risk-aware supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning-based policy optimization, together with safety-aware agentic reinforcement learning for tool use and multi-step reasoning in complex safety scenarios. We further introduce the Yuvion LLM RiskEval (YLRE), a collection of 93 benchmarks across four evaluation categories, covering diverse open and internal evaluations with a focus on safety, adversarial robustness, and real-world capability requirements. Across these evaluations, Yuvion LLM demonstrates clear advantages on safety-focused benchmarks and particularly strong robustness under adversarial conditions, while maintaining solid overall capability. Notably, Yuvion-8B outperforms most state-of-the-art baselines, including substantially larger models such as GPT-5.4 and Qwen3-MAX, on several safety tasks.

AI.tldr: Yuvion LLM is a language model designed with adversarial safety as a first-class objective, combining adversarially-aware data construction, safety-focused continued pretraining, and multi-task safety post-training. It introduces YLRE (93 benchmarks) and demonstrates strong adversarial robustness, with Yuvion-8B outperforming larger models like GPT-5.4 and Qwen3-MAX on safety tasks.
AI.motivation: Current LLM development overlooks the adversarial nature of safety failures — where users strategically attempt to evade safeguards via planning, tool use, and multi-step reasoning. This causes measured safety to overestimate real-world deployment robustness.
AI.method: Yuvion LLM employs: (1) adversarially-aware data construction, (2) knowledge-enhanced continued pretraining, (3) policy-grounded multi-task safety post-training (risk-aware SFT + RL-based policy optimization), and (4) safety-aware agentic RL for tool use and multi-step reasoning. Evaluation uses YLRE: 93 benchmarks across four categories.
AI.result: Yuvion LLM shows clear advantages on safety benchmarks and strong robustness under adversarial conditions while maintaining solid general capability. Yuvion-8B outperforms most SOTA baselines, including GPT-5.4 and Qwen3-MAX, on several safety tasks.
AI.conclusion: Treating adversarial robustness and agentic capability as first-class objectives yields significantly stronger real-world safety performance, even at smaller model scales, challenging the assumption that larger models are inherently safer.

title: GTI-mSEMP Framework : A Proposed Framework to Simulate Malware Propagation with Inclusion of Attacker-Defender Strategy
summary: The rapid proliferation of automated, multi-vector malware threats poses a significant risk to heterogeneous, resource constrained cyber-physical networks. Conventional epidemiological models often treat security defenses as static parameters, failing to capture the strategic, asymmetric maneuvers between an attacker and a defender. To address the gap, this paper proposes a Game-Theory-Integrated Modified Multi- Wireless Sensor Epidemic Malware Propagation (GTI-mSEMP) framework. This paper analyzed and compared the operational trajectories of Susceptible (S) and Recovered (R) node populations across three different operational regimes: Balanced Matchup, Exploit Surge and Hardened Defense. Numerical simulation results capture the real-time transient dynamics of the network state variables, demonstrating how the epidemic curve shifts when either the defensive or offensive scaling vectors hold an efficiency advantage. The proposed mathematical and numerical framework provides a rigorous foundation that can be deployed in highly adversarial network environments to evaluate dynamic malware propagation and predict localized node population states.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a game-theory-integrated epidemiological model (GTI-mSEMP) for malware propagation in cyber-physical wireless sensor networks, analyzing attacker-defender dynamics across three operational regimes to capture transient node population states under asymmetric strategic maneuvers.
AI.motivation: Conventional epidemiological malware models treat security defenses as static parameters, failing to capture the strategic, asymmetric interactions between attackers and defenders in resource-constrained cyber-physical networks facing automated multi-vector threats.
AI.method: The authors propose the Game-Theory-Integrated Modified Multi-Wireless Sensor Epidemic Malware Propagation (GTI-mSEMP) framework, which incorporates game-theoretic attacker-defender dynamics into a compartmental epidemiological model. Numerical simulations compare Susceptible (S) and Recovered (R) node population trajectories under three operational regimes: Balanced Matchup, Exploit Surge, and Hardened Defense.
AI.result: Numerical simulations capture real-time transient dynamics of network state variables, demonstrating how the epidemic curve shifts when either the defensive or offensive scaling vectors hold an efficiency advantage. The framework successfully models the differential impact of asymmetric strategies on susceptible and recovered node populations.
AI.conclusion: The GTI-mSEMP framework provides a rigorous mathematical and numerical foundation for evaluating dynamic malware propagation and predicting localized node population states in highly adversarial network environments.

title: PEBS: Per-rater Empirical-Bayes Shrinkage for RLHF Reward-Model Calibration
comment: Accepted at the ICML 2026 Workshop on Pluralistic Alignment. Code: https://github.com/deadsmash07/pebs-pluralistic
summary: Reward models for Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) pool preferences across thousands of annotators and fit one global affine calibrator, collapsing raters with systematically different rating-scale offsets and slopes into a single average-rater fit that does not match any individual annotator. PEBS is a per-rater empirical-Bayes shrinkage estimator: it fits per-rater affine calibrators on a held-out slice of each annotator's ratings and applies Morris-James-Stein empirical-Bayes shrinkage toward the population mean, in closed form and without retraining the reward model. On PRISM, PEBS reduces within-user held-out RMSE by 8.58% over the pooled population-slope baseline. The procedure replicates on PluriHarms harm ratings (Qwen-2.5 base, in-family) with a +9.66% RMSE reduction over the same population-slope baseline. PEBS is a closed-form post-hoc estimator for annotator-specific affine calibration in RLHF reward modeling; it leaves the reward base model unchanged and estimates only the rater-level map used at inference time for new ratings.

AI.tldr: PEBS is a post-hoc, per-rater empirical-Bayes shrinkage estimator that fits individual affine calibrators for each annotator without retraining the reward model, significantly reducing held-out RMSE compared to the standard global affine calibration approach in RLHF reward modeling.
AI.motivation: Standard RLHF reward models collapse diverse annotator preferences into a single global affine calibrator, ignoring systematic inter-rater differences in rating-scale offsets and slopes. This "average-rater" fit fails to represent any individual annotator's preference structure, degrading personalized alignment.
AI.method: PEBS fits per-rater affine calibrators on a held-out slice of each annotator's ratings, then applies Morris-James-Stein empirical-Bayes shrinkage toward the population mean. This is a closed-form, post-hoc estimator requiring no reward model retraining. At inference, only the rater-level calibration map is applied to the unchanged base reward model.
AI.result: On the PRISM dataset, PEBS achieves an 8.58% reduction in within-user held-out RMSE over the pooled population-slope baseline. On PluriHarms harm ratings (Qwen-2.5 base, in-family), it yields a 9.66% RMSE reduction over the same baseline.
AI.conclusion: Per-rater empirical-Bayes shrinkage provides a simple, computationally efficient, post-hoc solution for personalized affine calibration in RLHF reward models, improving predictive accuracy without modifying the underlying reward model.

title: Verifiable Geometry Problem Solving: Solver-Driven Autoformalization and Theorem Proposing
summary: Geometry Problem Solving have increasingly adopt the neuro-symbolic paradigm, combining neural intuition with symbolic rigor. However, current frameworks suffer from severe bottlenecks in two core stages: autoformalization, which treats multimodal translation as a static task decoupled from downstream solver compatibility, and theorem prediction, where solvers frequently hit a deductive impasse due to fixed rule libraries. To address these, we propose SD-GPS, a solver-driven framework that treats the symbolic solver as an execution oracle throughout both formalization and deduction. First, Solver-Driven Autoformalization unifies supervised formal-language adaptation and solvability-guided reinforcement learning into a single module built on QwenVL3-2B, making executability the central training signal. Second, Verified Theorem Proposing introduces an impasse-aware agent that proposes local auxiliary lemmas from current proof states, ensuring soundness by filtering all proposals through symbolic verification. Empirical evaluations on Geometry3K and PGPS9K demonstrate that SD-GPS consistently outperforms existing MLLM, neural, and neuro-symbolic methods across standard completion, multiple-choice, and cross-modal reference regimes, proving that closing the loop between multimodal perception and symbolic execution significantly improves geometric reasoning, offering profound insights into how neural agents can be grounded by formal systems to achieve verifiable problem-solving capabilities.

AI.tldr: SD-GPS is a solver-driven neuro-symbolic framework for geometry problem solving that integrates solver feedback into both autoformalization (via solvability-guided RL) and theorem prediction (via impasse-aware lemma generation with symbolic verification), achieving state-of-the-art results on Geometry3K and PGPS9K.
AI.motivation: Current neuro-symbolic geometry solvers suffer from two bottlenecks: (1) autoformalization treats multimodal translation as static and decoupled from downstream solver compatibility, and (2) theorem prediction relies on fixed rule libraries causing deductive impasses. The authors argue that the solver itself should serve as an execution oracle throughout the entire pipeline to close the loop between perception and formal deduction.
AI.method: SD-GPS consists of two key components: (1) Solver-Driven Autoformalization, which unifies supervised formal-language adaptation with solvability-guided reinforcement learning on QwenVL3-2B, using executability as the central training signal; and (2) Verified Theorem Proposing, an impasse-aware agent that generates local auxiliary lemmas from current proof states and filters all proposals through symbolic verification to ensure soundness.
AI.result: SD-GPS consistently outperforms existing MLLM, neural, and neuro-symbolic methods on Geometry3K and PGPS9K across standard completion, multiple-choice, and cross-modal reference evaluation regimes.
AI.conclusion: Closing the loop between multimodal perception and symbolic execution significantly improves geometric reasoning. The work demonstrates that grounding neural agents with formal systems via solver-driven feedback yields verifiable problem-solving capabilities.

title: CrossLangFuzzer: Differential Testing of Cross-Language JVM Compilers
summary: Modern JVM software increasingly integrates multiple programming languages, such as Java, Kotlin, Groovy, and Scala, within a single application. Supporting such interoperability requires JVM compilers to perform cross-language compilation while reconciling subtle semantic differences across language boundaries. Errors in this process can lead to critical miscompilations, yet existing compiler testing techniques focus exclusively on isolated, singlelanguage compilation. To address this gap, we present CrossLangFuzzer, the first differential testing framework for cross-language JVM compilation. CrossLangFuzzer leverages the Kotlin compiler's unified intermediate representation (IR) to synthesize cross-language test programs. It further applies seven mutation operators to diversify generated test programs and improve bug-finding capability. Evaluated on the latest versions of five major JVM compilers, CrossLangFuzzer uncovered 32 confirmed bugs, including 15 in Kotlin, 4 in Groovy, 7 in Scala 3, 2 in Scala 2, and 4 in Java. CrossLangFuzzer is open-source at https://github.com/XYZboom/CrossLangFuzzer

AI.tldr: CrossLangFuzzer is the first differential testing framework for cross-language JVM compilation, leveraging Kotlin's unified IR to synthesize multilingual test programs and using mutation operators to uncover 32 confirmed bugs across Java, Kotlin, Groovy, and Scala compilers.
AI.motivation: Modern JVM applications increasingly blend multiple languages (Java, Kotlin, Groovy, Scala), requiring compilers to handle cross-language interoperability with subtle semantic differences. Existing compiler testing techniques only target single-language compilation, leaving cross-language compilation errors undetected and creating a critical testing gap.
AI.method: CrossLangFuzzer uses the Kotlin compiler's unified intermediate representation (IR) as a foundation to synthesize cross-language test programs. It employs seven mutation operators to diversify generated test cases and applies differential testing: the same cross-language program is compiled by multiple JVM compilers, and behavioral discrepancies across compilers signal potential bugs.
AI.result: Evaluated on five major JVM compilers (latest versions), CrossLangFuzzer found 32 confirmed bugs: 15 in Kotlin, 4 in Groovy, 7 in Scala 3, 2 in Scala 2, and 4 in Java.
AI.conclusion: Cross-language compilation on the JVM is a significant, previously untested source of compiler bugs. CrossLangFuzzer demonstrates that differential fuzzing across language boundaries is effective and practically impactful, as evidenced by the 32 confirmed bugs discovered across all major JVM compilers.

title: When Search Agents Should Ask: DiscoBench for Clarification-Aware Deep Search
summary: Search agents powered by large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to solve complex information-seeking tasks, requiring multi-step retrieval and reasoning to fulfill user goals. However, existing benchmarks often assume that user queries are complete and explicit, overlooking the fact that real-world search requests are frequently vague, underspecified, or even factually incorrect. In deep search scenarios, such ambiguity can propagate along multi-step reasoning chains and lead agents toward incorrect search trajectories. To address this gap, we introduce DiscoBench, a benchmark for clarification-aware deep search, designed to evaluate whether search agents can proactively identify ambiguity, ask effective clarification questions, and recover correct reasoning paths through user interaction. DiscoBench contains 211 samples and 463 ambiguity instances across 11 real-world domains, covering four ambiguity types. We further design a user simulator for multi-turn interaction and evaluate model performance from four perspectives: task utility, ambiguity detection, interaction strategy, and cost efficiency. Experiments on representative LLMs show that ambiguity detection and effective clarification are distinct capabilities, and that repeatedly searching instead of asking for clarification often performs worse than direct guessing, highlighting a critical gap between retrieval ability and interactive problem-solving in current search agents.

AI.tldr: DiscoBench is a benchmark for evaluating whether LLM-based search agents can detect ambiguous queries, ask effective clarification questions, and recover correct reasoning paths through multi-turn user interaction, revealing that current agents struggle with proactive clarification compared to retrieval alone.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks assume user queries are complete and explicit, but real-world search requests are often vague, underspecified, or factually incorrect. In deep search scenarios with multi-step reasoning chains, such ambiguity can propagate and lead agents toward incorrect trajectories. No prior benchmark evaluates agents' ability to proactively identify and resolve ambiguity through clarification.
AI.method: The authors introduce DiscoBench with 211 samples and 463 ambiguity instances across 11 domains, covering four ambiguity types. They design a user simulator for multi-turn interaction and evaluate LLM-based search agents along four dimensions: task utility, ambiguity detection, interaction strategy, and cost efficiency. Representative LLMs are tested on their clarification-seeking and reasoning-recovery capabilities.
AI.result: Ambiguity detection and effective clarification are shown to be distinct capabilities. Repeatedly searching instead of asking for clarification often performs worse than direct guessing, exposing a critical gap between retrieval ability and interactive problem-solving in current search agents.
AI.conclusion: Current LLM-powered search agents lack robust clarification-seeking behavior, and retrieval prowess does not compensate for this deficiency. The work underscores the need for developing agents that can interactively resolve ambiguity to improve deep search performance.

title: Robust Harmful Features Under Jailbreak Attacks: Mechanistic Evidence from Attention Head Specialization in Large Language Models
comment: 323 pages, 19 figures. Accepted at ICML 2026 as a Oral presentation
summary: Jailbreak attacks bypass LLM safety alignment, yet their mechanisms remain poorly understood. We provide evidence that attacks do not comprehensively eliminate safety features, but instead selectively suppress specific attention heads. We identify two functionally differentiated types: Adversarially Compromised Heads (ACHs) concentrated in early layers, which are suppressed under attacks, and Safety-Aligned Heads (SAHs) in mid-layers, which maintain robust activations even when attacks succeed. Ablation studies support the causal role of ACHs and the contribution of SAHs to robust activations: suppressing a small number of ACHs is sufficient to induce jailbreak-like behavior on normally refused inputs, while removing SAHs substantially weakens mid-layer safety activations. Token-level attribution further shows that ACH suppression is driven specifically by attack-template tokens, providing a mechanistic account of why attacks can bypass refusal decisions through ACH suppression while leaving internal safety signals sustained by SAHs -- a phenomenon we term Robust Harmful Features. To validate the practical significance of this robustness, we show that simply reading these persistent activations -- without any training -- yields competitive aggregate detection performance with strong adversarial robustness.

AI.tldr: Jailbreak attacks don't eliminate LLM safety features but selectively suppress specific early-layer "Adversarially Compromised Heads" (ACHs), while mid-layer "Safety-Aligned Heads" (SAHs) remain robustly activated — a phenomenon termed "Robust Harmful Features." This persistent safety signal can be read directly for competitive jailbreak detection without any training.
AI.motivation: Existing work lacks a mechanistic understanding of how jailbreak attacks bypass LLM safety alignment. The authors aim to uncover the internal attention-head-level mechanisms underlying successful jailbreaks, moving beyond surface-level behavioral observations.
AI.method: The authors analyze attention head activations across layers under both normal and jailbroken conditions. They identify two functionally distinct head types (ACHs and SAHs), validate their causal roles through ablation studies (suppressing ACHs induces jailbreak-like behavior; removing SAHs weakens safety activations), conduct token-level attribution to trace ACH suppression to attack-template tokens, and evaluate detection performance by reading persistent SAH activations.
AI.result: (1) ACHs in early layers are suppressed during jailbreaks; SAHs in mid-layers remain robustly active. (2) Ablating a small number of ACHs suffices to jailbreak normally refused inputs.
