(3) ACH suppression is driven by attack-template tokens. (4) Reading SAH activations without training yields competitive jailbreak detection with strong adversarial robustness.
AI.conclusion: Jailbreak attacks exploit a dissociation between early-layer ACHs (suppressed) and mid-layer SAHs (persistent). This "Robust Harmful Features" phenomenon explains how attacks bypass refusal while internal safety signals survive, and it enables simple, training-free, adversarially robust detection methods.

title: Retroactive Advantage Correction: Closed-Form V-Trace Bias Correction for Delay-Aware RLHF
comment: Accepted at the ICML 2026 Workshop on Reinforcement Learning from World Feedback (RLxF). Code: https://github.com/deadsmash07/rac-rlxf-code
summary: Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) in production does not always have a synchronous reward signal. Code-execution verifiers, slow judge ensembles, and queued human review can return several gradient steps after the rollout that produced them, breaking the synchronous-reward assumption underlying standard PPO. We address this gap with Retroactive Advantage Correction (RAC): each pending slow completion is queued, aged through a non-negative kernel, and reinjected as a clipped residual into the next optimiser step's advantage. We prove that under an unbiased clipped importance ratio, the cumulative RAC correction is exactly unbiased when the effective delay kernel reinjects all of its mass, and carries a bias linear in the unreinjected fraction otherwise; at the no-delay identity kernel it reduces to V-trace. On a tabular Markov decision process (MDP) proof-of-concept, RAC reduces the closed-form policy bias by up to 47.9x at the two-slow-channel configuration, beating wait-for-slow at lower wall-clock cost. RAC integrates with PPO and GRPO through a two-line reward-manager patch.

AI.tldr: RAC (Retroactive Advantage Correction) solves the problem of delayed/asynchronous rewards in RLHF by queuing pending signals, aging them through a non-negative kernel, and reinjecting them as clipped residuals into advantage estimates — reducing policy bias by up to 47.9× over naive approaches.
AI.motivation: Standard PPO assumes synchronous rewards, but production RLHF systems often involve delays from code-execution verifiers, slow judge ensembles, or human review queues. These delays break the synchronous-reward assumption, causing bias in advantage estimation and suboptimal policy updates. Existing solutions like "wait-for-slow" incur high wall-clock cost.
AI.method: RAC queues each pending slow completion, ages it through a non-negative kernel, and reinjects it as a clipped residual into the next optimizer step's advantage. The method is theoretically analyzed: under an unbiased clipped importance ratio, the cumulative RAC correction is exactly unbiased when the effective delay kernel reinjects all mass, and carries bias linear in the unreinjected fraction otherwise. At the no-delay identity kernel, RAC reduces to V-trace.
AI.result: On a tabular MDP proof-of-concept, RAC reduces closed-form policy bias by up to 47.9× at the two-slow-channel configuration compared to baselines, while beating wait-for-slow at lower wall-clock cost.
AI.conclusion: RAC is a principled, lightweight solution (two-line reward-manager patch) that integrates seamlessly with PPO and GRPO, effectively handling asynchronous delayed rewards in production RLHF pipelines.

title: RelBall: Relation Ball with Quaternion Rotation for Knowledge Graph Completion
summary: Real-world knowledge graphs are often incomplete, lacking many valid facts. Knowledge Graph Completion (KGC) aims to predict missing links using known triples, thereby enhancing graph coverage. A key challenge is modeling diverse relational patterns such as symmetry, antisymmetry, inversion, composition and semantic hierarchy. Existing models such as RotatE can capture symmetric, antisymmetric, inverse, and commutative composition patterns, yet struggle with non-commutative composition. Rotate3D addresses this by introducing non-commutativity via three-dimensional rotations, but still fails to capture the semantic hierarchies prevalent in knowledge graphs. Moreover, both models cannot effectively model one-to-many relations. To overcome these limitations, we propose RelBall, which extends Rotate3D with two innovations. First, our model introduces modulus transformation to model hierarchies, driving abstract concepts toward smaller moduli and concrete instances toward larger ones. Second, it introduces a tail-centric relation ball to model one-to-one, one-to-many, many-to-one, and many-to-many relations. RelBall offers the following advantages: (1) coverage of all relational patterns, including the ones mentioned above; (2) an interpretable hierarchical representation where the modulus directly reflect semantic levels; (3) support for one-to-one, one-to-many, many-to-one, and many-to-many relations. Experiments on multiple datasets demonstrate RelBall's competitive link prediction performance against various baselines.

AI.tldr: RelBall extends Rotate3D with modulus transformation for semantic hierarchy modeling and tail-centric relation balls for handling all cardinality patterns (1-1, 1-N, N-1, N-M), achieving competitive KGC performance.
AI.motivation: Existing KGC models like RotatE cannot capture non-commutative composition, while Rotate3D (which adds 3D rotations for non-commutativity) fails to model semantic hierarchies and struggles with one-to-many relations. A unified model covering all these relational patterns is needed.
AI.method: RelBall builds on Rotate3D with two key innovations: (1) modulus transformation that maps abstract concepts to smaller moduli and concrete instances to larger ones, encoding semantic hierarchies in the vector norms; (2) a tail-centric relation ball that models cardinality patterns by representing relations as regions (balls) centered on tail entities rather than fixed vectors.
AI.result: Experiments on multiple benchmark datasets show RelBall achieves competitive link prediction performance against various baselines.
AI.conclusion: RelBall successfully unifies modeling of all major relational patterns (symmetry, antisymmetry, inversion, commutative and non-commutative composition, hierarchy) and all cardinality patterns, with the added benefit of interpretable hierarchical representations where modulus directly reflects semantic levels.

title: Humanizing Automatically Generated Unit Test Suites with LLM-Based Refactoring
summary: Search-based test generation tools such as EvoSuite produce compilable and high-coverage unit tests at scale, but their suites are often hard to read and maintain. LLMs can generate more natural tests, yet direct generation remains brittle, with compilation rates of only 51-78% in our study. We introduce TestHumanizer, a hybrid SBST+LLM approach that uses LLMs as controlled refactoring layers over compilable SBST suites to improve naming, structure, and developer-oriented clarity while preserving behavior and compilation validity. We evaluate TestHumanizer on 350 classes from Defects4J and SF110. EvoSuite generates 15 suites per class, and each suite is refactored under three context configurations using gpt-4o and mistral-large-2407, yielding 31,500 refactorings. TestHumanizer reaches 88-98% compilation rates, close to EvoSuite's 100% baseline and clearly above direct LLM generation. Structural coverage is largely preserved, typically within 1-2 percentage points, and 86-95% of refactorings satisfy a composite faithful-refactoring threshold. Refactored suites also improve predicted readability, reduce control-flow and cognitive complexity, and mitigate structural smells. The summary-based setting offers the most robust trade-off, while long code-centric prompts are more prone to hallucination-induced failures. A developer study on 30 classes and 444 test methods confirms significant gains in perceived readability and willingness to adopt, with Wilcoxon p less than 0.01 and substantial inter-rater agreement. Overall, LLMs are most effective not as standalone generators but as validation-gated refinement layers over robust SBST outputs.

AI.tldr: TestHumanizer uses LLMs as a controlled refactoring layer over EvoSuite-generated test suites to improve readability and maintainability while preserving compilation validity and coverage. The hybrid approach achieves 88-98% compilation rates versus 51-78% for direct LLM generation, with minimal coverage loss and significantly improved developer-perceived readability.
AI.motivation: Search-based software testing (SBST) tools like EvoSuite produce compilable, high-coverage unit tests at scale, but the generated suites suffer from poor readability, unnatural naming, and high structural complexity, hindering developer adoption and maintenance. Meanwhile, direct LLM-based test generation yields more natural code but suffers from low compilation rates (51-78%). The work aims to combine the strengths of both paradigms.
AI.method: TestHumanizer takes EvoSuite-generated compilable test suites and applies LLMs (gpt-4o, mistral-large-2407) as refactoring layers under three context configurations: summary-based, code-centric short, and code-centric long prompts. The refactoring targets naming, structure, and clarity improvements while preserving behavior. Evaluation spans 350 classes from Defects4J and SF110, with 15 EvoSuite suites per class, yielding 31,500 refactorings. A composite faithful-refactoring threshold is used to validate behavior preservation, and a developer study with 30 classes and 444 test methods assesses perceived readability and adoption willingness.
AI.result: TestHumanizer achieves 88-98% compilation rates, approaching EvoSuite's 100% baseline and far exceeding direct LLM generation. Structural coverage is preserved within 1-2 percentage points. 86-95% of refactorings meet the faithful-refactoring threshold. Refactored suites show improved predicted readability, reduced control-flow and cognitive complexity, and fewer structural smells. The summary-based prompting configuration offers the most robust trade-off, while long code-centric prompts increase hallucination-induced failures. The developer study confirms significant gains in perceived readability and willingness to adopt (Wilcoxon p < 0.01, substantial inter-rater agreement).
AI.conclusion: LLMs are most effective not as standalone test generators but as validation-gated refinement layers operating over robust SBST outputs. The hybrid SBST+LLM paradigm yields the best of both worlds: compilation guarantees and high coverage from SBST, combined with human-readable structure and naming from LLM refactoring.

title: From Signals to Transfer: A Factorised Study of Probe-Based Uncertainty Estimation in Large Language Models
summary: Probe-based uncertainty estimation (UE) has emerged as a prominent approach to detect hallucinations in Large Language Models (LLMs) by learning uncertainty from internal model signals. Yet, recent methods vary simultaneously across feature design, training data construction, and evaluation setting, obscuring what actually drives performance. To address this issue, we propose a factorised study of probe-based UE under matched conditions. Our results show that raw hidden states and attention features are difficult to outperform in-domain. However, under distribution shift, structured and compressed features are more robust, suggesting that in-domain performance alone is insufficient to measure progress. Furthermore, prompting and label construction significantly affect probe behaviour. Building on these best-practice findings, we train benchmark-based pretrained probes that transfer reasonably well to open-ended factual generation, providing a stable off-the-shelf baseline. Our work encourages more deployment-oriented evaluation of probe-based uncertainty estimators. The code repository is available at https://github.com/ponhvoan/ProbeUE.

AI.tldr: A factorised study of probe-based uncertainty estimation for LLM hallucination detection, revealing that in-domain performance is misleading, distribution-shift robustness matters more, and prompting/label construction significantly affect probe behavior. Pretrained probes are offered as a stable baseline.
AI.motivation: Existing probe-based uncertainty estimation methods vary across multiple dimensions (feature design, training data, evaluation settings) simultaneously, making it unclear which factors actually drive performance. A controlled, factorised study is needed to disentangle these variables.
AI.method: The authors conduct a factorised (ablative) study under matched conditions, systematically varying feature representations (raw hidden states, attention, structured/compressed features), training data construction, prompting strategies, and evaluation across both in-domain and distribution-shift settings. They then train benchmark-based pretrained probes and test transfer to open-ended factual generation.
AI.result: Raw hidden states and attention features perform best in-domain but degrade under distribution shift, where structured/compressed features show greater robustness. Prompting and label construction significantly influence probe behavior. Benchmark-pretrained probes transfer reasonably to open-ended generation, providing a stable off-the-shelf baseline.
AI.conclusion: In-domain performance alone is an insufficient metric; deployment-oriented evaluation under distribution shift is critical. The work encourages more rigorous, standardised evaluation of probe-based uncertainty estimators for LLM hallucination detection.

title: Global Explanations for Multivariate Time Series Forecasting Models via $K$-Order Markov Approximations
comment: Accepted at the Workshop on Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI), International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence (IJCAI 2026)
summary: While many explainable AI (XAI) methods have been proposed, most are not designed for time-series forecasting models and often rely on the implicit assumption that timestamp features are independent. This assumption ignores the fundamental property of temporal dependence and can lead to explanations that violate the sequential and causal structure of the data. We introduce \textsc{KARMA}, a method for explaining time-series predictors by constructing a Markov surrogate model that captures the temporal dependencies learned by the predictor. Our approach revolves around three main aspects: identifying the minimal history length $K$ that is predictively sufficient for the model, estimating the best-fitting $K$-order Markov transition kernel from the discretized history space, and a five-level global explanation hierarchy that can be derived from the Markov transition kernel, which we illustrate using real-world weather data (Beijing PM 2.5). We also certify using complex synthetic data with known true causal edges that KARMA (i) recovers the data causal structure as learned by the model via a controlled experiment and (ii) identifies temporal dependencies better than established attribution methods such as TimeSHAP.

AI.tldr: KARMA introduces a Markov surrogate model-based method for explaining time-series forecasting models that respects temporal dependencies, identifies the minimal sufficient history length, estimates a K-order Markov transition kernel, and provides a five-level global explanation hierarchy, outperforming methods like TimeSHAP on both real and synthetic data.
AI.motivation: Existing XAI methods for time-series forecasting often assume feature independence, violating the sequential and causal structure inherent in temporal data. There is a need for an explanation method that explicitly captures temporal dependencies learned by the predictor.
AI.method: KARMA constructs a Markov surrogate model in three steps: (1) identifying the minimal predictively sufficient history length K, (2) estimating the best-fitting K-order Markov transition kernel from the discretized history space, and (3) deriving a five-level global explanation hierarchy from the kernel. Validation uses real-world Beijing PM 2.5 weather data and controlled experiments on synthetic data with known causal edges.
AI.result: KARMA successfully recovers the data causal structure as learned by the model in controlled synthetic experiments and identifies temporal dependencies more accurately than TimeSHAP, an established attribution method.
AI.conclusion: By embedding temporal dependence into the explanation framework via a Markov surrogate, KARMA provides causally and sequentially faithful global explanations for time-series predictors, advancing beyond independence-assuming XAI methods.

title: Lifted Causal Inference
comment: Accepted to the Annals of Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence journal
summary: Lifted inference exploits indistinguishabilities in probabilistic graphical models by using a representative for indistinguishable objects, thereby speeding up query answering while maintaining exact answers. In this article, we show how lifting can be applied to efficiently compute causal effects in relational domains. More specifically, we introduce parametric causal factor graphs (PCFGs) to incorporate causal knowledge in lifted models and give a formal semantics of interventions therein. We further present the Lifted Causal Inference (LCI) algorithm to compute causal effects on a lifted level, thereby drastically speeding up causal inference compared to propositional inference, e.g., in causal Bayesian networks. In addition, we present partially directed parametric causal factor graphs (PD-PCFGs) as a generalisation of PCFGs to handle partial causal knowledge and extend LCI to perform lifted causal inference in a PD-PCFG, thereby extending the applicability of lifted causal inference to a broader range of models requiring less prior knowledge about causal relationships.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces parametric causal factor graphs (PCFGs) and a Lifted Causal Inference (LCI) algorithm that extends lifted inference techniques to causal reasoning in relational domains, achieving significant speedups over propositional methods. It also generalizes PCFGs to partially directed PCFGs (PD-PCFGs) to handle incomplete causal knowledge.
AI.motivation: Causal inference in relational domains is computationally expensive when performed at the propositional level (e.g., in causal Bayesian networks). Lifted inference has proven effective for probabilistic queries by exploiting symmetries, but its application to causal effect computation remains underexplored. The authors aim to bridge this gap by adapting lifted inference to the causal setting, enabling efficient, exact causal effect estimation in large relational models.
AI.method: The authors propose (1) parametric causal factor graphs (PCFGs), which integrate causal knowledge into lifted probabilistic models using factorization and a formal intervention semantics; (2) the Lifted Causal Inference (LCI) algorithm, which computes causal effects directly at the lifted level by exploiting indistinguishability; and (3) partially directed parametric causal factor graphs (PD-PCFGs), which relax the requirement for fully specified causal directions, along with an extended LCI algorithm for PD-PCFGs.
AI.result: LCI drastically speeds up causal effect computation compared to propositional inference in causal Bayesian networks, maintaining exact answers. The PD-PCFG extension broadens applicability to models with only partial causal knowledge, reducing the prior knowledge burden without sacrificing correctness.
AI.conclusion: Lifted inference can be effectively extended to causal reasoning, yielding substantial computational gains. The PCFG formalism and LCI algorithm provide a principled framework for exact lifted causal inference, while PD-PCFGs increase practical applicability by accommodating incomplete causal specifications.

title: Govern the Repository, Not the Agent: Measuring Ecosystem-Level Risk in AI-Native Software
summary: Autonomous coding agents now open and merge pull requests in shared repositories at scale, and the field evaluates them the way it has always evaluated components, one agent at a time, on isolated benchmark tasks. Yet agents that each pass their own tests still leave repositories that accumulate problems no single contribution accounts for. We ask whether this problem belongs to the individual agent or to the repository where it accumulates. We study integration friction, the cost of integrating a contribution into a codebase that other contributors are concurrently changing. Across more than 930,000 agent-authored pull requests, we measure how much of the variation in friction stays with the repository after the contribution, its author, its size, and its agent are accounted for. About half does, and it survives full controls. In the same repositories, agent-authored contributions concentrate this repository-level friction roughly twice as much as human ones (intraclass correlation 0.30 versus 0.16), a gap that holds after controlling for codebase size, age, task shape, process maturity, and merge path. The risk is a property of the ecosystem, not the agent. AI-native software is therefore better measured and governed at the ecosystem level than one agent at a time.

AI.tldr: Agent-authored pull requests exhibit "integration friction" that is primarily a property of the repository ecosystem rather than the individual agent. Repository-level factors account for roughly half the variation in friction, and agent contributions concentrate this friction roughly twice as much as human contributions. This suggests AI-native software should be evaluated and governed at the ecosystem level.
AI.motivation: Current evaluation of autonomous coding agents is done in isolation on benchmark tasks, but in real shared repositories, individually competent agents collectively produce emergent integration problems. The authors investigate whether this integration friction is attributable to individual agents or to the repository ecosystem where contributions accumulate.
AI.method: Analysis of over 930,000 agent-authored pull requests, measuring how much variation in integration friction remains attributable to the repository after controlling for contribution, author, size, and agent. Intraclass correlation (ICC) is used to compare friction concentration between agent-authored and human-authored contributions, with controls for codebase size, age, task shape, process maturity, and merge path.
AI.result: Roughly half of the variation in integration friction persists at the repository level after full controls. Agent-authored contributions concentrate repository-level friction at an ICC of 0.30 versus 0.16 for human contributions — approximately twice as much — a gap that survives all controls.
AI.conclusion: Integration friction is an ecosystem-level property, not an agent-level one. AI-native software development should be measured and governed at the ecosystem level rather than evaluating one agent at a time.

title: Mitigating LLM-based p-Hacking by Preregistering for the Next LLM
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate, classify, and annotate data whose outputs feed downstream hypothesis tests. However, LLM-based research is easy to p-hack: a researcher can tune the prompts, decoding parameters, or output format until a desired result is reached. We propose a protocol to mitigate p-hacking in LLM-based research: preregistering the experiment and eligible models, and then running it on the first eligible LLM that is released after the preregistration. The researcher finalizes the procedure on current models, preregisters the analysis plan together with a set of eligible future models, and runs the confirmatory analysis on the first eligible model released afterward. Because this model does not exist at commitment time, it cannot be hacked against; furthermore, configurations that hack one model frequently do not transfer to the next. We evaluate the protocol on two tasks whose true values are known. Across 20 models from four providers and 11 LLM-analysis configurations, the protocol would have blocked successful transfer of the p-hack in 73.9% and 72.7% of cases in the two tasks. Additional analyses reveal that mitigation remains substantial under several stress tests. Finally, putting money where our mouth is, we followed our own protocol and preregistered our experiment. The preregistered experiment confirmed the protocol's effectiveness: out of the 7 configurations that hacked the prior model, the hacking failed to carry over in 6 configurations on the first eligible model released afterward.

AI.tldr: Researchers can easily p-hack LLM-based experiments by tweaking prompts or parameters until desired results appear. This paper proposes a preregistration protocol using future LLM releases as holdout models to prevent such p-hacking, and validates its effectiveness both retrospectively and through a preregistered experiment.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used as research tools for generating and annotating data that feed into hypothesis tests. However, the flexibility in prompt engineering, decoding parameters, and output formatting creates a severe p-hacking risk: researchers can iteratively tune configurations until statistical significance is achieved. This threatens the validity of LLM-based scientific research, yet existing solutions (e.g., train/test splits) are inadequate because there is no natural holdout set when every model and configuration is available at experimentation time.
AI.method: The authors propose a preregistration protocol where researchers: (1) develop and finalize their analysis procedure on currently available LLMs, (2) preregister the complete analysis plan along with a set of eligible future models, and (3) run the confirmatory analysis exclusively on the first eligible model released after preregistration. Because the future model does not exist at commitment time, it cannot be p-hacked. The protocol is evaluated retrospectively on two ground-truth tasks across 20 models from four providers with 11 analysis configurations, measuring whether configurations that successfully hacked one model would transfer their hacked results to the next. The authors also conducted their own preregistered experiment to prospectively validate the protocol.
AI.result: In the retrospective evaluation, the protocol blocked successful transfer of p-hacks in 73.9% and 72.7% of cases across the two tasks. Stress tests showed mitigation remains substantial under various conditions. In the prospective preregistered experiment, 6 out of 7 configurations that hacked the prior model failed to carry over to the first eligible future model, confirming the protocol's effectiveness.
AI.conclusion: Preregistering LLM-based research with future model releases as holdout sets is a practical and effective safeguard against p-hacking. The protocol is lightweight, does not constrain legitimate exploratory analysis, and leverages the natural staggered release of LLMs to create genuinely independent confirmatory samples. The authors advocate for its adoption as a research standard and demonstrate its feasibility by successfully following it themselves.

title: Halt Fast! Early Stopping for Certified Robustness
summary: Randomized Smoothing (RS) provides rigorous robustness guarantees for neural networks without architectural constraints, yet its adoption is limited by extreme computational costs. Standard RS requires tens of thousands of model evaluations per input and forces practitioners to commit to fixed sample sizes a priori. In this work, we present a novel meta-learning framework for anytime-valid certified robustness that adaptively deploys computational resources. By using a lightweight meta-learner to predict image-specific priors for a sequential E-process, we achieve a 20-fold reduction in sample complexity compared to traditional methods while maintaining rigorous statistical guarantees. Beyond raw efficiency, we demonstrate how anytime-validity enables adaptively allocating compute based upon application-specific risk thresholds, a form of resource triage impossible under classic certification frameworks. That this is achievable while also providing similar certification performance demonstrates that our approach provides a pathway for real-time, safety-critical certification deployments.

AI.tldr: A meta-learning framework for anytime-valid certified robustness that reduces sample complexity by 20x compared to standard Randomized Smoothing, while maintaining rigorous statistical guarantees and enabling adaptive compute allocation based on risk thresholds.
AI.motivation: Standard Randomized Smoothing requires tens of thousands of model evaluations per input with fixed sample sizes determined in advance, making it computationally prohibitive for real-time and safety-critical deployments. The authors aim to overcome this adoption barrier by enabling adaptive, on-the-fly resource allocation without sacrificing statistical rigor.
AI.method: The authors propose a meta-learning framework that trains a lightweight meta-learner to predict image-specific priors. These priors inform a sequential E-process, enabling anytime-valid statistical inference. This allows the certification procedure to adaptively decide how many Monte Carlo samples to draw per input, stopping early when sufficient evidence is accumulated or allocating more compute to ambiguous cases.
AI.result: The method achieves a 20-fold reduction in sample complexity compared to traditional Randomized Smoothing while maintaining rigorous statistical guarantees. Certification performance remains comparable to standard approaches, demonstrating that efficiency gains do not come at the cost of certified accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Anytime-valid certification via meta-learning makes Randomized Smoothing viable for real-time, safety-critical applications by enabling adaptive resource triage based on risk thresholds, a capability impossible under classic fixed-sample certification frameworks.

title: Training Observable Control Policies to Expose Agent State Through Actions
summary: Physical or operational constraints often impose communications limitations on autonomous agents. Such limitations complicate monitoring or multiagent coordination. Even when strong communications are absent, some information may still be available. The remainder of the relevant agent state may be reconstructed via estimation. The actions taken by an agent are a potential source of information -- as the agent interacts with the environment, these actions may be observed even in the absence of explicit communication. We investigate using actions to estimate the state of an agent, using reinforcement learning to develop policies which make the estimation problem more tractable. Policy observability is encouraged through the training reward and is analyzed using simulation of the trained agent. In an aircraft tracking problem a policy with enhanced observability is found that has minimal impact on nominal task performance.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates using an agent's observable actions to estimate its internal state when explicit communication is unavailable, and employs reinforcement learning to train policies that intentionally make state estimation easier for external observers, with minimal sacrifice to task performance.
AI.motivation: Physical or operational constraints often limit explicit communication between autonomous agents, complicating monitoring and multi-agent coordination. However, actions taken by agents interacting with the environment may still be observed. The paper is motivated by the insight that these observable actions carry implicit information about the agent's internal state, which could be leveraged for state estimation if policies are designed with observability in mind.
AI.method: The authors propose using reinforcement learning to train agent policies that enhance policy observability — making the state estimation problem more tractable for external observers. They incorporate an observability-promoting term into the training reward function, incentivizing the agent to act in ways that reveal information about its internal state. The trained policies are then analyzed via simulation.
AI.result: In an aircraft tracking problem, the method successfully produced a policy with enhanced observability. Critically, this policy achieved better state estimability while imposing only minimal impact on nominal task performance, demonstrating a favorable trade-off between observability and primary mission objectives.
AI.conclusion: Agent actions can serve as a viable information channel for state estimation in communication-constrained environments. Reinforcement learning can be effectively used to train policies that intentionally reveal internal state through observable actions, balancing observability with task performance.

title: JD Oxygen AI Item Center (Oxygen AIIC) V1: An Industrial-Scale LLM/VLM-Centric Solution for Item Understanding, Management, and Applications
summary: JD$.$com, one of the world's largest e-commerce platforms, serves over 700 million active users and millions of merchants, with a catalog of tens of billions of SKUs. At this scale, high-quality, structured item knowledge underpins a better consumer experience, lower management costs, and higher operational efficiency-yet producing and serving it poses three industrial-scale challenges: fast-emerging concepts, high-quality knowledge production for massive SKUs, and diverse downstream requirements. To address these challenges, we present the JD Oxygen AI Item Center (Oxygen AIIC), an industrial-scale platform built on LLMs/VLMs for item-knowledge production and service. Oxygen AIIC is built around four core pillars: (i) ontology engineering driven by efficient human-AI collaboration, which supports the dynamic evolution and agile expansion of an ontology with millions of entries; (ii) a "Semantic Search then Discrimination"(S2D) knowledge identification architecture that, combined with throughput improvement strategies, enables scalable, extensible, and high-throughput AI Item Library production for tens of billions of SKUs; (iii) self-evolving item-understanding LLMs/VLMs that improve in a stable and controllable manner, enabling knowledge production with 94.2% precision and 82.8% recall; and (iv) a unified item tunnel that serves as the data and service hub. Oxygen AIIC now covers tens of thousands of JD categories and processes hundreds of millions of item updates per day on Huawei Ascend NPUs. It has accumulated hundreds of billions of item-knowledge assets. Deployed across core business scenarios-including search, recommendation, operations, category planning-Oxygen AIIC has delivered measurable gains at scale. Search-traffic coverage reaches 80.4%, item-information quality issues drop by 37%, the automated fill rate of core attributes during item listing exceeds 80%.

AI.tldr: JD.com presents Oxygen AIIC, an LLM/VLM-powered industrial platform for large-scale item-knowledge production and service, addressing challenges of fast-emerging concepts, massive SKU scale, and diverse downstream needs through ontology engineering, a Semantic Search then Discrimination architecture, self-evolving models, and a unified data hub, achieving significant measurable business impact.
AI.motivation: At JD.com's scale (700M+ users, millions of merchants, tens of billions of SKUs), producing and serving high-quality structured item knowledge faces three industrial-scale challenges: (1) fast-emerging concepts requiring agile ontology evolution, (2) high-quality knowledge production for massive SKUs, and (3) diverse downstream requirements across search, recommendation, and operations.
AI.method: Oxygen AIIC is built on four pillars: (i) human-AI collaborative ontology engineering supporting millions of entries with dynamic evolution; (ii) a "Semantic Search then Discrimination" (S2D) knowledge identification architecture with throughput improvements for scalable, high-throughput AI Item Library production; (iii) self-evolving item-understanding LLMs/VLMs that improve in a stable, controllable manner; (iv) a unified item tunnel serving as the central data and service hub. The system runs on Huawei Ascend NPUs.
AI.result: The platform achieves 94.2% precision and 82.8% recall in knowledge production, covers tens of thousands of JD categories, processes hundreds of millions of item updates daily, and has accumulated hundreds of billions of item-knowledge assets. In deployment: search-traffic coverage reaches 80.4%, item-information quality issues drop by 37%, and core attribute automated fill rate during item listing exceeds 80%.
AI.conclusion: Oxygen AIIC demonstrates that LLM/VLM-driven, ontology-grounded knowledge production can be effectively scaled to industrial e-commerce requirements, delivering measurable improvements across multiple core business scenarios while maintaining high precision and recall.

title: Mitigating Position Bias in Transformers via Layer-Specific Positional Embedding Scaling
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) still struggle with the ``lost-in-the-middle'' problem, where critical information located in the middle of long-context inputs is often underrepresented or lost. While existing methods attempt to address this by combining multi-scale rotary position embeddings (RoPE), they typically suffer from high latency or rely on suboptimal hand-crafted scaling strategies. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a layer-specific positional embedding scaling~(LPES) method that assigns distinct scaling factors to each layer. LPES achieves a more balanced attention distribution without fine-tuning model parameters or increasing inference delay. A specially designed genetic algorithm is employed to efficiently select the optimal scaling factors for each layer by incorporating Bézier curves to significantly reduce the search space. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LPES effectively mitigates positional attention bias and delivers consistent improvements across multiple long-context benchmarks, yielding up to an $11.2$\% accuracy gain on the key-value retrieval dataset.

AI.tldr: LPES tackles the lost-in-the-middle problem in LLMs by assigning genetically-optimized, layer-specific scaling factors to rotary position embeddings, improving long-context retrieval without fine-tuning or added latency.
AI.motivation: LLMs suffer from the lost-in-the-middle problem where middle-context information is underrepresented. Existing multi-scale RoPE solutions either incur high latency or rely on suboptimal hand-crafted scaling heuristics, motivating an automated, efficient, layer-aware approach.
AI.method: LPES assigns distinct RoPE scaling factors to each transformer layer. A genetic algorithm searches for optimal per-layer scaling factors, with the search space drastically reduced via Bézier curve parameterization. The method requires no fine-tuning and adds no inference latency.
AI.result: LPES consistently improves performance across multiple long-context benchmarks, achieving up to an 11.2% accuracy gain on the key-value retrieval dataset, effectively mitigating positional attention bias.
AI.conclusion: Layer-specific positional embedding scaling with genetic optimization is an effective, zero-overhead solution to the lost-in-the-middle problem, outperforming prior multi-scale RoPE approaches.

title: What Was That Again? Certified Robustness for Automatic Speech Recognition
summary: Automatic Speech Recognition systems are notoriously both sensitive to adversarial and benign perturbations. While this has been repeatedly demonstrated using reference datasets, detecting such behaviors in deployed systems is incredibly challenging, due to the absence of oracle knowledge of the true transcription. We demonstrate that employing a certification-inspired mechanism can significantly decrease WER, increase recall, and decrease the Spearman correlation between confidence and WER. We achieve this through a dual-gate diagnostic pipeline: a Two-Sided Atomic Audit that accumulates statistical wealth to certify both token existence and adversarial exclusion, and a Rank-Based Tournament that selects the winning sequence. Our evaluations across four diverse architectures demonstrate up to a 55% relative reduction in Word Error Rate, while also providing granular word- and sentence-level certifications to enhance acoustic security.

AI.tldr: ASR systems are vulnerable to perturbations, and detecting failures in deployment is hard without ground truth. The authors propose a certification-inspired dual-gate pipeline combining a Two-Sided Atomic Audit (sequential statistical testing for token existence and adversarial exclusion) with a Rank-Based Tournament for sequence selection. Across four architectures, this achieves up to 55% relative WER reduction and provides word- and sentence-level security certifications.
AI.motivation: ASR systems are sensitive to both adversarial and benign perturbations, a vulnerability repeatedly shown on reference datasets. However, detecting such failures in deployed systems is extremely challenging because there is no oracle ground-truth transcription available. Existing confidence-based metrics correlate poorly with actual WER, making it difficult to trust model outputs in the wild.
AI.method: The authors propose a dual-gate diagnostic pipeline: (1) A Two-Sided Atomic Audit that performs sequential statistical hypothesis testing to accumulate evidence, certifying both that a token genuinely exists in the transcription (existence) and that adversarial perturbations are absent (exclusion). This yields granular word- and sentence-level certifications. (2) A Rank-Based Tournament that selects the winning transcription sequence from candidate outputs, leveraging the statistical wealth accumulated during the audit stage. Together, these mechanisms provide certified decisions without requiring oracle knowledge of the true transcription.
AI.result: Evaluated across four diverse ASR architectures, the approach yields up to a 55% relative reduction in Word Error Rate (WER). It also increases recall and decreases the Spearman correlation between model confidence scores and WER, indicating that the pipeline provides more reliable indicators of transcription quality than raw confidence. Granular word- and sentence-level certifications are demonstrated.
AI.conclusion: A certification-inspired mechanism can substantially improve ASR robustness in deployment settings where ground truth is unavailable. The dual-gate diagnostic pipeline not only reduces WER significantly but also provides interpretable, fine-grained certifications that enhance acoustic security, bridging the gap between offline benchmark evaluations and real-world deployment reliability.

title: COOPA: A Modular LLM Agent Architecture for Operations Research Problems
summary: Operations Research (OR) provides a rigorous framework for high-stakes decision-making, but effective OR modeling requires substantial domain knowledge, mathematical abstraction, and solver expertise. Recent LLM-based systems automate parts of this pipeline, yet remain limited by low accuracy on complex problems, opaque outputs, and narrow solver support. We propose COOPA (COoperative OPerations Agent), a modular LLM-agent architecture for interpretable and scalable OR decision support. It combines three components: iterative confidence-based modeling, which generates multiple candidate formulations, self-evaluates them across modeling dimensions, and selects one using a max-min confidence criterion; element-level provenance and confidence explanations, which link variables, parameters, constraints, and objectives to quoted source text and provide an audit trail for human verification; and multi-solver routing to specialized optimizer agents for different OR problem classes. Across three OR benchmarks, eight LLM backbones, and four baselines under identical conditions, COOPA achieves the best macro-average accuracy on six of eight backbones and improves over the strongest baseline by up to 6.7 percentage points. A within-system ablation isolates the contribution of iterative confidence-based modeling, while additional analyses and case studies illustrate the value of source traceability and multi-solver dispatch.

AI.tldr: COOPA is a modular LLM-agent system for OR modeling that combines iterative confidence-based formulation selection, element-level provenance tracing, and multi-solver routing. It achieves state-of-the-art accuracy across benchmarks and LLM backbones, outperforming baselines by up to 6.7 points while providing interpretable, auditable outputs.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based OR modeling systems suffer from three key limitations: (1) low accuracy on complex problems, (2) opaque outputs that hinder human verification, and (3) narrow solver support that limits applicability across diverse OR problem classes. There is a need for a system that is simultaneously more accurate, interpretable, and broadly applicable.
AI.method: COOPA employs a three-component modular architecture: (1) Iterative confidence-based modeling — generating multiple candidate formulations, self-evaluating them across modeling dimensions, and selecting the best via a max-min confidence criterion; (2) Element-level provenance and confidence explanations — linking every model component (variables, parameters, constraints, objectives) to quoted source text for full auditability; (3) Multi-solver routing — dispatching problems to specialized optimizer agents based on problem class.
AI.result: Evaluated across three OR benchmarks, eight LLM backbones, and four baselines under identical conditions, COOPA achieved the best macro-average accuracy on six of eight backbones and improved over the strongest baseline by up to 6.7 percentage points. Ablation studies confirm the contribution of iterative confidence-based modeling, and case studies demonstrate the practical value of source traceability and multi-solver dispatch.
AI.conclusion: COOPA demonstrates that a modular, confidence-driven, and provenance-aware LLM-agent architecture can significantly advance automated OR decision support, offering both improved accuracy and human-interpretable outputs across diverse problem types and solver ecosystems.

title: Ontology-Guided Evidence Path Inference for Multi-hop Knowledge Graph Question Answering
summary: Knowledge graph question answering (KGQA) aims to answer natural-language questions by reasoning over structured facts. Existing multi-hop KGQA methods mainly rely on topic-centered expansion, which faces two key challenges: the search space rapidly grows with noisy mixed-type paths, and retrieved paths may fail to satisfy the semantic constraints of complex questions. To address these challenges, we propose OPI, an ontology-guided evidence path inference framework for multi-hop KGQA. OPI introduces a relation-centric ontology graph to capture the head-tail type constraints of relations, providing a compact interface for answer-side constraints. Based on this ontology graph, OPI first introduces a bidirectional retrieval mechanism by mapping the predicted answer type to compatible final-hop relations and combining topic-side prefix expansion with answer-side final-hop matching, thereby suppressing noisy mixed-type expansion. OPI further adopts an iterative refinement strategy to reassess retrieved paths and candidate answers under the question context, filtering type-compatible but question-irrelevant evidence for more reliable answer prediction. Experiments on WebQSP, CWQ, and MetaQA show that OPI substantially reduces the search space, improves Hit@1/F1 by 4.6/5.0 points on WebQSP and 8.9/3.3 points on CWQ over the strongest prior results, and achieves near-saturated Hit@1 on MetaQA with the retrieval module alone.

AI.tldr: OPI is an ontology-guided framework for multi-hop KGQA that uses a relation-centric ontology graph to constrain answer-side path search, combining bidirectional retrieval with iterative refinement to suppress noisy paths and improve answer accuracy, achieving SOTA results on WebQSP, CWQ, and MetaQA.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-hop KGQA methods rely on topic-centered expansion, which suffers from two problems: (1) the search space explodes with noisy mixed-type paths, and (2) retrieved paths often violate semantic constraints of complex questions. A more principled mechanism is needed to incorporate answer-side type constraints during evidence path retrieval.
AI.method: OPI first constructs a relation-centric ontology graph capturing head-tail type constraints of relations. Then it employs (1) bidirectional retrieval: predicting the answer type from the question, mapping it to compatible final-hop relations, and intersecting topic-side prefix expansion with answer-side final-hop matching to suppress mixed-type noise; and (2) iterative refinement: reassessing retrieved paths and candidate answers under the question context to filter type-compatible but question-irrelevant evidence for more reliable prediction.
AI.result: On WebQSP, OPI improves Hit@1/F1 by 4.6/5.0 points over the strongest prior results. On CWQ, gains are 8.9/3.3 points. On MetaQA, the retrieval module alone achieves near-saturated Hit@1. The method substantially reduces the search space across all benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating ontology-guided answer-side type constraints via bidirectional retrieval and iterative refinement effectively addresses the search space explosion and semantic mismatch problems in multi-hop KGQA, yielding significant performance gains and near-saturated results on simpler datasets like MetaQA.

title: Low-Agreeableness Persona Conditioning for Safe LLM Fine-Tuning
summary: Recent work has shown that fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) for social warmth degrades factual reliability and increases sycophancy. We investigate a related but distinct failure mode: warmth fine-tuning also weakens adversarial safety, making models more susceptible to jailbreaks and harmful output generation. We examine whether this reflects an inherent consequence of empathetic adaptation or an artifact of data construction. To address this, we introduce a persona-driven rewriting pipeline that conditions user turns on low agreeableness and pairs this with warm, de-escalating assistant responses. Across three experiments on four models, our approach reduces jailbreak susceptibility and harmful output rates relative to generic warmth fine-tuning baselines, while preserving conversational warmth. Representational probing provides suggestive evidence that this conditioning reduces the geometric alignment between warmth and compliance directions in latent space. These results show that safer empathetic fine-tuning is achievable through data design alone, without safety labels, harm detectors, or changes to the training objective.

AI.tldr: Warmth fine-tuning of LLMs degrades adversarial safety (increasing jailbreak susceptibility). The authors introduce a persona-driven data pipeline using low-agreeableness user personas paired with warm assistant responses, which reduces harmful outputs and jailbreak rates while preserving conversational warmth — without needing safety labels or modified training objectives.
AI.motivation: Prior work showed warmth fine-tuning impairs factual reliability; this paper identifies a novel failure mode: warmth fine-tuning also weakens adversarial safety. The authors investigate whether this safety degradation is inherent to empathetic adaptation or an artifact of how training data is constructed.
AI.method: A persona-driven rewriting pipeline: user turns are conditioned on a low-agreeableness persona, paired with warm, de-escalating assistant responses. This curated dataset is used for fine-tuning. The approach is evaluated across three experiments on four models, with representational probing used to analyze geometric alignment between warmth and compliance directions in latent space.
AI.result: The proposed approach reduces jailbreak susceptibility and harmful output rates compared to generic warmth fine-tuning baselines, while preserving conversational warmth. Probing analysis suggests the conditioning reduces alignment between warmth and compliance representations, offering a mechanistic explanation.
AI.conclusion: Safer empathetic fine-tuning is achievable through data design alone — without safety labels, harm detectors, or training objective changes. The persona-driven conditioning effectively decouples warmth from harmful compliance.

title: FoggyTrust: Robust Federated Learning with Hierarchical Trust Networks
summary: Byzantine-robust federated learning seeks to protect distributed model training from malicious or corrupted clients without requiring access to their private data. FLTrust addresses this challenge by introducing a trusted server-side root dataset that assigns trust scores to client updates for more robust aggregation. In this work, we propose FOGGYTRUST, a hierarchical extension of FLTrust that localizes trust computation to fog nodes, allowing the framework to better handle globally heterogeneous data while preserving robustness within locally homogeneous client groups. We further show that this two-level architecture can simultaneously address distribution mismatch in trust estimation and client drift across groups by combining local trust-based aggregation with heterogeneity-aware global optimizers such as FedAdam and SCAFFOLD. Across benchmark datasets, FOGGYTRUST achieves its strongest gains on more challenging heterogeneous settings, particularly on CIFAR-10 under Krum and Trim attacks, where it achieves an over 50% improvement over FLTrust. We also test FOGGYTRUST in a real-world safari dataset to show the promise of hierarchical trust networks for robust federated learning in socially impactful, safety-critical settings such as distributed wildlife monitoring.

AI.tldr: FOGGYTRUST extends FLTrust with a hierarchical fog architecture that localizes trust scoring to fog nodes, combining local trust-based aggregation with heterogeneity-aware optimizers (FedAdam, SCAFFOLD) to handle non-IID data. It achieves >50% improvement over FLTrust on CIFAR-10 under Byzantine attacks and demonstrates real-world applicability on a safari wildlife monitoring dataset.
AI.motivation: FLTrust, while effective for Byzantine-robust federated learning, relies on a single global root dataset for trust estimation. This creates distribution mismatch when client data is globally heterogeneous (non-IID), and fails to address client drift across diverse groups. A hierarchical approach is needed to preserve robustness while accommodating data heterogeneity.
AI.method: FOGGYTRUST introduces a two-level hierarchical architecture where fog nodes perform localized trust computation using FLTrust's root-dataset-based scoring within locally homogeneous client groups. At the global level, it integrates local trust-based aggregation with heterogeneity-aware optimizers (FedAdam and SCAFFOLD) to simultaneously mitigate distribution mismatch in trust estimation and cross-group client drift.
AI.result: On benchmark datasets, FOGGYTRUST shows strongest gains under challenging heterogeneous settings. On CIFAR-10 with Krum and Trim attacks, it achieves over 50% improvement compared to vanilla FLTrust. The method also demonstrates promise on a real-world safari dataset for distributed wildlife monitoring.
AI.conclusion: Hierarchical trust networks via fog computing effectively address the limitations of centralized trust estimation in FLTrust, enabling robust federated learning under both Byzantine attacks and severe data heterogeneity. The approach shows practical viability in safety-critical, socially impactful deployment scenarios.

title: AI-Driven Synthesis for High-Tech System Design: Automating Innovation
summary: This article addresses the combinatorial complexity inherent in modern high-tech system design by presenting automation-in-design (AiD) as a transformative paradigm. We propose computational design synthesis (CDS), a framework utilising deep learning and generative AI to automate the creation of novel systems. Two case studies (e-drive system design and spatial dimensioning problem) serve as proof-points for this approach. The AI-driven methods used in the case studies represent a fundamental shift in engineering, advancing from simulation-based optimisation towards autonomous design with minimal human supervision.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Automation-in-Design (AiD) via Computational Design Synthesis (CDS), a deep learning and generative AI framework that automates novel system creation, demonstrated through e-drive design and spatial dimensioning case studies, marking a shift from simulation-based optimization toward autonomous engineering design.
AI.motivation: Modern high-tech systems suffer from combinatorial complexity that overwhelms traditional manual and simulation-based design approaches. There is a need for a paradigm shift that can handle this complexity through automation, reducing human supervision while maintaining or improving design quality.
AI.method: The authors introduce Computational Design Synthesis (CDS), a framework that leverages deep learning and generative AI to automate the synthesis of novel engineering systems. The approach is validated through two proof-of-concept case studies: (1) e-drive system design and (2) a spatial dimensioning problem.
AI.result: Both case studies serve as proof-points demonstrating the viability of AI-driven autonomous design. The results indicate a fundamental shift from traditional simulation-based optimisation to generative, minimally supervised design processes capable of handling combinatorial complexity.
AI.conclusion: AiD and CDS represent a transformative paradigm in engineering design, enabling a transition from human-intensive simulation-based optimisation to autonomous design synthesis with minimal human intervention, with broad implications for complex system development.

title: Do Speech Emphasis Models Generalize across Languages and Emotions?
summary: Prosodic emphasis varies across languages, emotions, and speaking styles, yet existing emphasis detection models are largely trained and evaluated on monolingual neutral read speech. We introduce MMEE (Multilingual Multi-Emotion Emphasis), a corpus of 10,000 professionally recorded expressive utterances (14.13 hours) across 7 languages and 34 emotion/style categories, with three-level perceptual labels (10 annotations per sample). We benchmark two state-of-the-art architectures under monolingual, cross-lingual, multilingual, cross-emotion, cross-dataset, and data-scale settings. Monolingual models show limited zero-shot transfer, degrading across typologically distant languages, while multilingual training substantially improves robustness. Models transfer robustly between high- and low-arousal emotions; bidirectional transfer between synthetic and perceptual benchmarks suggests shared prosodic structure; and performance stays robust even at smaller training scales.

AI.tldr: Introduces MMEE, a multilingual multi-emotion emphasis corpus (7 languages, 34 emotion/style categories, 10K utterances), and benchmarks emphasis detection models showing that multilingual training improves robustness, cross-emotion transfer works well between arousal levels, and performance remains stable at smaller data scales.
AI.motivation: Existing emphasis detection models are narrowly trained on monolingual neutral read speech, limiting their generalizability across languages, emotions, and speaking styles. There is a need for a diverse, perceptually annotated corpus and systematic benchmarking to understand model behavior under varied conditions.
AI.method: Created MMEE: 10,000 professionally recorded utterances across 7 languages and 34 emotion/style categories, with three-level perceptual emphasis labels (10 annotators per sample). Benchmarked two SOTA architectures under six conditions: monolingual, cross-lingual, multilingual, cross-emotion, cross-dataset, and varying data scales.
AI.result: Monolingual models show poor zero-shot transfer, especially across typologically distant languages. Multilingual training significantly boosts cross-lingual robustness. Models transfer well between high- and low-arousal emotions. Bidirectional transfer between synthetic and perceptual benchmarks indicates shared prosodic structure. Performance remains robust even at reduced training data scales.
AI.conclusion: Multilingual multi-emotion training is key to building robust, generalizable emphasis detection systems. The MMEE corpus provides a valuable resource for future research, and the findings highlight that prosodic emphasis shares structural properties across emotional and dataset boundaries.

title: HybridCodec: Modeling Discrete and Continuous Representations for Efficient Speech Language Models
summary: Discrete audio representations have become increasingly popular for building multimodal text-audio systems and integrating audio capabilities into Large Language Models (LLMs). However, numerous studies report performance degradation on various downstream tasks due to information loss during discretization. To address this, we propose a novel approach combining temporally compressed discrete tokens with dimensionality-reduced continuous residuals. Our framework consists of a hybridized discrete-continuous focal modulation codec and a hybrid Transformer. This architecture performs autoregressive inference in the discrete domain, coupled with non-autoregressive prediction and continuous residual upsampling. Experimental results show that our approach significantly improves the retention of speaker characteristics compared to discrete-only methods, while simultaneously reducing the number of required autoregressive steps.

AI.tldr: Proposes a hybrid discrete-continuous audio codec and Transformer that combines temporally compressed discrete tokens with dimensionality-reduced continuous residuals, improving speaker characteristic retention while reducing autoregressive steps compared to discrete-only methods.
AI.motivation: Discrete audio representations are popular for text-audio LLMs but suffer from information loss during discretization, degrading downstream task performance. The authors aim to mitigate this degradation while maintaining the benefits of discrete representations.
AI.method: A hybridized discrete-continuous focal modulation codec paired with a hybrid Transformer. Autoregressive inference operates in the discrete domain, complemented by non-autoregressive prediction and continuous residual upsampling. The discrete tokens are temporally compressed, and continuous residuals undergo dimensionality reduction.
AI.result: Significant improvement in retaining speaker characteristics relative to discrete-only baselines, along with a reduction in the number of autoregressive steps required.
AI.conclusion: The hybrid discrete-continuous framework effectively addresses the information loss problem in audio discretization, offering a favorable trade-off between the efficiency of discrete autoregressive modeling and the fidelity of continuous representations.

title: Tandem Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has significantly improved the reasoning capability of large language models, reaching expert or even superhuman performance in domains such as competition math. However, whether weaker agents and humans can actually harness this capability is far less certain, with RLVR documented to drift reasoning toward idiosyncratic patterns such as poor readability and language mixing. Tandem training is a recently introduced paradigm that targets this compatibility problem: a trained, stronger senior co-generates each rollout with a frozen, weaker junior, and the two are rewarded as a team, so the senior is pushed to reason in ways the junior can follow. Yet this paradigm has so far been demonstrated only in proof-of-concept settings, leaving open whether it scales to the long chains of thought of the modern RLVR pipeline. In this work, we propose Tandem Reinforcement Learning (TRL), which carries the tandem training paradigm into RLVR. In TRL, the senior and a frozen junior alternate stochastically to co-generate the reasoning, the resulting generation is rewarded, and the standard GRPO loss is applied to the senior. Training Qwen3-4B-Instruct on competition math, we find that TRL matches vanilla GRPO on solo reasoning capability while three properties emerge together from the same rollout structure: stronger handoff robustness with the junior, reduced distributional drift from the junior, and a chain-of-thought more legible to the junior. Our results demonstrate a promising route for RLVR with practical payoffs in multi-model communication and human compatibility.

AI.tldr: TRL extends tandem training into RLVR by having a senior model and frozen junior model stochastically alternate in co-generating reasoning chains. Training Qwen3-4B-Instruct on competition math shows TRL matches vanilla GRPO in solo reasoning while improving junior compatibility, handoff robustness, and chain-of-thought legibility.
AI.motivation: RLVR improves LLM reasoning to expert/superhuman levels but introduces idiosyncratic patterns (poor readability, language mixing) that make reasoning inaccessible to weaker models and humans. Prior tandem training showed promise for this compatibility problem but only in proof-of-concept settings, not with modern long chain-of-thought RLVR.
AI.method: TRL: A senior model and frozen junior model stochastically alternate turns to co-generate reasoning chains. The full generation is rewarded, and standard GRPO loss is applied only to the senior. Evaluated by training Qwen3-4B-Instruct on competition math benchmarks.
AI.result: TRL matches vanilla GRPO on solo reasoning performance. Simultaneously, three properties emerge: (1) stronger handoff robustness with the junior, (2) reduced distributional drift from the junior's perspective, and (3) more legible chain-of-thought for the junior model.
AI.conclusion: TRL demonstrates a viable path for RLVR that yields practical benefits in multi-model communication and human compatibility, without sacrificing the senior model's individual reasoning capability.

title: Enhancing Numerical Prediction in LLMs via Smooth MMD Alignment
summary: Despite their strong general capabilities, large language models (LLMs) often remain unreliable when outputs must be numerically precise. A key reason is the training objective: standard cross-entropy treats numeric tokens as unstructured categories and ignores the metric structure of their values. We address this mismatch with Smooth Maximum Mean Discrepancy (SMMD), which builds on the classic MMD by incorporating value-distance kernels over numeric tokens and graph-based smoothness. With this kernel defined over a numeric sub-vocabulary, SMMD aligns the predicted numeric distribution to the target via kernel matching and smooths the prediction-target residual over the induced kernel graph to encourage local consistency. We evaluate SMMD on four numeric-target tasks: mathematical reasoning, arithmetic calculation, clock-time recognition, and chart question answering, across multiple open-weight LLM and VLM backbones. SMMD consistently improves accuracy over both cross-entropy and recent numeric-target losses; analyses show complementary effects between MMD and smoothness and underscore the importance of distance-based kernel design. Code is available at https://github.com/Zuozhuo/smmd-loss.

AI.tldr: SMMD proposes a loss function that replaces standard cross-entropy for numeric token prediction by incorporating value-distance kernels and graph-based smoothness via Maximum Mean Discrepancy, yielding consistent accuracy improvements across math, arithmetic, time recognition, and chart QA tasks.
AI.motivation: LLMs produce unreliable numerically precise outputs because cross-entropy treats numeric tokens as unstructured categories, ignoring the metric structure (e.g., 42 is closer to 43 than to 7). A loss function that respects numeric distance is needed.
AI.method: Smooth Maximum Mean Discrepancy (SMMD) extends classic MMD by: (1) defining value-distance kernels over a numeric sub-vocabulary, (2) aligning predicted and target numeric distributions via kernel matching, and (3) applying graph Laplacian smoothness regularization over the induced kernel graph to enforce local consistency in prediction-target residuals.
AI.result: SMMD consistently outperforms both standard cross-entropy and recent numeric-target losses across four tasks (mathematical reasoning, arithmetic calculation, clock-time recognition, chart QA) on multiple open-weight LLM and VLM backbones. Ablations confirm complementary effects between MMD and smoothness components, and the critical role of distance-based kernel design.
AI.conclusion: SMMD effectively addresses the numeric precision gap in LLMs by injecting metric-aware supervision. The approach is model-agnostic, broadly applicable to numeric generation tasks, and demonstrates that respecting the ordinal/interval structure of numbers during training yields reliable accuracy gains.

title: Continual Learning for Sequential Personalization of Small Language Models: A Stability Monitoring Analysis
summary: Small Language Models (SLMs) are increasingly being considered for deployment on edge devices such as laptops, enabling private, low-latency, and locally personalized applications. However, personalization requires models to adapt over time to evolving user- or task-specific data, placing them in a continual learning setting. This creates the risk of catastrophic forgetting, where learning new information degrades performance on previously learned tasks or broader model capabilities. Recent benchmarks such as TRACE have shown that continual fine-tuning can significantly degrade the general abilities of aligned large language models. In this work, we present a study for sequential LoRA personalization of SLMs. We save model checkpoints after each adaptation stage and evaluate them on current tasks, previously seen tasks, and a fixed reference set. This checkpoint-level protocol enables us to monitor task performance, forgetting, and reference set drift over time. We show that lightweight reference set distributional diagnostics can reveal model-specific instability patterns during sequential LoRA personalization of SLMs, including cases where task-level metrics alone hide harmful adaptation. We hope this can highlight new research avenues for monitoring stability of SLMs in a continual learning setting.

AI.tldr: Analyzes how sequential LoRA fine-tuning of small language models on edge devices causes catastrophic forgetting; proposes checkpoint-level monitoring with reference set distributional diagnostics to detect instability that task-level metrics alone may miss.
AI.motivation: SLMs deployed on edge devices require continual personalization to user-specific data, but this creates catastrophic forgetting risks. Existing benchmarks (e.g., TRACE) show continual fine-tuning degrades LLM general abilities, yet monitoring approaches for SLMs in this setting remain underdeveloped. Task-level metrics alone may hide harmful adaptation.
AI.method: Sequential LoRA personalization of SLMs with checkpoint-level evaluation protocol: after each adaptation stage, model checkpoints are saved and evaluated on (1) the current task, (2) previously seen tasks, and (3) a fixed reference set. Lightweight reference set distributional diagnostics are applied to detect model-specific instability patterns.
AI.result: Reference set distributional diagnostics reveal model-specific instability patterns during sequential LoRA personalization. Importantly, task-level metrics alone can fail to surface harmful adaptation, meaning distributional drift on a fixed reference set provides complementary signals that expose hidden degradation.
AI.conclusion: The checkpoint-level protocol combined with reference set diagnostics offers a more complete monitoring framework for SLM stability under continual learning. The authors hope this opens new research directions for ensuring safe, stable personalization of SLMs on edge devices.

title: KG2Cypher: Data-Centric Pipeline for Building Enterprise Text-to-Cypher Systems
summary: Enterprise Knowledge Graphs (KGs) are increasingly used for internal search, analytics, and question answering, but building natural-language interfaces for private enterprise graphs remains costly. We present KG2Cypher, a data-centric pipeline for building enterprise text-to-Cypher systems from existing KGs. KG2Cypher first constructs an executable Cypher query from observed graph facts and then uses LLMs to generate its associated natural-language question. The resulting Text-Cypher pairs are validated with an LLM judge and human validation, and are converted into candidate-aware SFT data. The trained generator is served with class-conditioned schema prompting, entity retrieval, and LoRA-based inference. We evaluate KG2Cypher in Korean enterprise settings, where short search-style queries and schema paraphrases make language grounding difficult. LoRA SFT improves execution-result F1 from 0.806 to 0.950 on broadcast-program queries and from 0.70 to 0.92 on company queries. In an 11-class setting, KG2Cypher achieves 95.2% exact match, 99.9% execution rate, and 0.964 execution-result F1.

AI.tldr: KG2Cypher is a data-centric pipeline that automatically generates natural-language-to-Cypher training pairs from existing enterprise KGs by reverse-generating questions from graph queries, then fine-tunes LLMs with LoRA to achieve high-accuracy text-to-Cypher translation in Korean enterprise settings.
AI.motivation: Building natural-language interfaces for private enterprise KGs is costly due to the lack of labeled Text-to-Cypher training data. Existing approaches struggle with short search-style queries and schema paraphrases, especially in non-English languages like Korean.
AI.method: KG2Cypher employs a data-centric pipeline: (1) construct executable Cypher queries from observed graph facts, (2) use LLMs to reverse-generate natural-language questions for each query, (3) validate resulting Text-Cypher pairs via an LLM judge and human review, (4) convert validated pairs into candidate-aware supervised fine-tuning (SFT) data. The trained generator is served using class-conditioned schema prompting, entity retrieval, and LoRA-based inference.
AI.result: LoRA SFT improves execution-result F1 from 0.806 to 0.950 on broadcast-program queries and from 0.70 to 0.92 on company queries. In an 11-class setting, KG2Cypher achieves 95.2% exact match, 99.9% execution rate, and 0.964 execution-result F1.
AI.conclusion: The data-centric reverse-generation approach effectively overcomes the scarcity of labeled Text-to-Cypher data in enterprise settings, and combining candidate-aware SFT with class-conditioned prompting and LoRA yields robust, near-production-ready performance for Korean enterprise KG question answering.

title: TeRoR: Decoupled Temporal Rotation with Relational Circular Region for Temporal Knowledge Graph Embedding
summary: In recent years, with the emergence of Temporal Knowledge Graphs (TKGs), research on learning entity and relation representations in TKGs has attracted increasing attention, giving rise to a large number of TKG embedding methods. TeRo is a simple and efficient temporal knowledge graph embedding approach. However, TeRo does not do well in modeling the mapping properties of various relations, such as one-to-many, many-to-one, and many-to-many. Meanwhile, it also has limitations in the expression of temporal information. To address these issues, we propose a novel TKG embedding method named TeRoR. This method divides the temporal evolution of entity embeddings, and conducts independent rotation transformations on head and tail entities in the complex vector space to strengthen temporal information modeling capacity. In terms of relational characteristics, we train a radius to constrain the rotated and translated head entities within a circular region centered on the tail entity, which effectively captures the diverse mapping properties of relations. Experimental results demonstrate that TeRoR achieves competitive performance against state-of-the-art models on four distinct TKG datasets.

AI.tldr: TeRoR improves upon the TeRo TKG embedding method by introducing independent rotation transformations for head and tail entities in complex vector space and a radius-based circular constraint to better model temporal information and diverse relation mapping properties (one-to-many, many-to-one, many-to-many).
AI.motivation: Existing TKG embedding method TeRo has two key deficiencies: (1) it poorly models various relational mapping properties such as one-to-many, many-to-one, and many-to-many; (2) it has limited capacity in expressing temporal information. These limitations motivate the development of a more expressive temporal knowledge graph embedding approach.
AI.method: The proposed TeRoR method addresses these issues through two mechanisms: (1) it decomposes the temporal evolution of entity embeddings and applies independent rotation transformations on head and tail entities in complex vector space, thereby strengthening temporal information modeling; (2) it trains a radius parameter to constrain rotated and translated head entities within a circular region centered on the tail entity, enabling effective capture of diverse relation mapping properties.
AI.result: Experimental results on four distinct TKG datasets show that TeRoR achieves competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art models.
AI.conclusion: TeRoR effectively mitigates TeRo's shortcomings in modeling relation mapping properties and temporal information expression, offering a competitive TKG embedding method validated across multiple benchmark datasets.

title: Output-Space Allocation Costs for Calibration-Guided LLM Compression: An Empirical Study
summary: Training-free compression methods for large language models (LLMs) often use calibration data to guide compression decisions. ROCKET, a recent method combining sparse-dictionary factorization with multi-choice knapsack problem (MCKP) allocation, derives its per-layer factorization from an output reconstruction objective but uses weight-space Frobenius error as the MCKP allocation cost. We investigate whether aligning the allocation cost with the output-space objective improves compressed model fidelity. On Qwen3-8B at 50\% compression, our ROCKET-ActCost achieves +0.8 percentage points higher average accuracy across 8 zero-shot benchmarks (53.1\% vs 52.3\%), but increases WikiText perplexity by 16\% (61.46 vs 52.98). This accuracy-perplexity tradeoff reveals that different allocation objectives favor different downstream metrics. The high correlation ($>$0.99) between weight-space and output-space errors limits allocation divergence, explaining the modest effect size. On Llama-3.2-1B at 20\% compression, the two methods produce near-identical results (53.3\% vs 53.5\% accuracy, 14.45 vs 14.66 PPL), suggesting that the effect of the cost function is minor at lower compression ratios.
