AI.tldr: Replacing weight-space Frobenius error with an output-activation-based cost in ROCKET's MCKP allocation step yields a small accuracy gain on Qwen3-8B at high compression but worsens perplexity, revealing a tradeoff; at low compression ratios the cost function choice is effectively inconsequential.
AI.motivation: ROCKET uses an output reconstruction objective for per-layer factorization but a weight-space Frobenius error for cross-layer allocation via MCKP. The authors hypothesize that aligning the allocation cost with the output-space objective could improve compressed model fidelity.
AI.method: The authors propose ROCKET-ActCost, which substitutes the MCKP allocation cost from weight-space Frobenius error to an output-activation-based reconstruction error. They evaluate on Qwen3-8B (50% compression) and Llama-3.2-1B (20% compression) across 8 zero-shot benchmarks and WikiText perplexity.
AI.result: On Qwen3-8B at 50% compression, ROCKET-ActCost achieves +0.8 pp average accuracy (53.1% vs 52.3%) but 16% higher perplexity (61.46 vs 52.98). The two cost functions correlate >0.99, limiting allocation divergence. On Llama-3.2-1B at 20% compression, results are near-identical (53.3% vs 53.5% accuracy; 14.45 vs 14.66 PPL).
AI.conclusion: Different allocation objectives favor different downstream metrics, revealing an accuracy-perplexity tradeoff. The extremely high correlation between weight-space and output-space errors explains the modest effect size, and at lower compression ratios the cost function choice is negligible.

title: Are Time-Series Foundation Models Ready for E-Nose Data? An Empirical Assessment of Their Embeddings
summary: Inspired by advances in natural language processing and computer vision, "time-series foundation models" (TSFMs) have recently been introduced with the promise of strong generalization across diverse time-series tasks, including forecasting, classification, and anomaly detection, as well as across domains such as healthcare, climate science, and manufacturing. However, their utility for gas-sensing data remains largely unexplored. To address this gap, this paper systematically evaluates recent TSFMs on electronic nose (E-Nose) data. In particular, we investigate whether embeddings produced by representative TSFMs, including Chronos-2 and MOMENT, provide effective representations for gas identification and concentration prediction. Specifically, we show that fine-tuning is necessary to achieve satisfactory performance on E-Nose data, and fusing TSFM embeddings with representations learned by specialized predictive models can further improve the performance, suggesting both the potential and limitations of current TSFMs for gas-sensing applications.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically evaluates time-series foundation models (TSFMs) on electronic nose (E-Nose) gas-sensing data, finding that fine-tuning is necessary and that fusing TSFM embeddings with specialized model representations improves performance for gas identification and concentration prediction tasks.
AI.motivation: While TSFMs have shown strong generalization across diverse time-series tasks and domains (healthcare, climate, manufacturing), their utility for gas-sensing data remains largely unexplored, creating a gap this paper aims to address.
AI.method: Systematic evaluation of representative TSFMs (Chronos-2, MOMENT) on E-Nose data. The study investigates whether TSFM embeddings provide effective representations for two tasks: gas identification (classification) and concentration prediction (regression). It further examines fine-tuning strategies and embedding fusion with specialized predictive models.
AI.result: Fine-tuning is necessary to achieve satisfactory performance on E-Nose data. Fusing TSFM embeddings with representations learned by specialized predictive models further improves performance, suggesting that current TSFMs have both potential and limitations for gas-sensing applications.
AI.conclusion: Current TSFMs show promise but are not off-the-shelf solutions for gas-sensing tasks; task-specific fine-tuning and representation fusion with domain-specialized models are needed to unlock their full potential.

title: SHIFT: Gate-Modulated Activation Steering for Knowledge Conflict Mitigation in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) enhances LLMs by incorporating external knowledge to support response generation. However, conflicts between retrieved context and parametric knowledge have emerged as a critical challenge in RAG systems. To mitigate such conflicts, numerous studies have attempted to identify and edit knowledge-related internal neurons, aiming to improve the ability of LLMs to rely on contextual evidence during generation. However, these neuron-level approaches may introduce unintended cascading effects that compromise the general capabilities of LLMs, as the modified neurons are often entangled with broader model behaviors and functionalities. In this paper, we introduce SHIFT, a novel framework that reformulates neuron-level modification as learnable gate modulation, allowing LLMs to adaptively regulate internal activations for knowledge conflict resolution. Technically, our SHIFT equips LLMs with a lightweight gate module and optimizes fewer than 0.01% trainable parameters while keeping the backbone model frozen. During generation, the gate module adjusts the model's internal representations to adaptively leverage contextual and parametric knowledge. Extensive experiments on six datasets validate the effectiveness of our SHIFT in comparison with various competing baselines. All datasets and code are available at https://github.com/OpenBMB/SHIFT.

AI.tldr: SHIFT proposes a learnable gate modulation framework for resolving knowledge conflicts in RAG systems, replacing neuron-level editing. It uses a lightweight gate module (<0.01% trainable parameters) that adaptively regulates internal activations, allowing LLMs to balance contextual and parametric knowledge without compromising general capabilities.
AI.motivation: Existing neuron-level approaches for resolving RAG knowledge conflicts (identifying and editing knowledge-related neurons) can cause unintended cascading effects that degrade the LLM's general capabilities, because modified neurons are entangled with broader model functionalities.
AI.method: SHIFT reformulates neuron-level modification as learnable gate modulation. A lightweight gate module is attached to a frozen backbone LLM, with fewer than 0.01% of parameters being trainable. During generation, the gate module adaptively adjusts internal representations to regulate the influence of contextual versus parametric knowledge.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on six datasets demonstrate that SHIFT outperforms various competing baselines in resolving knowledge conflicts while preserving the model's general abilities.
AI.conclusion: SHIFT provides an effective, parameter-efficient solution for knowledge conflict resolution in RAG systems by using adaptive gate modulation instead of direct neuron editing, avoiding degradation of the LLM's broader capabilities.

title: Textual Belief States for World Models: Identifiable Representation Learning Under Strict Mediation
summary: World models in partially observed environments rely on latent representations that summarize interaction history, but in many modern LLM-based architectures predictive performance fails to reflect representation quality due to history bypass, rendering the latent state unidentifiable. Strict latent state mediation, requiring predictions to depend only on the latent state and action, is a classical principle that resolves this, but enforcing it in text-based settings is an open challenge: textual latent states are discrete and non-differentiable, precluding variational training, and expressive LLM decoders readily ignore the bottleneck. We show how to make strict mediation work in the text domain. We formalize why it is necessary, showing that strict mediation makes representation quality empirically testable while history-leaky architectures break this connection. We then introduce textual latent states, which are discrete, interpretable, and variable-length, and factorized GRPO (fGRPO), a tree-structured reinforcement learning method that enforces strict mediation during training. Experiments on TextWorld and ScienceWorld show preserved one-step prediction accuracy alongside up to 57\% gains in representation quality and 98\% improvements in rollout performance, increasing with task complexity and horizon.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses the problem of "history bypass" in LLM-based world models, where predictive performance does not reflect latent representation quality. The authors propose textual latent states (discrete, interpretable, variable-length) and factorized GRPO (fGRPO), a tree-structured RL method that enforces strict latent state mediation during training. Experiments show preserved prediction accuracy with up to 57% gains in representation quality and 98% improvements in rollout performance.
AI.motivation: In LLM-based world models for partially observed environments, latent representations that summarize interaction history are essential. However, expressive LLM decoders can ignore the latent bottleneck and rely directly on raw history ("history bypass"), making the latent state unidentifiable and representation quality untestable. Strict latent state mediation—where predictions depend only on the latent state and action—is a classical solution, but enforcing it in discrete text domains is challenging because textual latents are non-differentiable (precluding variational training) and LLM decoders easily bypass the bottleneck.
AI.method: The authors (1) formalize why strict mediation is necessary, proving it makes representation quality empirically testable while leaky architectures break this property; (2) introduce textual latent states that are discrete, interpretable, and variable-length; and (3) propose factorized GRPO (fGRPO), a tree-structured reinforcement learning method that enforces strict mediation during training by structuring the optimization to force predictions through the latent bottleneck.
AI.result: Experiments on TextWorld and ScienceWorld benchmarks show that the approach preserves one-step prediction accuracy while achieving up to 57% gains in representation quality metrics and up to 98% improvements in rollout (multi-step simulation) performance. These gains increase with task complexity and horizon length.
AI.conclusion: Strict mediation is both necessary and feasible in text-based world models. By combining discrete textual latent states with factorized GRPO, the approach yields latent representations that are both high-quality and empirically verifiable, overcoming the history bypass problem that plagues standard LLM-based architectures.

title: NLL-Guided Full-Attention Layer Selection for Training-Free Sliding-Window Adaptation
summary: Hybrid attention models that mix full and sliding-window attention across layers offer a promising approach to efficient long-context inference, but the critical question of \emph{which layers} should retain full attention remains unsolved. Existing methods use either fixed periodic patterns or attention-based heuristics that may not capture what matters for downstream accuracy. We propose NLL-guided layer selection, a training-free method that directly measures each layer's importance by computing the negative log-likelihood degradation on answer tokens when that layer uses sliding-window instead of full attention. On LongMemEval with Qwen3-4B, our method achieves 64.6\% accuracy using only 1/4 full-attention layers, matching the 1/2-FA periodic baseline (65.0\%) while halving the computational budget. NLL-guided selection outperforms the SWAA-reported periodic 1/4-FA baseline by 10.4 percentage points and a matched LightTransfer-style baseline by 26.4 percentage points. De-confounding analysis shows the signal is consistent with long-range attention needs rather than generic layer sensitivity. The method requires only $\sim$15 minutes of one-time calibration, advancing the efficiency-accuracy Pareto frontier for long-context LLM deployment.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a training-free method for selecting which layers in a hybrid attention model should retain full attention, using negative log-likelihood degradation on answer tokens as a direct importance signal. The method achieves near-identical accuracy to baselines using half the full-attention layers and significantly outperforms existing heuristics.
AI.motivation: Hybrid attention models combining full and sliding-window attention across layers are promising for efficient long-context inference, but the optimal assignment of full attention to specific layers remains an open problem. Existing approaches (fixed periodic patterns or attention-based heuristics) fail to accurately capture which layers matter most for downstream task accuracy.
AI.method: NLL-guided layer selection: a training-free calibration method that measures each layer's importance by computing the degradation in negative log-likelihood (NLL) on answer tokens when that layer is switched from full attention to sliding-window attention. Layers with the largest NLL increase are deemed most important and retain full attention. The calibration requires approximately 15 minutes of one-time computation.
AI.result: On LongMemEval with Qwen3-4B, the method achieves 64.6% accuracy using only 1/4 full-attention layers, matching the 1/2-FA periodic baseline (65.0%) at half the computational cost. It outperforms the SWAA-reported periodic 1/4-FA baseline by +10.4 pp and a LightTransfer-style baseline by +26.4 pp. De-confounding analysis confirms the signal reflects genuine long-range attention needs rather than generic layer sensitivity.
AI.conclusion: NLL-guided layer selection advances the efficiency-accuracy Pareto frontier for long-context LLM deployment by providing a principled, lightweight method to identify attention-critical layers, enabling substantial computational savings with minimal accuracy loss.

title: CBD: API-Only LLM Black-Box Unlearning through Controlled Behavioral Divergence
summary: Edge devices increasingly invoke large language models (LLMs) through API services for context aware edge intelligence, while edge generated data may be collected to improve LLMs and may introduce sensitive, copyrighted, harmful, or outdated information into model behavior. Machine unlearning offers a practical way to remove the influence of undesired data without retraining LLMs. However, existing methods still face two gaps. The first is API only black box access, where target model parameters and internal logits are unavailable. The second is how to preserve retained utility when unlearning target data and retained data share highly similar prompt structures or semantic patterns. To address these challenges, we propose Controlled Behavioral Divergence (CBD), an API only black box unlearning framework. CBD uses two auxiliary models to create controlled behavioral divergence between retained inputs and unlearning target inputs, converts this divergence into an unlearning relevance score, and routes unlearning related prompts away from the target LLM. To improve discrimination accuracy under high similarity between target and retained data, CBD constructs a gradient statistics based discriminative basis by estimating empirical Fisher matrices and solving a regularized generalized eigenvalue problem, guiding the unlearning signal toward target specific information rather than shared prompt structures. Compared with eleven white box and gray box unlearning baselines, CBD achieves a better unlearning utility trade off and its performance varies little across settings. On ToFU forget10, CBD approaches the retrained reference on the forget set while raising model utility to 74.90, about 15% above the second best baseline. On WMDP, it lowers hazardous knowledge accuracy to 25.68, near random guessing, while preserving MMLU accuracy of 52.67. Code is at https://github.com/DGL-codes/CBD.

AI.tldr: CBD is an API-only black-box machine unlearning framework for LLMs that uses two auxiliary models to create controlled behavioral divergence, routing unlearning-related prompts away from the target model. It constructs a gradient-statistics-based discriminative basis via empirical Fisher matrices and a regularized generalized eigenvalue problem to distinguish target-specific from shared information, achieving superior unlearning-utility trade-offs compared to 11 white-box and gray-box baselines.
AI.motivation: Edge devices generate data that may contain sensitive, copyrighted, harmful, or outdated content, which can be introduced into LLMs when that data is used for model improvement. Machine unlearning is needed to remove undesired data influence without full retraining. Existing methods suffer from two gaps: (1) API-only black-box access where model parameters and internal logits are unavailable, and (2) difficulty preserving retained utility when target and retained data share highly similar prompt structures or semantic patterns.
AI.method: CBD (Controlled Behavioral Divergence) employs two auxiliary models to induce controlled behavioral divergence between retained and unlearning target inputs, converting this divergence into an unlearning relevance score for routing prompts away from the target LLM. To handle high similarity between target and retained data, CBD constructs a gradient-statistics-based discriminative basis by estimating empirical Fisher matrices and solving a regularized generalized eigenvalue problem, which steers the unlearning signal toward target-specific information rather than shared prompt structures.
AI.result: CBD achieves a better unlearning-utility trade-off than 11 white-box and gray-box baselines, with consistent performance across settings. On ToFU forget10, it approaches retrained-reference performance on the forget set while achieving model utility of 74.90 (~15% above second-best). On WMDP, it reduces hazardous knowledge accuracy to 25.68 (near random guessing) while preserving MMLU accuracy of 52.67.
AI.conclusion: CBD demonstrates that effective machine unlearning is feasible under strict API-only black-box constraints, even when target and retained data are semantically similar. The Fisher-based discriminative basis successfully isolates target-specific information, enabling strong unlearning without sacrificing retained utility.

title: Position Bias Correction is Insufficient for One-Pass Attention Sorting
summary: Long-context language models suffer from position bias, where information in middle positions is underutilized. Attention Sorting addresses this by iteratively reordering documents based on attention patterns, but its multiple sort-and-generate cycles increase deployment cost. We hypothesize that position bias is the primary bottleneck and propose Debiased One-Pass Attention Sorting, which estimates a per-prompt position-bias curve from the low-attention majority of documents and uses it to correct raw attention scores (via subtraction or division) to enable single-pass sorting. Our experiments on two models refute this hypothesis in the tested setting: on LLaMA-2-7B-32K-Instruct, debiasing produces identical results to uncalibrated single-pass sorting (94.83\% containment accuracy), while on YaRN-Llama-2-7b-64k, debiasing improves accuracy by 8.67 percentage points but remains 14.84pp behind iterative sorting, closing only 37\% of the gap. These results suggest that position-bias correction is insufficient to match iterative sorting, and that repeated reordering provides additional benefits beyond bias correction.

AI.tldr: Position bias causes long-context LMs to underutilize middle-position information. The authors test whether correcting attention scores with a per-prompt position-bias curve can match iterative Attention Sorting in a single pass. Results show debiasing helps modestly on one model but fails to close most of the gap, suggesting iterative reordering provides benefits beyond bias correction.
AI.motivation: Attention Sorting effectively mitigates position bias by iteratively reordering documents, but its multiple sort-and-generate cycles are computationally expensive. The authors hypothesize that position bias is the primary bottleneck and that a one-pass approach with explicit bias correction could match iterative sorting's performance at lower cost.
AI.method: Debiased One-Pass Attention Sorting: (1) estimate a per-prompt position-bias curve from the low-attention majority of documents; (2) correct raw attention scores using either subtraction or division by the estimated bias curve; (3) perform single-pass document sorting based on corrected scores. Evaluated on LLaMA-2-7B-32K-Instruct and YaRN-Llama-2-7b-64k against both uncalibrated single-pass and iterative Attention Sorting baselines using containment accuracy.
AI.result: On LLaMA-2-7B-32K-Instruct, debiasing yields identical results to uncalibrated single-pass sorting (94.83% containment accuracy). On YaRN-Llama-2-7b-64k, debiasing improves accuracy by 8.67 percentage points over uncalibrated single-pass but remains 14.84pp behind iterative sorting, closing only 37% of the performance gap.
AI.conclusion: The hypothesis that position bias is the primary bottleneck is refuted in the tested setting. Position-bias correction alone is insufficient to match iterative Attention Sorting, indicating that repeated reordering confers additional benefits — potentially through iterative refinement of document relevance estimates — that a single-pass correction cannot replicate.

title: Deployment-Side Adaptiveness in Multi-Horizon Volatility Forecasting
comment: Accepted for KDD 2026 Machine Learning in Finance Workshop
summary: In financial forecasting, predictive performance depends not only on which model is trained, but also on how the trained model is deployed. We study this issue in multi-horizon volatility forecasting. Our starting point is that a trained multi-output (MIMO) forecaster does not define a single deployable predictor: by changing the inference-time rollout rule, the same trained model induces a family of forecasts with different accuracy and cost profiles. Across 20 stock-volatility series, three forecast horizons, and architectures ranging from linear models to PatchTST, we find that non-default rollout rules often improve over standard MIMO deployment. However, the best fixed rule varies substantially across architectures and horizons, making any single static replacement unreliable. We therefore evaluate validation-based deployment policies over the induced rule family. Under the primary MSE objective, validation-selected singletons provide a low-cost improvement over default MIMO, while small rule subsets recover much of the benefit of larger ensembles at substantially lower inference cost. We also find that policy rankings are metric-sensitive: MSE-selected policies do not transfer uniformly to QLIKE, a finance-standard volatility loss. These results show that inference-time deployment is a meaningful source of adaptiveness in financial forecasting, and that trained volatility forecasters should be evaluated not only by their architecture, but also by their deployment policy.

AI.tldr: Multi-horizon volatility forecasting can be improved not by changing the model architecture, but by optimizing how a trained MIMO forecaster is rolled out at inference time. Different rollout rules yield distinct accuracy-cost trade-offs, and the best rule varies by architecture and horizon. Validation-based selection policies can recover ensemble-level gains at lower cost, but optimal policies are metric-dependent (MSE vs. QLIKE).
AI.motivation: Prior work on financial volatility forecasting focuses almost exclusively on model architecture and training. The authors identify a gap: the inference-time deployment strategy (rollout rule) of a multi-output (MIMO) forecaster is typically treated as fixed, yet it induces a whole family of possible forecasts. No systematic study exists on how deployment choices affect predictive performance in financial forecasting.
AI.method: The authors train multi-output (MIMO) forecasters across 20 stock-volatility series, three forecast horizons, and multiple architectures (linear models through PatchTST). For each trained model, they generate a family of forecasts by varying the inference-time rollout rule (e.g., direct multi-step, recursive, hybrid). They then evaluate validation-based deployment policies — including singleton selection and small rule subsets — under both MSE and QLIKE loss functions.
AI.result: Non-default rollout rules often outperform standard MIMO deployment, but no single fixed rule is universally best across architectures and horizons. Validation-selected singletons improve over default MIMO at low cost. Small rule subsets recover much of the benefit of larger ensembles with substantially lower inference cost. Policy rankings are metric-sensitive: MSE-selected policies do not transfer well to QLIKE.
AI.conclusion: Inference-time deployment is a significant and underappreciated source of adaptiveness in financial volatility forecasting. Trained forecasters should be evaluated not solely by architecture but jointly by their deployment policy. Deployment policy selection constitutes a practical, low-cost lever for improving forecast accuracy.

title: Learning Complementary Action Modeling from Automotive Maintenance Instructions
summary: A minute lexical variation can reverse the procedural meaning of an instruction even when the rest of the sentence remains unchanged. In automotive maintenance instructions, this pattern often appears when an action phrase turns an instruction into its procedural counterpart. The entities, modifiers, and surrounding context remain largely invariant, while the action phrase determines the procedural relation. We define this task as Complementary Action Modeling (CAM). Given a maintenance instruction, the goal is to identify or generate its procedural counterpart by modifying the action phrase while preserving the remaining sentence context. This task focuses on three aspects: distinguishing complementarity from surface similarity, controlling generation at the action-phrase level, and evaluating relational correctness using retrieval, overlap-based, and human evaluation. Using a German automotive maintenance dataset, we examine these questions through candidate matching and controlled Seq2Seq generation. The results show that complementary maintenance instructions are best modeled as procedural associations grounded in subtle lexical cues. They should therefore not be treated as ordinary cases of sentence similarity or synonym-based paraphrasing.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Complementary Action Modeling (CAM), a task focused on identifying or generating the procedural counterpart of a maintenance instruction by altering only the action phrase while preserving surrounding context. Using a German automotive dataset, the authors show that such complementarity relies on subtle lexical cues and should not be conflated with surface-level sentence similarity or synonym-based paraphrasing.
AI.motivation: Minute lexical variations can completely reverse the procedural meaning of an instruction even when the rest of the sentence is unchanged. This phenomenon is prevalent in automotive maintenance instructions, where a single action phrase distinguishes an instruction from its procedural counterpart. Existing approaches that treat this as sentence similarity or synonym-based paraphrasing fail to capture the relational, complementary nature of such pairs.
AI.method: The authors define the CAM task with three evaluation dimensions: distinguishing complementarity from surface similarity, controlled generation at the action-phrase level, and relational correctness. They employ candidate matching and controlled Seq2Seq generation on a German automotive maintenance dataset, and evaluate using retrieval-based metrics, overlap-based metrics, and human evaluation.
AI.result: Complementary maintenance instructions are best modeled as procedural associations grounded in subtle lexical cues. Standard sentence similarity and synonym-based paraphrasing methods are inadequate for capturing this complementarity.
AI.conclusion: CAM should be treated as a distinct task centered on procedural relations signaled by fine-grained lexical variation, rather than being subsumed under generic paraphrase or similarity frameworks.

title: A Study of Temporal Fusion Strategies for Named Entity Recognition in Historical Texts
summary: Temporal variation poses a unique challenge for named entity recognition (NER) in historical texts, where entities drift in surface form and salience across time. While language models (LMs) have made progress in various NLP tasks, their ability to reason about temporality, especially in diachronic contexts, remains limited or at least, questionable. In this paper, we systematically study how temporal metadata can be structurally embedded into NER models using a range of lightweight fusion strategies. We experiment with both absolute and relative temporal representations, injected into Transformer-based architectures via early or late fusion mechanisms such as cross-attention, adapters, and concatenation. Our evaluations on French and German historical datasets reveal that late fusion strategies yield more robust and temporally generalisable performance, particularly in early and noisy periods.

AI.tldr: The paper systematically investigates lightweight fusion strategies (cross-attention, adapters, concatenation) for embedding temporal metadata into Transformer-based NER models, evaluating absolute vs. relative temporal representations on French and German historical datasets, finding that late fusion yields more robust, temporally generalizable performance.
AI.motivation: NER on historical texts suffers from temporal variation — entities shift in surface form and salience across time. While LMs excel at many NLP tasks, their capacity for temporal reasoning in diachronic contexts remains questionable. The work is motivated by the need to structurally incorporate temporal metadata into NER models to handle these temporal drifts.
AI.method: The authors experiment with lightweight fusion strategies to inject temporal metadata into Transformer-based NER architectures. They compare absolute vs. relative temporal representations and evaluate early vs. late fusion mechanisms: cross-attention, adapter modules, and feature concatenation. Experiments are conducted on French and German historical datasets.
AI.result: Late fusion strategies consistently outperform early fusion approaches, providing more robust and temporally generalizable NER performance. The benefit is particularly pronounced in early historical periods and noisy data conditions where temporal signals are most critical.
AI.conclusion: Late fusion of temporal metadata into Transformer-based NER models is a practical and effective approach for handling diachronic variation in historical texts, enabling better cross-period generalization without requiring heavy architectural modifications.

title: Class-frequency Guided Noise Schedule for Diffusion Models
summary: In this paper, we are the first to examine the correlations between class frequency and the multi-scale noise schedule within diffusion models. For score-based generative models, low-density regions often lead to inaccurately estimated scores, thereby compromising the generation quality. Although the multi-scale noise schedule can alleviate this issue during the diffusion process, low-frequency classes still face the challenge of large low-density regions, resulting in more inaccurate estimated scores than high-frequency classes. Furthermore, high-frequency classes tend to dominate the score space, causing a convergence of most data points towards generating samples from these classes. Consequently, samples generated within low-frequency classes exhibit suboptimal quality and limited diversity. To address this challenge, we propose the \textit{Class-frequency Guided (CFRG)} noise schedule, leveraging the insight that low-frequency classes should be endowed with larger-scale noises. To illustrate the effectiveness of our method, we conduct experiments on various tasks, including image generation, image classification, and text-to-image generation, using imbalanced datasets, \textit{i.e.}, CIFAR-100-LT, and ImageNet-LT. By employing the CFRG noise schedule, we achieve substantial improvements over baselines, manifesting the crucial role of frequency statistics in noise schedule design.

AI.tldr: This paper reveals that class frequency strongly correlates with optimal noise schedules in diffusion models—low-frequency classes suffer from larger low-density regions and worse score estimation. The authors propose Class-frequency Guided (CFRG) noise schedule, which assigns larger-scale noises to low-frequency classes, achieving significant improvements on imbalanced datasets like CIFAR-100-LT and ImageNet-LT across image generation, classification, and text-to-image tasks.
AI.motivation: In diffusion models, low-density regions lead to inaccurate score estimation, degrading generation quality. Although multi-scale noise schedules help, low-frequency classes still face disproportionately large low-density regions, yielding poorer score estimates than high-frequency classes. Additionally, high-frequency classes dominate the score space, causing generated samples to collapse toward frequent classes—resulting in low-quality, low-diversity outputs for rare classes.
AI.method: The authors propose the Class-frequency Guided (CFRG) noise schedule, which is grounded in the key insight that low-frequency (rare) classes should receive larger-scale noise injections during the diffusion process. This mitigates the disproportionately large low-density regions that plague under-represented classes, improving score estimation accuracy specifically for those classes.
AI.result: Experiments on imbalanced datasets (CIFAR-100-LT, ImageNet-LT) across image generation, image classification, and text-to-image generation tasks show that CFRG yields substantial improvements over baselines, validating that class frequency statistics are critical to noise schedule design.
AI.conclusion: Class frequency is a crucial yet previously overlooked factor in designing noise schedules for diffusion models. By explicitly accounting for class imbalance through the CFRG noise schedule, low-frequency class generation quality and diversity can be significantly improved, demonstrating the importance of frequency-aware noise scheduling.

title: VASAE: Naming SAE Dictionary Directions with Vocabulary-Aligned Anchoring
comment: 14 pages, 7 figures. Accepted to the 2nd Workshop on Compositional Learning at ICML 2026
summary: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) provide useful decompositions of Transformer residual streams, but their learned features are usually named post hoc rather than directly connected to the Transformer's token vocabulary. We introduce Vocabulary-Aligned Sparse Autoencoder (VASAE), a method that trains SAE features under vocabulary-aligned anchoring and assigns each feature an intrinsic token name: the token string whose embedding is nearest to that feature. Without reducing reconstruction quality compared with a standard SAE, VASAE produces dictionaries with vocabulary-aligned features. Using a 0.8 cutoff on the nearest-token alignment score, dictionaries trained on GPT-2-small post-residual streams align about 90% of features in layers 0--10. In Llama-3.1-8B, representative shallow and middle-layer dictionaries contain strongly aligned features, including 92.8% in the shallow layer, while the representative final-layer dictionary shows limited alignment. After subtracting the sentence-level mean sparse code, case studies show that many remaining intrinsic token names are relevant to nearby input tokens. These results suggest that vocabulary-aligned anchoring can connect learned features to intrinsic token names during training, complementing post hoc interpretation of learned dictionaries.

AI.tldr: VASAE trains sparse autoencoders with vocabulary-aligned anchoring, assigning each learned feature an intrinsic token name (the nearest token embedding). It achieves ~90% feature alignment in GPT-2-small layers 0–10 and 92.8% in Llama-3.1-8B shallow layers, without sacrificing reconstruction quality versus standard SAEs.
AI.motivation: Standard SAE features are typically named post hoc, lacking intrinsic connections to the Transformer's token vocabulary. The authors aim to bridge this gap by directly anchoring learned dictionary features to token embeddings during training, enabling immediate interpretability through intrinsic token names.
AI.method: VASAE modifies the standard SAE training objective by introducing vocabulary-aligned anchoring: each dictionary feature is encouraged to align with a specific token embedding. The nearest token embedding (by cosine similarity or similar metric) becomes the feature's intrinsic token name. A 0.8 cutoff on alignment score filters features. Experiments span GPT-2-small (post-residual streams, layers 0–10) and Llama-3.1-8B (shallow, middle, and final layers). The method also subtracts sentence-level mean sparse codes for refined case studies.
AI.result: With a 0.8 alignment cutoff, ~90% of features in GPT-2-small layers 0–10 are vocabulary-aligned. Llama-3.1-8B shallow-layer dictionaries reach 92.8% alignment, middle layers show strong alignment, but final-layer alignment is limited. After subtracting sentence-level mean sparse codes, many intrinsic token names remain relevant to nearby input tokens. Reconstruction quality matches standard SAEs.
AI.conclusion: Vocabulary-aligned anchoring successfully connects learned SAE features to intrinsic token names during training, offering a complementary approach to post hoc dictionary interpretation without compromising reconstruction fidelity. Alignment is strong in early and middle layers but diminishes in the final layer of larger models.

title: The Simulacrum: Decision-Theoretic Pretraining for Near-Optimal Time-Series Forecasting and Inference
summary:
We introduce a neural network-based framework for learning time series estimators through a process we term decision-theoretic pretraining. Analysts specify a generative world, a distribution over data-generating processes, and a target decision objective. A neural network trained on stratified simulations from this world approximates the corresponding optimal decision rule, yielding a neural estimator that provides forecasts, parameter estimates, predictive intervals, or model-selection for zero-shot inference on previously unseen time series.
  The joint specification of the generative world and objective enables the estimators to directly approximate process-level, finite-sample properties: near-optimal risk, bias control, minimax performance, and uniform calibration. Our experiments demonstrate that these neural estimators can outperform traditional baselines such as maximum likelihood estimation and model selection via AICc, for the same model structural model classes. Furthermore, even when trained purely on simulations of structural models, they achieve competitive or state-of-the-art forecasting accuracy on major real-world benchmarks, compared with statistical, neural or large pre-trained models.
  We illustrate the framework by addressing two longstanding challenges: finite-sample bias and miscalibration in AR(p) models, and the forecast combination puzzle. These applications highlight the approach's main advantage: its ability to approximate solutions to analytically intractable or computationally prohibitive time series problems, including complex structural equations or optimality criteria. Ultimately, by enabling explicit control over decision-theoretic trade-offs, the framework equips analysts with highly efficient estimation tools tailored to their specific analytical needs.

AI.tldr: A neural network framework called "decision-theoretic pretraining" is proposed, where networks are trained on simulated time series data against a specified decision objective, yielding estimators that directly optimize finite-sample properties and can outperform traditional methods on both synthetic and real-world benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Traditional time series estimators (e.g., MLE, AICc) often rely on asymptotic theory and are not optimized for finite-sample performance on specific decision objectives. Many analytically intractable or computationally prohibitive time series problems remain unsolved. The authors aim to provide a general-purpose framework for learning estimators that directly approximate optimal decision rules for user-specified generative worlds and objectives.
AI.method: The framework involves: (1) an analyst specifies a generative world (distribution over data-generating processes) and a target decision objective (e.g., forecasting, parameter estimation, model selection); (2) a neural network is trained on stratified simulations from this world to approximate the corresponding optimal decision rule; (3) the resulting "neural estimator" performs zero-shot inference on unseen time series. The approach is demonstrated on two challenges: finite-sample bias/miscalibration in AR(p) models and the forecast combination puzzle.
AI.result: Neural estimators trained via this framework outperform traditional baselines (MLE, AICc) on structural model classes. When trained purely on simulations of structural models, they achieve competitive or state-of-the-art forecasting accuracy on major real-world benchmarks, rivaling statistical, neural, and large pre-trained foundation models.
AI.conclusion: Decision-theoretic pretraining enables explicit control over trade-offs like risk, bias, calibration, and minimax performance. It provides a practical way to tackle analytically intractable time series problems and equips analysts with tailored, highly efficient estimation tools for their specific needs.

title: An Empirical Analysis of Factual Errors in Human-Written Text and its Application
summary: Factual Error Detection (FED), which is the task of identifying factually incorrect spans in a given text, has long been recognized as an important research problem. However, with the rapid rise of large language models (LLMs), research attention has shifted toward factual errors specific to LLM-generated text (hallucinations) and their detection. As a result, the detection of factual errors in human-written text has been relatively neglected. To address this gap, we first distill a taxonomy of human-induced factual errors by analyzing corrections of newspaper articles, a representative source of text that is guaranteed to be human-written and contains few grammatical errors. Our analysis revealed that there are characteristic categories such as kanji misconversions and numeral classifier errors, which are not focused in existing hallucination benchmarks. Based on the taxonomy, we then evaluate the FED capability of vanilla LLMs on synthesized realistic test cases and real corrections. Experimental results demonstrated that even high-performance LLMs such as GPT-5.4 achieved only word-level F1 score of 52% on the synthetic evaluation data, highlighting the task difficulty. Furthermore, a detailed analysis by detection difficulty revealed the current state of FED.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the neglected problem of factual error detection (FED) in human-written text, proposes a taxonomy of human-induced factual errors derived from newspaper corrections, and evaluates LLMs on this task, revealing that even advanced models like GPT-4 achieve only ~52% word-level F1, underscoring the difficulty of FED.
AI.motivation: Research on factual error detection has shifted toward detecting hallucinations in LLM-generated text, leaving FED in human-written text relatively understudied. The authors aim to fill this gap by systematically characterizing human factual errors and benchmarking LLM performance on this task.
AI.method: (1) The authors distilled a taxonomy of human-induced factual errors by manually analyzing corrections from newspaper articles — a source guaranteed to be human-written and largely free of grammatical errors. (2) Based on this taxonomy, they constructed synthesized realistic test cases and also used real-world corrections. (3) They evaluated the FED capability of vanilla LLMs (e.g., GPT-4) on both synthetic and real data, measuring word-level F1 scores and conducting difficulty-stratified analysis.
AI.result: The taxonomy revealed error categories characteristic of human writing — such as kanji misconversions and numeral classifier errors — that are absent from typical hallucination benchmarks. On synthetic evaluation data, even the best LLM (GPT-4) achieved only a 52% word-level F1 score, indicating substantial room for improvement. A fine-grained analysis by detection difficulty further characterized the current limitations of LLMs on FED.
AI.conclusion: FED in human-written text remains a challenging open problem that current LLMs handle poorly. The proposed taxonomy and benchmark offer a foundation for future work, and the difficulty-stratified analysis highlights specific areas where detection capabilities need improvement.

title: Aurora: A Leverage-Aware Spectral Optimizer
summary: We show that for tall matrix parameters, like projection matrices in the MLP layers, the Muon update can have row norms that are arbitrarily non-uniform. This can lead to a self-reinforcing feedback loop whereby neurons receive persistently small updates and eventually do not contribute meaningfully to network outputs. This problem is effectively mitigated by an additional row normalization step, but current methods do this in a way that moves the Muon update geometry away from the polar factor of the momentum matrix, which we find is undesirable. We propose Aurora, an optimizer that enforces row-uniformity of matrix parameter updates while respecting Muon's polar factor geometry. Aurora outperforms Muon in our pre-training experiments and, when combined with existing methods, achieves state-of-the-art performance among spectral optimizers on the optimizer track of the modded-nanoGPT speedrun. Additionally, we find that Aurora's empirical gains over Muon scale with the MLP expansion factor, suggesting that Aurora may allow for effective training of very wide MLP layers.

AI.tldr: Aurora is a novel optimizer that addresses Muon's issue of non-uniform row updates in tall matrix parameters (e.g., MLP projection matrices) by enforcing row-uniformity while preserving the desirable polar factor geometry. It outperforms Muon and achieves state-of-the-art among spectral optimizers on modded-nanoGPT.
AI.motivation: Muon updates for tall matrices can produce arbitrarily non-uniform row norms, causing a feedback loop where some neurons receive persistently tiny updates and become "dead" (non-contributing). Existing row-normalization fixes distort Muon's polar factor geometry, which the authors find undesirable. There is a need for a method that enforces row-uniformity without sacrificing this geometry.
AI.method: Aurora is an optimizer that applies row-normalization to Muon-style updates for matrix parameters while explicitly respecting the polar factor geometry of the momentum matrix — i.e., it projects updates onto a geometry-preserving manifold rather than naively normalizing rows post hoc.
AI.result: Aurora outperforms Muon in pre-training experiments and achieves state-of-the-art results among spectral optimizers on the modded-nanoGPT speedrun optimizer track. Gains over Muon scale with the MLP expansion factor, suggesting benefits for very wide MLP layers.
AI.conclusion: Aurora successfully mitigates Muon's row-norm non-uniformity problem while retaining the beneficial polar factor geometry. It offers a promising direction for training architectures with wide MLP layers and advances the state of spectral optimization.

title: From Black-Box to Clinical Insight: A Multi-Stage Explainable Framework for Speech-Based Cognitive Impairment Detection
summary: Speech-based cognitive impairment detection offers a noninvasive, accessible alternative to costly biomarker assays, yet transformer-based models remain clinically uninterpretable. We propose a multi-stage explainability framework that translates black-box transformer predictions into clinically grounded narratives by integrating SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP)-based token attribution, theory-informed linguistic features, and a four-stage LLM reasoning pipeline using LLaMA-3.1-70B-Instruct. Built on the SpeechCARE-Adaptive Gating Network multimodal screening model (F1 = 72.11% on the NIA PREPARE benchmark), the framework maps model outputs to four cognitive-linguistic dimensions, including lexical richness, syntactic complexity, and semantic coherence. Physician evaluation on 70 stratified English samples demonstrated strong alignment with patient-level cognitive profiles, and a System Usability Scale score of 82/100 indicated high potential for clinical workflow integration.

AI.tldr: A multi-stage explainability framework using SHAP token attribution, linguistic features, and LLaMA-3.1-70B-Instruct translates black-box transformer predictions for cognitive impairment detection into clinically grounded narratives, achieving strong physician alignment and an 82/100 System Usability Scale score.
AI.motivation: Transformer-based models for speech-based cognitive impairment detection are clinically uninterpretable, limiting their adoption despite offering a noninvasive, accessible alternative to costly biomarker assays.
AI.method: A multi-stage explainability framework combining (1) SHAP-based token attribution to identify influential speech tokens, (2) theory-informed linguistic features mapped to four cognitive-linguistic dimensions (lexical richness, syntactic complexity, semantic coherence), and (3) a four-stage LLM reasoning pipeline using LLaMA-3.1-70B-Instruct to generate clinically grounded narratives. This is built atop the SpeechCARE-Adaptive Gating Network multimodal screening model (F1=72.11% on NIA PREPARE).
AI.result: Physician evaluation on 70 stratified English samples showed strong alignment with patient-level cognitive profiles, and a System Usability Scale score of 82/100 indicated high potential for clinical workflow integration.
AI.conclusion: The framework effectively bridges the interpretability gap in transformer-based cognitive screening, translating model outputs into clinically meaningful narratives and demonstrating readiness for real-world clinical integration.

title: Learning to Reason with Curriculum II: Compositional Generalization
summary: Compositional generalization, the ability to solve complex problems by combining solutions to simpler sub-problems, is a fundamental capability of both natural and artificial intelligence, and a key mechanism underlying chain-of-thought reasoning. However, the theoretical underpinnings of compositional generalization remain poorly understood: when and why does decomposing a problem into parts yield more efficient learning than solving it directly? We study this question through the canonical problem of learning to simulate semiautomata (predicting the outcome of $T$ steps of sequential computation), a model that captures state tracking, regular language recognition, and modular arithmetic. We show that an autocurriculum-based approach building on Part I of this series, recursively decomposing longer sequences into shorter sub-problems, learning to solve them, and composing the solutions, achieves dramatically better statistical complexity than direct methods. (i) For a setting inspired by supervised fine-tuning (SFT) where the learner receives interactive feedback on intermediate states of the computation, curriculum facilitates learning from only $2^{\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{\log T})}$ tokens of supervision; i.e., subpolynomial in the sequence length $T$, overcoming the $Ω(T)$ token barrier required by direct simulation. (ii) For a setting inspired by reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), where the learner improves a pre-trained reference model using an outcome verifier, we show that curriculum reduces the requirement on the reference model from coverage at the full sequence length $T$ to coverage at a shorter block length $B \ll T$, an exponentially weaker condition.

AI.tldr: This paper studies the theoretical foundations of compositional generalization, showing that curriculum-based recursive decomposition of sequential computation tasks yields exponentially better sample complexity than direct methods in both supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) settings.
AI.motivation: Compositional generalization is central to chain-of-thought reasoning and intelligence, yet its theoretical basis — specifically, when and why problem decomposition enables more efficient learning — remains poorly understood. This work aims to provide rigorous theoretical answers.
AI.method: The authors model compositional generalization through the lens of learning semiautomata (T-step sequential computation), capturing state tracking, regular language recognition, and modular arithmetic. They propose an autocurriculum-based approach that recursively decomposes long sequences into shorter sub-problems, learns to solve them, and composes the solutions. The analysis spans two settings: (i) an SFT-inspired setting with interactive feedback on intermediate states, and (ii) an RLVR-inspired setting using an outcome verifier to improve a pre-trained reference model.
AI.result: (i) In the SFT setting, curriculum enables learning from only 2^{Õ(√log T)} tokens of supervision — subpolynomial in sequence length T — overcoming the Ω(T) token barrier required by direct simulation. (ii) In the RLVR setting, curriculum reduces the coverage requirement on the reference model from full sequence length T down to a much shorter block length B ≪ T, an exponentially weaker condition.
AI.conclusion: Curriculum-based recursive decomposition provides strong theoretical justification for compositional generalization: it provably enables exponentially more sample-efficient learning by breaking long-range sequential tasks into composable sub-problems, with implications for designing more efficient training paradigms in both SFT and RLVR contexts.

title: ToxiREX: A Dataset on Toxic REasoning in ConteXt
summary: We introduce a new, contextual, multilingual dataset called ToxiREX: Toxic REasoning in ConteXt. The dataset consists of threads of Reddit comments and structured characterizations of what the comments imply, following a systematic toxic reasoning schema developed in a previous paper. Using the schema allows us to capture and explain implicit and context-dependent toxicity, while supporting mappings to existing toxicity taxonomies. The dataset includes comments in six languages (English, Arabic, Turkish, Spanish, German, and Dutch), collected from posts connected to specific major events (e.g. the 2023 Turkey earthquakes; the Russian invasion of Ukraine). We describe the context-preserving preprocessing of the threads. We create a training set of 125 thousand comments which is annotated by a commercially available LLM, and a test set of just under three thousand comments that is annotated by native speakers. We show that apparent disagreements in the test set annotations often reflect defensible alternative interpretations rather than noise. Finally, we provide baseline results by prompting and fine-tuning language models. To produce these results, we develop evaluation strategies for our hierarchical, schema-based predictions. While models perform better than random, there remains a lot of room for improvement, showing the task to be challenging. ToxiREX is the first dataset to simultaneously incorporate multiple languages, conversational context, and implicit toxicity, while using the toxic reasoning schema for rich, structured annotations. Dataset available at: https://github.com/cltl/toxirex

AI.tldr: ToxiREX is a multilingual, contextual dataset of Reddit comment threads annotated with a structured toxic reasoning schema. It covers six languages, links toxicity to real-world events, uses LLM-assisted annotation at scale, and provides baseline model results showing the task remains challenging.
AI.motivation: Existing toxicity detection datasets often lack conversational context, multilingual coverage, and the ability to capture implicit, context-dependent toxicity. The authors aim to fill this gap by providing a resource that explains *why* and *how* toxicity arises in context, using a systematic reasoning schema that maps to existing taxonomies.
AI.method: The authors collected Reddit comment threads linked to major events (e.g., Turkey earthquakes, Russia-Ukraine war) in six languages: English, Arabic, Turkish, Spanish, German, and Dutch. They preserved conversational context during preprocessing. A training set of ~125K comments was annotated using a commercial LLM; a test set of ~3K comments was annotated by native speakers. The annotation framework follows a previously developed toxic reasoning schema that captures structured characterizations of implied toxicity. Baseline evaluations were conducted via prompting and fine-tuning language models, using newly developed evaluation strategies for schema-based hierarchical predictions.
AI.result: Apparent disagreements among native-speaker annotators on the test set often reflected defensible alternative interpretations rather than noise. Baseline models outperformed random baselines but left substantial room for improvement, demonstrating the task's difficulty. The dataset is the first to simultaneously combine multiple languages, conversational context, implicit toxicity, and the toxic reasoning schema.
AI.conclusion: ToxiREX provides a uniquely challenging benchmark for context-aware, multilingual, and implicit toxicity detection. The structured reasoning schema enables richer analysis than traditional toxicity labels. The performance gap between current models and the task complexity highlights significant opportunities for future research in nuanced, explainable toxicity detection.

title: Reduction of Probabilistic Chemical Reaction Networks
summary: Programming adaptive behaviors at the cellular level is a long-standing goal that raises the question of how probabilistic computation can be implemented in biochemical systems. Chemical reaction networks (CRNs) provide such a substrate and have been shown to realize probabilistic models, including hidden Markov models and factor graphs, with dynamics reproducing Bayesian inference and belief propagation. However, encoding these algorithms typically requires prohibitively large reaction networks, and classical CRN reduction techniques do not directly apply. By recovering the factor graph structure encoded in Napp--Adams-compiled CRNs, we transport recent factor-graph reduction results to their chemical implementations, obtaining significantly smaller CRNs while preserving the belief-propagation fixed points on surviving variables.

AI.tldr: This paper bridges factor graph reduction techniques with chemical reaction network (CRN) compilations, enabling significantly smaller CRNs that preserve belief-propagation fixed points for probabilistic cellular computation.
AI.motivation: Programming adaptive probabilistic behaviors at the cellular level using CRNs is promising but suffers from prohibitively large reaction networks when encoding algorithms like hidden Markov models and factor graphs. Classical CRN reduction techniques fail to address this, motivating a need for principled reduction methods that preserve key inferential properties.
AI.method: The authors recover the factor graph structure embedded in CRNs compiled via the Napp–Adams method, then transport recent factor-graph reduction results (e.g., variable elimination, structural simplifications) directly to the chemical implementation level, yielding reduced CRNs that maintain fixed points of belief propagation on surviving variables.
AI.result: Significantly smaller chemical reaction networks are obtained that retain the belief-propagation fixed points on the remaining (non-eliminated) variables, preserving the inferential semantics of the original probabilistic model.
AI.conclusion: Factor graph reduction can be successfully lifted to the CRN domain via the Napp–Adams compilation, offering a principled pathway to compact biochemical implementations of probabilistic inference without sacrificing correctness at the fixed-point level.

title: Dialogue to Detection: A Multimodal Hybrid NLP Pipeline for Insurance Fraud Detection
summary: Insurance fraud imposes substantial financial losses and operational inefficiencies, raising premiums and impacting trust among legitimate policyholders. Early detection at FNOL remains a persistent challenge. Existing approaches rely largely on private, text-only datasets, limiting progress on multimodal methods that integrate linguistic, behavioural, and speaker-based indicators. We introduce a synthetic multimodal framework that replicates FNOL conditions. It generates agent-customer dialogue transcripts and two-speaker audios, performs ASR and diarisation. Downstream modules combine NER, regex-based feature extraction, LLM-RAG retrieval, and speaker embeddings in a rule-based risk score to flag narrative reuse, structural inconsistencies, and cross-case voice repetition while balancing sensitivity and false positives. Dataset validation and component-level evaluations show stability and transfer potential, offering a reproducible baseline beyond text-only fraud detection.

AI.tldr: A synthetic multimodal framework for insurance fraud detection at First Notice of Loss (FNOL) that integrates dialogue transcripts, speaker audio, ASR, diarisation, NER, regex features, LLM-RAG retrieval, and speaker embeddings into a rule-based risk scoring system.
AI.motivation: Existing insurance fraud detection methods are limited to private, text-only datasets, hindering progress on multimodal approaches that combine linguistic, behavioural, and speaker-based indicators for early detection at FNOL.
AI.method: The authors construct a synthetic multimodal framework simulating FNOL conditions: generating agent-customer dialogue transcripts and two-speaker audios, applying ASR and diarisation. Downstream, they employ NER, regex-based feature extraction, LLM-RAG retrieval, and speaker embeddings within a rule-based risk scoring system to flag narrative reuse, structural inconsistencies, and cross-case voice repetition.
AI.result: Dataset validation and component-level evaluations demonstrate stability and transfer potential of the framework.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a reproducible, multimodal baseline for fraud detection that extends beyond text-only approaches, with demonstrated stability and transfer potential.

title: The Weakest Link Tells It All: Outcome-Supervised Process Reward Modeling via Learnable Credit Assignment
summary:
Process reward models (PRMs) enhance the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs) by providing fine-grained feedback, yet training PRMs typically requires expensive stepwise annotations. Outcome-supervised PRMs offer a scalable alternative by learning from final-answer correctness alone, but this introduces a fundamental *credit assignment* challenge, i.e., attributing outcomes to responsible reasoning steps. Existing approaches rely on either uniform or causal assignment, both of which fail to anchor credit in step correctness and thus hinder process error identification.
  In this work, we propose Outcome-Supervised Process Reward Modeling via **L**earnable **C**redit **A**ssignment (**LCA**), an outcome-supervised PRM framework that jointly learns credit assignment and reward modeling under the principle of *Weakest Link Assignment: a reasoning chain is as strong as its weakest link*. To address mutual dependence between credit assignment and reward modeling, we formalize outcome-supervised PRM as a Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) problem and introduce Softmax-Weighted-Sum (SWS) pooling, an MIL pooling technique tailored for strong dependence and redundancy among reasoning states. We prove Bayes consistency of our algorithm under mild assumptions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that **LCA** consistently outperforms state-of-the-art outcome-supervised PRMs across multiple tasks and backbones. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/LCA.

AI.tldr: LCA proposes an outcome-supervised Process Reward Model that jointly learns credit assignment and reward modeling using Weakest Link Assignment, formalized as Multiple Instance Learning with a novel Softmax-Weighted-Sum pooling, outperforming existing methods without requiring expensive stepwise annotations.
AI.motivation: Training PRMs typically requires costly stepwise annotations. Outcome-supervised PRMs avoid this but suffer from the credit assignment problem—correctly attributing final outcomes to individual reasoning steps. Existing uniform or causal assignment methods fail to anchor credit in actual step correctness, limiting their ability to identify process errors.
AI.method: The authors formalize outcome-supervised PRM as a Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) problem under the "Weakest Link Assignment" principle (a reasoning chain is only as strong as its weakest step). They jointly learn credit assignment and reward modeling, introducing Softmax-Weighted-Sum (SWS) pooling—an MIL pooling technique designed for strong dependence and redundancy among reasoning states. The algorithm's Bayes consistency is proved under mild assumptions.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show that LCA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art outcome-supervised PRMs across multiple tasks and backbones.
AI.conclusion: LCA provides an effective, scalable, and theoretically grounded framework for outcome-supervised PRM training, overcoming the credit assignment bottleneck via MIL-based joint optimization with SWS pooling.

title: The Signal-Coverage Matrix: Stratifying Type and Semantic Errors in Statement Autoformalization
summary: Headline type-correctness (TC\%) of LLM autoformalization has climbed from $\sim$53\% to $\sim$76\% in two years, yet this scalar conceals which errors each method resolves. We propose a signal-coverage matrix that crosses the Lean elaborator (pass/fail) with a semantic-equivalence judgment (equivalent/not), sorting every output into one of four cells: true success (TS), type-only (TO), semantic-only (SO), or both fail (BF). On ProofNet\# and MiniF2F-test with DeepSeek V4-Pro across Vanilla, Lean-Retry, Sample-Filter, and Stratified Autoformalization (SAF): (1) the +34 to +36 TS gain across the three elab-feedback methods is $\sim$64\% type-stratum recovery, with SO flat on net (87.5\% of original semantic errors rescued, 8 newly created). (2) The TO-to-TS rate is 23/61 for each method (Wilson 95\% CI [26.6\%, 50.3\%]), and this stratum-level recovery rate predicts $Δ$TS on held-out methods to within 2/186 and renders $Δ$TC linear in the Vanilla elab-fail rate across six (model, dataset) cells ($R^2=0.96$). (3) The two judges disagree by 26 to 37 pp on elab-feedback outputs (vs. 7 pp on Vanilla), with 30 to 56\% of symbolic-judge false negatives traceable to elaborator-forced rewrites. The persistent residual reduces to two gold-formalization errors. TC\% gains should be credited by which cell moved, not by the scalar alone.

AI.tldr: Autoformalization evaluation using a 2×2 signal-coverage matrix (elaborator pass/fail × semantic equivalence) reveals that recent TC% gains are largely "type-stratum recovery" (fixing type errors without improving semantics), with persistent semantic gaps and systematic judge disagreements traced to elaborator-forced rewrites.
AI.motivation: The scalar TC% metric (climbing from ~53% to ~76%) obscures *which* errors each autoformalization method actually resolves. The authors argue that understanding the composition of improvements—whether they fix type errors, semantic errors, or both—is critical for crediting methodological progress accurately.
AI.method: The paper proposes a **signal-coverage matrix** crossing the Lean elaborator outcome (pass/fail) with a semantic-equivalence judgment (equivalent/not), yielding four cells: True Success (TS), Type-Only (TO), Semantic-Only (SO), and Both Fail (BF). This framework is applied to four autoformalization approaches—Vanilla, Lean-Retry, Sample-Filter, and Stratified Autoformalization (SAF)—using DeepSeek V4-Pro on ProofNet# and MiniF2F-test.
AI.result: (1) The +34–36pp TS gain across elaborator-feedback methods is ~64% type-stratum recovery; SO is flat net (87.5% of original semantic errors rescued but 8 new ones created). (2) The TO→TS conversion rate is 23/61 per method (Wilson 95% CI [26.6%, 50.3%]), and this stratum-level recovery rate predicts ΔTS on held-out methods within 2/186 and renders ΔTC linear in the Vanilla elaborator-fail rate (R²=0.96 across six cells). (3) The two judges disagree by 26–37pp on elaborator-feedback outputs (vs. 7pp on Vanilla), with 30–56% of symbolic-judge false negatives attributed to elaborator-forced rewrites. The persistent residual reduces to two gold-formalization errors.
AI.conclusion: TC% gains should be credited by identifying *which cell moved* in the signal-coverage matrix rather than by the scalar alone. The matrix reveals that recent improvements are predominantly type-stratum recovery, with semantic quality largely unchanged, and highlights systematic judge disagreement as a confound in evaluation.

title: Flexformer: Flexible Linear Transformer with Learnable Attention Kernel
summary:
Transformer models rely on attention mechanism to capture long-range dependencies but suffer from quadratic complexity, limiting their scalability to long sequences. Kernel-based linear attention reduces this complexity but typically relies on fixed or weakly learnable kernels, restricting expressiveness and performance. In this work, we propose Flexformer, a flexible linear Transformer that learns attention kernels in a fully data-driven manner. Flexformer builds on random Fourier feature-based linear attention and treats spectral frequencies as trainable parameters, enabling the model to learn a broad family of attention kernels.
  We develop both stationary and nonstationary variants, with the latter offering strictly greater expressiveness.
  Extensive experiments on language modeling and sequence classification demonstrate that Flexformer consistently outperforms baselines. Moreover, Flexformer can be effectively distilled from pretrained Transformers to recover softmax attention and exhibits strong kernel transferability across domains, achieving both high efficiency and competitive performance on long-sequence tasks.

AI.tldr: Flexformer proposes a fully data-driven kernel learning approach for linear attention, treating Fourier spectral frequencies as trainable parameters to learn flexible attention kernels, outperforming fixed-kernel baselines on long-sequence tasks.
AI.motivation: Standard Transformer attention has quadratic complexity, limiting long-sequence scalability. Existing kernel-based linear attention methods rely on fixed or weakly learnable kernels that restrict expressiveness, creating a need for more flexible, data-driven kernel learning in linear attention.
AI.method: Flexformer builds on random Fourier feature-based linear attention, making spectral frequencies trainable parameters to learn attention kernels in a fully data-driven way. Both stationary and nonstationary variants are developed, with the nonstationary variant providing strictly greater expressiveness. The method also supports distillation from pretrained Transformers to recover softmax-like attention.
AI.result: Flexformer consistently outperforms baselines on language modeling and sequence classification. It can be distilled from pretrained Transformers to recover softmax attention and demonstrates strong kernel transferability across domains, achieving high efficiency and competitive performance on long-sequence tasks.
AI.conclusion: A fully data-driven, learnable kernel approach to linear attention (Flexformer) effectively bridges the gap between efficiency and expressiveness, offering a scalable alternative to standard softmax attention for long-sequence processing.

title: A Tree-of-Thoughts Inspired Hybrid Approach for Legal Case Judgement Summarization using LLMs
summary: In recent times, Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly being used for legal case judgement summarization. Most prior works have tried traditional extractive and abstractive summarization of case judgements. However, hybrid or extractive-abstractive techniques have not been explored much. In this work, we propose a novel tree-of-thoughts inspired extractive-abstractive summarization approach for legal judgement summarization. We conduct experiments using two popular LLMs, DeepSeek and LLama, and compare among extractive, abstractive and extractive-abstractive summarization. Our experiments show that the proposed extractive-abstractive prompt provides better summaries compared to other types of LLM prompts.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a tree-of-thoughts-inspired hybrid extractive-abstractive approach for legal judgment summarization using LLMs (DeepSeek, LLama), demonstrating that the combined prompt method outperforms purely extractive or abstractive prompts.
AI.motivation: Legal case judgment summarization has been dominated by either extractive or abstractive methods, with hybrid extractive-abstractive approaches remaining largely unexplored. The authors aim to fill this gap by leveraging LLMs with a structured reasoning paradigm.
AI.method: A novel tree-of-thoughts inspired extractive-abstractive summarization prompt is designed. Experiments are conducted using two LLMs — DeepSeek and LLama — comparing three summarization paradigms: extractive-only, abstractive-only, and the proposed extractive-abstractive hybrid approach.
AI.result: The proposed extractive-abstractive prompt consistently yields better-quality summaries compared to purely extractive or abstractive LLM prompts across both DeepSeek and LLama models.
AI.conclusion: Hybrid extractive-abstractive prompting guided by tree-of-thoughts reasoning enhances LLM performance on legal judgment summarization, suggesting this combined paradigm is a promising direction for legal NLP tasks.

title: PerturbCellRL: Verifier-Guided Reinforcement Learning for Single-Cell Perturbation Prediction
summary: Single-cell perturbation models can reduce costly wet-lab screening by predicting how cells respond transcriptionally to interventions. While recent generative models improve population-level prediction, individual generated cells are not explicitly checked for biological consistency. We introduce PerturbCellRL, a reinforcement learning (RL) framework that post-trains a pretrained single-cell transcriptomic generator using a suite of cell-level verifiers as rewards. These verifiers define four rewards: Pearson top-k similarity, RMSE top-k proximity, DE Spearman, and Pathway activity. The Pathway activity verifier rewards cells whose pathway responses match known perturbation biology. We evaluate PerturbCellRL on multiple genetic and chemical perturbation benchmarks. Across these benchmarks, PerturbCellRL improves over the pretrained flow-matching generator on reward-aligned evaluation metrics and a held-out evaluation metric. Moreover, PerturbCellRL remains competitive with state-of-the-art methods on population-level metrics. Together, these results frame trustworthy single-cell prediction as verifier-guided generative alignment, moving beyond matching expression distributions toward predictions whose single-cell perturbation effects are explicitly checked for biological consistency.

AI.tldr: PerturbCellRL is a reinforcement learning framework that post-trains pretrained single-cell transcriptomic generators using cell-level verifiers as rewards, explicitly checking individual generated cells for biological consistency rather than relying solely on population-level distribution matching.
AI.motivation: Current single-cell perturbation models focus on population-level prediction quality but do not explicitly verify whether individual generated cells are biologically consistent with known perturbation biology. This gap limits trustworthiness of generative models for downstream use.
AI.method: PerturbCellRL post-trains a pretrained flow-matching generator via RL, using a suite of four cell-level reward verifiers: Pearson top-k similarity, RMSE top-k proximity, DE (differential expression) Spearman correlation, and Pathway activity, the latter specifically rewarding alignment with known perturbation pathway responses.
AI.result: Across multiple genetic and chemical perturbation benchmarks, PerturbCellRL improves over the pretrained flow-matching generator on both reward-aligned evaluation metrics and a held-out evaluation metric, while remaining competitive with state-of-the-art methods on population-level metrics.
AI.conclusion: Trustworthy single-cell perturbation prediction can be framed as verifier-guided generative alignment, explicitly checking single-cell perturbation effects for biological consistency rather than merely matching expression distributions.

title: Can LLMs Judge Better Than They Generate? Evaluating Task Asymmetry, Mechanistic Interpretability and Transferability for In-Context QA
summary: LLM-as-a-Judge and self-evaluation pipelines implicitly assume that evaluation is easier than generation. We test this in a controlled in-context QA setting where a context passage is the sole information source and each model judges the answer it generated, removing the parametric-knowledge confound of open-domain comparisons. Across four benchmarks (SQuAD 2.0, DROP, HotpotQA, MuSiQue) and two models, evaluation is not uniformly easier: generation accuracy exceeds self-evaluation on three of four, with multi-hop MuSiQue the exception. Attention analysis reveals why: evaluation attends to context 3--5x less than generation does and barely reads the candidate answer. LoRA fine-tuning confirms the asymmetry is not a training artifact: generation fine-tuning induces over-acceptance and evaluation fine-tuning degrades generation. These findings challenge core assumptions in self-evaluation pipelines.

AI.tldr: The paper challenges the assumption that self-evaluation is easier than generation. In controlled in-context QA experiments, generation accuracy exceeds self-evaluation on three of four benchmarks. Attention analysis reveals evaluation attends to context 3-5x less than generation and barely reads candidate answers, confirming a fundamental asymmetry.
AI.motivation: LLM-as-a-Judge and self-evaluation pipelines rest on an implicit assumption that evaluating an answer is easier than generating one. This assumption has not been rigorously tested in controlled settings that isolate in-context reasoning from parametric knowledge confounds.
AI.method: Controlled in-context QA experiments across four benchmarks (SQuAD 2.0, DROP, HotpotQA, MuSiQue) using two models.
