Each model judges its own generated answer using only a provided context passage. Attention analysis quantifies how much evaluation vs. generation attends to context and candidate answers. LoRA fine-tuning experiments test whether the asymmetry is a training artifact by fine-tuning for generation (inducing over-acceptance) and evaluation (degrading generation).
AI.result: Generation accuracy exceeds self-evaluation accuracy on three of four benchmarks (SQuAD 2.0, DROP, HotpotQA), with multi-hop MuSiQue as the exception. Evaluation attends to context 3-5x less than generation and barely reads the candidate answer. LoRA fine-tuning confirms asymmetry is not a training artifact: generation fine-tuning causes over-acceptance, while evaluation fine-tuning degrades generation performance.
AI.conclusion: The findings directly challenge core assumptions underlying self-evaluation pipelines and LLM-as-a-Judge frameworks, demonstrating that evaluation is not uniformly easier than generation and that the two processes rely on fundamentally different attention mechanisms.

title: Layerwise Progressive Freezing: A Training Scaffold for Depth-Scalable Binary Networks
comment: arXiv admin note: substantial text overlap with arXiv:2601.22660
summary: Training binary neural networks (BNNs) from scratch is dominated by the straight-through estimator (STE), whose forward/backward mismatch produces severe accuracy degradation as networks deepen. We study an orthogonal axis: when and where binarization is enforced during training. We introduce StoMPP (Stochastic Masked Partial Progressive Binarization), which gradually replaces clipped weights and activations with their hard binary counterparts layer by layer from input to output, using stochastic partial masks with soft refresh. StoMPP delivers two complementary benefits. As a standalone training rule, it provides a fully STE-free procedure that improves over vanilla STE with gains that grow with depth (ResNet-50 BNN: +18.0/+13.5/+3.8 on CIFAR-10/100/ImageNet), and the pattern holds across ResNet-18/34/50, MobileNetV2, and BERT fine-tuning. Composed with surrogate gradients by applying STE only to frozen entries, it reaches +27.1/+19.8/+17.7 over vanilla STE on the same setting. Underlying both regimes is a single mechanistic finding: progression order is decisive. Forward layerwise progression prevents depth collapse, reverse progression collapses to near-chance, and binary-weight networks (without binary activations) are insensitive to order. We trace this asymmetry to activation-induced gradient blockades: a committed binary activation severs gradient flow upstream, and ordering controls when these blockades form. To isolate the progression's contribution from any benefit conferred by STE, we conduct all ablations in the STE-free regime; the resulting characterization (schedule, refresh, ordering, dynamics) thus reflects the progression itself rather than its interaction with surrogate gradients.

AI.tldr: StoMPP introduces a progressive, layerwise binarization schedule using stochastic partial masks, achieving substantial accuracy gains over STE-based BNN training. Forward progression order is crucial—reverse order collapses performance—due to activation-induced gradient blockades. When combined with STE on frozen entries, gains are even larger.
AI.motivation: Standard STE training for BNNs suffers from a forward/backward mismatch that worsens with depth. The authors investigate an orthogonal axis: the timing and ordering of binarization enforcement during training, seeking an STE-free alternative and a mechanistic understanding of why progression order matters.
AI.method: StoMPP (Stochastic Masked Partial Progressive Binarization) progressively replaces clipped real-valued weights/activations with hard binary versions, moving layer-by-layer from input to output. It uses stochastic partial masks with soft refresh. The method is evaluated in two regimes: (1) fully STE-free, and (2) composed with STE applied only to frozen (already binarized) entries. Ablations isolate the progression mechanism independently from STE interactions.
AI.result: STE-free StoMPP outperforms vanilla STE, with gains growing with depth: ResNet-50 BNN achieves +18.0/+13.5/+3.8 on CIFAR-10/100/ImageNet. With STE on frozen entries: +27.1/+19.8/+17.7. Forward layerwise progression prevents depth collapse; reverse progression collapses to near-chance accuracy. Binary-weight-only networks (no binary activations) are insensitive to ordering, implicating activation-induced gradient blockades.
AI.conclusion: Progression order is decisive in BNN training: forward ordering prevents gradient blockades caused by committed binary activations severing upstream gradient flow. StoMPP provides an effective STE-free training procedure and, when combined with STE on frozen entries, achieves state-of-the-art BNN accuracy. The mechanistic findings carry implications for deep BNN training design.

title: MultiHashFormer: Hash-based Generative Language Models
summary: Language models (LMs) represent tokens using embedding matrices that scale linearly with the vocabulary size. To constrain the parameter footprint, prior work proposes hashing many tokens into a single vector within encoder-only models. While this offers parameter efficiency, many-to-one collisions prevent its use in causal LMs. In this paper, we propose MultiHashFormer, a new framework that allows hash-based autoregression. Each token is represented as a unique hash signature, a short sequence of discrete hash IDs, generated by multiple independent hash functions. A Hash Encoder compresses this signature into a single latent vector for processing by a Transformer decoder. Then, a Hash Decoder generates the hash signature of the next token, which is then mapped back to text. We evaluate our approach at the 100M, 1B and 3B parameter scales, demonstrating that MultiHashFormer consistently outperforms standard Transformer LMs across multiple benchmarks. Furthermore, we show that our model handles multilingual vocabulary expansion with a constant parameter footprint without any modifications.

AI.tldr: MultiHashFormer introduces hash-based autoregressive language modeling by representing tokens as multi-hash signatures, processed through a Hash Encoder-Transformer-Decoder pipeline. It outperforms standard Transformers at 100M–3B scales and supports multilingual vocabulary expansion without extra parameters.
AI.motivation: Standard LMs use embedding matrices that scale linearly with vocabulary size, leading to large parameter footprints. Prior hash-based approaches (many-to-one hashing) offer parameter efficiency but cause collisions that break autoregressive generation, limiting them to encoder-only models. The authors aim to enable hash-based parameter-efficient causal LMs.
AI.method: MultiHashFormer uses multiple independent hash functions to map each token to a unique hash signature (a short sequence of discrete hash IDs). A Hash Encoder compresses this signature into a single latent vector, which is processed by a standard Transformer decoder. A Hash Decoder then predicts the next token's hash signature autoregressively, which is subsequently mapped back to text.
AI.result: MultiHashFormer consistently outperforms standard Transformer LMs across multiple benchmarks at the 100M, 1B, and 3B parameter scales. It also demonstrates effective multilingual vocabulary expansion with a constant parameter footprint, requiring no architectural modifications.
AI.conclusion: Hash-based autoregression is viable and effective for causal LMs. MultiHashFormer achieves superior performance to standard Transformers while maintaining parameter efficiency, offering a promising direction for scaling LMs without proportional embedding growth.

title: RS-Diffuser: Risk-Sensitive Diffusion Planning with Distributional Value Guidance
summary: Offline reinforcement learning enables policy learning from fixed datasets without additional environment interaction, making it appealing for safety-critical applications where online exploration is costly or unsafe. Diffusion-based decision-making methods have recently achieved strong performance in offline RL by modeling rich, multimodal trajectory distributions. However, existing diffusion planners are typically risk-neutral and therefore may overlook rare but catastrophic outcomes that are crucial in real-world deployment. In this work, we propose RS-Diffuser, a risk-sensitive offline diffusion planning framework that combines diffusion-based trajectory generation with distributional value critics. RS-Diffuser learns a diffusion planner over future state trajectories, a separate inverse dynamics model for action decoding, and a Monte Carlo distributional critic that estimates the full return distribution of candidate plans through quantile regression. At sampling time, we incorporate a risk-sensitive guidance signal into the denoising process, using gradients computed from tail-aware objectives such as Conditional Value at Risk to steer generation toward desired risk profiles. As a result, a single trained model can flexibly produce risk-averse, risk-neutral, or risk-seeking behaviors by changing only the inference-time risk parameter. Extensive experiments on risk-sensitive D4RL and risky robot navigation benchmarks demonstrate that RS-Diffuser achieves state-of-the-art performance, improving both overall return and worst-case robustness while reducing safety violations.

AI.tldr: RS-Diffuser is a risk-sensitive offline diffusion planning framework that combines trajectory diffusion models with distributional value critics. By incorporating tail-aware risk objectives (e.g., CVaR) into the denoising process, a single model can flexibly produce risk-averse, risk-neutral, or risk-seeking behaviors at inference time, achieving SOTA on risk-sensitive D4RL and robot navigation benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing diffusion-based offline RL planners are risk-neutral and may overlook rare but catastrophic outcomes. In safety-critical applications, this is a critical limitation, motivating the need for a risk-sensitive planning approach that can explicitly control the trade-off between expected return and worst-case robustness.
AI.method: RS-Diffuser consists of three components: (1) a diffusion planner that models future state trajectory distributions; (2) an inverse dynamics model for action decoding; and (3) a Monte Carlo distributional critic using quantile regression to estimate the full return distribution. At sampling time, risk-sensitive guidance is injected into the denoising process via gradients from tail-aware objectives (e.g., Conditional Value at Risk), enabling flexible risk-profile selection purely at inference.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on risk-sensitive D4RL and risky robot navigation benchmarks demonstrate state-of-the-art performance. RS-Diffuser improves both overall return and worst-case robustness while reducing safety violations compared to existing methods.
AI.conclusion: RS-Diffuser demonstrates that integrating distributional critics with diffusion-based trajectory generation enables flexible, risk-aware decision-making in offline RL. A single trained model can adapt to diverse risk preferences at inference time, offering a practical solution for safety-critical deployment scenarios.

title: Mechanism-Driven Monitors for Preemptive Detection of LLM Training Instability
summary: Frontier large language model training consumes massive accelerator fleets and long wall-clock computation, making stability failures costly when they occur. After a numerical or a hyperparameter fault has already destabilized the training dynamics, it may continue for thousands of steps while loss and gradient norms still appear normal. We study mechanism-driven detection of training instability by deriving internal monitors from the functional role of each critical module and from the earliest computational sites where failures are expected to produce measurable signatures. For low-precision flash attention, we monitor the spectral entropy of a QK bilinear decomposition, whose first-order term becomes abnormal before the loss fully collapses. For MoE routers, we derive indicators from their role in expert selection. Our fault-injection experiments on low-precision attention, large learning-rate, and combined faults show that these signals provide distinct signatures for different failures, triggering thousands of steps before loss divergence.

AI.tldr: Proposes mechanism-driven internal monitors for early detection of training instability in large language models, using spectral entropy of QK decomposition for attention and expert-selection indicators for MoE routers, detecting failures thousands of steps before loss divergence.
AI.motivation: Training large frontier LLMs consumes massive compute resources and long wall-clock time. Numerical or hyperparameter faults can destabilize training silently for thousands of steps while loss and gradient norms appear deceptively normal, making late detection extremely costly. The authors aim to catch failures early by exploiting domain knowledge of module internals.
AI.method: Mechanism-driven monitoring: derive internal signals from the functional role of each critical module at the earliest computational sites where failures produce measurable signatures. For low-precision flash attention, they monitor the spectral entropy of a QK bilinear decomposition (first-order term abnormalities precede full loss collapse). For MoE routers, they derive indicators from expert-selection behavior. Fault-injection experiments test low-precision attention faults, large learning-rate faults, and combined faults.
AI.result: The proposed internal signals provide distinct, interpretable signatures for different failure modes. They trigger detection thousands of training steps before loss divergence occurs, enabling early intervention.
AI.conclusion: Mechanism-driven internal monitoring is an effective strategy for early detection of training instabilities in large-scale LLM training, outperforming reliance on surface-level metrics like loss and gradient norms, which can remain normal long after destabilization begins.

title: Difference of Convex Programming in the Wasserstein Space with Applications to MMD Optimization
summary: Optimizing functionals over the space of probability measures is now ubiquitous in machine learning. A widely used approach is to perform the optimization directly over the Wasserstein space, but many objective functionals of practical interest are non-convex along Wasserstein geodesics, making the analysis of standard first-order methods challenging. In this work, we study a class of objectives over the Wasserstein space that admit a difference-of-convex (DC) decomposition and we lift the classical convex-concave procedure (CCCP) to this setting. Under smoothness and strong convexity assumptions on the convex components of the decomposition, we prove almost stationarity along the iterates of the resulting algorithm. Our main focus is on the Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) and the Energy Distance (ED) functionals, for which we develop explicit Wasserstein DC decompositions, and establish local convergence of the scheme under mild assumptions. Empirically, we show that well-chosen DC decompositions yield faster and more stable convergence than Wasserstein gradient descent on these MMD objectives.

AI.tldr: The paper lifts the classical convex-concave procedure (CCCP) to the Wasserstein space for optimizing non-convex functionals over probability measures. Using a difference-of-convex (DC) decomposition, it proves almost stationarity of iterates and demonstrates faster, more stable convergence than Wasserstein gradient descent on MMD and Energy Distance objectives.
AI.motivation: Many objective functionals in machine learning over Wasserstein space are non-convex along Wasserstein geodesics, making first-order methods difficult to analyze. Existing convex optimization tools don't directly apply, motivating a structured approach via DC decompositions.
AI.method: The authors propose lifting the convex-concave procedure (CCCP) to the Wasserstein space by exploiting difference-of-convex (DC) decompositions of objective functionals. They assume smoothness and strong convexity on the convex components, prove almost stationarity of iterates, and develop explicit Wasserstein DC decompositions for MMD and Energy Distance functionals.
AI.result: Theoretical results establish almost stationarity along CCCP iterates under smoothness and strong convexity assumptions. For MMD and Energy Distance, explicit DC decompositions are derived with local convergence guarantees. Empirically, well-chosen DC decompositions yield faster and more stable convergence than Wasserstein gradient descent.
AI.conclusion: The Wasserstein CCCP framework provides a principled way to optimize non-convex functionals over probability measures, with MMD and Energy Distance as key applications. DC decompositions offer both theoretical convergence guarantees and practical improvements in optimization speed and stability.

title: From Tokens to States: LLMs as a Special Case of World Models and the Continuous Path Beyond
summary: The AI community has framed the relationship between large language models (LLMs) and world models as a dichotomy: LLMs predict tokens; world models simulate reality. Yann LeCun argues in 2022 that reaching general intelligence requires abandoning autoregressive token prediction in favour of latent-space architectures. This framing is unnecessarily binary. Two claims will be defended. First, LLMs are a degenerate special case of world models: the state space is the set of all token sequences, the only action is appending one token, and world models are therefore a strict generalisation of LLMs, not a replacement. Second, there is a natural continuous spectrum from NTP to JEPA, with multi-token prediction, future-summary prediction, and next-latent prediction as intermediate stations already populated by current research. Moving along this spectrum relaxes the LLM constraints one by one. It also progressively surrenders the two practical advantages that make LLMs trainable at scale: internet-scale self-supervised data, and a transformer architecture co-designed for discrete token prediction. Both are examined as open research questions: the data question (the cliff from self-supervised text to instrumented action-labelled environments) and the architecture question (whether the transformer generalises to continuous-state prediction, or whether a new primitive is needed).

AI.tldr: The paper challenges the dichotomy between LLMs (token prediction) and world models (reality simulation), arguing that LLMs are a degenerate case of world models, and that a continuous spectrum of research—from next-token prediction to JEPA—already exists, progressively relaxing LLM constraints while raising open questions about data and architecture.
AI.motivation: To refute the binary framing—exemplified by LeCun's 2022 argument—that positions autoregressive LLMs and latent-space world models as mutually exclusive paths to general intelligence, and to instead show they are points on a continuum.
AI.method: Conceptual analysis and argument by construction: (1) formally showing that LLMs are a special case of world models with state = token sequences, action = append token; (2) mapping intermediate architectures (multi-token prediction, future-summary prediction, next-latent prediction) onto a continuous spectrum from NTP to JEPA; (3) identifying the practical trade-offs as constraints are relaxed.
AI.result: Two claims are defended: LLMs are a degenerate special case of world models (not a replacement), and a natural spectrum from NTP to JEPA exists with existing research populating intermediate points. Relaxing constraints surrenders two key LLM advantages—internet-scale self-supervised data and the transformer architecture optimized for discrete tokens—posing open research problems: the data cliff and architecture generalizability.
AI.conclusion: The LLM-vs-world-model dichotomy is a false binary; progress toward general intelligence lies in navigating the identified spectrum while solving the data and architecture challenges that emerge as LLM constraints are progressively relaxed.

title: NormGuard: Reward-Preserving Norm Constraints in Flow-Matching Reinforcement Learning
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training improves the reward alignment of flow-based generators, but often degrades perceptual quality in ways that are not captured by the reward proxy. We identify a simple structural signature of this drift: across three post-training methods (NFT, AWM, DPO), RL fine-tuning inflates the per-step velocity norm $\|v_θ\|$ by $5\%$ to $15\%$ relative to the reference. A form of norm inflation has been studied in classifier-free guidance (CFG), where rescaling the velocity back to a reference norm at inference time can mitigate the resulting artifacts. However, this inference-time correction does not transfer cleanly to RL: rescaling $v_θ$ to match $\|v_{\text{ref}}\|$ at inference time neither improves reward nor fixes the quality degradation, because the inflation is co-adapted into the model weights. Furthermore, an adjoint sensitivity analysis shows that velocity magnitude rescaling carries no coherent first-order reward signal at the batch level, indicating that suppressing norm inflation is unlikely to remove a consistently reward-carrying component. Since inference-time renormalization fails while norm suppression carries no reward cost, training-time intervention is the appropriate strategy. Together, these findings motivate \methodname, a hinge penalty that activates only when $\|v_θ\|$ exceeds $\|v_{\text{ref}}\|$ and composes additively with any velocity-local base loss. Across two base models, three post-training methods, and two reward proxies, \methodname consistently improves MLLM-judged image quality and forensic realism while preserving reward, with gains that amplify under few-step inference and are not explained by early stopping.

AI.tldr: RL post-training inflates flow-matching velocity norms, degrading perceptual quality. Inference-time rescaling fails because the inflation is co-adapted into weights and lacks a coherent reward signal. The authors propose a hinge penalty on velocity norm excess during training, which preserves reward while improving image quality across multiple settings.
AI.motivation: RL post-training for flow-based generative models improves reward alignment but introduces perceptual quality degradation not captured by the reward proxy. The authors aim to identify the structural cause of this quality drift and develop a principled intervention that mitigates it without sacrificing reward.
AI.method: The authors first diagnose velocity norm inflation (5–15% increase in ||v_θ||) across three RL post-training methods (NFT, AWM, DPO). They test inference-time renormalization to reference norms and conduct adjoint sensitivity analysis, showing norm rescaling carries no coherent first-order reward signal. Based on these findings, they propose a hinge penalty that activates only when ||v_θ|| exceeds ||v_ref||, composable with any velocity-local base loss, and applied during training.
AI.result: Inference-time renormalization fails to restore quality or improve reward. Adjoint analysis confirms velocity magnitude rescaling lacks a consistent reward signal. The proposed hinge penalty consistently improves MLLM-judged image quality and forensic realism while preserving reward across two base models, three post-training methods, and two reward proxies, with gains amplifying under few-step inference and not attributable to early stopping.
AI.conclusion: Velocity norm inflation is a structural signature of RL-induced quality drift in flow-based generators. Since inference-time correction fails and norm suppression incurs no reward penalty, training-time intervention via a hinge penalty is both effective and well-motivated, offering a simple, plug-and-play solution for preserving perceptual quality during RL post-training.

title: Cognitive Episodes in LLM Reasoning Traces Enable Interpretable Human Item Difficulty Prediction
summary: Predicting human item difficulty is central to educational assessment, where reliable estimates support fairness and effective test construction. Existing methods often depend on costly human calibration or item-level textual representations, providing limited evidence about the cognitive processes that make items difficult. We argue that difficulty should be viewed not only as a property of item text, but also as an observable consequence of the problem-solving burden an item induces. Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) offer scalable process evidence through reasoning traces, but such evidence must be structured to support interpretable modeling. To this end, we introduce Epi2Diff (Episode to Difficulty), a framework that maps LRM reasoning traces into cognitively grounded episode sequences. These episodes group trace segments into functional problem-solving states, enabling difficulty to be modeled through reasoning scale, effort allocation, and state transitions. Epi2Diff extracts compact episode-dynamic features and combines them with semantic item representations for human difficulty prediction. Experiments on four real-world human difficulty datasets show that Epi2Diff consistently outperforms strong baselines, including fine-tuned small language models, LLM in-context learning, and supervised LLM adaptation. On SAT-derived classification benchmarks, Epi2Diff achieves an 8.1% average relative gain over supervised LLM fine-tuning baselines. Further analyses show that harder items induce more effortful, iterative, and implementation-centered episode dynamics, rather than merely longer responses. These results demonstrate that cognitive episodes in LRM reasoning traces provide a predictive and interpretable process representation for human item difficulty, offering a new lens for educational measurement with reasoning models.

AI.tldr: Epi2Diff maps Large Reasoning Model (LRM) reasoning traces into cognitively grounded episode sequences to predict human item difficulty. It outperforms strong baselines on four datasets, showing that harder items involve more effortful, iterative, and implementation-centered episode dynamics rather than merely longer responses.
AI.motivation: Existing difficulty prediction methods rely on costly human calibration or shallow item-level text features, failing to capture the underlying cognitive processes that make items difficult. The authors argue that difficulty is a consequence of problem-solving burden, and LRM reasoning traces can provide scalable process evidence — but only if properly structured for interpretable modeling.
AI.method: Epi2Diff groups LRM reasoning trace segments into functional problem-solving states (episodes), then extracts compact episode-dynamic features — reasoning scale, effort allocation, and state transitions. These process features are combined with semantic item representations to predict human difficulty. The framework uses supervised learning over the combined feature set.
AI.result: Epi2Diff consistently outperforms baselines including fine-tuned small language models, LLM in-context learning, and supervised LLM adaptation across four real-world datasets. On SAT-derived classification benchmarks, it achieves an 8.1% average relative gain over supervised LLM fine-tuning. Analyses reveal harder items induce more effortful, iterative, implementation-centered episode dynamics rather than simply longer responses.
AI.conclusion: Cognitive episodes extracted from LRM reasoning traces provide a predictive and interpretable process representation for human item difficulty, offering a new lens for educational measurement that leverages reasoning models' observable problem-solving behavior.

title: Accelerating Hierarchical Sparse Predictive Coding with Hybrid Amortized Inference
summary: Hierarchical predictive coding provides an interpretable framework for perception as error-driven inference in multi-layer generative models, while sparse coding imposes parsimonious latent representations through explicit sparsity constraints. Their combination yields hierarchical sparse predictive coding models with appealing computational and neuroscientific properties, but practical use is often limited by the cost of iterative latent inference. In such models, each input may require many recurrent refinement steps before a useful sparse representation is obtained, and this burden becomes more severe as the hierarchy deepens. We study this bottleneck by holding the hierarchical sparse energy fixed and varying the inference procedure. The comparison includes four schemes: classical iterative inference based on ISTA, an accelerated MFISTA reference, structurally informed amortized inference using a LISTA-style bottom-up encoder adapted to the hierarchical model, and a hybrid method in which this fast amortized initialization is followed by a small number of corrective energy-based refinement steps. Under this shared objective, we measure reconstruction quality, sparsity, latency, and stability on static image benchmarks. The results show that a shallow LISTA-style initializer plus short corrective recurrence improves over pure amortization while remaining much faster than long iterative inference.

AI.tldr: The paper studies inference speed bottlenecks in hierarchical sparse predictive coding by comparing four inference schemes—ISTA, MFISTA, LISTA-style amortized inference, and a hybrid (amortized initialization + few iterative refinements)—finding that the hybrid approach balances reconstruction quality and speed.
AI.motivation: Hierarchical sparse predictive coding models are computationally appealing but suffer from slow iterative latent inference, which worsens with deeper hierarchies. The authors aim to identify faster inference procedures without altering the underlying energy objective.
AI.method: Four inference schemes are compared under a fixed hierarchical sparse energy: (1) classical ISTA-based iterative inference, (2) accelerated MFISTA, (3) structurally informed amortized inference via a LISTA-style bottom-up encoder adapted to the hierarchy, and (4) a hybrid method combining amortized initialization with a small number of corrective energy-based refinement steps. Evaluation uses static image benchmarks measuring reconstruction quality, sparsity, latency, and stability.
AI.result: The shallow LISTA-style initializer followed by short corrective recurrence outperforms pure amortization and achieves competitive reconstruction quality while being substantially faster than full iterative inference.
AI.conclusion: A hybrid inference strategy—fast amortized bottom-up initialization plus a few energy-based refinement steps—offers the best trade-off between inference latency and representational quality in hierarchical sparse predictive coding.

title: Vision-Default, Prior-Override: Causal Mechanisms of Perception-Knowledge Conflict in Vision-Language Models
summary: Vision-language models must reconcile visual evidence with memorized world knowledge when the two conflict. How they resolve this conflict shapes the reliability of multimodal systems, yet prior work characterizes it behaviorally without a component-level causal account. We combine activation patching across three granularities (residual stream, attention heads, and MLP sublayers) with model-component ablation studies and mechanistic analysis. Across three VLM families, we find that visual grounding emerges by default, whereas prior grounding depends on a small set of causally necessary attention heads (2.5-4.8%) concentrated in the second half of the network. These heads enable answers from stored world knowledge (e.g., "red" for a strawberry) despite conflicting visual input. Ablating them flips predictions from knowledge-grounded to visually grounded answers in 68-96% of cases under prior-knowledge prompts, but changes only 0.8-7.5% of visually grounded predictions, establishing an asymmetric causal structure. The identified heads decompose into routing heads, which modulate information flow, and writing heads, which directly project answer tokens into the residual stream. This structure is consistent across model families and scales, revealing a sparse causal circuit underlying perception-knowledge conflict in VLMs.

AI.tldr: Vision-language models resolve perception-knowledge conflicts through a sparse set of attention heads concentrated in later layers, which asymmetrically enable knowledge-grounded predictions while visual grounding emerges by default.
AI.motivation: Prior work characterizes how VLMs handle conflicts between visual evidence and memorized world knowledge only behaviorally, lacking a component-level causal account. Understanding the mechanistic circuits underlying this resolution is critical for multimodal system reliability.
AI.method: The authors apply activation patching at three granularities (residual stream, attention heads, MLP sublayers), combined with model-component ablation studies and mechanistic analysis, across three VLM families at multiple scales.
AI.result: Visual grounding emerges by default, while knowledge grounding depends on a sparse set of attention heads (2.5-4.8%) concentrated in the second half of the network. Ablating these heads flips 68-96% of knowledge-grounded predictions to visually grounded ones under prior-knowledge prompts, but only 0.8-7.5% in the reverse direction, revealing an asymmetric causal structure. These heads decompose into routing heads (modulating information flow) and writing heads (projecting answer tokens into the residual stream), with consistent structure across model families and scales.
AI.conclusion: A sparse, interpretable causal circuit underlies perception-knowledge conflict resolution in VLMs. The asymmetry — knowledge grounding requires dedicated heads while visual grounding is the default — has implications for understanding and controlling multimodal model behavior.

title: Pepti-drift: Toxicity-Repulsive Drifting for Antigen-Conditioned Discrete Peptide Generation
summary: Peptides are a promising therapeutic modality that combine the chemical tunability of small molecules with the target specificity of macromolecular therapeutics. However, designing antigen-specific binding peptides while avoiding toxicity remains a major challenge for therapeutic peptide discovery. Here, we present Pepti-drift, a toxicity-aware latent refinement framework that generates peptide candidates through a single antigen-conditioned drift step. In a peptide embedding space, Pepti-drift learns to attract generated peptide latents toward antigen-matched binding peptides while repelling them from toxicity-associated regions. This is challenging because binding-promoting physicochemical features often overlap with toxicity-associated features in peptide representation space. To address this, we introduce a warm-up strategy to stabilize this competing objective by first learning binding-oriented attraction and then increasing toxicity repulsion. Pepti-drift achieves highly efficient generation, running 16.2-fold faster than PepMLM and 1,092.0-fold faster than PepTune. Generated peptides show 100% validity, 98.1% uniqueness, the highest sequence diversity, and near-zero cross-antigen reuse. Further evaluation indicates consistently reduced toxicity and hemolysis risk across most peptide-length ranges while retaining target-related predictive binding signal. Pepti-drift thus provides a fast, scalable, and controllable framework for antigen-specific peptide design that directly encodes safe-and-active properties.

AI.tldr: Pepti-drift is a toxicity-aware latent refinement framework that generates antigen-specific binding peptides in a single drift step, balancing binding affinity with safety by learning to attract peptide latents toward binding targets while repelling them from toxicity-associated regions in embedding space.
AI.motivation: Designing antigen-specific binding peptides that avoid toxicity is a major challenge because binding-promoting physicochemical features often overlap with toxicity-associated features in peptide representation space. Existing methods lack efficient, controllable generation that simultaneously optimizes for both binding and safety.
AI.method: Pepti-drift operates in a peptide embedding space using a single antigen-conditioned drift step. It employs a dual-objective latent refinement: attraction toward antigen-matched binding peptides and repulsion from toxicity-associated regions. A warm-up strategy stabilizes training by first learning binding-oriented attraction, then progressively increasing toxicity repulsion to handle the competing objectives.
AI.result: Pepti-drift is 16.2× faster than PepMLM and 1,092.0× faster than PepTune. Generated peptides achieve 100% validity, 98.1% uniqueness, highest sequence diversity, and near-zero cross-antigen reuse. Toxicity and hemolysis risk are consistently reduced across most peptide-length ranges while retaining target-related predictive binding signal.
AI.conclusion: Pepti-drift provides a fast, scalable, and controllable framework for antigen-specific peptide design that directly encodes both safe and active properties, addressing a critical bottleneck in therapeutic peptide discovery.

title: USAD: Uncertainty-aware Statistical Adversarial Detection
summary: Statistical adversarial detection (SAD) treats detection as a two-sample test. Given a reference set of clean examples (CEs) and a batch of queries, potentially containing an unknown mixture of CEs and adversarial examples (AEs), SAD decides whether the query distribution drifts away from the CE distribution while controlling the false-alarm rate. Existing SAD-based methods mainly use maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) to measure the distributional discrepancy. However, MMD's distributional properties limit its ability to capture characteristic uncertainty patterns of AEs that are crucial for detection: AEs typically exhibit abnormal feature spread (i.e., global uncertainty) and instability under perturbations (i.e., local uncertainty). To close the gap, we propose Uncertainty-aware Statistical Adversarial Detection (USAD), which explicitly captures these uncertainty patterns with two new statistics: (1) Variance Discrepancy (VD), which measures the difference in feature spread between AEs and CEs to capture global uncertainty differences. (2) Perturbation-based Covariance Discrepancy (PCD), which compares feature covariance under Gaussian perturbations to capture local uncertainty differences. By aggregating VD and PCD, USAD achieves superior detection performances over baseline methods against various adversarial attacks, highlighting the importance of considering characteristic behaviors of AEs for effective SAD. Our code is available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/USAD.

AI.tldr: USAD introduces two uncertainty-aware statistics—Variance Discrepancy (VD) for global uncertainty and Perturbation-based Covariance Discrepancy (PCD) for local uncertainty—to improve statistical adversarial detection over MMD-based methods.
AI.motivation: Existing SAD methods using MMD fail to capture characteristic uncertainty patterns of adversarial examples: abnormal feature spread (global uncertainty) and instability under perturbations (local uncertainty). This gap limits detection performance.
AI.method: USAD proposes two new statistics: (1) Variance Discrepancy (VD) to measure differences in feature spread between AEs and CEs, capturing global uncertainty; (2) Perturbation-based Covariance Discrepancy (PCD) to compare feature covariance under Gaussian perturbations, capturing local uncertainty. These are aggregated within the SAD framework for detection.
AI.result: USAD achieves superior detection performance over baseline methods against various adversarial attacks, demonstrating the importance of modeling AE-specific uncertainty behaviors in SAD.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly modeling global and local uncertainty patterns of adversarial examples significantly improves statistical adversarial detection, outperforming traditional MMD-based approaches.

title: WattLayer: Get Layers Right to Estimate Inference Energy of Neural Networks
summary: The widespread adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has led to increasing concerns about energy consumption, yet there is a lack of standardized methodologies to accurately estimate AI inference energy consumption, particularly across various tasks and architectures. In this study, we propose a task independent, layer-wise energy estimation model for AI architectures. Our model is evaluated on a large dataset of more than 100,000 layers for 295 neural network architectures across 3 widely-used tasks and 3 distinct hardware platforms. Our approach achieves a median error of 19.6%, outperforming state-of-the-art methods. We further show that layer-wise decomposition generalize to new tasks without complete retraining, by leveraging shared layers across architectures. It offer tools, insights and a precise methodology to empower stakeholders in designing energy-efficient AI systems.

AI.tldr: Proposes a task-independent, layer-wise energy estimation model for AI inference, evaluated on 100K+ layers across 295 architectures, 3 tasks, and 3 hardware platforms, achieving 19.6% median error and outperforming SOTA methods.
AI.motivation: Rising AI adoption raises energy consumption concerns, but standardized methodologies to accurately estimate inference energy across diverse tasks and architectures are lacking.
AI.method: A task-independent, layer-wise energy estimation model that decomposes energy prediction at the granularity of individual neural network layers, enabling generalization across architectures and tasks by leveraging shared layers.
AI.result: Achieves a median error of 19.6% on a large-scale dataset of over 100,000 layers from 295 neural network architectures across 3 tasks and 3 hardware platforms, outperforming state-of-the-art methods. Layer-wise decomposition generalizes to new tasks without full retraining.
AI.conclusion: The proposed methodology offers precise tools and insights for stakeholders to design energy-efficient AI systems, demonstrating that layer-wise modeling is both accurate and generalizable.

title: Applicability of memorization indicators for early spotting of overfitting while recalibrating sEMG-decoders on low sample sizes
summary: Deep learning models for surface electromyography (sEMG) can benefit substantially from subject-specific (re-)calibration, since no sufficiently large and diverse datasets are available to train fully generic decoders. However, for user acceptance, the number of repetitions that can realistically be collected during calibration is severely limited, which increases the risk of overfitting and, in extreme cases, can even degrade performance compared to the uncalibrated model. Classical overfitting indicators such as validation performance and regularization with early stopping are difficult to apply in this low-sample regime, as they require additional held-out data that is rarely available in practical calibration scenarios. In this work, we investigate a recently proposed class of memorization indicators based solely on the activation statistics of rectified linear units (ReLU) in deep neural networks, which can be computed directly from training data without any extra validation set. We conduct a transferlearning experiment on a benchmark sEMG dataset, where a convolutional neural network is first pre-trained on multiple subjects and subsequently fine-tuned on individual users using only a small number of repetitions. During calibration, we monitor both decoding performance and the activation behaviour of the last hidden layer. Our results provide first evidence that decreases in test accuracy during fine-tuning are ac companied by characteristic changes in activation rates, indicating that activation-based memorization indicators are a promising tool for early spotting of unsuccessful learning in low-sample sEMG calibration settings.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates using ReLU activation statistics as memorization indicators to detect overfitting during subject-specific calibration of sEMG deep learning models when only very limited training data is available, without requiring a held-out validation set.
AI.motivation: Subject-specific calibration of sEMG decoders is essential for practical usability, but the small number of calibration repetitions that users tolerate creates a severe overfitting risk. Traditional overfitting countermeasures (validation monitoring, early stopping) are impractical because they require held-out data that is unavailable in real-world low-sample calibration scenarios.
AI.method: The authors employ a transfer learning pipeline: a CNN is pre-trained on multi-subject sEMG data (benchmark dataset), then fine-tuned per individual user with only a few repetitions. During fine-tuning, they simultaneously track decoding accuracy and ReLU activation statistics (specifically activation rates) in the last hidden layer, using these as memorization indicators that require only training data.
AI.result: Decreases in test accuracy during fine-tuning are accompanied by characteristic changes in ReLU activation rates, providing initial evidence that activation-based memorization indicators can signal unsuccessful learning (overfitting) in low-sample sEMG calibration.
AI.conclusion: ReLU activation-based memorization indicators are a promising, validation-free tool for early detection of overfitting in subject-specific sEMG model calibration, addressing a key practical barrier to user acceptance.

title: GNBAN: Graph Neural Basis Attention Networks for Long-Horizon Forecasting over Large Entity Sets
summary: Demand forecasting at the bottom of a retail hierarchy requires predicting tens of thousands of correlated long-horizon series across products, stores, and regions. Modern systems must scale across massive catalogs, capture shared demand dynamics, and remain interpretable enough to be trusted. Classical statistical methods need a separate model per series and are hard to manage at scale; deep autoregressive models struggle as the joint state grows to tens of thousands of dimensions; and recent graph-based forecasters, while capturing cross-entity dependencies, often produce opaque long-horizon forecasts. We propose GNBAN (Graph Neural Basis Attention Network), an end-to-end architecture combining heterogeneous graph representation learning with an interpretable basis-decomposition head. Retail data are represented directly as a heterogeneous graph derived from the relational schema, so a single model serves the entire catalog. Rather than predicting the horizon directly, GNBAN decomposes each forecast into trend, seasonal, and generic components. Its key innovation is a per-basis attention mechanism: each basis function keeps its own learnable query and retrieves information independently from the entity's historical neighborhood, letting different bases specialize to distinct temporal patterns while preserving interpretability. On two large-scale benchmarks, M5 Walmart and Favorita Grocery Sales, evaluated under matched protocols, GNBAN improves volume-weighted WRMSSE by roughly 4-5% over a matched graph baseline. Qualitative analysis shows the learned decomposition exposes trend, seasonal, and residual demand drivers without post-hoc explanation methods. These results demonstrate that scalable relational forecasting and interpretable forecast decomposition can be achieved together in a unified graph-based framework.

AI.tldr: GNBAN is a graph neural network for large-scale retail demand forecasting that combines heterogeneous graph representation learning with an interpretable basis-decomposition head, using per-basis attention to let trend, seasonal, and residual components specialize independently, achieving ~4–5% WRMSSE improvement on M5 and Favorita benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Retail demand forecasting at scale requires predicting thousands of correlated, long-horizon time series. Classical statistical methods don't scale well (one model per series), deep autoregressive models struggle with high-dimensional joint states, and existing graph-based forecasters produce opaque long-horizon forecasts. There is a need for a single unified model that is scalable, captures shared dynamics across entities, and produces interpretable forecasts.
AI.method: GNBAN represents retail data as a heterogeneous graph derived directly from the relational schema (products, stores, regions). A single model serves the entire catalog. Instead of directly predicting the horizon, it decomposes each forecast into trend, seasonal, and generic basis components using a basis-decomposition head. The core innovation is per-basis attention: each basis function has its own learnable query and independently retrieves information from the entity's historical neighborhood, enabling specialization to distinct temporal patterns while maintaining interpretability.
AI.result: On M5 Walmart and Favorita Grocery Sales benchmarks under matched protocols, GNBAN improves volume-weighted WRMSSE by roughly 4–5% over a matched graph baseline. Qualitative analysis shows the learned decomposition exposes trend, seasonal, and residual demand drivers without post-hoc explanation methods.
AI.conclusion: Scalable relational forecasting and interpretable forecast decomposition can be achieved simultaneously within a unified graph-based framework, as demonstrated by GNBAN's empirical and qualitative results.

title: FlexMoE: One-for-All Nested Intra-Expert Pruning for MoE Language Models
summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models scale model ability with sparsely activated experts, making this architecture a standard recipe for modern large models. However, sparse activation does not remove the deployment burden of storing and serving all experts, and the available deployment budget can vary substantially across devices, users, and workloads. Existing MoE compression methods are still largely fixed-budget, typically optimizing one compressed endpoint at each chosen target budget. We study a different setting: converting a large pretrained MoE LLM into a nested family of deployable subnetworks across budgets. Our method first ranks expert FFN channels by their importance, then lets each expert learn a discrete action to prune its channels. By gradually increasing cost pressure, a single action-training run exports a series of action masks from high to low budgets, each of which identifies a reliable smaller subnetwork nested in the ranked base model. Moreover, we use a single recovery fine-tune at a mid pruning budget (40%) to recover degraded model quality and transfer the recovered model to other unseen budgets. Overall, our framework surpasses recent MoE compression baselines. Specifically, on Qwen2-57B-A14B, our method retains ~99.8% of base performance while pruning 50% of routed expert parameters even without fine-tuning. For deployment, our pruned subnetworks deliver real memory reduction and throughput gains, and further support realtime online budget switching with kernel-level co-design.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a method to convert a pretrained MoE language model into a nested family of subnetworks across different budgets, using expert channel ranking and learned discrete pruning actions under increasing cost pressure, achieving ~99.8% performance retention at 50% parameter pruning without fine-tuning on Qwen2-57B-A14B.
AI.motivation: Existing MoE compression methods are fixed-budget (optimizing one compressed endpoint per target), but deployment budgets vary substantially across devices, users, and workloads. Sparse activation does not eliminate the storage and serving cost of all experts. A method is needed to produce a nested family of subnetworks spanning multiple budgets from a single training run.
AI.method: The method first ranks expert FFN channels by importance. Each expert then learns a discrete action (via action masks) to prune its channels. By gradually increasing cost pressure during training, a single run exports a series of action masks from high to low budgets, each identifying a smaller subnetwork nested within the ranked base model. A single recovery fine-tune at a mid-range pruning budget (40%) is used to recover quality and transfer to unseen budgets.
AI.result: On Qwen2-57B-A14B, the method retains ~99.8% of base performance while pruning 50% of routed expert parameters, even without fine-tuning. Pruned subnetworks deliver real memory reduction and throughput gains, and support realtime online budget switching with kernel-level co-design.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework surpasses recent MoE compression baselines by enabling elastic, nested subnetworks across multiple deployment budgets from a single training run, with strong performance retention and practical deployment benefits.

title: A Comparison of Fusion Techniques for Multi-Modal Human Activity Recognition on the HARMES Dataset
summary: Recent advances in Human Activity Recognition (HAR) from wearable sensors have shown that multi-modal deep learning models consistently outperform their uni-modal counterparts. Modalities can include IMUs, RGB cameras, audio signals, and others. One important aspect of multi-modal deep learning is the sensor fusion approach we apply. Over recent years, multiple fusion paradigms have been proposed for multi-modal HAR. However, to the best of our knowledge, no head-to-head comparison of these paradigms exists on a common multi-modal HAR benchmark dataset. To address this research gap, we systematically compare seven state-of-the-art sensor fusion methods on the recently released HARMES dataset, which comprises 61 hours of fully labeled IMU, audio, and ambient humidity data. The chosen dataset focuses on 15 household and personal hygiene activities of daily living (ADLs). By applying the seven different fusion techniques to a state-of-the-art multi-modal model architecture, we show that Gated Multi-modal Fusion achieves the highest macro F1-score (0.82), surpassing the concatenation-based late fusion HARMES paper baseline of 0.76 by +6pp under leave-one-participant-out evaluation. All code used in our experiments is made publicly available on GitHub.

AI.tldr: A systematic head-to-head comparison of seven sensor fusion paradigms for multi-modal Human Activity Recognition (HAR) on the HARMES dataset (IMU, audio, humidity). Gated Multi-modal Fusion achieved the best macro F1-score of 0.82, outperforming the concatenation-based late fusion baseline by +6 percentage points.
AI.motivation: Despite the proliferation of multi-modal deep learning models for wearable sensor-based HAR, no prior study has conducted a systematic, head-to-head comparison of different sensor fusion paradigms on a common benchmark dataset. This gap hinders informed selection of fusion strategies.
AI.method: The authors systematically compared seven state-of-the-art sensor fusion methods using a shared multi-modal model architecture. Evaluation was performed on the HARMES dataset (61 hours of labeled IMU, audio, and ambient humidity data covering 15 ADL activities) under leave-one-participant-out cross-validation.
AI.result: Gated Multi-modal Fusion achieved the highest macro F1-score of 0.82, surpassing the concatenation-based late fusion baseline (0.76) by +6 percentage points.
AI.conclusion: Gated fusion mechanisms provide a clear performance advantage over simpler concatenation-based late fusion for multi-modal HAR. The authors release all code publicly to facilitate reproducibility and further research.

title: Towards Automating Scientific Review with Google's Paper Assistant Tool
summary:
Artificial intelligence is driving a revolution in scientific discovery, accelerating everything from hypothesis generation to mathematical theorem proving. However, this rapid acceleration is creating a systemic challenge: traditional human peer review cannot scale to match the influx of AI-assisted science. Ultimately, to resolve this tension, we must also deploy AI to accelerate the verification and review process itself. To frame the discussion around this transition, we propose a taxonomy consisting of four progressive levels of AI-human collaboration in scientific evaluation, and discuss various trade-offs involved with each.
  As a step toward this future, we introduce the Paper Assistant Tool (PAT), an agentic AI framework built for deep scientific review and verification. PAT ingests full scientific manuscripts and produces a comprehensive evaluation, checking theoretical results, validating experiments, suggesting improvements, and identifying potential flaws. By utilizing inference scaling techniques, PAT is able to identify deeper issues than a single model call alone, achieving a 34% improvement over zero-shot recall on mathematical errors in the SPOT benchmark. Pilot deployments of PAT as a pre-submission tool for authors at two major Computer Science conferences -- STOC and ICML -- demonstrate its ability to identify critical errors and suggest substantive improvements to research papers. By catching errors early, PAT eases the cognitive burden placed on referees, while preserving their control over the outcomes of the review process.

AI.tldr: Proposes a four-level taxonomy for AI-human collaboration in scientific peer review and introduces PAT (Paper Assistant Tool), an agentic AI framework that performs deep review of manuscripts, achieving 34% improvement over zero-shot methods on mathematical error detection and demonstrated successfully at STOC and ICML conferences.
AI.motivation: The accelerating pace of AI-assisted scientific discovery is outpacing the capacity of traditional human peer review, creating a systemic bottleneck. To resolve this, AI must be deployed to accelerate the verification and review process itself.
AI.method: The authors propose a four-level taxonomy of progressive AI-human collaboration in scientific evaluation. They then introduce PAT, an agentic AI framework that ingests full manuscripts and performs comprehensive evaluation (checking theory, validating experiments, suggesting improvements, identifying flaws). PAT employs inference scaling techniques to achieve deeper issue detection beyond single-model calls.
AI.result: PAT achieves a 34% improvement over zero-shot recall on mathematical error detection in the SPOT benchmark. Pilot deployments at STOC and ICML conferences demonstrate PAT's ability to identify critical errors and suggest substantive improvements pre-submission, reducing reviewer cognitive burden while preserving human control.
AI.conclusion: AI-assisted review tools like PAT can help resolve the scalability crisis in peer review by catching errors early and supporting — rather than replacing — human referees, offering a practical pathway toward AI-augmented scientific evaluation.

title: TA-SparseMG: Trend-Aware Sparse Forecasting via Multi-Scale Gating for Long-Term Time Series
summary: Long-term time series forecasting finds extensive applications in domains such as power demand, traffic flow, meteorological observation, and renewable energy dispatch. Forecasting dynamically varying long-term time series poses inherent challenges, including statistical nonstationarity, local high-frequency disturbances, and coupled cross-period dependencies, which make it difficult for lightweight models to balance parameter efficiency and forecasting performance. To address this issue, this study presents TA-SparseMG, a lightweight cross-period forecasting model built on SparseTSF's sparse cross-period modeling framework. It incorporates three key modules: a trend-aware reversible instance normalization module, a scale-adaptive gated denoising module, and a multiscale gated-attention MLP forecasting module. The trend-aware normalization module captures input-window statistics and calibrates forecast-window distributions, effectively mitigating distribution shift. The scale-adaptive gated denoising module performs feature smoothing and residual suppression before period rearrangement, thereby reducing interference from high-frequency perturbations. The multiscale gated attention prediction module strengthens the prediction head's adaptive representational capacity via conditional gating and feature modulation. Extensive experiments across multiple LTSF benchmarks demonstrate that the proposed TA-SparseMG consistently achieves superior, stable performance. Ablation studies confirm that each module independently improves distribution adaptation, input robustness, and cross-period feature mapping capability.

AI.tldr: TA-SparseMG is a lightweight long-term time series forecasting model that extends SparseTSF with three modules — trend-aware normalization, scale-adaptive gated denoising, and multiscale gated-attention MLP — to address nonstationarity, high-frequency disturbances, and cross-period dependencies, achieving superior performance on LTSF benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Long-term time series forecasting faces three core challenges: statistical nonstationarity (distribution shift), local high-frequency disturbances (noise), and coupled cross-period dependencies. Existing lightweight models struggle to balance parameter efficiency with forecasting performance under these conditions.
AI.method: TA-SparseMG builds on the SparseTSF sparse cross-period modeling framework and introduces: (1) a trend-aware reversible instance normalization module that captures input-window statistics and calibrates forecast-window distributions to mitigate distribution shift; (2) a scale-adaptive gated denoising module that performs feature smoothing and residual suppression prior to period rearrangement to reduce high-frequency perturbation interference; and (3) a multiscale gated-attention MLP forecasting module that enhances adaptive representational capacity via conditional gating and feature modulation.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across multiple LTSF benchmarks show that TA-SparseMG consistently achieves superior and stable performance. Ablation studies confirm that each module independently contributes to improved distribution adaptation, input robustness, and cross-period feature mapping capability.
AI.conclusion: The three proposed modules — trend-aware normalization, scale-adaptive gated denoising, and multiscale gated-attention MLP — each provide independent and complementary benefits, collectively enabling TA-SparseMG to effectively address the key challenges in long-term time series forecasting while maintaining a lightweight parameter footprint.

title: Graph Dimensionality Reduction for Contextual Bandits: Structure-Specific Regret Bounds under Approximate Smoothness and Noisy Eigenspaces
summary: Contextual bandits with graph-structured arms arise in recommendation, citation retrieval, and social advertising, where arms connected on a graph tend to share reward signal. Standard dimensionality reduction ignores this structure, inflating exploration cost by a factor of $d/k$. We propose GraphDR-LinUCB, which projects arm features onto the graph's low-frequency spectral subspace and runs linear UCB in the resulting $k$-dimensional space. We prove the first $\wtO(k\sqrt{T})$ regret bound for spectral-projection-based contextual bandits, reducing dimension dependence from $d$ to $k$; a perturbation argument extends this to noisy graphs, with an explicit penalty for reward-smoothness mismatch and graph-estimation error. Our central theoretical finding is that the high-frequency reward component need not incur a worst-case linear-in-$T$ penalty: its actual cost depends on its realized impact along the played path, not on its total energy. A simple spectral comparison between subspaces ($Γ_k$) predicts which reducer wins on a given dataset, correctly calling five of six real-dataset outcomes without any fitted threshold. Across a synthetic benchmark and six real datasets (MovieLens, Amazon, LastFM, ogbn-arxiv, MIND), GraphDR-LinUCB reduces cumulative regret by $15\times$ over full-dimensional LinUCB and outperforms competing graph-aware methods on five of six; the single failure is precisely where the graph's spectral subspace is misaligned with the reward.

AI.tldr: GraphDR-LinUCB projects contextual bandit arm features onto a graph's low-frequency spectral subspace, achieving a $\tilde{O}(k\sqrt{T})$ regret bound. The method reduces regret up to 15× vs. full-dimensional LinUCB and introduces $\Gamma_k$, a spectral alignment metric that predicts which reducer wins on a given dataset.
AI.motivation: Standard contextual bandit algorithms operate in the full d-dimensional feature space, but when arms are graph-structured (e.g., in recommendation or social advertising), the reward signal primarily lives in a low-frequency k-dimensional subspace (k ≪ d). Ignoring this structure inflates exploration cost by a factor of d/k, motivating a method that exploits graph smoothness for efficient dimension reduction.
AI.method: GraphDR-LinUCB projects arm features onto the graph Laplacian's low-frequency spectral subspace (top-k eigenvectors), then runs standard LinUCB in the reduced k-dimensional space. The authors prove a $\tilde{O}(k\sqrt{T})$ regret bound using a novel analysis showing the high-frequency reward component's cost depends on its realized path impact rather than total energy. A perturbation argument extends this to noisy/estimated graphs, with an explicit penalty term for reward-smoothness mismatch and graph-estimation error. They also introduce $\Gamma_k$, a spectral subspace comparison metric that predicts relative method performance without fitting.
AI.result: On a synthetic benchmark and six real datasets (MovieLens, Amazon, LastFM, ogbn-arxiv, MIND), GraphDR-LinUCB achieves up to 15× cumulative regret reduction over full-dimensional LinUCB and outperforms competing graph-aware methods on five of six datasets. The $\Gamma_k$ metric correctly predicts the winner on five of six datasets without any fitted threshold. The single failure case occurs precisely when the graph's spectral subspace is misaligned with the reward.
AI.conclusion: Spectral projection onto the graph's low-frequency subspace is both theoretically justified and empirically effective for contextual bandits with graph-structured arms. The key insight is that high-frequency reward components do not inherently incur linear regret—their cost depends on realized path impact—enabling dimension reduction from d to k without sacrificing regret guarantees. The $\Gamma_k$ metric offers a practical, tuning-free diagnostic for choosing the right subspace reducer.

title: Two-Stage Fine-Tuning for Protein Sequence Generation with Targeted Amino-Acid Composition
summary: Protein language models are standard priors for biological sequence generation, but steering them toward explicit distributional design targets remains largely unexplored. We study a constrained protein generation problem in which sequences must match a desired amino-acid (AA) composition profile while preserving plausible sequence statistics and diversity. The motivating application is synthetic feed protein design, where the AA composition of dietary proteins directly determines their nutritional value. We propose a two-stage pipeline in which domain-adaptive fine-tuning (FT) on an in-domain protein dataset is followed by iterative reward-weighted FT via reinforcement learning (RL) anchored against the FT model as a frozen reference. We evaluate the pipeline on two AA compositions and find that FT brings the average composition close to the target, while the subsequent RL enforces specific sequence constraints that FT alone cannot satisfy. We additionally evaluate the design choices of the proposed composition reward term against two baselines and an ablated variant, isolate the contribution of each training stage, and verify that AA composition alignment is achieved without degrading sequence quality.

AI.tldr: A two-stage pipeline combining domain-adaptive fine-tuning with iterative reward-weighted reinforcement learning is proposed to generate protein sequences matching target amino-acid composition profiles, motivated by synthetic feed protein design, achieving composition alignment without degrading sequence quality.
AI.motivation: Protein language models serve as effective priors for sequence generation, but explicit control over distributional properties—specifically amino-acid composition—remains underexplored. The motivating application is synthetic feed protein design, where dietary protein AA composition directly determines nutritional value, necessitating methods that can steer generation toward prespecified composition targets while maintaining plausible sequence statistics and diversity.
AI.method: A two-stage pipeline: (1) Domain-adaptive fine-tuning (FT) on an in-domain protein dataset to bring average composition near the target; (2) Iterative reward-weighted FT via reinforcement learning (RL) with a frozen FT model as reference anchor, using a composition-based reward term to enforce specific sequence constraints that FT alone cannot satisfy. The reward design is evaluated against two baselines and an ablated variant.
AI.result: FT alone brings average AA composition close to the target; subsequent RL enforces specific sequence-level composition constraints that FT cannot fully satisfy. AA composition alignment is achieved without degrading sequence quality. Ablation confirms distinct contributions of each training stage, and the proposed reward term outperforms baseline and ablated alternatives.
AI.conclusion: The proposed two-stage FT+RL pipeline effectively steers protein language models toward explicit AA composition targets, enabling nutritional optimization for synthetic feed protein design while preserving sequence plausibility and diversity. The approach demonstrates that RL-based reward fine-tuning can enforce distributional constraints beyond what domain-adaptive FT alone can achieve.

title: RECAST: Model Reconstruction via Counterfactual-Aware Wasserstein Geometry under Limited Data
comment: Accepted at the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2026)
summary: Counterfactual explanations (CFs) help understand machine learning models by identifying minimal input changes that would lead to alternative model outcomes. Recent work demonstrates their utility for reconstructing black-box models, enabling third-party auditing of opaque decision systems for fairness and accountability. Still, CF-based reconstruction may suffer from decision boundary shifts, overfitting, and restrictive assumptions requiring online query access to target platforms. We propose REconstruction via Counterfactual-Aware waSserstein opTimization (RECAST) under limited data and restricted access, a behavioral surrogate model based on Wasserstein barycentric prototypes. Our approach addresses decision boundary shifts by incorporating CFs as informative, though less representative, samples for both classes, maintaining high surrogate fidelity in low-sample regimes without requiring online access during reconstruction. To enhance fairness auditing, our method enables systematic group fairness diagnostics. Experiments on real-world datasets and various setups show that RECAST effectively achieves high fidelity and query efficiency, as well as stable results even when the access is limited and noisy.

AI.tldr: RECAST proposes a behavioral surrogate model for black-box auditing using counterfactual explanations and Wasserstein barycentric prototypes, achieving high fidelity under limited data and restricted access without requiring online queries, while enabling systematic fairness diagnostics.
AI.motivation: Existing counterfactual-based black-box model reconstruction methods suffer from decision boundary shifts, overfitting, and restrictive assumptions requiring online query access. There is a need for a reconstruction method that works under limited data, restricted access, and noisy conditions while supporting fairness auditing.
AI.method: RECAST uses Wasserstein barycentric prototypes to build a behavioral surrogate model. It incorporates counterfactuals as informative samples for both classes, mitigating decision boundary shifts. The approach works in low-sample regimes without online access during reconstruction and includes systematic group fairness diagnostics.
AI.result: Experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate RECAST achieves high surrogate fidelity and query efficiency, with stable performance even under limited and noisy access conditions.
AI.conclusion: RECAST effectively reconstructs black-box models under data and access constraints, outperforming prior methods in fidelity and robustness while enabling fairness auditing through group-based diagnostics.

title: Dual-Learning based Penalized Multi-Align Clustering for Multi-View Incomplete and Disorderly Data
summary:
Multimodal feature fusion can effectively capture complex patterns in real-world data by integrating complementary information from different modalities. However, in many applications, such as boiler combustion monitoring, equipment failure, inconsistent sensor sampling frequencies, and network delays often cause missing modalities and temporal asynchrony. These issues lead to incomplete and disorderly multimodal data. To address them, previous studies have proposed several data fusion methods that align cluster centers before fusion. However, these methods have two key limitations. First, they cannot guarantee accurate sample-level alignment of data pairs. Second, they do not address significant discrepancies in data sizes across different classes, which may affect subsequent fusion performance.
  To address these problems, we propose a dual-learning based penalized multi-align clustering model, named DLPMAC. The dual-learning mechanism enables the model to learn prior knowledge from each modality, including semantic and structural information. This helps preserve semantic consistency and structural similarity across modalities at both local and global levels. In addition, the penalized multi-align module performs multi-to-multi data alignment through a penalty mechanism. It allows one sample to form data pairs with different samples from other modalities, thereby improving data-pair alignment accuracy. The penalty mechanism also prevents data aggregation, avoiding the case where excessive samples are linked to a single sample. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of DLPMAC in addressing data alignment and fusion challenges from both sampling and clustering perspectives.

AI.tldr: DLPMAC is a dual-learning penalized multi-align clustering model that addresses missing modalities and temporal asynchrony in multimodal data fusion by preserving semantic/structure consistency and using a penalty mechanism to improve sample-level alignment accuracy without data aggregation.
AI.motivation: Real-world multimodal applications suffer from missing modalities and temporal asynchrony caused by sensor failures and network delays, rendering data incomplete and disorderly. Existing alignment methods that align cluster centers before fusion fail to guarantee accurate sample-level alignment and ignore class-imbalance issues that degrade fusion performance.
AI.method: DLPMAC employs: (1) a dual-learning mechanism that learns prior semantic and structural knowledge from each modality to preserve cross-modal consistency at local and global levels; (2) a penalized multi-align module that enables multi-to-multi sample pairing across modalities, where a penalty mechanism improves alignment accuracy while preventing excessive samples from linking to a single sample (data aggregation).
AI.result: Experimental results demonstrate DLPMAC's effectiveness in addressing data alignment and fusion challenges, validated from both sampling and clustering perspectives.
AI.conclusion: DLPMAC effectively resolves incomplete and asynchronous multimodal data fusion by combining dual learning for semantic/structural preservation with penalized multi-alignment for accurate, non-aggregative sample pairing, outperforming existing cluster-center alignment approaches.

title: Benchmarking on Tasks That Matter: Dataset Selection for Preserving Model Rankings
comment: Accepted to the 32nd ACM SIGKDD Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining (KDD 2026)
summary:
Benchmarks of machine learning models often include many datasets, making evaluation expensive. For efficiency, it is preferable to perform evaluations on small, representative datasets instead. The selection of such subsets typically relies on heuristics and is rarely analyzed for the robustness of the resulting model rankings.
  We introduce a framework to perform the task of selecting datasets subsets with an evaluation of how different selection strategies preserve the global model rankings. Our framework includes bootstrap aggregation, which provides valid confidence intervals, allowing a principled comparison of selection strategies. We consider clustering, design criteria (A/D-optimality), random baselines, and greedy farthest-first (FAFI). For the latter, we derive upper bounds on selection quality in terms of ranking errors as a function of the number of selected datasets.
  Empirically, in time series classification (TSC, 112 datasets) and in a supplementary natural language processing benchmark derived from MTEB (57 tasks), several selection strategies improve rank preservation compared with random subsets, including simple FAFI. In contrast, in recommender systems (30 datasets), the improvement of strategies over random selection is small and typically statistically insignificant. For TSC, our best-performing strategy achieves a Spearman correlation of 0.95 with the full benchmark model rankings using only five selected datasets. Additional experiments indicate that the effectiveness of selection approaches depends on both the quality of dataset representations and the scale of the benchmarking regime.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a principled framework for selecting small, representative subsets of datasets from large benchmarks while preserving model rankings. Using bootstrap aggregation for valid confidence intervals, the authors compare clustering, optimal design criteria, farthest-first traversal (FAFI), and random baselines. On time series classification, FAFI achieves 0.95 Spearman correlation with full rankings using only 5 of 112 datasets; gains are smaller in recommender systems and moderate in NLP.
AI.motivation: Full machine learning benchmarks are expensive to evaluate due to many datasets. Practitioners resort to heuristic subset selection without analyzing whether resulting model rankings remain robust. A principled, statistically sound framework for subset selection with ranking preservation guarantees is missing.
AI.method: The framework evaluates dataset subset selection strategies by measuring rank preservation against full benchmarks. It employs bootstrap aggregation to construct valid confidence intervals for ranking metrics, enabling rigorous comparison. Strategies compared include: (1) clustering-based selection, (2) A- and D-optimality design criteria, (3) greedy farthest-first traversal (FAFI), and (4) random baselines.
